t.tihau gradiste@47.2,23.3:
The Someș river makes its way through the hills of north-western Romania between Cluj and Baia Mare, and near the small town of Jibou, in Sălaj county, it passes through a narrow valley guarded on its slopes by the remains of a Roman fort. The site, known locally as Grădiște, which simply means old fort, lies above the village of Tihău, close to Surduc and Gâlgău Almașului.

The Romans conquered Dacia in the early second century under Trajan and held it for about a hundred and seventy years. The north-western frontier of the province ran through these hills, and the line of forts, watchtowers and walls along it is now part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacian Limes, a UNESCO site inscribed in 2024. The fort at Tihău guarded the Someș valley, a natural route into the province. What remains is mostly earthworks and foundations, but the setting, with the river below and the hills around, makes the military logic clear.

Jibou is known for its botanical garden, one of the largest in Romania, laid out around the Wesselényi castle, a Baroque palace built by a Hungarian noble family. The Sălaj region has a strong mixed heritage, with Romanian and Hungarian communities and wooden churches in many villages, some of them centuries old.

The riding in this part of Transylvania is relaxed and rural. The roads along the Someș valley and over the hills toward Zalău, Dej and Baia Mare are generally decent, with gentle curves through farmland, orchards and forest. Smaller roads can be potholed and narrow, and horse-drawn carts are still common, as are dogs. Romania requires a vignette, the rovinieta, for cars on national roads, but motorcycles are exempt. The Maramureș, north of Baia Mare, with its famous wooden churches and traditional villages, is within reach for a day ride.

Jibou, about six kilometres away, has fuel, shops and food. Local cuisine is hearty: sarmale, cabbage rolls; ciorbă, sour soup; and the plum brandy, pălincă, offered with pride. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with mild weather and green hills.
The Cerna is a mountain river in south-western Romania, flowing through a long, deep valley between the Mehedinți and Cerna mountains before reaching the old spa town of Băile Herculane. The Domogled-Valea Cernei National Park protects this valley and the mountains around it, a landscape of limestone cliffs, gorges, caves and some of the largest old-growth beech forests in Europe, part of the UNESCO site for the ancient and primeval beech forests of the Carpathians and other regions of Europe. Iauna Craiovei, at these coordinates, is a high forested area in the park between Cornereva, Isverna and Rusca.

The beech forests here have been growing undisturbed for centuries, and their trees are huge. The park is also known for its karst landscape, with caves, sinkholes and underground rivers, and its flora includes Mediterranean species that survive thanks to the mild climate of the southern valleys. Bears, wolves and lynx live in the forests, and the black pine of Banat, a local variety, grows on the cliffs.

Băile Herculane, at the southern end of the valley, has been a spa since Roman times, when soldiers bathed in its thermal springs, which were dedicated to Hercules. In the nineteenth century, under the Habsburgs, it became a fashionable resort, with grand hotels and baths, many of which are now in a sad state of decay, which gives the town a melancholy charm.

The road up the Cerna valley from Băile Herculane is a beautiful ride, following the river through gorges and forest, with the cliffs rising on both sides. It becomes narrower and rougher as it goes, and the upper sections may be unpaved. The roads over the mountains toward Cornereva and Isverna are remote and often in poor condition, with gravel and potholes. This is not a place for a heavy road bike on a tight schedule. Weather in the mountains can change quickly.

Fuel is scarce in the mountains; Băile Herculane, Orșova and Padeș, about twenty-four kilometres away, are the nearest options. Local food includes mountain cheeses, smoked meats and trout. Late spring and early autumn are the best times to visit.
t.surduc deasupra vaii hraii@47.3,23.4:
Surduc is a village in the Someș valley in Sălaj county, north-western Romania, where the river cuts a narrow path through hills on its way toward Baia Mare. Above the village, on a ridge overlooking the valley of the Hrăii stream, there are traces of a Roman watchtower, part of the frontier of the province of Dacia. The nearby villages of Tihău and Băbeni, and the town of Jibou, are all close by.

The Romans held Dacia from the early second century until about 271, and the north-western frontier of the province ran through these hills. It was not a continuous wall like Hadrian's Wall, but a network of forts, watchtowers and earthworks that watched the valleys and passes. The frontier, the Dacian Limes, was added to the UNESCO list in 2024 as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire. The watchtower above the Hrăii valley is one of many small sites along this line, and what remains is mostly earthworks, but the position, with views over the valley, shows how the Romans used the landscape to keep watch.

The Someș valley was a natural route between Transylvania and the plains to the north-west, and it remained important long after the Romans left. The region has a mixed heritage, with Romanian and Hungarian villages, Orthodox and Reformed churches, and old wooden churches, some of which are beautifully painted inside. Surduc is also known for a large reservoir on the Hrăii river nearby, a popular spot for fishing and walks.

The riding here is rural and relaxed. The roads along the Someș valley are generally decent, with gentle curves, while side roads into the hills can be rough and narrow. Expect horse-drawn carts, livestock and dogs, and watch out for potholes. The roads toward Zalău and the Meseș mountains, or north toward Baia Mare and the Maramureș, offer more interesting riding.

Jibou, about seven kilometres away, has fuel and shops. Local food includes sarmale, mămăligă, polenta, and plum brandy. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with mild weather and green hills.
t.clit fata chicerii@47.3,23.4:
Northern Sălaj is quiet country: low wooded hills, hay meadows, plum orchards and villages strung along the Someș river and its side valleys, with wooden churches and haystacks built around poles in the fields. Cliț is a small village near Băbeni, and the point named Fața Chicerii lies in the hills above it. Names in this list follow the pattern of the Romanian archaeological record, a village and then the local name of a hillside, and in this part of Sălaj many such points belong to the line of watchtowers and small forts of the Roman frontier of Dacia, which UNESCO recognised in 2024. I cannot vouch for what remains on this particular slope; many sites are little more than a grassy bump or a scatter of stones in a meadow.

The context is fascinating, though. After Trajan conquered the Dacians in the early second century, the Romans held this province for about 170 years, and the frontier in northwest Dacia ran along the Meseș mountains and the Someș, centred on the great fort and town of Porolissum near Zalău. Watchtowers on the hills passed signals along the line, and the views from the ridges still make clear why they were placed where they are.

The riding is gentle and rural. The main road along the Someș valley follows the river and the railway between Jibou and Dej, with long curves and few towns, while side roads into the hills turn narrow, patched and sometimes unpaved. Horse carts, cattle and slow tractors are part of the traffic, and village dogs take their job seriously. Late spring, when the meadows bloom, and early autumn, when the forests colour and the plum brandy stills are working, are the most rewarding times.

Jibou, about fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with dependable fuel, shops and simple restaurants, and it has a baroque castle of the Wesselényi family with a large botanical garden. Villages like Băbeni and Lozna have small shops and sometimes a bar. Bring cash, water and a basic tool kit, because services are thin in the hills, and accept the invitation to a glass of pălincă if offered; refusing is harder than drinking.
t.glod toaca glodului 2@47.3,23.7:
East of Jibou the Someș river squeezes through a narrower valley, and around Ileanda the hills close in, wooded and steep, with villages tucked wherever there is room for a few houses and gardens. Glod is a tiny settlement in these hills, and Toaca Glodului is the local name of a height above it; toaca, by the way, is the wooden board struck to call monks to prayer, and hills with that name often have a commanding view. Like many points with this naming pattern in Sălaj, it is listed with the Roman frontier of Dacia, where watchtowers and small forts guarded the approaches to the province. On the ground you should expect little more than traces in a field or woodland, so come for the setting.

And the setting is a good one. The Someș here is broad and brown, with willows on the banks and herons fishing in the shallows. The railway follows the river through short tunnels and over bridges, and the slopes above are covered in oak and beech forest that turns copper in October. Small farms still mow by hand in places, and the haystacks dotted across the meadows are straight out of an old painting.

The main road along the valley, which runs between Jibou and Dej, has smooth stretches and a relaxed rhythm of curves following the river, with little traffic apart from local cars and the occasional truck. Turn off into the side valleys, toward villages like Rus or Gâlgău, and things get rougher: broken tarmac, gravel, mud after rain and steep grades. A light adventure bike is ideal; a heavy tourer will cope on the main road but feel nervous on the tracks. Watch for animals and horse carts, especially around dusk.

Ileanda has a few shops and probably a bar, but for fuel and a proper meal you are better off in Jibou to the west or Dej to the east, both larger towns. Copalnic-Mănăștur, to the north over the hills toward Maramureș, is another option. If you have time, keep riding north into Maramureș itself, where the wooden churches with their tall spires are among the most beautiful buildings in Romania and the road over the hills offers some of the best scenery in the country.
t.tihau dealul cucului@47.2,23.3:
Dealul Cucului means cuckoo hill, and the name fits the place: a low, wooded rise above the village of Tihău, close to the town of Jibou in the Someș valley of Sălaj county, where in spring the cuckoo's call echoes across the meadows. The point belongs to the network of archaeological sites along the Roman frontier of Dacia in the northwest of the province, near the confluence of the Almaș and Someș rivers, a strategic spot where valleys meet and roads cross. As with many of these sites, there may be little to see on the surface, but the location makes sense once you look at the map.

Jibou, six kilometres away, is a small town with a big surprise: the Wesselényi castle, a baroque palace of a Hungarian noble family, now home to one of the largest botanical gardens in Romania, with greenhouses, Japanese gardens and collections of plants from around the world. It is an unexpectedly elegant place for a walk after a ride through the countryside. The town also has a railway junction and a few shops and cafés around the centre.

The riding around Tihău is relaxed and rural. The roads follow the river valleys, with gentle curves, small villages and fields of maize and sunflowers. Side roads lead into the hills, toward Gâlgău Almașului and Creaca, where the tarmac often gives way to gravel and dirt, and the landscape becomes more wooded and remote. Watch for horse-drawn carts, which are still common here, and for cattle and sheep being moved along the roads in the evening. Summers can be hot and thunderstorms frequent, while autumn brings mild weather and colourful forests.

Jibou has fuel, supermarkets and simple restaurants, and it is the best base for exploring the area. Zalău, the county capital, is about thirty kilometres away and has more services, as well as a county museum with finds from Porolissum, the great Roman city on the frontier. Local food is hearty: sour soups called ciorbă, sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with meat and rice, and polenta with cheese and sour cream. Accept the hospitality, and you will find the people of Sălaj warm and curious.
t.teregova la hideg@45.2,22.3:
Teregova is a village in the narrow corridor between the Banat mountains and the Țarcu range in western Romania, where the Timiș river flows north toward the plain and a low pass leads south to the Cerna and the Danube. This corridor has been a route since ancient times: the Roman road from Dierna, on the Danube, to Tibiscum, near Caransebeș, ran through here, linking the river crossing with the heart of the province of Dacia. La Hideg is a local place name near the village, and the point is listed among the sites of the Roman frontier of Dacia, the UNESCO site recognised in 2024. As with many such sites, the remains may be hard to spot, but the logic of the location is clear.

The landscape is beautiful: green meadows, beech and oak forests, and mountains rising on both sides. The village is known for its traditional music and costumes, and the people are proud of their Banat heritage, a mix of Romanian, German, Serbian and other cultures. To the east, the Țarcu mountains rise to over two thousand metres, and to the west, the Semenic mountains offer forests and ski slopes.

The main road through Teregova, the DN6 or E70, is a major route between Timișoara and Bucharest, and it is busy with trucks, so take care. But it is also a scenic road, with long curves through the valley and a climb over the pass toward Domașnea and Mehadia. Side roads into the mountains offer quieter riding, especially the road to Semenic, which climbs through forests with tight bends. The Cerna valley, to the southeast, with the old spa town of Băile Herculane, is a spectacular gorge between limestone cliffs, and the road along it is a favourite with riders.

Teregova has a few shops and bars, and fuel may be available on the main road, but Caransebeș, about thirty kilometres north, is the nearest town with full services. Băile Herculane, to the south, has hotels and restaurants. Local food includes hearty soups, grilled meats and fresh trout from the mountain streams. Watch for horse-drawn carts and animals on the roads, especially in the villages, and be careful at night, when visibility can be poor.
t.turzansk tserkva of saint michael the ar:
The wooden church of Saint Michael the Archangel in Turzańsk stands on a gentle slope in the foothills of the Bieszczady mountains, in the far southeast of Poland, near the borders with Slovakia and Ukraine, with its onion domes rising above the trees. It was built in the early nineteenth century by the Lemko or Boyko communities, the Ruthenian highlanders who once lived in these mountains, and it is one of the wooden tserkvas of the Polish and Ukrainian Carpathian region listed by UNESCO in 2013. Inside, an iconostasis of painted icons separates the nave from the sanctuary, and the church is still used for Orthodox services.

The history of this region is poignant. After the Second World War, the Lemko and Boyko populations were deported, first to the Soviet Union and then, in 1947, to western Poland, in Operation Vistula, and many villages were abandoned. Some churches survived, others were destroyed or fell into ruin. Today, the Bieszczady are among the least populated areas of Poland, a land of forests, meadows and wildlife, including wolves, bears, lynx and bison.

The riding in the Bieszczady is fantastic. The Great Bieszczady Loop, a road circling the mountains, offers endless curves through forests and valleys, with views over the hills and the Solina reservoir, the largest artificial lake in Poland. Traffic is light, especially on weekdays, though summer weekends bring more visitors. Roads can be narrow and bumpy, and wildlife crossings are common, especially at dusk. Winters are snowy and cold, and the best riding season runs from May to October, with autumn colours especially beautiful.

Komańcza and Rzepedź, nearby villages, have small shops, a few restaurants and accommodation, and Lesko, about eighteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with full services, including fuel. Sanok, a bit further, has an open-air museum of folk architecture with many wooden buildings from the region, and a museum of icons. Local food includes pierogi, hearty soups and proziaki, a soda bread baked on a hot plate, often served with garlic butter. The Bieszczady narrow-gauge forest railway, near Cisna, is a fun excursion.
t.historic centre of the city of san juan:
San Juan del Río grew up as a stop on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road that ran north from Mexico City to the silver mines of Zacatecas and on to Santa Fe in New Mexico, and its historic centre is one of the sites along that route listed by UNESCO in 2010. For centuries, mule trains, wagons and travellers passed through here, stopping at inns and crossing the river on the stone bridge built in the early eighteenth century, which still stands. The centre has plazas, churches, convents and colonial houses of pink and grey stone, and a relaxed provincial atmosphere, despite the city's growth as an industrial centre.

San Juan del Río is known for its opals, mined in the surrounding hills and sold in shops around the centre, and for its basketry and wicker crafts. The nearby town of Tequisquiapan, about twenty kilometres north, is a Pueblo Mágico famous for its wine and cheese route, with vineyards, cheese makers and a lively square, and it holds a wine and cheese fair every year. Bernal, further north, sits beneath one of the largest monoliths in the world, the Peña de Bernal, a huge rock rising above the village.

The riding here is mostly on the high plateau, at around two thousand metres, with long, straight roads through farmland and dry hills. The federal highway 57, linking Mexico City with Querétaro, passes through San Juan del Río and is very busy with trucks, so it is better to take smaller roads where possible. The roads north to Tequisquiapan, Bernal and the Sierra Gorda offer more variety, climbing into the mountains with winding roads, forests and spectacular views. The climate is dry and temperate, with a rainy season in summer.

San Juan del Río has fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels, and all the services you need. Local food includes gorditas, barbacoa, cooked slowly in an underground pit and served on Sunday mornings, and the cheeses of the region, especially the fresh panela and aged varieties from Tequisquiapan. The city's market is a good place to try local specialities. Querétaro city, about fifty kilometres northwest, offers even more, with its aqueduct and colonial centre.
t.powroznik tserkva of saint james the les:
Hidden among the hills of the Beskid Sądecki, close to the Slovak border in southern Poland, the little wooden church at Powroźnik is one of the oldest of its kind still standing in the country. Its oldest parts date from around 1600, and it belongs to the group of wooden tserkvas of the Carpathian region listed by UNESCO in 2013. A tserkva is an Eastern-rite church, and this one was built by the Lemkos, the Rusyn highlanders who farmed these valleys for centuries until most were forcibly resettled after the Second World War. Today it serves as a Catholic church, but the shape tells its origin story at once: a tower with a bulging onion-like cap, stepped shingle roofs and dark timber walls weathered almost black.

If it is open, the interior has painted walls and an iconostasis, the screen of icons that separates the sanctuary from the nave. Even from the churchyard, though, the craftsmanship stands out: every shingle cut by hand, every joint pegged rather than nailed.

The valley it sits in leads up towards Krynica-Zdrój, the grand old spa town a few kilometres away, famous for mineral water pump rooms, wooden villas and the naive painter Nikifor, whose small, bright pictures of churches and the town now hang in a museum there. Muszyna, just down the road, is smaller and calmer, with the ruin of a castle above the Poprad river.

The riding is a pleasure. Narrow roads follow the streams through mixed beech and fir forest, with gentle climbs, plenty of bends and farms scattered across clearings. Along the Poprad valley the road towards Piwniczna runs close to the river and the Slovak frontier, with steep wooded slopes on both sides. Surfaces vary from good to patched, and in spring you will meet mud on the minor roads from forestry work. Autumn is the season to aim for, when the beeches turn copper and the air smells of woodsmoke.

For practical needs Muszyna, about four kilometres off, has fuel and shops, and Krynica, a few kilometres further, has everything from cafés to grand hotels. Try the local mineral waters at a pump room, or sit with a coffee and a slice of cake, which is a serious business in any Polish spa town.
t.grosii tiblesului preluci@47.5,24.2:
The Țibleș massif rises like a dark green wall between Maramureș and the Bistrița country of northern Romania, an old volcanic range topped by the Țibleș peak at around eighteen hundred metres. On its southern flanks, above the village of Groșii Țibleșului, lie the forests of Preluci, part of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe that UNESCO has protected as one sprawling, multi-country site. These are woods left largely to themselves, where old beeches grow huge, fall, rot and feed the next generation without a forester in sight.

You will not ride into the reserve itself, and you should not try; the value lies in its being untouched. What you can do is ride the valleys around it and feel the scale. The villages here belong to the Țara Lăpușului, the Land of Lăpuș, one of the most traditional corners of Romania, with wooden houses, carved gates, haystacks shaped by hand and horse carts still doing real work. Sunday mornings bring people out in embroidered blouses, and the wooden churches with their steep shingled spires are part of the same tradition that made the churches of Maramureș famous.

The roads vary wildly. Some county roads are freshly laid and flow beautifully along the streams; others turn into broken tarmac, potholes and stretches of gravel with little warning. To the east, the Șetref pass links Maramureș with the Bistrița valley in a pleasant, wooded climb, a good way to string the region together. Expect dogs, livestock and children on the road in every village, and slow right down through them. Brown bears live in these mountains, and seeing one cross the road at dusk is not rare.

The best months are late spring, when the beech leaves are a startling fresh green, and early October, when the forest goes bronze and gold and the mornings are crisp. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms that can wash gravel across the roads.

Fuel is the thing to think about. The hamlets have none, and the nearest reliable towns are Săliștea de Sus, about sixteen kilometres away, or Târgu Lăpuș to the west. Village shops sell bread, cheese and cold drinks, and someone will usually point you to a family offering a meal and a room if you ask politely.
t.village of calnic@45.9,23.7:
Câlnic, a small village south of Sebeș in Alba county, is home to one of the strangest fortresses among the Saxon sites of Transylvania. Unlike most of its neighbours, it began not as a fortified church but as a noble residence. In the thirteenth century a local count built a stone keep here, surrounded by walls and a moat. Later the villagers bought it, added a chapel and storerooms, and turned it into a peasant refuge, where families could shelter from raids behind the walls. The result, still ringed by water on parts of its perimeter, is part of the Villages with Fortified Churches in Transylvania World Heritage site.

The keep, a tall square tower with small windows, dominates the interior, and the courtyard is often quiet, with flowers and old wooden galleries. The village around it has the long, straight streets and gabled houses typical of Saxon settlements, though most of the original German-speaking families left after 1990.

What makes Câlnic stand out for riders is its location. A few kilometres away, Săsciori sits on the Transalpina, the road that climbs south from Sebeș over the Parâng mountains to Novaci in Oltenia. It is the highest paved road in Romania, peaking at over two thousand metres, and in good weather it is one of the great rides of Europe: a long climb through forest, past reservoirs, then up onto open alpine meadows with switchbacks, sheepfolds and enormous views. It closes in winter, usually from late autumn until late spring or early summer, and even in summer the weather at the top can turn cold and foggy in minutes. Watch out for sheep, dogs, and loose gravel on the hairpins, and for cars stopping suddenly to photograph the view.

The area around Câlnic is gentler, with rolling hills, orchards and vineyards along the Sebeș valley. Sebeș itself, a busy town with a fine Saxon church, is the main supply point, while Săsciori, about six kilometres away, has fuel and a few shops. Fill up before starting up the Transalpina, as there is nothing reliable on the high section. In the village, a quiet hour at the fortress and a picnic of bread, cheese and fruit is the ideal warm-up before the mountain.
t.svydovets@48.2,24.2:
The Svydovets is a long, high ridge in the Ukrainian Carpathians, rising above the upper Tisza valley near the town of Rakhiv in Zakarpattia. Its southern and northern slopes hold some of the wildest primeval beech forest left in Europe, protected as part of the Carpathian Biosphere Reserve and included in the UNESCO site of Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe. Above the trees lie broad alpine meadows, the polonyna, where Hutsul shepherds traditionally drove their flocks each summer, with glacial lakes tucked below the ridge.

This is a place of big landscapes and deep tradition. The Hutsuls, the highland people of this part of the Carpathians, are known for their carved wooden churches, embroidered clothing, long trembita horns and a rich folklore of forest spirits. Food is hearty and simple: banosh, a cornmeal porridge cooked with sour cream and topped with sheep's cheese, bryndza, and mushroom soups. Rakhiv likes to call itself the highest town in Ukraine, and a monument near the village of Dilove claims to mark the geographical centre of Europe, a title several places contest.

Honesty matters more than romance here, though. Ukraine is at war, and travel conditions can change quickly. Before considering any trip, check official advice from your government, entry requirements and the security situation in the region. The area sits close to the Romanian border, and border zones may have restrictions.

If and when conditions allow, the riding is rugged. The main road follows the Tisza valley along the Romanian frontier, with mountains rising steeply on both sides, and minor roads branch up side valleys towards villages and logging tracks. Surfaces range from decent to terrible, with deep potholes, broken tarmac and gravel, and many forest roads are suitable only for dual-sport bikes. Weather in the mountains is changeable, with heavy rain and fog common. Plans for a large ski resort on the Svydovets have met strong opposition from environmental groups, who see the forest as irreplaceable.

Rakhiv, about sixteen kilometres away, is the main town, with fuel, shops and basic services. Elsewhere supplies are sparse. Carry spare fuel if you venture into the side valleys, along with water, food and a good map, and do not rely on mobile coverage in the high country.
t.component of esztramos hill@48.5,20.8:
Esztramos is a lumpy limestone hill rising from the valley of the Bódva in north-eastern Hungary, a stone's throw from the Slovak border. For much of the twentieth century it was quarried for limestone and iron ore, and in the process the miners broke into caves hidden inside it, full of crystal formations. The Rákóczi Cave, the best known of them, has delicate aragonite crystals and pools, and the hill now forms part of the Caves of Aggtelek Karst and Slovak Karst, a World Heritage site shared between the two countries. Visits to the cave are limited and usually need to be booked, so check before you count on getting inside.

The karst region around here is riddled with caves, more than a thousand of them on both sides of the border. The most famous is the Baradla Cave at Aggtelek, a short ride west, a vast underground system with huge chambers and an underground passage that continues into Slovakia, where it becomes the Domica cave. Concerts are sometimes held in one of the halls because the acoustics are so good.

The region has a long industrial history too. Rudabánya, a few kilometres south, was a mining town for centuries, and in the 1960s fossils of an ancient ape were found in its old open-cast mine, giving the name Rudapithecus to a species that lived here millions of years ago. Szendrő, the nearest small town, has the remains of a castle and a quiet main street.

For riding, the Bódva valley and the surrounding hills offer gentle, unhurried roads through farming villages, woods and meadows. This is one of the poorest and least visited parts of Hungary, so traffic is light, but road surfaces can be rough, with potholes, broken edges and patched tarmac. Horse carts and slow farm vehicles share the roads, and dogs often run out from village yards. Across the border in Slovakia, the Slovak Karst plateau has more dramatic scenery, with gorges and cliffs.

Fuel is sparse in the small villages. The nearest larger town listed is Moldava nad Bodvou in Slovakia, about twenty-one kilometres away, while Edelény and Szendrő on the Hungarian side are closer for basics. Village shops sell bread, sausages and soft drinks, and a bowl of goulash or a plate of lángos in a local inn makes a satisfying stop.
t.church of st leonard@49.7,20.5:
The hills around Limanowa in southern Poland have a nickname that suits them perfectly: the Beskid Wyspowy, the Island Beskids. Instead of forming a continuous ridge, the summits rise individually from the surrounding valleys like islands from a sea, each one wooded, rounded and separate. Driving through the area is a constant game of spotting the next hump on the horizon. The famous wooden church of St Leonard stands at Lipnica Murowana, in the hills to the north of here, and it is one of the Wooden Churches of Southern Lesser Poland listed by UNESCO in 2003.

St Leonard's is a small Gothic church built of larch, probably in the late fifteenth century, with a steep shingled roof sweeping almost to the ground and a covered walkway around the base, designed to protect worshippers from the weather. The interior is decorated with painted walls and altars, and it is a quiet, intimate space. The church sits beside a stream on the edge of the village, among old trees, and occasionally the stream floods into the churchyard.

Lipnica Murowana itself has a lively tradition. Every Palm Sunday, the village holds a competition for the tallest Easter palm, made from willow branches, dried flowers and grasses, and some of them reach astonishing heights, raised by teams of men with ropes and poles. The village square is also unusually grand for a small place, a reminder that it once had town rights.

The riding in the Island Beskids is a pleasure. Roads wind between the hills, through woods and farmland, with frequent climbs and descents and plenty of bends. Surfaces vary, and some minor roads are narrow and patched. Traffic is moderate, but tractors and slow vehicles are common, and villages often stretch along the road, so you need to watch for pedestrians and dogs. Autumn is especially beautiful, when the beeches turn gold and copper on every hill.

Limanowa, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel, shops and restaurants. Try pierogi or a bowl of żurek, sour rye soup, in a roadside inn, and look out for oscypek, the smoked sheep's cheese of the Polish mountains, sold at stalls along the roads.
t.caseiu cetatele samvm caseiu samum@47.2,:
On a terrace above the river Someș, near the village of Cășeiu, a few kilometres from Dej in northern Transylvania, the Romans built a fort they called Samum. It guarded the northern edge of their province of Dacia, which they conquered in the early second century after two hard wars against the Dacian king Decebalus. The fort controlled the valley and the routes into the province, and today its outline can still be traced in the fields, with low walls and earthworks where archaeologists have uncovered gates, towers and barracks. In 2024 the Dacian frontier was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

The Someș valley is broad and fertile, with fields, orchards and villages strung along the river, and low hills on either side covered in woods and pastures. In summer the valley is warm and green, in autumn full of the smell of plums and woodsmoke, and in winter often wrapped in mist.

Dej, the nearest town, has long been linked to salt. The salt mines of the area were exploited since Roman times, and the town has a fine Gothic Reformed church in its centre, a reminder of the many communities, Romanian, Hungarian and others, that have shaped Transylvania. Cluj-Napoca, the region's main city, lies about an hour south-west.

The riding is relaxed rather than dramatic. Main roads follow the valley, carrying a fair amount of traffic, including trucks, while minor roads branch into the hills towards villages with wooden churches, fruit trees and haystacks. Surfaces on minor roads can be rough, and horse carts, dogs and livestock are common. For more spectacular riding, the mountains of the Rodna and Maramureș lie to the north and east, a few hours away.

Dej, about four kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Try a bowl of ciorbă, the sour soup that comes in many versions, with tripe, beans or meatballs, or a plate of sarmale, cabbage rolls served with polenta and sour cream. If someone offers you a glass of homemade plum brandy, be careful: it is strong, and you have a bike to ride.
t.muncel muchia poienii lupului@47.3,23.8:
The name is a mouthful, and a good one: the Ridge of the Wolf's Clearing, on the hill of Muncel, above the Someș valley north-east of Dej. Somewhere along this wooded crest the Romans kept a lookout on the northern border of Dacia, watching the valleys for movement from the free tribes beyond. Watchtowers like this one were the eyes of the frontier, signalling to the forts below, and the site is part of the Dacian frontier inscribed by UNESCO in 2024. On the ground, expect very little: perhaps a low mound, a ditch or scattered stones under the trees. It is a place for imagination and a walk rather than a monument.

The hills here form the edge of the Transylvanian basin, a rolling patchwork of pastures, hay meadows, beech and oak woods, and orchards of plums and apples. In late spring, the meadows are full of wildflowers, and in summer the hay is cut by hand in many places and stacked in tall ricks around wooden poles. Shepherds still move flocks across the hills, often accompanied by large, protective dogs that are best given a wide berth.

The villages nearby, Vad, Poiana Blenchii and Gâlgău, are small and scattered, with wooden and stone houses, churches and wells. Life follows the seasons and the rhythm of the farm, and visitors are rare enough to attract curious looks and, often, warm hospitality.

The roads are a mixed bag. The main road along the Someș valley is good but can be busy, while minor roads into the hills quickly become narrow, patched and steep, and some turn to gravel or dirt. A dual-sport bike is the right tool for exploring the higher tracks, and rain turns them into mud quickly. Further east, the mountains of Rodna and the Bârgău valley offer more dramatic scenery and excellent riding roads, including the pass towards Bucovina.

Dej, about thirteen kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. Village shops sell basics, bread, cheese and drinks. If you are invited into a home, expect generous food, perhaps polenta with cheese and sour cream, and a glass of homemade plum brandy offered with insistence; a polite refusal on account of riding is usually understood.
t.kuziy trybushany@47.9,24.1:
The river Tisza runs fast and green out of the Ukrainian Carpathians, and for many kilometres it forms the border between Romania and Ukraine. On the Ukrainian bank, the forests of Kuziy and Trybushany are among the primeval beech woods protected in the Carpathian Biosphere Reserve and listed by UNESCO as part of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe. From the Romanian side, around Valea Vișeului, you look across the river at steep, wooded slopes where the trees have grown and died without interference for centuries.

This corner of Romania is Maramureș, one of the most traditional regions in Europe, where wooden churches with tall, slender spires rise above the villages, and several of them are themselves World Heritage sites. People still wear traditional dress on Sundays and holidays, haystacks are built by hand, and carved wooden gates stand in front of many homes. Sighetu Marmației, the main town, has a sobering memorial museum in a former prison where the communist regime held and killed political prisoners. Further west, at Săpânța, the Merry Cemetery is famous for its colourful wooden crosses painted with scenes and humorous verses about the lives of the dead.

A short ride east, at Vișeu de Sus, a narrow-gauge steam railway, the mocănița, still runs up the Vaser valley into the mountains, originally built to carry timber and now popular with visitors.

The riding here is beautiful but slow. Roads follow the river valleys, winding through villages and forests, with views of the mountains. Surfaces vary from good to poor, with potholes and patches. Traffic is light, but horse carts, livestock and dogs are common, and villages often stretch along the road for miles. The border area may have police and border guard checkpoints. Weather is changeable, with cold winters and warm summers, and heavy rain can cause flooding.

A word on the map: Rakhiv is listed as the nearest larger town, but it lies in Ukraine. The border crossing at Sighet is the nearest, and Ukraine remains at war, so check current advice before considering a crossing. On the Romanian side, fuel and services are available in Sighetu Marmației and Vișeu de Sus. Try tochitură, a pork stew with polenta and egg, and a glass of horincă, the local plum brandy.
t.ileanda dealul ciuha@47.3,23.6:
Ileanda is a village in the north of Sălaj county, where the river Someș swings north-west out of the Transylvanian basin through a valley flanked by wooded hills. On the hill called Ciuha, above the village, the Romans had a post on the northern edge of their province of Dacia, one of the watchtowers and forts that guarded the frontier from the second to the third century. The site belongs to the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia, inscribed by UNESCO in 2024. Do not expect a ruin with walls to wander through: what survives is mostly earthwork and traces in the ground, and the joy lies in the climb and the view rather than the remains.

The Someș valley here is narrow and winding, with the railway, the road and the river squeezed between hills, and villages strung along the bottom. The hills are covered with beech and oak forests, meadows and orchards, and in spring and autumn they are particularly beautiful. Village life follows traditional rhythms, with hay meadows cut by hand, cattle driven to pasture, and wooden churches standing among the houses.

Jibou, a little way downstream, has a remarkable botanical garden, one of the largest in Romania, laid out in the grounds of a Baroque castle that belonged to the Wesselényi family, Hungarian nobles who played a part in the region's history. It makes a pleasant break on a hot day, with greenhouses, ponds and shady paths.

The riding is relaxed and scenic, following the river valley through villages and forests, with gentle curves and occasional climbs. The main road can be busy with trucks, while minor roads into the hills are quieter but rougher, with potholes, gravel and sometimes dirt. Horse carts, livestock and dogs are common, and villages often stretch along the road. The weather is continental, with hot summers, cold winters and changeable conditions in spring and autumn.

Fuel is limited in the villages. The nearest larger town listed is Copalnic Mănăștur, about twenty kilometres away, and Jibou and Dej are the main towns in either direction along the valley. Village shops sell bread, cheese and drinks. Try a bowl of balmoș, polenta cooked with sheep's cheese and butter, a traditional shepherd's dish, at a guest house or inn.
t.voineasa crac gauri@45.4,23.6:
North of the Jiu Valley, the land rises steeply into the Șureanu and Parâng mountains, a wild region of high ridges, deep valleys, spruce forests and alpine meadows. Crac-Găuri lies up in this high country, linked by name to the old routes that crossed the mountains in Roman times, when Dacia was a province and soldiers watched the passes between the Transylvanian basin and the south. Little is visible today, and the remoteness is half the attraction: this is mountain land, where shepherds bring their flocks to high pastures in summer and the forest stretches for miles.

The Jiu Valley below is coal country. Petroșani, Petrila and the surrounding towns grew around the mines, and in the communist period the miners were a powerful force, famously descending on Bucharest in the early 1990s in violent episodes that shaped the country's post-revolution politics. Most of the mines have closed, and the towns have struggled, but there are efforts to develop tourism, especially winter sports in the mountains around Straja and Parâng.

The Transalpina road passes nearby, climbing over the Parâng mountains from the Lotru valley towards Novaci, at over two thousand metres the highest road in Romania. The junction at Obârșia Lotrului, a crossroads in the middle of the mountains, is a meeting point for riders, with roads heading north, south and east. The high section is closed in winter, usually from late autumn until early summer, and even in summer fog, rain and cold can arrive quickly. Vidra lake, along the Lotru valley, is a large reservoir surrounded by forest.

The riding here is among the best in Romania, with long climbs, hairpins and huge views, but surfaces can be variable, with gravel, potholes and occasional landslides. Traffic is light on weekdays but heavy on summer weekends. Watch for sheep, cattle and dogs on the road, and for drivers stopping suddenly to take photos. Bears are common in these mountains.

Fuel is not available in the high mountains. The nearest towns are Petrila, about seventeen kilometres away, and Petroșani, so fill up before climbing. Mountain huts and stalls along the Transalpina sell grilled sausages, cheese and polenta, and a hot bowl of soup at a cabana is welcome on a cold day.
From the outside, the church in Dębno Podhalańskie looks like a sturdy wooden barn with a steep shingled roof and a squat tower, the kind of building you might ride past without a second glance. Step inside and the walls explode with colour: every surface covered in stencilled and painted patterns, animals, plants and geometric figures, dating back to around 1500, one of the best-preserved medieval painted interiors in Poland. The church, built of larch in the late fifteenth century, is part of the UNESCO listing of Wooden Churches of Southern Małopolska, a group of Gothic timber churches that show the skill of local carpenters who built without nails.

The village lies in the Podhale region, a stone's throw from the Dunajec river, with the Pieniny range to the east and the jagged peaks of the Tatras visible to the south on clear days. Just beyond lies Lake Czorsztyn, a reservoir created by a dam, with two castles facing each other across the water: Niedzica on one side and the ruins of Czorsztyn on the other. Rafting down the Dunajec gorge on traditional wooden boats steered by local highlanders in felt hats is a classic Pieniny experience.

The riding is superb. The roads around the lake and through the hills toward Frydman and Łapsze offer beautiful views, with flowing curves and a few steep climbs. The area has a strong highland culture, with wooden houses, sheep farms and the smoky scent of oscypek, the local smoked sheep's cheese, sold by the roadside. Watch out for cyclists and slow-moving tourist traffic in summer, and remember that the weather in the mountains can turn quickly.

Fuel and services are available in Nowy Targ, about thirteen kilometres away, a market town of thirty-four thousand known as the capital of Podhale. Smaller villages around the lake have restaurants, guesthouses and cafés. Try kwaśnica, a sour cabbage soup with pork, or grilled oscypek with cranberry sauce. The church is still in use, so be respectful of services, and remember that it may close for conservation work or limited hours, so check before you go.
t.town of aculco@20.1,-99.8:
Aculco is a quiet stone town in the northwest of the State of Mexico, on the high plateau at well over two thousand metres, where the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the colonial road to the north, passed through on its way from Mexico City. The town was a staging post, and its well-preserved centre, with a broad plaza, the Franciscan church and convent of San Jerónimo and old houses built of pinkish stone, is part of the UNESCO listing for the route. It was here, in November 1810, that royalist troops defeated Miguel Hidalgo's insurgent army, an early setback in the War of Independence that people still mention with a kind of local pride.

The region is home to Otomí communities, known in their own language as Ñähñu, and their crafts and traditions are woven into daily life. The countryside is a mix of pasture, cornfields and oak forest, and Aculco is known for its dairy farms, producing cheeses, cream and cajeta sold in shops around the plaza. Just outside town, the Tixhiñú waterfall drops over a curtain of basalt columns, and the Peña de Ñadó, a huge rock outcrop, attracts climbers and hikers.

The riding is a pleasure: winding roads across the high plateau, with views of volcanic hills and farmland, and very little traffic once you leave the main highway between Mexico City and Querétaro. The air is cool, even cold in the mornings, so dress in layers. Watch for topes, livestock and potholes, especially after the rainy season. The best months are from October to April, when the skies are clear and blue.

Aculco is a small town, and while you may find a fuel station on its outskirts, the nearest larger town is Acambay, about sixteen kilometres away, with more services. Plan your fuel stops carefully if you are heading deeper into the hills. In town, eat at the market or in one of the small restaurants around the plaza, where you can try barbacoa, slow-cooked lamb, or quesadillas made with the local cheese, followed by a sweet from one of the dairy shops.
t.udava@49.2,22.2:
Out where Slovakia, Poland and Ukraine meet, the eastern Carpathians fold into long, rounded ridges covered in beech forest so continuous that from a high point it looks like a green sea. Udava is one of the Slovak pieces of the UNESCO Primeval Beech Forests listing, protected within Poloniny National Park, the most easterly and least populated corner of the country. Here the forest has been left to its own rhythms for a very long time: giant trees, fallen trunks covered in fungi and moss, a dense understory of young growth wherever light breaks through. Wolves, lynx, brown bears and even European bison roam the area, and the dawn chorus in May is unforgettable.

The human history is just as layered. This was the land of the Rusyns and the Boyko and Lemko peoples, with wooden churches dotted through the valleys, many of them listed by UNESCO in their own right. After the Second World War, entire villages on both sides of the border were emptied by deportations and resettlement, and in places you will find only a cemetery, an orchard gone wild or a lone church to mark where a village stood. On the Polish side, the Bieszczady mountains became a byword for wilderness for exactly that reason.

Riding here is about solitude rather than speed. Roads are narrow, sometimes bumpy, winding along valleys and over passes with few villages and even fewer cars. On the Polish side, the Great Bieszczady Loop through Cisna, Wetlina and Ustrzyki Górne is a classic, with long flowing sections and wide views from the passes. On the Slovak side, the roads around Snina and the Starina reservoir, which supplies drinking water to much of eastern Slovakia, are quieter still. Watch for wildlife, forestry trucks and wet leaves, and remember that the weather can turn fast in the hills.

Services are sparse. Snina, about twenty kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, with fuel, shops and places to eat; Cisna on the Polish side is a small village with guesthouses and a station. Fill up whenever you can. Simple inns serve hearty soups, pierogi on the Polish side and bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese, on the Slovak side.
t.muncel caramida@47.3,23.8:
In northern Transylvania, where the Someș river winds through low hills between Dej and Beclean, the Roman Empire once ran out of land and patience. The province of Dacia, conquered by Trajan in the early second century, had a long and complicated frontier, and in 2024 parts of it were added to the UNESCO Frontiers of the Roman Empire. Muncel–Cărămidă is one of those components, a small military site above the valley near Poiana Blenchii, part of a network of watchtowers and forts that guarded the northern edge of the province. The big fort of Porolissum, near Zalău to the west, with its reconstructed gate, gives you a sense of what the bigger garrisons looked like.

There is little to see here beyond earthworks and scattered stones, but the landscape is worth the visit. The hills are a patchwork of small fields, orchards and woodland, with villages of wooden houses, painted gates and churches with tall spires. Horse-drawn carts still share the road with cars, and haystacks dot the meadows in late summer. The Someș valley is broad and fertile, and the river meanders lazily between willows and poplars.

The riding is gentle and rural. The main road along the Someș is busy with trucks, but the side roads through the hills are quiet, winding and sometimes rough, with potholes, gravel and the occasional dog chasing your wheels. The villages are close together, so speed limits change often, and police speed traps are common. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the hills are green or golden and the air is cool; summer can be hot and dusty.

Dej, about fifteen kilometres away, is a town of thirty-eight thousand with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. It has long been linked to salt mining, and its old centre has a fine Gothic Reformed church. Cluj-Napoca, an hour away, is the region's lively capital. Eat at a roadside restaurant serving ciorbă, sour soup, sarmale, stuffed cabbage rolls, and papanași, fried doughnuts with sour cream and jam, if you have room.
t.church of saint nicholas@47.7,24.0:
Budești is one of the old villages of the Cosău valley in Maramureș, the far northern corner of Romania, where traditional life has survived longer than almost anywhere else in Europe. Its wooden church of St Nicholas, built in the seventeenth century, is a masterpiece of the local carpentry tradition: a dark timber body with a tall, steep shingled roof and a slender spire that seems to pierce the sky. Inside, the walls are covered with painted scenes from the Bible, and among the church's treasures is a coat of chain mail said to have belonged to Pintea the Brave, a legendary outlaw hero of the region. The church is one of eight in the UNESCO listing of the Wooden Churches of Maramureș.

The villages here are full of character: wooden houses with carved gates, haystacks in the meadows, horse carts on the roads and people in traditional dress on Sundays and holidays. Nearby Breb, Sârbi and Hoteni are similar villages, and many families still make horincă, a strong plum brandy distilled twice. A short ride north, Săpânța has the famous Merry Cemetery, with brightly painted wooden crosses carved with humorous epitaphs about the lives of the dead.

The riding in Maramureș is a joy, if you take it slowly. The roads in the valleys are narrow and winding, with potholes, livestock and horse carts. The DN18 from Baia Mare climbs over the Gutâi pass, with a series of tight hairpins through the forest, and descends into the valley of the Mara toward Sighetu Marmației. Cavnic, eleven kilometres away, is a small mining and ski town with fuel and services. The weather in the mountains can be cold and wet, even in summer, and winters are snowy.

Fuel is available in Cavnic and in larger villages along the main roads, but not in every village, so plan ahead. Guesthouses in the area are often family-run and serve home-cooked food: ciorbă, sour soup, sarmale, cabbage rolls, and balmoș, a cornmeal porridge with sheep's cheese and butter. A glass of horincă will be offered as a welcome, and refusing it politely takes skill.
t.church of the holy archangels@47.5,23.9:
The wooden church at Rogoz stands in the Lăpuș country, a quieter, lesser-known corner of Maramureș, south of the mountains and away from the main tourist circuits. Built in the seventeenth century and dedicated to the Holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel, it is unusual in shape: the roof is asymmetric and overhangs deeply on one side, and the eaves are supported by carved wooden brackets shaped like horse heads, a detail that seems to come straight out of folk tradition. Inside, the walls are painted with scenes from the Bible, including a vivid Last Judgement. It is one of the eight churches in the UNESCO listing of the Wooden Churches of Maramureș.

The Lăpuș valley is green and gentle, with meadows, orchards and small villages. The Țibleș mountains rise to the east, covered in beech and spruce forests, with high pastures where shepherds spend the summer. The local people are known for their crafts, including pottery, wood carving and textiles, and for their festivals, when you can hear traditional music and see people in folk costumes.

The roads in the Lăpuș country are narrow and winding, often with potholes and patched surfaces, and they pass through villages where horse carts, cows and geese have the right of way. The road along the Lăpuș river is pleasant, with gentle curves and views of the valley, and the routes over the hills toward the Gutâi pass or into the Țibleș mountains are more challenging. Weather can be changeable, with summer storms and early snow in autumn.

Târgu Lăpuș, the main town of the area, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Suciu de Sus, nine kilometres away, is a larger village. Rogoz and Dămăcușeni are small villages with basic shops. Ask in the village for the church key if it is locked; someone usually knows who has it. Local guesthouses serve hearty food: tochitură, a pork stew with polenta and egg, or mici, grilled minced-meat rolls, with mustard and a cold beer, best once the bike is put away for the night.
t.cugir batrana@45.6,23.4:
South of the town of Cugir, the land rises into the Șureanu mountains, a sprawling range of beech and spruce forests, high meadows and rounded summits in the heart of the Southern Carpathians. This is the country of the Dacians, the people who ruled much of present-day Romania before the Roman conquest in the early second century. Their capital, Sarmizegetusa Regia, and a ring of mountain fortresses lie in the Orăștie mountains to the west, and they are listed by UNESCO as the Dacian Fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains. Bătrâna, on the high ground above the Cugir valley, belongs to the network of ancient sites scattered across these hills, where Dacians and Romans watched each other across the ridges.

The mountains are wild and lightly populated. Shepherds bring their flocks up to the high pastures in summer, and the forests are home to bears, wolves and lynx. The rivers are clear and cold, tumbling down rocky valleys, and the views from the summits reach across the Transylvanian plateau to the north and the Jiu valley to the south.

For riders, the big attraction is the Transalpina, the highest paved road in Romania, which crosses the Parâng mountains from Șugag, through the Lotru valley, to Novaci, reaching more than two thousand metres at its highest point. It is a spectacular road, with hairpins, long climbs and views over endless ridges, but it is open only in the warmer months, usually from early summer to autumn, and the weather at the top can be cold, foggy and windy even in July. The surface is generally good, but watch for sheep, dogs, cows and gravel, and the road can be busy with tourists on weekends.

Services are scarce in the mountains. Petrila, about twenty kilometres away in the Jiu valley, is an old coal-mining town with fuel and shops, and Șugag and Cugir have basic services. Fill your tank before heading into the hills, and carry water and warm clothing. Mountain huts and guesthouses along the Transalpina serve grilled meat, cheese and polenta, and the sheep's cheese, fresh from the shepherds, is delicious.
t.trampoiele grohasu mic@46.1,23.1:
In the Apuseni mountains of western Romania, gold has shaped the land and its people for two thousand years. The Romans came for it after conquering Dacia, organising the mining from a centre at Ampelum, today the town of Zlatna, whose name comes from the Slavic word for gold. Trâmpoiele, on the high ground near Almașu Mare, is one of the many small sites connected to that Roman presence, where mining, settlement and watch posts dotted the hills. A little further north, the mining landscape of Roșia Montană, with its Roman galleries cut deep into the rock, was listed by UNESCO in 2021 and gives the clearest idea of how the ancient gold was won.

The Apuseni are a range of limestone and volcanic rock, with karst plateaus, caves, gorges and forests. Near Bucium, the Detunata hills show off columns of basalt, rising from the forest like organ pipes. The villages are scattered across the hills, with wooden houses and small fields, and the people, known as Moți, have a reputation for independence, resilience and skill in woodwork.

The riding is challenging and rewarding. The roads around Zlatna and Almașu Mare wind through steep valleys and over passes, with tight curves and changing surfaces, from fresh tarmac to broken asphalt and gravel. Traffic is light, but watch for logging trucks, horse carts and animals. The weather in the mountains is changeable, with frequent rain and fog, and snow can linger on the higher roads well into spring. Zlatna itself shows the scars of later mining and smelting, but nature is slowly recovering.

Zlatna, about eleven kilometres away, has fuel, shops and a few places to eat, and Alba Iulia, the historic city with its star-shaped Habsburg fortress, is about an hour's ride east. Almașu Mare and Balșa are small villages with basic shops. In the mountains, look for guesthouses serving balmoș, cornmeal with cheese, and tocăniță, a meat and vegetable stew. The local plum brandy, țuică, is everywhere, and it is strong.
t.trezenea gura teghisului@47.1,23.1:
The Meseș mountains are a low, forested ridge in northwestern Transylvania, and for the Romans they formed a natural wall at the edge of the province of Dacia. Along the ridge, they built a chain of forts, watchtowers and earthworks, and the big fort of Porolissum, near Zalău, was the key to it all, guarding a pass through the mountains used by traders and travellers. In 2024, much of this frontier was listed by UNESCO as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire – Dacia, and the site between Treznea and Gura Teghișului is one of its components. On the ground, there is little more than a line of ditches, banks and the foundations of towers, hidden in the forest.

Treznea also carries a much more recent memory. In September 1940, after northern Transylvania was transferred to Hungary, Hungarian troops killed dozens of Romanian and Jewish villagers here, and a memorial in the village remembers the victims. It is a sobering stop, and a reminder of how many borders have shifted across this region.

The landscape is rolling and green, with meadows, orchards and oak and beech forests. The villages are scattered along the valleys, with wooden houses, churches and wells, and the pace of life is slow. The roads are narrow and winding, often with poor surfaces, potholes and gravel, and you will share them with horse carts, cows and sheep. The ride over the Meseș ridge, between Zalău and Cluj, has some nice curves and views, but beware of trucks on the main road.

Zalău, nine kilometres away, is a town of over sixty thousand with fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, and its history museum displays finds from Porolissum. Treznea and Aghireș are small villages with basic shops. If you have time, visit the reconstructed gate and walls of Porolissum, which give a vivid idea of the Roman presence. Try local dishes such as ciorbă de burtă, tripe soup with garlic and sour cream, or a plate of grilled meats with polenta and pickles.
t.domogled valea cernei ciucevele cerne@45:
The Cerna valley in southwestern Romania is a deep limestone gorge between the Mehedinți and Cerna mountains, with cliffs, caves and forests rising steeply on both sides. The Domogled–Valea Cernei National Park protects this wild landscape, and its beech forests, some of them untouched for centuries, became part of the UNESCO listing of Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe in 2017. The park is also home to a rare variety of black pine that grows on the steep limestone slopes, and to bears, wolves, lynx and chamois, as well as horned vipers and a remarkable variety of butterflies.

At the southern end of the valley lies Băile Herculane, one of the oldest spa towns in Europe. The Romans knew its hot springs as Ad Aquas Herculi and built baths here, and in the nineteenth century the Habsburgs turned it into an elegant resort, with grand bathhouses, hotels and a casino. Today, many of the old buildings are crumbling, but they still have a faded grandeur, and the hot springs still flow, with pools by the river where locals bathe for free.

The road up the Cerna valley from Herculane is one of the most scenic in Romania, following the river through the gorge, past cliffs, waterfalls and caves, with tight curves and views. Further north, the road continues over the mountains toward Baia de Aramă, but the surface deteriorates, and some sections may be gravel or broken tarmac, so check conditions before you go. Traffic is light, but watch for rockfalls, potholes and animals on the road. The weather is milder than in much of Romania, thanks to Mediterranean influences, but storms can be sudden and violent.

Services are limited in the valley. Băile Herculane, at the southern end, has fuel, shops and accommodation, and Tismana, about twenty-four kilometres away on the other side of the mountains, is a small town with a famous monastery and basic services. Fill up before heading into the mountains. Try local dishes such as sarmale, stuffed cabbage rolls, or grilled trout from the mountain streams, and finish with a glass of local plum brandy.
t.pianu de jos muncelu lautaorea@45.7,23.5:
High above the Sebeș and Cugir valleys, where the Șureanu foothills fold into long grassy shoulders, the Romans kept watch over the southern approaches to their province of Dacia. The name on the map, Muncelu-Lăutaorea, belongs to the ridge country above Pianu de Jos, and it is one of the many small frontier points that archaeologists have tied to the Roman defensive system here. Do not expect walls to lean on. What survives on these hilltops is usually a faint platform, a ditch you notice only when the light is low, and a view that explains everything about why a sentry was posted there.

The riding is the reason to come up. The lanes that climb out of the Pianu side are narrow, patched and occasionally graded gravel, so treat them as farm roads rather than touring tarmac, and expect a horse cart or a flock where the hedges close in. In return you get orchards, beech woods, hay meadows that still get cut by hand, and long looks south toward the Șureanu and Parâng ranges. Late spring and early autumn are kindest; July afternoons can bring heavy thunderstorms that turn clay tracks slick in minutes.

You are also close to one of Romania's great roads. Șugag, about thirteen kilometres away, sits on the DN67C, the northern end of the Transalpina, which follows the Sebeș river up past its reservoirs before climbing over the mountains to Novaci. If you have a spare day, this is the side from which to start it, and the gorge sections above Șugag are lovely even if you turn back before the high pass. The Transalpina's top section closes for the snowy months, so check before you commit.

Practically, villages like Pianu, Șugag and Jina have small shops and the occasional terrace bar, but for a reliable fill head for Cugir, the industrial town some eighteen kilometres off, or Sebeș on the main road to the north. Câlnic, on the same ride, adds a Saxon fortress-house to the day, and Alba Iulia's star-shaped citadel is not far beyond. Carry water up the ridge, keep your speed down through villages where dogs sleep in the road, and save the photographs for the evening, when the hills go gold and the old Roman logic of the place becomes obvious.
t.guga varful taglii@47.3,23.8:
Rugășești, Vad and Poiana Blenchii are the kind of villages most people drive past on the way to somewhere else, and that is precisely the charm of the hills that rise between them. The point marked as Guga, Vârful Țâglii, lies on this rolling country north of the Someș, roughly a dozen kilometres from Dej, in the band of land where Rome drew the northern edge of Dacia. A summit called Țâglii is the sort of place where a watchtower would have looked out across the Someș corridor toward the free tribes beyond, and the archaeological lists record a frontier site here.

On the bike, think in terms of slow pleasures. County roads around Vad and Rugășești wind through low hills of wheat, sunflower and pasture, with wooden gates carved in the Transylvanian manner and church towers popping up behind every crest. Tarmac quality changes without warning, and the final approach to any hilltop is likely to be a field track, so leave the heavy tourer at the bottom if the ground is wet. The light is best in the early evening, when the long shadows pick out old earthworks you would never see at noon.

Dej itself is a proper town with fuel, supermarkets and a market, and it has a long story of its own: salt from the nearby Ocna Dejului mines was shipped down the Someș for centuries, and the Reformed church in the centre is one of the finest Gothic buildings in this corner of Transylvania. The town is a sensible place for coffee and a meal before heading into the hills, and the riverside road along the Someș gives an easy, flowing ride either upstream toward Beclean or west toward Gâlgău.

Nature here is gentle rather than dramatic. Buzzards circle over the hay, storks nest on electricity poles in the villages, and in late summer the verges smell of wild thyme and dust. Ride respectfully: these are working farms, tracks belong to the people who use them, and a wave to the man on the tractor goes a long way. If the ride brings you back the same way, the return gives you the valley from the other side, which feels like a different landscape entirely.
t.galgau valea stramturei@47.3,23.7:
Strâmtură means a narrowing, and the name fits. Just outside Gâlgău, a small Sălaj village on the Someș, the valley pinches between wooded slopes, and the Roman frontier made use of exactly such pinch points to control movement along the river. The site listed as Valea Strâmturei belongs to that northern Dacian line, and like most of its neighbours it is earthwork and setting rather than standing masonry. You come for the geography and the sense of a border that ran through these quiet hills nearly two thousand years ago.

The river road is the backbone of the ride. Along the Someș between Dej and Jibou the road follows the water through a series of tight bends, with the railway on one side and steep woods on the other, and it is one of the nicer stretches of ordinary national road in northern Transylvania. Trucks use it, so pick your overtakes, and watch for gravel washed out of side valleys after rain. Spring brings the river up brown and fast, while October turns the beech and oak on the gorge walls to copper.

Gâlgău itself is tiny, around eight hundred people, with a shop and not much else, so plan your fuel. Ileanda, eight kilometres away, is a little larger, and Dej, about nineteen kilometres back east, is the dependable choice for a full tank and a cooked lunch. The villages on this stretch keep wooden churches and old peasant houses with deep eaves, and a slow ride through them reveals more than any museum.

If the ride is the variant that continues to Brâncovenești, you will be swapping Roman earthworks for a castle of the Kemény family on a bluff above the Mureș, a good contrast for one day. Either way, take a minute at the narrows with the engine off. You will hear the river, a train perhaps, a dog somewhere up the slope, and you will understand why a garrison commander once thought this was the place to stand.
t.gilau la castel@46.8,23.4:
Gilău is a market village on the Someșul Mic, the first real settlement west of Cluj-Napoca on the road toward the Apuseni mountains, and the place name La Castel says it plainly: there was a fortification here, and there still is one, layered through the centuries. Under the later castle grounds, archaeologists found a Roman auxiliary fort guarding the valley route into Dacia from the west, and the medieval and early modern castle that followed sits on the same strategic ground. Rome, Hungarian nobles and later owners all made the same calculation about this spot.

The village of about seven and a half thousand people has fuel, shops and places to eat, which makes it a useful stop rather than just a sight. From here the riding gets good quickly. Head upstream and the road climbs toward the Gilău lake and the Tarnița reservoir, with views over dark water, and the mountain roads beyond lead toward Mărișel and Beliș through spruce forest and open plateau farmland where haystacks stand in neat rows. Downstream, Cluj is a twenty-minute run, with all the traffic that implies.

The Apuseni roads are a mix. Some are newly laid and fast, others are rough, and the higher ones can hold snow late into spring and see fog roll in without warning. Cows, sheep and logging trucks are the main hazards. Summer is the obvious season, but September is better: quieter, clearer, and the forests start turning toward autumn colour on the high ground around Mărișel.

This is also a region of strong local food. Apuseni villages are known for smoked cheese, polenta with sour cream and cheese, and hearty soups, and the road-side stands sell honey and forest berries in season. Gilău sits on rides that also take in Roșia Montană, the old gold-mining landscape with Roman galleries that is now on the UNESCO list, so think of this stop as the gateway: a last solid meal and a full tank before the roads tighten and the villages thin out.
t.ighiu dealul magulici@46.1,23.5:
There is a hill above Ighiu called Măgulici, and from its slopes you look straight across the Mureș valley toward Alba Iulia, the old Roman Apulum. That view is the whole point. Apulum was the base of the Thirteenth Legion and the largest Roman centre in Dacia, and the hills around it were dotted with watch posts and small sites that kept an eye on the roads in and out. The frontier lists name a site on Dealul Măgulici, and while there is little to see on the ground beyond the lie of the land, standing there makes the Roman geography readable.

Ighiu itself is a commune of over six thousand people with small shops, and it lies in a pocket of vineyards and orchards between the Mureș and the Trascău mountains. The wine country around Alba Iulia has been planted since Roman times, and on a warm afternoon the slopes smell of grapes and dry grass. The roads up from Ighiu and Șard toward the hills are narrow and broken in places, and the last bit to any viewpoint will likely be gravel or grass.

The best riding nearby heads north and west into the Trascău, where the limestone gorges of Râmeț and the valley toward Întregalde give tight, slow, scenic roads with rock walls close on both sides. Further on lie the Apuseni proper. It is not fast country; it is the kind of riding where third gear is plenty and you stop often because the view keeps changing.

For fuel, meals and a proper bed, Alba Iulia is minutes away. Its star-shaped Alba Carolina citadel, built by the Habsburgs in the eighteenth century, is one of the largest of its type in Europe, and it was in this city that the union of Transylvania with Romania was proclaimed on 1 December 1918, still the national day. Walk the walls in the evening, then ride back to the hills in the morning light, when the Mureș valley lies under a thin mist and the old legionary town reappears as the sun burns it off.
t.salva roata lui todoran@47.3,24.4:
Salva is a railway village. Trains for the Maramureș line split off here from the route along the Someșul Mare, and the place has a slightly busy, crossroads feel for a commune of a little over four thousand people. The site called Roata lui Todoran, Todoran's wheel, sits right by the village in the Năsăud country of Bistrița-Năsăud, a region that marked the northern edge of Roman Dacia and later formed part of a Habsburg border regiment. Few places in Transylvania have been a frontier for quite so long.

Năsăud, four kilometres away, is the town to know. It was the seat of that frontier regiment and still has an air of civic pride out of proportion to its ten thousand inhabitants, with a well-known high school and a regional museum. The poet George Coșbuc was born in a village just up the valley, and the novelist Liviu Rebreanu also came from this area, so locals take their literature seriously. Fuel, groceries and a hot meal are easy there.

The riding is gentle and rewarding. North of Salva the road follows the Sălăuța valley up toward the Maramureș border and the Șetref pass, rising through hay meadows and spruce woods, and it is one of the better ways into Maramureș if you want to avoid main roads. East, the Someșul Mare valley leads toward Rodna and the mountains of the same name, the highest in the Eastern Carpathians. Surfaces vary from fresh tarmac to tired patchwork, and the railway crossings deserve a careful approach.

In high summer, hay is made by hand on the steep slopes and stacked around tall poles, and the smell carries onto the road. Storks are everywhere. Come in September if you can, when the hills are still green, the light is softer and the tourist traffic heading to Maramureș has thinned. Whatever the season, Salva is a hinge of a place: the Roman edge, the Habsburg edge, and the point where the land starts to rise toward the north.
t.dobsinska ice cave@48.9,20.4:
Step out of a warm summer day into the Dobšinská Ice Cave and the temperature drops to just below freezing within a few metres. The cave, on the northern edge of the Slovak Paradise in eastern Slovakia, holds a vast mass of ice, tens of thousands of cubic metres, with frozen floors, walls and columns that have built up over thousands of years. It was explored in 1870 by Eugen Ruffinyi, opened to visitors soon after, and became one of the first caves in Europe to be lit by electricity. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Caves of Aggtelek Karst and Slovak Karst, shared with Hungary.

The tour takes visitors down wooden steps through halls of ice, and the effect is magical, with blue and white surfaces reflecting the light. Bring a warm jacket, even in July, and good shoes; the walk from the car park up to the entrance is a steep twenty minutes or so. Opening is seasonal, typically from late spring to early autumn, so check before you go.

The Slovak Paradise national park around the cave is a plateau of limestone cut by deep gorges, with ladders, chains and footbridges leading hikers up waterfalls and through narrow canyons. It is one of the most unusual hiking areas in Central Europe. For riders, the roads around Dobšiná and Stratená are narrow and twisty, winding through forests and along the Hnilec valley, with the Palcmanská Maša reservoir offering a quiet place to rest.

The area is quite remote, with limited services. Dobšiná, six kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and Spišská Nová Ves, a town of nearly forty thousand, has everything you could need. Further north lies Spiš, with its huge castle and the medieval town of Levoča, home to Master Paul's carved altar. Try bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese, Slovakia's national dish, and keep an eye out for bears in the forest at dusk.
t.rogna la bontaua@47.3,23.6:
Rogna is a scatter of farms in the hills of northern Sălaj, close to the Someș valley and the border with Maramureș, and La Bontauă is the name the locals give to a piece of high ground where a Roman frontier site has been recorded. The northern edge of Roman Dacia ran through these hills, and the Romans placed watchtowers and small forts on high points to keep an eye on the river valleys and the free Dacians to the north. Today there is little to see apart from the shape of the land, but the view over the rolling hills makes it easy to imagine a sentry looking out across the valley.

The countryside around Ileanda and Rus is quiet and unspoiled, with hay meadows, orchards and patches of oak and beech forest. Villages are small, with wooden houses and churches, and traditional life is still visible, with horse carts on the roads, haystacks in the fields and geese in the yards. In spring, the meadows are full of wildflowers, and in autumn, the forests turn gold and red.

The roads here are narrow, winding and often in poor condition, with potholes, gravel and the occasional stretch of dirt. Take it slowly, especially on the climbs and descents, and watch out for animals and farm vehicles. The main road along the Someș, between Dej and Jibou, is better, with gentle curves along the river and views of the wooded valley.

Services are limited. Ileanda, five kilometres away, has a shop and perhaps a bar, but for fuel, head to larger towns such as Dej, Jibou or Copalnic Mănăștur. Carry water and snacks, and be prepared for basic conditions.
