To the north, Maramureș offers wooden churches, the Merry Cemetery at Săpânța and some of the most traditional rural culture in Europe, while Zalău and the Roman city of Porolissum lie to the south-west.
t.gorgany@48.5,24.3:
The Gorgany are the wildest part of the Ukrainian Carpathians, a range of sandstone peaks rising above dense forests in the Ivano-Frankivsk region. What makes them unusual are the gorgany themselves, the fields of loose stone blocks that cover the upper slopes and summits, formed by frost shattering the rock. Walking across them is slow and tiring, and the forests below, of spruce, beech and Swiss stone pine, are among the most pristine in Ukraine, with brown bears, wolves, lynx and red deer. The Gorgany nature reserve protects a part of this landscape.

The village of Bystrytsya lies at the edge of the range, in the valley of the Bystrytsia Nadvirnianska river, about four kilometres from the site. It is a quiet place, with wooden houses and a church, and forestry roads that lead into the mountains. Yaremche, about twenty kilometres away, is the main tourist town of the area, known for its waterfall on the Prut river, its wooden church and its market selling Hutsul crafts, wool, cheeses and honey.

The Hutsuls are the highland people of the Ukrainian Carpathians, known for their distinctive culture, music, wood carving, embroidery and the trembita, a long wooden horn used to communicate across the mountains. Their traditions are still alive in villages around Yaremche, Verkhovyna and Kosiv.

A realistic word about travel: Ukraine is at war, under martial law, and much official travel advice warns against all travel to the country. Even in the west, far from the front line, air raids happen, curfews apply and regulations can change quickly. If you are considering a visit, check the latest official advice, your insurance and the entry rules first. In peacetime, the roads from Ivano-Frankivsk to Yaremche and Bukovel are good, while mountain roads are rough and often unpaved. Fuel is available in towns such as Nadvirna and Yaremche, and the best season is summer, when the forests are green and the mountain meadows are in flower.
t.treznea coasta ciungii 2@47.1,23.0:
Treznea is a small village in the hills of Sălaj county, eleven kilometres east of Zalău, and its name carries a heavy weight in Romanian history. In September 1940, after northern Transylvania was transferred to Hungary by the Second Vienna Award, Hungarian troops entering the region killed scores of villagers here, Romanians and Jews, in one of the worst atrocities of that time. A memorial in the village remembers the victims. It is a sobering reminder that these quiet hills have seen terrible violence, and a short, respectful stop at the memorial is worth more than any viewpoint on the ride.

Coasta Ciungii is a hillside above the village, where a Roman frontier site, probably a watchtower, has been identified. The Meseș mountains, a low, forested ridge running north-east from Zalău, formed part of the western frontier of Roman Dacia, and the Romans built a line of towers and forts along it. The most important was Porolissum, near Moigrad, north of Zalău, a large military and civilian settlement whose stone gate, amphitheatre and walls have been partly reconstructed.

The riding in the Meseș hills is pleasant, with winding roads through forests of oak and beech, pastures and orchards, and views over the Transylvanian plateau to the east and the Sălaj valley to the west. Roads vary in quality, with some recently resurfaced and others full of potholes. The main road from Zalău to Cluj crosses the ridge at the Meseș pass, with curves and climbs, but also heavy traffic.

Zalău, a town of over sixty thousand, has fuel, supermarkets and a good county museum, with finds from Porolissum. In the villages, look out for local specialities such as smoked meats, cheese and pălincă, the strong fruit brandy of the region. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the forests are full of colour and the air is fresh. In wet weather, the clay lanes up to the ridge turn greasy, so stick to tarmac and walk the last bit if you want to stand where the Roman sentries stood.
t.tokaj wine region historic cultural land:
Some wine regions are famous for a grape. Tokaj is famous for rot. Here in north-eastern Hungary, where the volcanic Zemplén hills meet the Great Plain and the Bodrog flows into the Tisza, autumn mists from the rivers encourage noble rot on the grapes, shrivelling them and concentrating their sugar. The berries, picked one by one, become aszú, and the sweet wine made from them has been celebrated for centuries. A line attributed to Louis XIV calls it the wine of kings and the king of wines.

The region is a UNESCO cultural landscape, and its villages are full of cellars dug deep into the volcanic tuff, some of them labyrinths stretching for kilometres, their walls covered in a thick black mould that helps regulate humidity. Furmint and Hárslevelű are the main grapes, and alongside the sweet aszú, the region now produces excellent dry whites. Tarcal, the village closest to these coordinates, lies at the foot of the Tokaj hill, the Kopasz-hegy, an extinct volcano covered in vineyards, and its cellars are among the best known.

The riding is gentle and pleasant rather than demanding. Roads wind between vineyards and villages along the edge of the hills, with views across the flat plain to the south. The road up the Tokaj hill offers a fine panorama. North of the region, the Zemplén mountains have quieter forest roads with more bends, leading towards the Slovak border. Summer can be hot, autumn is the most beautiful season with the harvest and the mists, and spring brings fresh green to the vines. Watch for slow agricultural traffic and for potholes on minor roads.

Tokaj town, six kilometres away, has fuel and services, and its main street is lined with cellars and wine shops where you can taste before you buy. Tarcal itself has a few restaurants and wineries offering tastings. Remember that Hungary has a zero tolerance policy on alcohol for drivers, so taste only when your riding is done for the day, or buy bottles to take home. The confluence of the rivers at Tokaj is lovely in the evening, with fishermen on the banks and herons over the water.
t.component of plesivec plateau@48.6,20.4:
The Slovak Karst is a world of limestone plateaus and deep gorges in southern Slovakia, along the Hungarian border, and the Plešivec plateau is one of its great tablelands, a high, flat-topped block of rock rising steeply above the valleys of the Slaná and the Štítnik rivers. Its surface is a rolling steppe of grass and scrub, pitted with sinkholes, and beneath it lies a maze of caves and abysses, part of the UNESCO site of the Caves of Aggtelek Karst and Slovak Karst.

The plateau's steep edges are home to rare plants and animals, including species more typical of warmer regions, which thrive on the sunny limestone slopes. Below the surface, caves such as the nearby Gombasek cave, with its delicate straw stalactites, are open to visitors. The region also has a rich cultural heritage. Krásna Hôrka castle, on a hill near Rožňava, was one of the most impressive in Slovakia until a fire in 2012 destroyed its roofs, and restoration is ongoing. Betliar, nearby, has a beautiful manor house and park, once owned by the Andrássy family.

The riding around the plateau is excellent. The roads follow the valleys around its edges, with cliffs rising above you and the river beside, and climb into the surrounding hills with plenty of bends. The road through the Slovak Paradise and the Slovak Ore Mountains to the north offers some of the best riding in the country, with forested passes and quiet villages. Surfaces vary, with some potholes and patched sections, and traffic is light. Weather can be changeable; summer is warm, and autumn colours in the forests are spectacular.

Rožňava, nine kilometres away, is a town of nineteen thousand with fuel, shops and restaurants, and its central square, with a watchtower and a cathedral, is pleasant. The town grew rich from mining in the Middle Ages. Plešivec, a small town at the foot of the plateau, has basic services. Local food includes bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese, and hearty soups. On a clear day, standing on the edge of the plateau, you look out over a landscape of forests and valleys, and the silence is complete.
t.wooden churches of maramures@47.8,24.1:
Maramureș is a region in the far north of Romania, along the Ukrainian border, where traditions have survived more strongly than almost anywhere else in Europe. Its villages are known for their carved wooden gates, their haystacks and their wooden churches, eight of which form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Bârsana, in the valley of the Iza river, has one of them, a church built in the eighteenth century, with a tall slender spire and a steep shingled roof.

The wooden churches were built by the Orthodox and Greek Catholic communities of Maramureș, who were often not allowed to build in stone under Hungarian rule. They developed a distinctive style, with tall spires rising above the villages, and interiors covered in painted scenes from the Bible, often mixing religious themes with local life. Bârsana is also home to a large modern monastery, built of wood in traditional style since the 1990s, which has become a popular destination for pilgrims and visitors.

The riding in Maramureș is a joy. The roads follow the river valleys, winding between villages and over hills, with views of meadows, forests and mountains. Traffic is light, but expect horse-drawn carts, livestock and pedestrians on the roads, especially in villages. Surfaces vary, with some good main roads and some rough minor ones. The Prislop pass, to the east, crosses into Moldavia and Bukovina with fine views. Summer is the best season, with warm days and cool nights, and autumn colours are spectacular. Winters are cold and snowy.

Bârsana has basic services, and Sighetu Marmației, the main town of the region, has fuel and more choice. The local food is hearty: sarmale, cabbage rolls, mămăligă, polenta, and pălincă, a strong plum brandy. Many villages offer homestays where you can experience traditional life. The Merry Cemetery at Săpânța, with its brightly painted wooden crosses and humorous epitaphs, is a short ride north-west. Sunday mornings, when villagers in traditional dress walk to church, are a wonderful time to visit.
t.boita caput stenarum in rude@45.6,24.3:
The Olt does something improbable south of Sibiu. Instead of going around the Carpathians, it cuts straight through them, carving a deep, winding gorge between the Făgăraș and Lotru ranges, and for two thousand years that gorge has been one of the great gateways between Transylvania and Wallachia. At its northern mouth, near the village of Boița, the Romans built a fort they called Caput Stenarum, the head of the narrows, to guard the entrance.

The fort controlled the road through the gorge, which the Romans used to link their province of Dacia with the Danube. Later, the pass became known as the Red Tower Pass, after a medieval fortress whose ruins still stand nearby at Turnu Roșu, and it saw armies come and go for centuries, including Ottoman invasions. The remains of the Roman fort are modest, but the strategic logic of the site is obvious as soon as you look south and see the mountains closing in on the river.

The road through the gorge, the DN7, part of the E81, is spectacular in scenery but busy, carrying a lot of heavy traffic between Sibiu and Râmnicu Vâlcea, and roadworks for the new motorway have been a feature for years. Overtaking trucks on the winding road requires patience and care. If you want quieter riding, the Transfăgărășan, one of the most famous mountain roads in Europe, starts a few kilometres east at Cârțișoara, climbing over the Făgăraș mountains to Bâlea Lake at over two thousand metres; it is usually open only from early July to October.

Boița is a small village, and Tălmaciu, six kilometres away, is a town with fuel and shops. Sibiu, twenty kilometres north, is one of the most beautiful cities in Romania, with a Saxon old town of squares, towers and houses whose roof windows look like watching eyes. The Mărginimea Sibiului villages to the west, such as Sibiel and Rășinari, are known for their shepherding traditions and their cheese. The gorge is at its best in the early morning, when mist lifts from the river and the traffic has not yet built up.
t.chiuiesti muncelul chiuiestiului@47.3,23:
North of Dej, in the hills of Cluj county, the land rises into a rolling upland of pastures, orchards and beech woods, cut by small valleys and dotted with villages. Muncelul Chiuieștiului is one of the hilltops above the village of Chiuiești, and the name is listed among archaeological sites of the Roman frontier in Dacia, which in this region ran along the hills to protect the province from the free Dacians and other peoples to the north. What exactly stood on this hilltop is something to learn from the local signs rather than assume; much of the frontier here consisted of small watchtowers and earthworks that left only faint traces.

The landscape is the real draw. This is a quiet corner of Transylvania, far from the tourist routes, where traditional village life continues. Haymaking is still done by hand on the steep slopes, and wooden churches and old farmhouses can be found in the villages. The Someș valley, to the south, is broader and more developed, with the town of Dej, known for its salt mines and its Gothic Reformed church.

The riding is relaxed and rural. Minor roads wind through the hills between villages, with plenty of bends and gradient changes, but surfaces vary from good asphalt to broken tarmac and gravel. Traffic is light, but expect horse carts, cattle and village dogs. The views from the hilltops across the valleys are wide and peaceful. Spring brings fresh green and wildflowers, summer is warm, and autumn colours in the beech woods are lovely. Rain can make unpaved sections muddy.

Chiuiești and the neighbouring villages have small shops, but fuel is best found in Dej, fifteen kilometres away, a town of thirty-eight thousand with all services. The salt mine at Ocna Dej, and the larger and more famous one at Turda further south, are interesting visits. Village guesthouses offer traditional food: sarmale, ciorbă, cheese and homemade pălincă. In the evening, the sound of church bells drifts across the valleys, and the light on the hills is soft and golden.
t.cincsor cetate@45.8,24.9:
Between Sibiu and Făgăraș, the Olt flows through a broad valley, with the long wall of the Făgăraș mountains rising to the south, the highest in Romania, culminating in Moldoveanu at 2,544 metres. On the north bank, near the Saxon village of Cincșor, known in German as Kleinschenk, the Romans built a fort to guard the river crossing and the road along the valley. The site, known locally as Cetate, the fortress, lies in fields near the village, with only faint traces visible.

Cincșor itself is a typical Transylvanian Saxon village, with houses built in a continuous row along the street, their gables facing the road, and a fortified church surrounded by defensive walls in the centre. The Saxons, German settlers invited by the Hungarian kings in the twelfth century, built hundreds of these fortified churches across southern Transylvania to protect themselves from raids. Many Saxons emigrated to Germany after 1990, and the villages are now mixed, but the architecture remains.

The riding here is varied. The main road along the Olt valley, the DN1 between Sibiu and Brașov, is busy with trucks and fast traffic, so use it only to cover distance. The minor roads through the villages are quieter, with views of the mountains. The Transfăgărășan, one of the most spectacular mountain roads in Europe, begins a short distance west at Cârțișoara and climbs to Bâlea Lake, usually open from July to October. Summer is warm, and the mountains are often covered with clouds in the afternoon; mornings are clearer.

Cincșor has a guesthouse and basic services, and Făgăraș, seven kilometres away, is a town of thirty thousand with fuel and shops. Its fortress, a large moated castle, is one of the best preserved in Romania and houses a museum. Food in the region combines Romanian and Saxon traditions: try the hearty soups and the cakes. In the evening, the light on the Făgăraș mountains can be spectacular, with the peaks glowing pink above the dark valley, and the sounds of the village settling down for the night.
t.ciglean varful cigleanului 2@47.2,23.2:
The Roman province of Dacia had a northern frontier that ran along the hills of what is now Sălaj county, in north-western Romania, around the great fortress of Porolissum. Here the Limes was not a continuous wall but a network of watchtowers, small forts and earthworks set on hilltops with views over the valleys. Vârful Cigleanului, a hilltop near the village of Ciglean, close to Jibou, held one of these watchtowers, and the number in the name marks it as one of several in the area.

The Someș river flows past Jibou, cutting through the hills towards the north, and the landscape is a mix of forests, pastures and villages. Jibou has a botanical garden around the Wesselényi castle, a baroque mansion of a Hungarian noble family, and the garden is one of the most important in Romania, with greenhouses and collections of plants from around the world. Porolissum, about thirty kilometres south-west near Zalău, has impressive remains of a Roman fort and town, including a reconstructed gate.

The riding in Sălaj is rural and relaxed. Minor roads wind through the hills and villages, with gentle bends and views across the Someș valley, but surfaces vary and potholes are common. Traffic is light, with horse carts and livestock sharing the roads. The Meseș mountains, to the south-west, offer more winding roads through forests. Summer is warm, and spring and autumn are pleasant, with fresh green or golden colours. Rain can turn unpaved tracks to mud, so stay on asphalt unless you are equipped for it.

Ciglean is a tiny village, and Jibou, five kilometres away, is a town of eleven thousand with fuel and shops. Zalău, the county capital, has all services. Local food is hearty and simple, and village guesthouses offer homemade dishes and pălincă. If you are interested in the Roman frontier, a visit to Porolissum is essential, and the walk to a hilltop like Vârful Cigleanului gives a sense of how the Romans watched over this distant edge of their empire.
t.kezmarok@49.1,20.4:
Kežmarok sits at the foot of the High Tatras in northern Slovakia, and on a clear day the jagged peaks of the smallest high mountain range in Europe rise above the town like a wall. It is an old town with a mixed history: founded by German settlers in the Middle Ages, it was a free royal town and a centre of trade and crafts, and its wealthy citizens built a castle, churches and fine houses around the square.

The town's most remarkable building is its wooden articular church, built in 1717 by the Lutheran community at a time when Protestants were allowed to build churches only of wood, without stone foundations or towers, outside the town walls. The interior is a masterpiece of carved and painted wood, with galleries and a magnificent organ, and it is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Wooden Churches of the Slovak part of the Carpathian Mountain Area. Next to it stands the New Evangelical Church, a striking building of the late nineteenth century in an eclectic mix of styles, which contains the tomb of Imre Thököly, a Hungarian prince who led a rebellion against the Habsburgs.

The riding around Kežmarok is excellent. The roads along the foot of the Tatras, through Poprad and the resort villages of Starý Smokovec and Tatranská Lomnica, offer views of the mountains, and the road over the border into Poland, through the Belianske Tatras, is scenic. To the north, the Pieniny mountains and the Dunajec gorge are within reach. The roads are generally good, but traffic can be heavy in the Tatras in summer and during the ski season. The weather in the mountains changes quickly, with storms in summer afternoons.

Kežmarok, a town of sixteen thousand, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Its castle, a Renaissance fortress, houses a museum. The local food is hearty: bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese, kapustnica, sauerkraut soup, and pirohy, filled dumplings. The town hosts a folk festival in summer. From the square, looking up at the Tatras in the evening light, you understand why this town has been a gateway to the mountains for centuries.
t.var dealul taravailor@47.2,23.3:
Dealul Tărăvăilor is a hill above the village of Var, near Creaca and Jibou, in Sălaj county, north-western Romania, and like many hilltops in this part of the country, it held a Roman watchtower on the frontier of the province of Dacia. The Limes Porolissensis, as the northern frontier is known, was a system of towers, forts and earthworks guarding the roads leading to the great fortress of Porolissum, and the towers were placed on hills with views over the valleys, so that signals could pass quickly along the line.

The Someș valley runs through the area, and the hills on either side are covered with forests, pastures and orchards. The villages are small and traditional, with wooden houses, churches and farms, and life here moves at the pace of the seasons. The Meseș mountains, to the south-west, form a natural barrier between Transylvania and the Pannonian plain, and the Romans used them as part of their defensive line. Zalău, the county capital, has a museum of history and art with finds from Porolissum.

The riding in this part of Sălaj is rural and gentle. The roads wind through the hills and valleys, with views over the countryside, and traffic is light. Surfaces vary, with good asphalt on main roads and potholes and gravel on minor ones. Horse carts, livestock and village dogs share the roads, so ride carefully through villages. The climate is continental, with warm summers and cold winters, and spring and autumn are lovely, with fresh green or golden colours on the hills.

Var and Creaca are small villages with basic services, and Jibou, five kilometres away, is a town of eleven thousand with fuel and shops. The Wesselényi botanical garden in Jibou is worth a visit. Porolissum, to the south-west, has the impressive remains of a Roman fort and town, and is a must for anyone interested in the Roman frontier. Local food in village guesthouses is homemade and hearty. Climbing to a hilltop like Dealul Tărăvăilor, with the valley spread out below, gives a sense of how the Romans watched over this distant frontier.
t.vetel micia gradiste@45.9,22.8:
The Mureș flows west across Transylvania towards Hungary, and near the village of Vețel, just west of Deva, the Romans built one of the most important forts in their province of Dacia. Micia guarded the river and the road along the valley, the main route between Transylvania and the Pannonian plain, and around the fort grew a large civil settlement with baths, temples and an amphitheatre. Excavations have revealed much of it, though part of the site lies under a power station built in the twentieth century.

Micia was a garrison for auxiliary troops from across the empire, including units from Syria and North Africa, and inscriptions found here show the diversity of the people who lived in this frontier town. The amphitheatre, one of the few in Roman Dacia, has been partly excavated. The Mureș valley was also important for transporting gold and salt from the mines of the Apuseni mountains to the north. Deva, eight kilometres east, is dominated by a medieval citadel on a volcanic hill, reached by a funicular.

The riding around Vețel is mostly along the Mureș valley, where the main road is busy with trucks between Deva and Arad, and a motorway now runs parallel. The minor roads into the hills on either side are quieter and more interesting. To the south, the Poiana Ruscă mountains have winding roads through forests and villages. To the north, the Apuseni mountains offer some of the best riding in Romania. The Orăștie mountains, to the south-east, contain the Dacian fortresses, including Sarmizegetusa Regia, the capital of the Dacian kings before the Roman conquest.

Vețel is a village with basic services, and Deva, eight kilometres away, is a city of sixty-seven thousand with fuel, shops and restaurants. Hunedoara, south of Deva, has the spectacular Corvin Castle, one of the largest Gothic castles in Europe. The local food is hearty Romanian cuisine. The Roman site at Micia is not developed for visitors, but the location, with the river and the hills, helps you imagine the bustling frontier town that once stood here.
t.izvoarele nerei@45.1,22.1:
High in the Semenic mountains of south-western Romania, in the Banat region, the Nera river is born in a forest of ancient beech trees. The Izvoarele Nerei reserve, the springs of the Nera, protects one of the largest areas of virgin beech forest in Europe, with trees over thirty metres tall and centuries old, untouched by logging. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe.

The forest is a cathedral of grey trunks and green light, with fallen trees left to decay and provide habitats for insects, fungi and birds. Wolves, bears and lynx live in these mountains, though they are rarely seen. The Nera flows south from here through a dramatic limestone gorge, the Cheile Nerei, to the Danube, and the Cheile Nerei-Beușnița national park protects the gorge, with its waterfalls and the turquoise Lake of the Devil, Lacul Dracului. The Semenic plateau, above the forest, is a ski area in winter.

The riding in the Banat mountains is excellent. The road from Reșița to the Semenic plateau climbs through forests past the Văliug reservoir, with tight bends and steep gradients, and continues over the mountains. The roads around the Nera gorge and through the villages of the Almăj valley are winding and quiet. Surfaces vary, with some good asphalt and some rough or unpaved sections, so check conditions. The climate in the mountains is cooler and wetter than in the lowlands, with snow in winter, and fog can be thick.

Văliug is a small village with basic services, and Anina, sixteen kilometres away, is a former mining town with fuel and shops. Reșița, the county capital, has all services and a museum of steam locomotives. The local food in the Banat reflects its mixed heritage, with Romanian, Serbian, German and Hungarian influences. The Banat was home to the Danube Swabians, German settlers, whose villages can still be found. Walking in the virgin beech forest of Izvoarele Nerei, in the silence and green light, is an experience that stays with you.
t.rosia montana mining landscape@46.3,23.1:
Gold has been mined at Roșia Montană, in the Apuseni mountains of western Romania, for over two thousand years. The Romans, who called the place Alburnus Maior, dug an extensive network of galleries into the mountains to extract the gold, and some of these galleries survive, along with wax tablets found in the mines, recording contracts and daily life. In 2021, after years of controversy, the mining landscape of Roșia Montană was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The controversy was over a plan by a Canadian company to create a huge open-pit gold mine using cyanide, which would have destroyed much of the village and the Roman galleries. The plan sparked the largest protests in Romania since the fall of communism, in 2013, and was eventually abandoned. The village itself, with its old houses and churches, reflects a long history of mining, and the landscape around is marked by tailings ponds, old mining works and lakes created to provide water for the mills.

The riding in the Apuseni mountains is among the best in Romania. The roads wind through valleys and over passes, with forests, meadows and villages, and the views are wide and beautiful. The road from Abrud to Câmpeni and on to the Arieș valley is scenic, and the roads into the heart of the Apuseni, towards the Scărișoara ice cave and the Padiș plateau, are wild and often rough. Surfaces vary greatly, from good asphalt to broken roads and gravel. The climate in the mountains is cool and wet, and snow can close roads in winter.

Roșia Montană is a village with basic services, and Abrud, six kilometres away, is a small town with fuel and shops. Câmpeni, the main town of the area, has more services. The Detunata, a basalt hill near Abrud with columns of volcanic rock, is a striking natural monument. The local food is hearty mountain cuisine, and the Apuseni are known for their wooden crafts. Visiting the Roman galleries, deep inside the mountain, gives a sense of the scale and the hardship of ancient mining.
t.pausa arutela poiana bivolari@45.3,24.3:
The Olt is the river that cuts through the Carpathians, and wherever a river does that, an army will want to sit beside it. At Păușa, near Călimănești, the Romans built a small fort called Arutela to guard the road through the Olt valley, part of the defensive line that protected their province of Dacia after Trajan's conquest at the start of the second century. The fort's remains lie by the river, partly lost to floods and later works, and are included in the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing for Dacia, added by UNESCO in 2024.

The Olt valley here is narrow and dramatic, with steep forested slopes rising on both sides and the river flowing fast and green below. The monastery of Cozia, founded in the fourteenth century by the Wallachian prince Mircea the Elder, who is buried there, stands right by the road, with its beautiful Byzantine-style church and frescoes. The spa towns of Călimănești and Căciulata have long attracted visitors to their mineral waters.

The main road through the Olt valley is one of the key routes between Transylvania and Wallachia, and it is busy, with heavy truck traffic, frequent overtaking and narrow sections where the road squeezes between river and rock. Ride with care and patience, and avoid peak times if you can. The reward lies beyond: the Transfăgărășan, one of the most famous mountain roads in Europe, starts not far to the east, and the Transalpina is within reach to the west, both seasonal high roads closed for much of the year by snow.

Călimănești, about five kilometres away, has fuel, shops, restaurants and plenty of accommodation. Râmnicu Vâlcea, to the south, is a bigger town with every service. Local food is hearty: sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with meat and rice, mici, grilled sausages, and polenta with cheese and sour cream. The Horezu monastery and its famous pottery are an easy detour to the west.

Come in late spring or early autumn, when the forests are fresh or golden and the high roads open. Summer brings heat and crowds, winter snow and ice. Little of Arutela is left to see, so treat it as a pause by the river, a breath before the Cozia monastery and whichever mountain road you have chosen for the afternoon.
t.dumbraveni dealul podului 1@47.3,24.0:
The northern edge of Roman Dacia was a long line of watchtowers, small forts and earthworks drawn across the hills of what is now northern Transylvania, and Dealul Podului, the bridge hill, near Dumbrăveni, was one of the points along it. Watchtowers here kept an eye on the valleys that led north from the province, toward the lands of the free Dacians and other peoples beyond the frontier, and their remains, now mostly low earthworks in the fields and forest, are part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing for Dacia, added by UNESCO in 2024.

This is the valley of the Someș, a river that winds through rolling hills of pasture, orchards and small villages on its way north-west. The landscape is gentle and rural, with haystacks in the fields, horse-drawn carts on the roads, wooden gates and churches. Not far away stand the ruins of the Ciceu fortress, a medieval stronghold on a hilltop that once belonged to the princes of Moldavia, with wide views over the valley.

The riding is relaxed and pleasant, with roads winding through hills and villages, gentle curves and light traffic. Surfaces vary, with good asphalt on main roads and potholes and patched sections on smaller ones. Watch for horse-drawn carts, livestock, dogs and pedestrians in villages, and for farm vehicles at harvest time. The weather is continental, with hot summers, cold winters and changeable springs and autumns.

Ciceu-Giurgești and the nearby villages are small, with a shop or two and perhaps a bar. For fuel and wider choice, head for the larger towns: Beclean and Dej are both within reach, and Căianu Mic is about fourteen kilometres away. Local food is rustic and generous: ciorbă, sour soups with meat or vegetables, polenta with cheese and sour cream, and homemade cakes. In villages, you may be offered țuică, a strong plum brandy, which is a gesture of hospitality, though best declined politely if you are riding.

Come in late spring, when the meadows are full of flowers, or in early autumn, when the orchards are heavy with fruit and the forests begin to turn. The earthworks are faint and easily missed, so give yourself time, ask in the village if you are unsure, and enjoy the walk whether you find them or not.
t.capalna@45.8,23.6:
The Dacians liked their fortresses high, hidden and hard to reach, which is why the Roman legions of Trajan took two bloody wars at the start of the second century to conquer them. Căpâlna stands on a steep wooded hill above the Sebeș valley, a Dacian citadel with stone walls built in the distinctive murus dacicus technique, blocks of cut stone tied together with timber beams, and a tower that served as the last refuge. It is one of the six Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains listed by UNESCO in 1999, along with the capital Sarmizegetusa Regia, and it is one of the easier ones to reach, with a path climbing through the forest from the valley road.

The views from the top are lovely: the Sebeș river below, the wooded hills rolling away and the higher peaks of the Șureanu and Parâng ranges to the south. Walking among the walls, you get a feel for how the Dacian kingdom used its mountains, a network of strongholds controlling valleys, mines and roads.

For riders, the real treasure is the road. The Sebeș valley carries the northern end of the Transalpina, one of the highest and most spectacular roads in Romania, which climbs from Șugag past reservoirs and through the forest before rising above the treeline to cross the mountains at more than two thousand metres and drop south toward Novaci. The valley section near Căpâlna is twisty and scenic, with gorges and lakes, while the high part is exposed, often windy, and closed in winter, typically from late autumn until early summer. Check whether it is open before planning a crossing.

Șugag and Jina are small villages with basic shops, and Săsciori, about eight kilometres away, is a little larger. For a full tank and supermarkets, Sebeș, at the mouth of the valley, is the place. Jina, high on the plateau above the valley, is a village of shepherds known for its sheep's cheese and its strong pastoral traditions.

Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and the Transalpina usually open by summer. Midsummer weekends bring crowds to the high road. Climb up to the fortress in the early morning, when mist lies in the valley below, and you will understand why the Dacians trusted these hills to keep them safe.
t.feldioara cetateaua@45.8,24.7:
The Făgăraș mountains are the highest wall in Romania, and from the Olt valley at Ucea they rise like a grey and white curtain across the southern sky, with Moldoveanu and Negoiu, the country's two highest peaks, hidden somewhere in the ridge. Down in the valley, near the villages of Ucea de Jos and Feldioara, the Romans had a fort at a site called Cetățeaua, guarding the Olt route that formed part of the frontier system of Dacia. The remains, earthworks and fragments in the fields, are included in the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing for Dacia, added by UNESCO in 2024.

The Olt valley here is a broad, green corridor of fields, meadows and villages, with the Saxon and Romanian communities of the Țara Făgărașului, the land of Făgăraș, living side by side for centuries. Many villages have fortified churches or old wooden churches, and the region has a strong tradition of folk music and costume.

For riders, this is the gateway to the Transfăgărășan, one of the most famous roads in the world, which starts at Cârțișoara a short distance to the west and climbs in a series of dramatic hairpins to the Bâlea Lake at over two thousand metres, before tunnelling through the ridge and descending south toward Curtea de Argeș. The high section is open only in summer, usually from early July to the end of October, depending on snow, and it is busy with tourists, so ride early in the morning or on weekdays. The road along the Olt valley itself is flat and fast, with heavy truck traffic.

Ucea de Jos is a small village, and the nearest town with full services is Victoria, about six kilometres away, a town built in communist times around a chemical works, with fuel and supermarkets. Făgăraș, to the east, is a larger town with a well-preserved medieval fortress. Food in the region is hearty: mountain cheeses, smoked meats, cabbage rolls and the soups that Romanians eat with almost every meal.

Come in summer, when the Transfăgărășan is open and the meadows full of flowers, or in early autumn, when the forests turn and the high road is quieter. Look up at the mountains from the valley in the morning light, and plan your ascent.
t.levoca and the work of master paul in sp:
Master Paul of Levoča carved the tallest Gothic wooden altar in the world, and you can stand in front of it in the church of St James in the centre of this walled town in eastern Slovakia. Completed in the early sixteenth century, the altar rises almost nineteen metres, with life-size figures of the Virgin and saints in limewood, painted and gilded, under a forest of pinnacles. It is the masterpiece of a sculptor about whom little is known beyond his work, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of Levoča, Spiš Castle and the associated cultural monuments.

Levoča itself is a beautiful town, with its medieval walls largely intact, a large central square lined with Renaissance and Gothic houses, and a town hall with arcades. Next to the town hall stands a cage of shame, an iron cage in which petty criminals were once displayed to the public. The town was a rich German-speaking merchant centre in the Middle Ages, part of a group of Saxon towns in the Spiš region. Each July, a large Catholic pilgrimage climbs to the basilica on the Marian hill above the town.

The riding in Spiš is excellent. The region is a rolling landscape of fields and forests, with the High Tatras rising dramatically to the north-west, snow-capped for much of the year. Spiš Castle, one of the largest castle complexes in Central Europe, sits on a hill above Spišské Podhradie, a short ride east, and the view of its white walls is unforgettable. The roads are generally good, with long sweeps through the hills, though some minor roads are bumpy. Weather can change quickly, especially near the mountains, and winters are cold and snowy. The Slovak Paradise national park, to the south, offers gorges and forests.

Levoča has fuel, shops, restaurants and hotels; Spišská Nová Ves, ten kilometres away, is a larger town. Slovak food is hearty: bryndzové halušky, small potato dumplings with sheep cheese and bacon, soups, and grilled meats. Local beers are good and cheap. Visit the church early, before the groups arrive, and spend time looking at the altar figures; their faces are calm and individual, as if Master Paul had used his neighbours as models.
t.maramarosh@47.9,24.3:
On the map, the line between Romania and Ukraine runs along the Tisza river here, and on either side of it the Carpathians rise in forested ridges. Maramarosh is the old name for the whole region, Maramureș to Romanians, and it is also the name of a protected forest within the Carpathian Biosphere Reserve on the Ukrainian side, one component of the World Heritage inscription for ancient and primeval beech forests of the Carpathians and other regions of Europe. These are forests where beech trees have grown undisturbed since the last ice age, with giants several hundred years old and a richness of life that has vanished from most of Europe.

On the Ukrainian side, Rakhiv is the main town, near the slopes of Hoverla, the highest mountain in Ukraine at just over two thousand metres. Given the war, travel there is not a realistic option for most riders at present. On the Romanian side, the valleys of the Vișeu and the Tisza are the heart of traditional Maramureș, with wooden churches, carved gateways and villages where people still wear traditional dress on Sundays. At Vișeu de Sus, the Mocănița, a narrow-gauge steam railway, carries passengers and timber up the Vaser valley into the mountains.

The riding on the Romanian side is wonderful. The road along the Tisza runs with the river on one side and Ukraine just across the water on the other, with views of the forested hills. Further east, the roads climb toward the Prislop pass and the Rodna mountains, with long curves and big views. The surface varies from new to potholed, and there are horse-drawn carts, cows and dogs on the road. Weather in the mountains is unpredictable, with summer thunderstorms and snow in winter. The border zone has police presence, so carry your documents.

Fuel can be found in the larger villages and towns of the valleys, such as Vișeu de Sus and Sighetu Marmației, but stations are spread out. Bistra and Valea Vișeului are small. Maramureș food is simple and filling: sour soups, polenta with cheese and cream, smoked meats and plum brandy, called horincă here, offered generously. Stop by the Tisza and look across to the forests on the other side; they are among the wildest in Europe, and for now, they are best admired from a distance.
t.vatava cetatele@47.0,24.8:
For about a century and a half, the Roman province of Dacia was a wedge of empire pushed north of the Danube, and its eastern edge ran along the curve of the Carpathians through what is now central Romania. In 2024, UNESCO added the frontiers of the Roman Empire in Dacia to its list, a long chain of forts, watchtowers and earthworks. Vătava, in the upper Mureș valley, is one of the sites, with traces of a Roman fortification on a hill called Cetățele, the little fortresses. Not much is visible to the casual eye: earthworks, a few stones, the outline of a position chosen for its view along the valley.

The Mureș flows here from its source in the eastern Carpathians, cutting between the volcanic Călimani and Gurghiu mountains before emerging into the Transylvanian plateau. Vătava is a village of a couple of thousand people in this valley, surrounded by forests of beech and spruce, with meadows where haystacks are still made by hand. Upstream, the Mureș gorge between Toplița and Deda is one of the most beautiful valleys in Romania, with the river, the railway and the road squeezed together between forested slopes.

The riding in the upper Mureș valley is excellent. The main road follows the river with long curves and views of the mountains, and the side roads climb into the forests toward villages that see few visitors. The surface on the main road is generally good, but minor roads can be potholed or unpaved. Watch for horse carts, logging trucks and cows, and for local drivers overtaking in improbable places. Weather in the valley can be misty in the morning, and winters are cold and snowy. Bears live in these forests, and it is wise not to camp carelessly.

Vătava itself has little in the way of services. Reghin, a town of over thirty thousand downstream, is the nearest place for reliable fuel and supplies, and it is known for its violin-making workshops, which have supplied musicians for over a century. Food in the region is Transylvanian: sour soups, sarmale, cabbage rolls, and polenta with cheese. The Roman site is for those who enjoy imagining the past; stand on the hill and look down the valley, and you will see why the Romans chose this spot to watch.
t.salva dealul dumbrava@47.3,24.4:
The Someșul Mare valley around Năsăud was a frontier long before the Habsburgs made it one again. The Romans built watchtowers on the hills here to guard the northern edge of Dacia, and Salva - Dealul Dumbravă, the hill of the oak grove near the village of Salva, is one of the sites included in the UNESCO listing of the Dacian frontier in 2024. Sixteen centuries later, the Habsburg empire turned the region into a military border district, and the Năsăud border regiment, made up of local Romanian peasants, guarded the Carpathian passes in return for privileges and education.

That tradition of schooling left a mark. Năsăud, a town of about ten thousand, became a centre of Romanian culture in Transylvania, and two of the great Romanian writers grew up nearby: the poet George Coșbuc, born in the village of Hordou, now named after him, and the novelist Liviu Rebreanu, who spent his childhood in Maieru. Their memorial houses can be visited. Salva itself is a village of a few thousand, where the railway from Cluj to the north crosses the valley.

The riding is good and varied. The valley road follows the Someșul Mare with gentle curves, and further east, toward Rodna and the Rodna mountains, the landscape becomes more dramatic, with peaks over two thousand metres and forests reaching down to the river. The road over the Rotunda pass leads to Bucovina, and other roads climb toward Maramureș. Surfaces vary greatly, from new asphalt to potholes, and there are carts, cows and dogs on the road. Summer brings thunderstorms, and winter is snowy and cold. Autumn colours in the beech forests are superb.

Năsăud has fuel, shops and restaurants. Food here is typical of northern Transylvania: sour soups with lovage, polenta with cheese and sour cream, smoked meats and plum brandy. Traditional costumes are still worn for festivals, with their distinctive hats decorated with peacock feathers. The Roman site is modest, but the hill offers a view over the valley that the soldiers on watch would recognise. Climb up if you can, then roll back down to Năsăud for a strong coffee.
t.ilisua arcobara vicinal@47.2,24.1:
A Roman cavalry regiment kept its horses near the village of Ilișua, in the hills of northern Transylvania, for most of the time the province of Dacia existed. The fort, which modern archaeologists link with the ancient name Arcobara, was a large stone camp on the northern frontier, and its remains have been excavated over the years. It is part of the frontier of Roman Dacia listed by UNESCO in 2024. Today the site is a field with low walls and grassy mounds, and the neighbouring villages of Uriu, Cristeștii Ciceului and Braniștea go about their business around it.

This is the valley of the Someș, between Dej and Beclean, a gentle landscape of low hills, orchards and fields, with the river meandering through meadows. On a hill near Ciceu-Mihăiești stood the medieval fortress of Ciceu, which belonged for a time to the princes of Moldavia, including Stephen the Great, a reminder that this was contested ground between Transylvania and its neighbours. Dej, to the west, has a large salt mine, and salt was one of the reasons Rome wanted Dacia in the first place, along with gold.

The riding here is relaxed. The roads follow the valley and climb over low hills with easy curves, and traffic is light except on the main road between Dej and Bistrița. The surface varies, and in villages watch for horse carts, geese and children. The countryside is at its best in spring, when the orchards blossom, and in autumn, when the hills turn gold and the smell of plum brandy being distilled drifts from farmyards. Summer can be hot, and winter brings snow and fog.

The nearest places for fuel are Beclean and Dej, both within easy reach. The village shops sell basics, and a roadside restaurant will serve soups, grilled meats and polenta. The Roman site has information boards, but little else, so use your imagination: five hundred horsemen, their barracks and stables, their baths, and the long wait for trouble from the north. Then ride on along the Someș, which has been flowing past all of it, Romans included, without much interest.
t.agrij coasta lata@47.1,23.0:
The Meseș mountains are a modest ridge by Carpathian standards, but for the Romans they were a natural wall, and they built their frontier along it. The north-western edge of Dacia ran along these hills, with forts, watchtowers and walls guarding the passes from the plains of the Barbaricum beyond. Agrij - Coasta Lată, near the villages of Stârciu, Buciumi and Meseșenii de Jos, is one of the watchtower sites named in the World Heritage inscription of 2024. Nearby, at Buciumi, are the remains of a fort, and a little further north, at Moigrad, lies Porolissum, the largest Roman site in the region, with a reconstructed gate.

This is the county of Sălaj, a quiet region of rolling hills, forests and small villages, between Cluj and Oradea. Zalău, the county capital, sits at the foot of the Meseș, and Crasna, a town of six thousand, lies to the north-west. The landscape is pastoral and gentle, with meadows, orchards and beech woods, and the villages have small wooden churches, some of them centuries old. The pass over the Meseș, between Zalău and Cluj, was an important route since Roman times.

The riding is pleasant and quiet. The roads across the Meseș climb through forests with curves and views over the hills, and the minor roads wind through villages and valleys. The main road between Zalău and Cluj can be busy with trucks, but the side roads are calm. Surfaces vary, with potholes and gravel on minor roads. Expect carts, cows and dogs. Weather is generally mild, but there can be fog, rain and snow in winter. Autumn colours in the beech forests are lovely.

The villages near the watchtower are small; for fuel, head to Crasna or Zalău, both within easy reach. Food in Sălaj is typical of Transylvania: soups, stews, polenta with cheese and smoked meats. Local plum brandy is strong and offered with generosity. The watchtower site is little more than a mound in the forest, but the setting is beautiful, and a visit to Porolissum makes the history come alive. Stand on the ridge and look west over the plains, and you are looking at what the Romans called the land beyond the frontier.
t.turda potaissa dealul cetatii@46.6,23.8:
Turda sits on salt. Under the town, the Salina Turda, an old salt mine, has been converted into an extraordinary underground amusement park, with a Ferris wheel, a lake with rowing boats and a mini-golf course more than a hundred metres below the surface, inside vast chambers carved out over centuries. Above ground, on the hill called Dealul Cetății, the Romans built the camp of the Fifth Macedonian Legion, which moved here in the late second century to guard the heart of the province of Dacia. The legionary fortress of Potaissa, with its walls, gates and headquarters building, has been excavated, and it counts as one component of UNESCO's inscription of the Dacian frontier.

Turda has more history than its size suggests. In 1568, the Diet of Turda proclaimed freedom of religion in Transylvania, one of the earliest laws of its kind in Europe. In 1601, Michael the Brave, who had briefly united the three Romanian principalities, was murdered near the town; his tomb stands on a hill nearby. The surrounding landscape includes the Turda Gorge, a spectacular limestone canyon with cliffs over two hundred metres high and a path along the river, popular with hikers and climbers.

The riding is good. The motorways from Cluj and toward the south pass close to Turda, but the real fun is on the minor roads into the Trascău mountains to the west, with gorges, villages and forests. The road toward the Turda Gorge is narrow and twisty, and the road over the hills toward the Arieș valley and the Apuseni mountains offers curves and views. The surface varies from excellent to poor. Summer can be hot, and winter brings snow and fog. Watch for local driving habits, especially overtaking.

Turda has fuel, beds and plenty of places to eat. The cooking here is Transylvanian, with Hungarian influences: goulash, stuffed cabbage, sour soups and cakes. The salt mine is worth the queue for anyone who has never seen anything like it, and the air inside is said to be good for the lungs. The Roman fortress is on the hill above the town, and from its walls you look out over the valley of the Arieș, as the legionaries once did.
t.glod toaca glodului 1@47.3,23.6:
Between Dej and Jibou the Someș river squeezes through a narrow, winding valley, with the railway, the road and the river taking turns to cross each other. On the hills above, near the village of Glod and the larger villages of Rus and Ileanda, the Romans kept a watch on the north-western edge of Dacia, and Toaca Glodului is one of their watchtower positions, among the components of UNESCO's Dacian frontier listing. Toaca is the name of the wooden board struck in Romanian monasteries to call the monks to prayer, and the hill may owe its name to its shape or to some long-forgotten story.

This is a quiet corner of Transylvania, on the border between the counties of Sălaj and Maramureș, with hills covered in beech and oak, meadows and orchards, and villages of a few thousand people strung along the valley. To the north, the Lăpuș country, Țara Lăpușului, is one of the most traditional regions of Romania, with wooden churches and villages where life still follows the seasons. The Someș, swollen in spring, slows to a lazy green river in summer, and herons stand in the shallows.

The riding is relaxed and pretty. The valley road follows the river with gentle curves, and traffic is light, apart from the occasional truck and the horse carts that are still common here. Side roads climb into the hills toward Lăpuș and the Țibleș mountains, with more curves, steeper gradients and rougher surfaces. Watch for potholes and gravel, and for dogs that take an interest in motorcycles. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with mild weather and beautiful colours. Summer can be hot, and winter brings snow and ice.

The villages along the valley have small shops, and Ileanda has a few services, but for reliable fuel it is best to fill up in Dej or Târgu Lăpuș before heading into the hills. Local cooking is simple and hearty: soups, polenta, cheese, smoked bacon and plum brandy. The watchtower site itself is on a hill, reached by a walk through fields and forests, and there is little to see beyond earthworks. But the view over the Someș valley is lovely, and the silence of the hills is the real reward.
t.sintereag dealul oului@47.2,24.3:
Egg Hill, Dealul Oului, is a gentle rise near the village of Șintereag in Bistrița-Năsăud, and the Romans used it as a watch post on the north-eastern frontier of Dacia. Like the other sites in this area, it is part of the frontier listed by UNESCO in 2024, and like many of them, it is more a place to imagine than to see: a low hill, a few traces in the ground, a wide view over the valley of the Șieu and the hills toward Bistrița. Șintereag, a village of a few thousand, lies close by, with Șieu-Odorhei and Cociu as neighbours.

The nearby city of Bistrița is known around the world for a reason that has little to do with its real history: it appears in Bram Stoker's Dracula as the town where Jonathan Harker stays at the Golden Krone before heading to the count's castle. The real Bistrița was a prosperous Saxon trading town, with a fine Gothic Evangelical church and a tall tower. East of the city, the road climbs to the Tihuța pass, the Borgo pass of the novel, at over a thousand metres, before descending into Bucovina.

The riding is good, especially if you head east into the mountains. The road toward the Tihuța pass is a classic, with long curves, forests and views of the Călimani mountains. The roads around Șintereag are calmer, crossing gentle hills with farms and orchards. Surfaces vary, and there are horse carts and livestock on the roads. Watch for local drivers overtaking on blind bends. Weather in the hills is mild, but the mountains bring storms in summer and snow in winter.

Beclean, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and services, and Bistrița has everything. Food here is typical of northern Transylvania, with soups, polenta, cheese, smoked meats and cakes. Plum brandy is a local pride. The Roman site is quiet, often with just a farmer and a dog for company, so enjoy the view and the peace. Then, if the light is good, ride east to the Tihuța pass and see the mountains that Stoker never visited but described with such gothic relish.
t.costesti cetatuie@45.7,23.1:
The Dacians built their strongholds high in the Orăștie mountains, and the fortress of Costești-Cetățuie was one of the gateways to their heartland. Standing on a steep hill above the valley of the Grădiștea river, it was protected by walls built in the Dacian style, the murus dacicus, with large cut stone blocks bound by timber beams, and by earthen ramparts and palisades. It guarded the road up the valley to Sarmizegetusa Regia, the capital of King Decebalus, which the Romans captured in the wars of 101 to 106 that turned Dacia into a province. The fortresses of the Orăștie mountains are listed together by UNESCO.

The valley is quiet and green, with beech forests, meadows and scattered farms, and the villages of Orăștioara de Sus and Costești sit at its mouth. Up the valley, the road climbs toward Sarmizegetusa Regia, a sacred precinct with circular and rectangular sanctuaries made of andesite and limestone, set in the forest at around a thousand metres. The site is atmospheric and mysterious, especially in the morning mist, and it has become a place of pilgrimage for Romanians interested in their Dacian roots.

The riding is enjoyable. The road from Orăștie up the Grădiștea valley is narrow and twisty, with forests and the river beside it, and it has been improved in recent years, though the upper part can be rough. The surrounding hills offer quiet roads with curves and views, and further south, the Șureanu mountains and the Transalpina road, one of the highest in Romania, are within reach. Weather in the mountains is unpredictable, with summer storms and snow in winter. Watch for potholes, gravel and logging trucks.

The villages near the fortress have small shops and guesthouses, but for reliable fuel, Orăștie or Călan are the safe choices. What lands on the table here is Transylvanian, with soups, polenta, cheese and grilled meats. Guesthouses serve home-cooked meals with local ingredients. Climb to the fortress on foot, a steep but short walk, and look down the valley; this was the front door of the Dacian kingdom, and its guards would have seen any army coming from far away.
t.ideciu de sus dealul custurii@46.8,24.8:
Salt has shaped this part of Transylvania as much as any river. The hills of the eastern Transylvanian basin sit on enormous salt deposits, and the springs and lakes are often salty, as in Sărățeni, whose name says it all, and where a small salt museum explains the history. Ideciu de Sus, a village in the Mureș valley above Reghin, lies in this country, and the hill of Dealul Custurii nearby carried a Roman watchtower on the eastern frontier of Dacia, included in UNESCO's inscription of 2024. The Romans valued salt highly, and controlling the deposits was one reason they kept a watchful eye on these hills.

A little further east, the town of Praid has one of the largest salt mines in Europe, now partly open to visitors, and Sovata has a famous heliothermal lake, Lacul Ursu, the bear lake, whose salty water stays surprisingly warm at depth because of the way it traps the sun's heat. These are the hills of the Székely Land, where Hungarian is the language spoken in most villages, with carved wooden gates and painted churches. The valley of the Mureș, here broad and green, is lined with fields and orchards.

The riding is pleasant and varied. The road along the Mureș is fast and easy, and the side roads into the hills toward Sovata and Praid climb through forests with curves and views. The surface varies from good to rough, and there are horse carts and livestock on the roads. The Gurghiu mountains to the north offer remote roads through forests where bears are common. Weather is mild in summer, with occasional storms, and cold and snowy in winter. Autumn is particularly beautiful.

The villages around Ideciu have small shops; for fuel and services, Reghin, about seven kilometres away, is the obvious choice. Food in the region mixes Romanian and Hungarian traditions: goulash, kürtőskalács, the chimney cake roasted on a spit and rolled in sugar, soups and stews. The Roman site is modest, but the view over the valley is good, and the combination of salt, history and gentle hills makes for a fine day's riding. Finish with a float in a salt lake, if you have time; it is the best possible cure for a sore back.
t.geoagiu bai germisara dambul romanilor@4:
The Romans never met a hot spring they did not want to bathe in, and at Germisara, now Geoagiu-Băi, they found warm water bubbling from the ground in a valley at the edge of the Apuseni mountains. They built baths, carved pools into the rock and dedicated offerings to the nymphs and to the healing gods, including small gold plaques found by archaeologists in one of the pools. The site, called Dâmbul Romanilor, the Romans' hillock, sits on the World Heritage list as part of the Dacian frontier, together with the military fort of Germisara in the Mureș valley below. Today, Geoagiu-Băi is again a spa resort, with modern pools fed by the same warm springs.

The resort lies in a narrow valley among wooded hills, a few kilometres north of the town of Geoagiu and the Mureș river. It is a pleasant, slightly old-fashioned place, with hotels, guesthouses and a large open-air pool complex that is popular with Romanian families in summer. The Roman pools, cut into a travertine mound formed by the mineral-rich water, are next to the modern ones, and it is easy to imagine legionaries soaking away their aches here two thousand years ago.

The riding is good. The A1 motorway runs along the Mureș valley, but the real fun lies in the roads climbing north into the Apuseni mountains, toward the gold mining country of Roșia Montană and the Arieș valley. These roads are narrow and twisty, with forests, villages and views, and the surface varies from good to poor. To the south, across the Mureș, the Orăștie mountains and the Dacian fortresses beckon. Weather in summer is warm, with storms; winter brings snow in the hills.

Geoagiu has fuel and shops, and Orăștie and Deva, a short ride away, have everything. The kitchen in these parts is Transylvanian, with soups, stews, polenta and grilled meats, and the spa restaurants serve generous portions. After a day on the bike, an hour in the warm pools is the obvious cure, and you will be in good company: the Romans did exactly the same, and they left their thanks to the nymphs in gold.
t.stretch of the camino real between aculc:
For almost three centuries, wagon trains loaded with silver rolled north and south along the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road that linked Mexico City with the mining towns of the north and eventually with Santa Fe in what is now New Mexico. It was one of the longest trade routes in the Americas, carrying silver, mercury, goods, people and ideas across thousands of kilometres. In 2010 UNESCO listed a series of sites along the route, including stretches of the old road, bridges, haciendas and towns. This section, between Aculco and San Juan del Río, crosses the high plateau on the border between the State of Mexico and Querétaro.

Aculco is a pretty colonial town, designated one of Mexico's pueblos mágicos, with a main square, a church and stone houses. It is known for its dairy products, especially cheese, and for its waterfalls, the Cascadas de la Concepción and Tixhiñú, which plunge over basalt columns nearby. San Juan del Río, to the north, is a larger town with a historic centre, a long stone bridge built in the colonial period, and a tradition of opal and wine production in the surrounding area.

The old road itself survives in places as a cobbled track across the fields, with stone bridges over streams. Walking a stretch, you can imagine the mule trains, the soldiers and the merchants who passed this way. The landscape is open and rolling, with farmland, maguey plants and distant hills.

The riding is mixed. Highway 57, the main route between Mexico City and Querétaro, runs close by, a busy toll road with heavy truck traffic. The minor roads are quieter and more pleasant, but surfaces vary, and topes, the infamous Mexican speed bumps, appear without warning, often unmarked. Watch out for livestock, pedestrians and slow vehicles. The altitude here is over two thousand metres, so the air is cooler than you might expect, and afternoon thunderstorms are common in the rainy season, from June to September.

San Juan del Río has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Aculco has the basics. Try the local cheeses and a plate of barbacoa, slow-cooked lamb, a weekend specialty in the region. Check current travel advice, and avoid riding at night. The best time to visit is the dry season, from October to May.
t.agrij osoiul ciontului 2@47.1,23.0:
The Meseș hills are a long, wooded ridge in northwestern Romania, and for the Romans they were the edge of the world. Beyond them lay the free Dacians and the peoples of the great plain; on this side lay the province of Dacia, conquered by Trajan in the early second century. The valley of the Agrij river, which runs along the southern side of the ridge in Sălaj county, is dotted with archaeological sites, and Osoiul Ciontului is one of many places in the area where traces of ancient settlement have been recorded. There may be little to see at the spot itself, but the landscape around it is rich in history and quiet beauty.

The great site nearby is Porolissum, near the village of Moigrad, northeast of Zalău. It was the most important Roman town and military base on the northwestern frontier of Dacia, guarding a pass through the Meseș hills. The ruins include a reconstructed gate, the walls of the fort, an amphitheatre and the remains of a customs post, all set on a hilltop with sweeping views. It is one of the most impressive Roman sites in Romania, and it is rarely crowded.

Sălaj county is also known for its wooden churches, small, steep-roofed buildings of oak and shingle, often set in village graveyards on hillsides. Many date from the eighteenth century, and their interiors are painted with saints and scenes from the Bible. They are a lovely sight, especially in the evening light.

The riding here is relaxed and rural. The roads follow the valleys, with gentle bends and short climbs over the hills, through villages where horse-drawn carts are still common. Surfaces vary; the main roads are generally good, but minor roads can be potholed or gravel. Watch out for dogs, livestock and slow vehicles. The views from the ridge over the rolling countryside are wonderful, especially in spring and autumn.

Zalău, the county seat, is the place for fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. The villages around have small shops and bars, but services are limited. Try the local food: sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with meat and rice, or a hearty ciorbă, a sour soup. The weather is continental, hot in summer and cold in winter, with snow on the hills. Spring and autumn are the best seasons for riding.
t.dabaceni coama pietrar 1@47.3,23.6:
The Someș is the river of northern Transylvania, gathering its waters in the mountains and winding west through a broad, green valley towards Hungary. Around Rus and Ileanda, in the northeast of Sălaj county, the valley narrows between wooded hills, and the villages cling to the slopes above the river. Dăbâceni and the ridge called Coama Pietrar lie in this landscape, one of many recorded archaeological sites in the area, and like most of them it is more about the setting than about visible remains.

This part of Romania feels remote, even though it is not far from Cluj or Baia Mare. The villages are small and traditional, with wooden gates, haystacks and orchards of plums and apples. Many people still farm the land in the old way, with horses and hand tools, and the pace of life is slow. Ileanda has a small monastery and a few shops.

The area also carries painful memories. In September 1940, after northern Transylvania was transferred to Hungary, troops carried out a massacre in the nearby village of Treznea, killing dozens of Romanian villagers. A memorial stands there today. The history of this region is complex, with Romanians, Hungarians, Germans and Jews living side by side for centuries, and the scars of the twentieth century run deep.

The riding follows the Someș valley, with the road and railway sharing the narrow space between the river and the hills. It is a pleasant, winding road, with gentle bends and views of the water. Side roads climb into the hills, narrow and steep, with rough surfaces and spectacular views over the valley. To the north rise the Țibleș mountains, wilder and higher, with forests and few roads. Traffic is light, but watch for logging trucks, horse-drawn carts and livestock.

The nearest towns with full services are Dej, to the east, and Jibou, to the west, both with fuel, supermarkets and restaurants. The villages have small shops and bars where you can get a coffee or a cold drink. The weather is continental, with hot summers and cold, snowy winters. Spring brings blossom to the orchards, and autumn turns the hills gold and red. Slow down, enjoy the river, and wave to the people sitting outside their gates; they will wave back.
t.perisor corobana@47.3,24.2:
Țara Năsăudului, the Land of Năsăud, is a hilly corner of Bistrița-Năsăud county in northern Romania, and it has a strong sense of its own identity. In the eighteenth century the Habsburgs organised the villages here into a military frontier district, with a Romanian border regiment that defended the empire's eastern edge in return for freedom from serfdom. The people of the area were proud of that status, and the schools and institutions founded with the regiment's funds helped create a remarkable tradition of learning. Two of Romania's best-loved writers grew up nearby: the poet George Coșbuc, born in the village that now bears his name, and the novelist Liviu Rebreanu, whose books describe the lives of Transylvanian peasants.

Perișor and the hillside called Corobana lie near Zagra, in a valley north of the Someș. The site here is one of many recorded archaeological locations in the area, and the landscape is gentle and green, with rolling hills, meadows, orchards and patches of beech forest. To the north, the mountains rise: the Țibleș and the Rodna, with peaks over two thousand metres and snow well into spring.

Village life here is still traditional. People wear embroidered costumes on Sundays and festivals, haystacks dot the meadows, and wooden gates guard the farmyards. The local plum brandy, țuică or the stronger palincă, is offered to visitors with pride.

The riding is excellent. The roads wind through the hills and valleys with good views, little traffic and a variety of bends. Surfaces vary, from smooth new asphalt to potholed stretches and gravel. To the north, the road over the Rotunda pass towards Bucovina, or the climb towards the Rodna mountains, offer more challenging and spectacular riding. Watch for horse-drawn carts, livestock and dogs.

Năsăud is the nearest town with full services, including fuel, supermarkets and restaurants; Beclean and Bistrița are also close. The villages have small shops and bars. The weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters; in the mountains, snow can linger into May. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons for riding, with fresh green meadows or golden forests. Stop in a village, ask about the local festivals, and you may be invited in for a glass of something strong.
t.chornohora@48.1,24.4:
Chornohora, the Black Mountain, is the highest range of the Ukrainian Carpathians, a long ridge of rounded summits above the forests on the border between the Zakarpattia and Ivano-Frankivsk regions. Its highest peak, Hoverla, rises to 2,061 metres, the highest point in Ukraine, and on summer weekends it can be busy with hikers. Along the ridge to the southeast stands Pip Ivan, crowned by the ruins of an astronomical and meteorological observatory built by Poland in the 1930s, when this was the border with Czechoslovakia. Locals call it the White Elephant, and seeing it loom out of the mist is unforgettable.

The mountains are home to the Hutsuls, a highland people with a distinctive culture of colourful embroidered costumes, wooden churches, carved crafts and long alpine horns called trembitas, once used to send signals across the valleys. Sheep grazing on the high pastures, the polonyny, has been part of life here for centuries, and in summer you may see shepherds with their flocks on the slopes.

The forests are vast, with beech on the lower slopes and spruce higher up, and much of the area is protected as part of the Carpathian Biosphere Reserve. Some of the old-growth beech forests in the region are part of a UNESCO World Heritage site that spans many European countries. Bears, wolves, lynx and deer live in the woods.

The villages nearest the pin, Kvasy, Bohdan and Lazi, lie in the valleys of the Tisza and its tributaries, near the town of Rakhiv. Near the village of Dilove, a monument marks one of the places claimed as the geographic centre of Europe. The roads follow the rivers, winding through narrow valleys with steep, forested slopes. Surfaces range from good to very poor, with potholes, gravel and broken asphalt, and side roads into the mountains are often dirt tracks suitable only for off-road bikes.

Rakhiv has fuel, shops and simple restaurants. Try banosh, a dish of cornmeal cooked with cream and topped with cheese and crackling, a Hutsul specialty. The weather in the mountains is changeable, with rain and storms common in summer, and snow from autumn to late spring. Ukraine has been at war since 2022, and travel conditions, border rules and safety advice must be checked carefully before any trip.
t.stuzica bukovske vrchy@49.1,22.5:
At the very eastern tip of Slovakia, where the borders of Slovakia, Poland and Ukraine meet on the summit of Kremenec, lies a forest that has been left to itself for longer than anyone remembers. Stužica, in the Poloniny National Park, is one of the most valuable fragments of primeval beech forest in Europe, with trees several hundred years old, fallen trunks rotting slowly on the ground, and an extraordinary richness of fungi, insects and birds. It is part of the UNESCO site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a transnational listing that started with forests in Slovakia and Ukraine.

The Bukovské Vrchy, the hills around here, are a remote and thinly populated corner of Europe. The villages were home to Rusyns, an East Slavic people with their own language and Greek Catholic and Orthodox traditions, and wooden churches survive in several of them. In the twentieth century, much of the area was depopulated, partly by the construction of the Starina reservoir, which supplies drinking water to eastern Slovakia and led to the removal of several villages. Today wolves, bears, lynx and European bison live in the forests.

Riding into this area means following quiet valley roads from Snina toward the village of Nová Sedlica, the easternmost village in Slovakia, where the road ends. The route passes the Starina reservoir and winds through forested valleys, with gentle curves, some narrow stretches and broken asphalt in places. Traffic is minimal, but watch for forestry trucks, livestock and wildlife. In autumn the beech woods turn gold and the air smells of wet leaves and mushrooms. Winter brings snow and cold, and the area feels truly remote.

The Polish villages of Cisna and Lutowiska lie across the ridge, but there is no road crossing the border here, so treat this as a dead end. Nová Sedlica has a few guesthouses and simple food. Leave the bike at the trailhead, walk into the forest for an hour or so, and listen to the sounds of a place where humans have stepped back. It is a humbling and peaceful experience.
t.chiuiesti dealul crucii@47.3,23.8:
North of Dej, the Someș river winds through a land of soft hills, orchards and scattered villages, and on the ridges above it the Romans once kept watch over the northern frontier of their province of Dacia. Chiuiești, a commune of small villages spread across the hills, is one of the places where archaeologists have identified the remains of watchtowers on high points along the frontier, including one on the hill known as Dealul Crucii, the Hill of the Cross. Little survives above ground beyond low mounds and traces in the grass, but the sites are included in the World Heritage inscription of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire in Dacia, added in 2024.

Dacia was conquered by Trajan in two wars at the beginning of the second century AD and became a Roman province with its capital at Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa. The northern frontier ran through the hills of what is now Sălaj and Cluj counties, with forts, watchtowers and earthworks controlling the passes and valleys. The Romans withdrew from Dacia around 271, but their legacy endured in the Romanian language, which descends from Latin, something every Romanian schoolchild learns with pride.

The riding around Chiuiești is a pleasant mix of rural roads and hilly lanes. The main roads along the Someș valley are fairly busy, with trucks and cars heading between Dej and Baia Mare, but the side roads into the hills are quiet, winding through orchards, pastures and woods with frequent climbs and descents. Surfaces vary greatly, from new asphalt to broken roads and gravel tracks, so an adventure bike is an advantage if you want to explore. Watch out for horse-drawn carts, which are still common in rural Romania, as well as cattle and dogs.

Chiuiești itself has small shops but no proper services. Dej, about fifteen kilometres away, is a town of nearly forty thousand people with fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants. The area around Dej is also known for its salt, with the salt mine at Ocna Dejului nearby. Local food is hearty: sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with meat and rice, mămăligă, a polenta-like dish, and strong plum brandy called țuică or pălincă. Ride up to the ridge if the track allows, look out over the hills and the Someș valley, and imagine a Roman sentry staring north into the forests.
t.valea lesului ticlau@47.3,23.5:
The Someș river does most of the work here.
