Flowing west and then north out of Transylvania, it has carved a valley through the hills of Sălaj county, and near the villages of Lozna and Letca the slopes close in, wooded and steep, with small clearings and hay meadows. On the ridges above, the Romans built watchtowers to guard the northern edge of Dacia, and the remains near Valea Leșului and Țiclău are among the sites included in the UNESCO frontier listing. Today they are little more than grassy hollows and stone scatters, visited by archaeologists and the occasional curious walker.

The countryside is beautiful in a quiet, unassuming way. Haystacks stand in the meadows, built around central poles in the traditional way, and wooden gates and old houses with carved details still appear in the villages. In spring the meadows are full of flowers, and in autumn the woods turn red and gold. This is a region where traditional farming has survived longer than in most of Europe, and the result is a landscape of great richness for wildlife, from butterflies to birds of prey.

The road along the Someș valley through Jibou and toward Dej is the main route, with gentle curves and generally decent asphalt, following the river through the narrowing valley. Side roads up into the hills are narrow, often rough, and sometimes turn into gravel or dirt tracks, which can become muddy and slippery after rain. Railway lines follow the river too, and level crossings are frequent. Traffic is light, but horse-drawn carts and livestock are a regular sight, and village dogs can be enthusiastic about chasing bikes.

Lozna and Letca are small villages with basic shops. For fuel and proper services, head for Jibou, a town of about eleven thousand people around eighteen kilometres away, which also has a baroque castle built by the Wesselényi family and a well-known botanical garden. Local food in Sălaj is rich and comforting: soups soured with borș, grilled meats and pancakes filled with sweet cheese. Find a spot by the river, switch off the engine, and watch the water slide past under the wooded slopes. It is the kind of place where an hour disappears without you noticing.
t.hurez dealul prislop 5@47.0,22.9:
Some frontiers look dramatic on the map and modest on the ground, and the Roman watchtower site on Dealul Prislop near Hurez is a good example. Here, in the hills of Sălaj county in northwestern Romania, archaeologists have identified a series of small towers on high ground along the western frontier of Roman Dacia, which ran along the Meseș mountains and the hills around them. The towers were part of a chain of observation posts linked by signals, controlling movement across the frontier, and they are now included in the UNESCO listing of the Dacian frontier. Little is visible except low mounds and the shape of the land, but the views from the ridges explain why the Romans chose these spots.

The area lies between the Crasna and Barcău river valleys, in a landscape of rolling hills, woods and small farming villages. Nearby, near Zalău, lies Porolissum, the most important Roman site in the region, a large fortified town with a reconstructed gate and an amphitheatre. It controlled the main pass through the Meseș mountains and was a hub of trade between the province and the free Dacians beyond the frontier.

The riding is rural and varied. Roads link the villages of Cizer, Stârciu and Mal with occasional climbs and gentle curves through woods and fields. Surfaces range from fairly smooth asphalt to rough patches and gravel, so take care, especially after rain. Traffic is minimal, but watch out for carts, livestock and the occasional tractor. The higher ground offers wide views over the hills toward the Plopiș and Meseș ranges. Spring and autumn are lovely; summer can be hot, and winter muddy or snowy.

Services are limited in the villages. Crasna, about fifteen kilometres away, is the nearest larger place with fuel and shops, while Zalău, the county seat, has a full range of amenities. Local food includes sour soups, stuffed cabbage and plum brandy, and village shops sell bread, cheese and drinks. Make a quiet stop here, perhaps on a ridge with a view, and think of the soldiers who stood watch on these hills almost two thousand years ago, scanning the horizon for trouble. Then head on to Porolissum to see the frontier at its most impressive.
t.voislova gara cfr@45.5,22.5:
The Bistra valley is a natural corridor, and armies have known it for millennia. Running east from Caransebeș toward the Iron Gate of Transylvania and the Hațeg basin, it was the route by which Trajan's legions advanced on the Dacian heartland in the wars of AD 101 to 106, and later the road that linked Roman forts and towns along the way. Near the village of Voislova, by the railway station, the remains of a Roman site have been identified as counted within the UNESCO serial site of the Dacian frontier, a reminder of how important this valley was to the Roman presence in the province.

The landscape is lovely: a broad green valley with the Țarcu mountains rising to the south and the Poiana Ruscă mountains to the north, small villages strung along the road, and the Bistra river running clear and fast. To the east, the Iron Gate of Transylvania pass leads into the Hațeg country, home to the ruins of Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, the Roman capital of Dacia, and to fossil sites where dwarf dinosaurs have been found. Oțelu Roșu, a former steelworks town, sits at the western end of this stretch.

Riding the valley road is easy and enjoyable. The DN68 runs along the river with long, gentle curves and good views of the mountains, before climbing over the Iron Gate pass in a series of bends through beech forest. Traffic is moderate, with trucks heading between the Banat and Transylvania, but it is usually manageable. Side roads into the mountains toward Poiana Mărului or the Muntele Mic area climb steeply and get rough higher up. Spring and autumn are especially pleasant, and the beech woods on the pass turn spectacular colours in October.

Voislova and the neighbouring villages have small shops and cafés, while Oțelu Roșu, about seven kilometres away with over ten thousand people, has fuel stations and more services. Caransebeș, further west, is a larger town with everything you might need. Local food is Banat cuisine, influenced by Austrian, Hungarian and Serbian traditions, with excellent sausages, soups and pastries. Pause by the station, look up the valley toward the mountains, and think of the legions marching east. Then ride on toward Sarmizegetusa, where their story is written in stone.
t.treznea carbunarea@47.1,23.1:
Treznea is a quiet village in the hills southeast of Zalău, the kind of place where the loudest sound is a cockerel or a tractor. Yet its name carries a heavy weight in Romanian memory. In September 1940, shortly after northern Transylvania was transferred to Hungary under the Second Vienna Award, Hungarian troops entering the area killed dozens of villagers here, Romanians and Jews, and burned houses. A memorial in the village commemorates the victims. It is a sombre reminder that the beautiful hills of Transylvania have seen terrible things.

The Roman frontier ran close by, along the Meseș mountains, and the site at Cărbunarea near Treznea is one of the points identified as part of the defensive system that guarded the northwestern edge of Dacia. The Meseș ridge was a natural barrier, and the Romans fortified it with watchtowers, earthworks and forts, including the great fortress of Porolissum to the north. These sites form part of the UNESCO listing of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire in Dacia.

The riding around Treznea is a pleasure for anyone who likes quiet, hilly roads. The village sits in the valley of the Agrij river, and roads lead up into the Meseș mountains through forests of beech and oak, with steep climbs, tight bends and views over the hills. Surfaces can be patchy, with gravel and potholes, especially on minor roads. The main road between Zalău and Cluj-Napoca crosses the Meseș ridge nearby, with a well-known climb and curves that local riders enjoy, though it carries significant truck traffic. Weather in the hills can change quickly, and fog is common in autumn.

Treznea is small, with basic shops. Zalău, about nine kilometres away and home to over sixty thousand people, has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and accommodation. Local food includes hearty soups, grilled meats and pancakes, and you will often be offered pălincă, the strong fruit brandy of the region. Take a moment at the memorial, then ride up into the Meseș hills to find a view. The contrast between the peaceful landscape and its history is striking, and it is worth remembering both.
t.chiuiesti dealul podului@47.3,23.9:
The hills above the Someș valley northeast of Dej roll away in long green waves, and the commune of Chiuiești sprawls across them in a scatter of hamlets, each tucked into its own fold of land. Dealul Podului, the Hill of the Bridge, is one of the ridges where traces of a Roman watchtower have been found, part of the chain of observation points that guarded the northern frontier of Dacia. The frontier was not a wall but a network of forts, towers and roads, and the Romans placed their towers where they could see far across the valleys and signal to one another. The site is one of the components of the World Heritage site of the Dacian frontier, although on the ground you will see little more than the shape of the hill and perhaps a low mound.

The Romans are only one layer of history here. The villages have wooden churches, some centuries old, and the Someș valley was a route for salt, timber and cattle long before and after the Romans. The region was part of the Kingdom of Hungary for centuries, then the Habsburg Empire, before becoming part of Romania in 1918, and you will still hear Hungarian spoken in some places alongside Romanian.

For riders, this is exploring country. The main road through the Someș valley offers easy cruising with gentle curves, but the side roads into Chiuiești climb into the hills on narrow lanes that turn rough, steep and occasionally unpaved. Expect potholes, loose gravel and mud after rain, and share the road with horses and carts, cattle and village dogs. The views from the ridges are lovely, especially in the evening, when the light turns golden over the hills and the villages. Spring wildflowers and autumn colours make those two seasons the best.

There are no real services in Chiuiești beyond small village shops. Dej, about thirteen kilometres away, has fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants. If you are hungry, try a bowl of ciorbă, a sour soup, or mici, grilled minced meat rolls, washed down with a cold beer if you have finished riding for the day. Find a high point with a view across the valleys, cut the engine, and enjoy the stillness. It is a beautiful, little-visited corner of Transylvania.
The Țibleș mountains rise like a dark wall between the Lăpuș country and the valleys of Maramureș, a volcanic range of dense spruce and beech forest topping out at nearly two thousand metres. On their slopes, near the source known as Izvorul Șurii above the village of Groșii Țibleșului, the forest feels almost untouched: springs bubbling out of mossy banks, fallen trunks covered in fungi, and a silence broken only by woodpeckers and the wind. This is bear country, and wolves and lynx roam these woods too. The area lies on the edge of the Maramureș region, famous for its wooden churches, carved gates and deeply traditional village life.

Maramureș is one of the few places in Europe where the old peasant culture has survived largely intact into the twenty-first century. Villages such as Botiza, a short ride away, are known for their woven rugs dyed with natural colours, and for their wooden churches with tall, slender spires. The UNESCO-listed wooden churches of Maramureș, built between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries, are scattered through the valleys to the north. Sunday mornings in the villages still see people walking to church in traditional dress, and haymaking is often done by hand with scythes.

The ride here is an adventure. Roads from Lăpuș or from the Iza valley climb into the mountains through forested valleys, becoming narrower, steeper and rougher as you go. The higher sections are often forest roads, gravel or dirt, which are best suited to adventure or dual-sport bikes and can become impassable after heavy rain or in winter. The asphalt stretches in the valleys have plenty of curves but also potholes and loose gravel. Watch out for logging trucks, horse-drawn carts and livestock. The views over the Maramureș hills and the distant Rodna mountains from the higher passes are superb.

Services are thin on the ground. Groșii Țibleșului, Botiza and Lăpuș have small shops, but for reliable fuel, head for Săliștea de Sus, Dragomirești or the town of Târgu Lăpuș, depending on your route. Food in Maramureș is simple and filling: polenta with cheese and sour cream, smoked meats, soups and the fiery plum brandy known locally as horincă. Bring water and supplies, find a spring in the woods and fill your bottle, and enjoy one of the wildest corners of the Carpathians.
t.varadia arcidava pusta@45.1,21.6:
Down in the southwestern corner of Romania, where the Banat plain gives way to the first hills of the Carpathians, the village of Vărădia sits on the edge of a gentle valley that opens toward Serbia. Here, at a place called Pustă, lie the remains of the Roman fort of Arcidava, one of the first stations on the road the Romans built from the Danube crossing at Lederata north into Dacia. Trajan's troops passed this way during the conquest, and the fort guarded the route for the century and a half that followed. Excavations have revealed the outline of the fortifications, and the site is now part of the UNESCO frontier listing.

The Banat is a region with its own identity, shaped by centuries of Habsburg rule after the Ottomans were driven out in the eighteenth century, when settlers came from Germany, Serbia, Slovakia and elsewhere. The landscape around Vărădia mixes vineyards, orchards and pasture with forested hills, and the climate is noticeably milder than in Transylvania. To the east rise the Anina mountains and the Semenic, and beyond them the wild Cerna valley, where the Domogled national park protects limestone gorges and old forests.

Riding in this part of the Banat is relaxed and scenic. The roads around Vărădia and Oravița wind gently through hills and villages, with moderate traffic and decent surfaces on the main routes. Oravița is the starting point of the famous railway to Anina, one of the oldest mountain railways in this part of Europe, and the road toward Anina climbs through forest with steady curves and views. Head east toward Bozovici and the Almăj valley, and the roads become quieter and more rural, with fine scenery. Summer can be hot, and spring is green and lovely.

Vărădia is a small village with basic shops. Oravița, around twelve kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel stations, cafés and supermarkets, and it also has a charming old theatre, said to be one of the oldest in Romania. Banat cuisine is a mix of Romanian, Serbian and Austrian influences, with grilled meats, sausages, cabbage dishes and pastries. Stop near the fort, look across the valley toward Serbia, and picture the Roman road heading north into the unknown, with legionaries marching toward the Carpathians.
t.avasaksa aavasaksa@66.4,23.7:
Aavasaksa is a wooded hill rising above the Torne river on the Finnish side of the border with Sweden, near the town of Ylitornio, just south of the Arctic Circle. It is a modest height, around 240 metres, but it has a remarkable history. In 1736 and 1737, a French expedition led by Pierre Louis Moreau de Maupertuis came to the Torne valley to measure the length of a degree of latitude near the pole, and their observations helped prove that the earth is flattened at the poles, as Newton had predicted. Over a century later, Aavasaksa became one of the points of the Struve Geodetic Arc, the chain of survey stations running from Norway to the Black Sea, inscribed by UNESCO in 2005.

The hill has long been a place of celebration. Because of its height and location, the midnight sun can be seen from the summit around midsummer, even though the hill lies just south of the Arctic Circle, and people have gathered here for midsummer festivities for centuries. A wooden lodge on the summit was built in the nineteenth century for an imperial visit, when Finland was a grand duchy under the Russian tsar. The view from the top over the Torne river, the forests and the Swedish village of Övertorneå across the water is wide and beautiful.

The riding in the Torne valley is a northern pleasure. The roads along the river, on both the Finnish and Swedish sides, run through forests of pine and birch, with long gentle curves and very little traffic. Surfaces are generally good, but frost damage can leave bumps and cracks, and gravel is common on minor roads. Reindeer wander freely on the roads, and they are a real hazard, especially at dusk. The riding season is short, from late May to September, with the midnight sun in June and July and autumn colours, called ruska, in early September. Mosquitoes can be fierce in summer.

Ylitornio, about ten kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafés, and Övertorneå, across the bridge in Sweden, has similar services. The road up the hill is short and steep, and the summit has a viewpoint. Local food includes reindeer, salmon from the river, and cloudberries in late summer. Ride up the hill, look over the valley, and imagine the French scientists in their wigs and coats, measuring the earth in the northern wilderness.
t.smolnik tserkva of saint michael the arc:
In the Bieszczady mountains of south-eastern Poland, close to the border with Ukraine, a wooden church stands on a gentle rise above the San valley at Smolnik. It is dedicated to St Michael the Archangel and built in the style of the Boyko people, with three log sections stepping up from east to west under shingled roofs. Since 2013 it has been part of the World Heritage Site of Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region in Poland and Ukraine.

The church tells a story of absence. Before the Second World War, the Bieszczady were home to Boyko and Lemko communities, mostly Greek Catholic or Orthodox, who built these churches in their villages. In the years after the war, especially during Operation Vistula in 1947, they were deported or resettled, and many villages vanished entirely, leaving only cemeteries, orchards gone wild and the occasional church. The Smolnik tserkva survived and was later used as a Roman Catholic church.

The landscape around Smolnik is wild by European standards. Beech and fir forests cover the slopes, and above them the poloniny, high grassy ridges, offer views into Ukraine and Slovakia. Wolves, lynx, brown bears and European bison live here, and you may see deer or foxes along the roads at dawn and dusk. The rivers are clear and cold, and the air smells of resin and hay in summer.

The Great Bieszczady Loop is what draws most bikes here, and road 896 through Smolnik and Lutowiska is part of the approach to it. The roads are narrow, winding and generally well surfaced, with few towns and light traffic outside the summer holidays. The section from Ustrzyki Górne to Wetlina and Cisna is especially beautiful. Watch for wildlife, logging trucks and occasional gravel on corners.

Services are sparse. Lutowiska, five kilometres away, is a small village with limited facilities; Ustrzyki Dolne, twenty-five kilometres north, has reliable fuel, shops and banks. Fill up before heading into the mountains. Simple guesthouses and mountain huts offer accommodation and food: pierogi, soups and local trout. The Bieszczady have a reputation as Poland's last frontier, a place for people seeking solitude, and an evening by a campfire with only the sound of the forest is the region's real gift.
t.spermezeu lazuri@47.3,24.2:
Spermezeu is a village in the hilly country of western Bistriţa-Năsăud county, in northern Transylvania, where low ridges covered with orchards, hayfields and beech woods roll between the Someş valley and the Ţibleş mountains. The site called Spermezeu - Lazuri belongs to the series of places along the northern edge of the Roman province of Dacia, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listed in Romania in 2024. Here the Romans watched the border with watchtowers and small fortifications on hilltops, and though little remains above ground, the commanding views explain why these spots were chosen.

Roman Dacia was conquered by Trajan in the early second century and held for about 170 years. Its northern frontier in this area did not follow a continuous wall but a chain of watchtowers, forts and earthworks along the hills, watching the valleys that led north into free Dacian territory. Archaeologists have found traces of towers, ditches and pottery, but the landscape has long since reclaimed most of it.

The region has deep literary roots. The novelist Liviu Rebreanu, one of the founders of the modern Romanian novel, was born in Târlişua, just a few kilometres from Spermezeu, and his books about peasant life in Transylvania draw on this very landscape. Near Năsăud, the poet George Coşbuc was born in the village that now bears his name.

Riding here is a matter of quiet, winding country roads with little traffic, linking villages with wooden churches, traditional houses and wells. Surfaces vary from good new asphalt to potholed stretches, and you will meet horse carts, cows and dogs. The hills offer pleasant curves and views of the mountains to the north. May and September tend to be loveliest, when the orchards are in blossom or full of fruit, and the light is soft. Summer can be hot, and winter brings snow and ice.

Spermezeu is a village with basic services. For fuel, head to Beclean on the Someş or the larger communes nearby such as Căianu Mic, seven kilometres away. Food in the region is rich and homemade: soups, cheeses, cured meats, and pălincă, the strong fruit brandy, offered as a sign of hospitality.
t.livezile poderei@47.2,24.6:
Leave Bistriţa eastwards on the DN17 and within minutes you are in Livezile, a long village strung out along the valley of the Bistriţa river where the Transylvanian hills start to bunch up towards the Eastern Carpathians. Poderei is the name of a hillside here where the Romans kept watch over the northern edge of their province of Dacia, and the site is one of the many small components of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listed in Romania in 2024. There is nothing to visit in the sense of ruins; what you get is the hill, the view up the valley and the knowledge that legionaries stared at the same ridges.

The road you are on has a famous literary destination. Bram Stoker sent Jonathan Harker through Bistritz in Dracula, staying at the Golden Krone before setting off by coach for the Borgo Pass. The pass is real, known in Romanian as Tihuţa, and the DN17 climbs over it towards Vatra Dornei and Bukovina. It is one of the finest rides in northern Romania: a steady climb through villages, then forest, then broad bends with views over wave after wave of hills. A hotel built near the summit trades shamelessly on the Dracula connection, and it is a fun place for a coffee.

Bistriţa itself was a Saxon town, Bistritz, founded by German colonists in the Middle Ages, and its Evangelical church with its tall tower dominates the old square. The tower was badly damaged by fire in 2008 and has been restored. The arcaded merchants' houses known as the Sugălete line one side of the centre.

This is fruit country, as the village name suggests: livezi means orchards in Romanian, and in late summer the roadside stalls are piled with plums and apples, while the smell of plum brandy being distilled hangs over some farmyards in autumn. Along the DN17 you share the road with trucks and local traffic, and villages bring speed limits, dogs and horse carts, so keep your eyes up.

Bistriţa, eight kilometres away, is a sizeable town with fuel, workshops, supermarkets and hotels, and it is the natural place to stock up before the climb. In winter the pass can be snowy and icy; from late spring to autumn it is a delight, and a sunset ride back down towards the town, with the hills glowing, is about as good as an evening gets in Transylvania.
t.dumbraveni@47.3,24.0:
Dumbrăveni sits in the quiet hill country above the Someş Mare, where the river curves west towards Dej and the land folds into low ridges, orchards and small woods of oak and hornbeam. Like several places on these rides, it marks a point on the old northern edge of Roman Dacia, one of the scattered watchtower and earthwork sites listed in 2024 as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire. Expect a hill and a view rather than masonry, and enjoy the feeling of being somewhere few travellers bother to stop.

Close by, at Ciceu-Giurgeşti and the village of Ciceu-Corabia, stood the medieval fortress of Ciceu, once an important stronghold. For a time in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries it belonged to the princes of Moldavia, a strange outpost of Stephen the Great's realm deep in Transylvania, granted as a fief by the Hungarian kings. Little of the castle survives, but the story says much about how fluid borders and loyalties were in this part of Europe.

The countryside is a living picture of traditional Transylvanian farming. Haystacks are built around tall poles, fields are often worked by hand or with horses, and the villages have neat houses with painted gates and tall wooden fences. Old wooden churches, some with very steep roofs and slender towers, survive in many villages, and the hills are full of birds: storks nesting on poles, buzzards circling, larks over the meadows.

The roads around Dumbrăveni are a mix. The main road along the Someş valley between Dej and Beclean is busy with trucks, but the small roads up into the hills are quiet and twisty, sometimes newly surfaced, sometimes broken and patched. After rain, mud from farm tracks can make corners slippery, and loose gravel is common. A gentle pace suits this kind of country.

Fuel and shops are available in Dej to the west or Beclean to the east, both on the main valley road, while the closest larger commune listed nearby, Căianu Mic, is about eleven kilometres away. In the villages, small shops sell drinks and snacks, and the people are friendly, if often surprised to see a foreign motorcyclist. A short chat, even in sign language, often ends with an offer of something to drink.
t.negreni poiana la arbore@47.3,23.5:
Somewhere in the hills of Sălaj county, between the villages of Lozna, Rus and Letca, a meadow called Poiana la Arbore, the clearing by the tree, marks one of the small Roman sites on the north-western frontier of Dacia. The name alone tells you what to expect: a glade, a ridge, perhaps a lone tree, and the faint traces of a watch post that once looked out over the Someş valley. The Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing in 2024 included many such places, and their value lies in the chain they form rather than in any single ruin.

The big Roman site in this area is Porolissum, near Moigrad, about an hour's ride to the west, where the Romans built a large fort and town guarding a pass through the Meseş hills. Walls, a gate and an amphitheatre have been excavated and partly reconstructed, and it is worth the detour if you want to see what the frontier looked like at its strongest.

The Someş river cuts through these hills in a narrow valley, with the railway and road squeezed alongside it. The landscape is green and wooded, with villages strung along the valley and scattered on the hillsides. In spring the meadows are full of flowers, and in autumn the beech woods turn copper and gold. Mornings often bring mist in the valley, which burns off by mid-morning.

Riding here is a mix of valley roads and hill lanes. The roads along the Someş offer flowing curves and pleasant scenery, while the side roads up into the hills are narrower, steeper and often rougher. Traffic is light, but watch for animals and farm vehicles. The region is far from the main tourist routes, which means peace and quiet, but also limited services.

Jibou, twenty-two kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, with fuel, shops and restaurants. It has a baroque castle built by the Wesselényi family, a Hungarian noble family, and a botanical garden in its grounds. In the villages, life follows the rhythm of the seasons, and the food is homemade: bread, cheese, smoked bacon and vegetables from the garden.
t.berzovia berzobis@45.4,21.6:
Only a handful of sentences survive from the Emperor Trajan's own account of his wars against the Dacians, and one of them mentions this place. Quoted by a later grammarian, it reads, in Latin, that from there we advanced to Berzobis, then to Aizi. Berzobis is the village now called Berzovia, in the Banat hills of south-western Romania, and the site of the Roman fort here, where the Fourth Legion Flavia Felix was stationed after the conquest, is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing in Romania inscribed in 2024.

The fort was one of the largest in Dacia, built to hold a whole legion at the start of the occupation, on the road that Trajan's armies followed from the Danube northwards into the heart of the Dacian kingdom. Excavations have revealed walls, buildings and finds, though the visible remains are modest. Standing in the fields here, it is easy to imagine columns of soldiers marching past, heading for the mountains around Sarmizegetusa.

The Banat is a region with a very mixed history: Romanians, Serbs, Germans, Hungarians, Czechs and others all lived here, and the traces of that diversity are everywhere, in churches, place names and food. Bocşa, nine kilometres away, and Reşiţa beyond it, are old industrial towns, the latter with one of the oldest ironworks in Romania, dating from the eighteenth century. The surrounding hills offer forests, rivers and quiet roads.

On the bike you get pleasant country roads through rolling hills and valleys, with good asphalt on the main routes and rougher surfaces on the smaller ones. South of Reşiţa, the road towards the Semenic mountains climbs through forests to high meadows, and to the south-west, the roads through the Caraş gorge and down to the Danube offer more dramatic scenery. Traffic is generally light, but watch for trucks near the industrial towns.

Bocşa can sort out fuel and a simple meal, while Reşiţa offers more choice. The local cuisine reflects the mix of cultures: Serbian grilled meats, German pastries and Romanian soups all appear on menus. A plate of mici, grilled minced meat rolls, with mustard and a cold beer is the classic roadside meal.
t.vihorlat@48.9,22.2:
Vihorlat is a range of old volcanoes in the far east of Slovakia, close to the Ukrainian border, and its higher slopes are covered with some of the last primeval beech forests in Europe. The trees here have grown, died and rotted without human interference for a very long time, and the forest is part of the transnational UNESCO site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, first listed in 2007 with sites in Slovakia and Ukraine and later extended across much of the continent.

A walk among these beeches feels different from an ordinary wood. Giant trunks rise straight and smooth to a high canopy, fallen trees lie where they fell, covered in moss and fungi, and young saplings fight for the light in the gaps. The forest is full of life: woodpeckers, owls, salamanders, and larger animals including wolves, lynx and brown bears. In autumn, the slopes turn copper and gold.

The most popular destination in the range is Morské oko, a lake formed by a landslide that dammed a valley, surrounded by beech forest, with a legend about a monster that lived in its depths and ate those who disturbed it. A road leads up from Remetské Hámre to a car park below the lake, and from there it is a short walk. Higher up, the rocky summit of Sninský kameň offers sweeping views across the hills of eastern Slovakia.

The riding around Vihorlat is quiet and lovely. Roads from Snina run south and west through rolling hills, villages and forest, with gentle curves and light traffic; to the north-east, the road to the Starina reservoir and the villages of the Poloniny region leads into the most remote corner of Slovakia. Road surfaces are generally fair but can be patched and bumpy in places, and forest roads may be closed to motor traffic.

This is the land of the Rusyns, an East Slavic people with their own language and Greek Catholic and Orthodox traditions, and wooden churches dot the hills. Snina, a town of over twenty thousand people eight kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try a plate of bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese and bacon, Slovakia's national dish, or local game. Spring and autumn are the most beautiful seasons, but even in high summer the forest stays cool and the roads are never crowded.
t.wooden tserkvas of the carpathian region:
In a narrow valley in the Low Beskids, close to the Slovak border in south-eastern Poland, stands the wooden church of Saint Paraskeva in Kwiatoń, often called the most beautiful of the Lemko churches. Built in the seventeenth century by the Lemkos, an East Slavic highland people who lived in these hills for centuries, it is one of the sixteen wooden tserkvas of the Carpathian region in Poland and Ukraine that UNESCO listed in 2013. Its silhouette is unmistakable: three towers rising in steps toward the west, each topped with onion-shaped domes and crosses, the walls covered in wooden shingles that have weathered to silver-grey.

The church's story is tied to one of the darker episodes of Polish history. In 1947, in Operation Vistula, the Lemko population was forcibly removed from these mountains and resettled in western and northern Poland, and many villages were abandoned. Churches were taken over by Catholic parishes or left to decay. Today, Kwiatoń is used as a Roman Catholic church, but its iconostasis and paintings remain, and the Lemko heritage of the area is slowly being remembered and celebrated.

The surrounding landscape is gentle mountain country, with rounded forested ridges, meadows and small villages strung along the streams. The roads from Gorlice through Uście Gorlickie toward the spa village of Wysowa-Zdrój are narrow, winding and quiet, with good surfaces in most places and plenty of opportunities to stop and photograph wooden churches, roadside shrines and old farmsteads. Further south, the border crossing to Slovakia opens up more empty roads.

This is also where the oil industry began. In the 1850s, the pharmacist Ignacy Łukasiewicz developed the kerosene lamp in this region, and the world's first oil wells were dug nearby, at Bóbrka near Krosno, where an open-air museum shows the old workings. During the First World War, the Battle of Gorlice in 1915 was fought across these hills, and the area is dotted with war cemeteries, many designed by the Slovak architect Dušan Jurkovič in wood and stone.

Grybów, around twelve kilometres away, and Gorlice have fuel and shops; the villages have small stores and guesthouses. Wysowa is known for its mineral waters. Try a plate of pierogi or a bowl of żurek, sour rye soup, and in autumn ask about local mushrooms, which the Beskids produce in abundance.
t.border ridge and gorna solinka valley@49:
The Bieszczady are the wildest mountains in Poland, a corner where the country meets Ukraine and Slovakia and the forest has had decades to reclaim the land. The border ridge, running along the frontier, and the valley of the upper Solinka, below it, are part of the Polish section of the Carpathian primeval beech forests, protected within Bieszczady National Park. There are no roads up here: the ridge is reached on foot, and the forest, with its old beeches, fir and sycamore, is home to wolves, lynx, brown bears, and the European bison that were reintroduced to the area.

The emptiness has a history. Before the Second World War, these valleys were full of villages of Boykos, a Ukrainian-speaking highland people, with wooden churches, mills and fields. After the war, in fighting between the Polish army and Ukrainian insurgents and in the deportations that followed, the population was removed and many villages vanished entirely. Today, all that remains in some valleys are fruit trees gone wild, the foundations of houses, overgrown cemeteries and roadside crosses. Walking through the meadows where Solinka and its neighbours once stood is a melancholy experience.

For riders, the Bieszczady are a favourite destination, mainly thanks to the Great Bieszczady Loop, the Wielka Obwodnica Bieszczadzka, a circuit of roads linking Lesko, Ustrzyki Górne, Wetlina, Cisna and Lake Solina. The road between Cisna, Wetlina and Ustrzyki Górne runs through forest and along valleys under the grassy high ridges called połoniny, with good curves, a few steep climbs and wonderful views. Surfaces are generally good, but watch out for gravel, wildlife and cyclists, and for heavy traffic on summer weekends. There are no road crossings into Ukraine along this stretch of the border, so plan your route accordingly.

Facilities are modest. Cisna and Wetlina are small villages with guesthouses, bars and limited shops; for reliable fuel and supplies, fill up in Lesko or Ustrzyki Dolne before heading into the mountains. Bring rain gear: the weather changes quickly, and fog can sit on the passes.

In the evening, in a wooden guesthouse in Wetlina, eat a plate of pierogi with local cheese or a bowl of bigos, the hunter's stew of cabbage and meat, and listen to the stories of people who came here to escape the city. The Bieszczady attract artists, dreamers and eccentrics, and the atmosphere in the evenings is half the reason to come.
t.hervartov@49.2,21.2:
Hervartov is a small village in the hills of north-eastern Slovakia, a few kilometres from Bardejov, and its wooden church of Saint Francis of Assisi is considered the oldest surviving wooden church in the country, built in the late Middle Ages in the Gothic style. It is one of eight wooden churches of the Slovak part of the Carpathian Mountain Area inscribed by UNESCO in 2008, alongside Greek Catholic, Protestant and Roman Catholic churches that together tell the story of the many faiths and peoples of this borderland.

The church is small and steep-roofed, built of spruce and covered in wooden shingles, with a tall tower crowned with a slender spire. Inside, the walls are covered with paintings, and the Gothic altars are a remarkable survival from an age when most of Europe's wooden churches were lost to fire, war or rebuilding in stone. Visiting usually requires contacting the local caretaker, so ask in the village or check in advance.

The surrounding landscape is gentle and pastoral, with rolling hills, meadows, forests and villages stretched along small streams in the foothills of the Low Beskids. The roads are narrow and quiet, often in decent condition, but with occasional patches of damage and farm traffic. It is lovely riding at a relaxed pace, with plenty of chances to stop at wooden churches, roadside crosses and small bars in the villages. To the north, the roads toward the Polish border and the Dukla Pass, the site of fierce fighting in 1944, are especially rewarding.

Bardejov, about seven kilometres away, is an essential stop. Its medieval town square, surrounded by Gothic and Renaissance burghers' houses, with the town hall in the middle and the Basilica of Saint Giles on one side, is one of the best-preserved in Central Europe and also a UNESCO site. The nearby spa of Bardejovské Kúpele has an open-air museum of folk architecture with wooden houses and churches.

Bardejov, a town of over thirty thousand people, has fuel stations, shops and restaurants. The Šariš region is known for its beer, brewed in Veľký Šariš near Prešov, and for hearty food: try kapustnica, sauerkraut soup with sausage and mushrooms, or potato pancakes. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the hills are green or golden and the roads are quiet.
t.banita jigoru mare@45.5,23.3:
High on a limestone outcrop above the village of Bănița, in the hills of south-western Transylvania, stand the ruins of a Dacian fortress. Bănița is one of the six Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains listed by UNESCO in 1999, part of the defensive system built around the capital of the Dacian kingdom, Sarmizegetusa Regia, in the first century BC and the first century AD. The kingdom's last great ruler, Decebalus, held out against Rome in two hard wars before Trajan's legions finally conquered Dacia in 106, an event recorded in stone on Trajan's Column in Rome.

The site is a short, steep hike up from the road, and the reward is a view over the rolling hills toward the Jiu valley and the high ridges of the Retezat and Parâng mountains. Only the foundations and parts of the walls remain, but standing on the rock, with the wind in the grass, you get a sense of why it was chosen: it controls the pass between the Hațeg country to the north and the Jiu valley to the south.

That pass is the road you are on. The DN66 crosses from Petroșani over the Merișor pass to Hațeg and Simeria, climbing through forest with good, flowing curves and fine views. Traffic is usually moderate, though heavy trucks use the route, and the surface is generally decent. The Hațeg country to the north is a lovely landscape of villages, castles and churches; the Hațeg Geopark is known for the fossils of dwarf dinosaurs found there, and the ruined Roman city of Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, the capital of Roman Dacia, lies nearby.

The area is also the gateway to some of Romania's best riding. South of Petroșani, the road through the Jiu Gorge winds through a narrow canyon toward Târgu Jiu, and to the east, the Transalpina, one of the highest roads in the country, crosses the Parâng mountains. Both are wonderful and best in summer and early autumn; the Transalpina is closed in winter.

Petrila, around twelve kilometres away, and Petroșani have fuel, shops and restaurants; the village of Bănița itself is small. In the area, eat a bowl of ciorbă, the sour soup that comes in endless varieties, and polenta with cheese and sour cream, mămăligă cu brânză și smântână, the comfort food of the Romanian countryside.
t.petrosani dealul botanilor@45.5,23.4:
Petroșani is the capital of the Jiu valley, a long trench between the Retezat, Vâlcan, Parâng and Șureanu mountains in south-western Romania, and for most of the twentieth century it was the heart of the country's hard-coal industry. The hills around the town, including Dealul Botanilor, look down on a landscape of mining towns, pit heads and miners' housing, with the high mountains rising all around. The coordinates put the hill on the edge of the valley, above the towns of Petrila and Petroșani.

The miners of the Jiu valley loom large in Romanian history. In 1977, they went on strike against the Ceaușescu regime, one of the few open challenges to communist rule. In 1990 and the following years, after the revolution, miners were brought to Bucharest several times in the episodes known as the mineriads, violently suppressing protesters. Since then, most of the mines have closed, and the valley has struggled with unemployment and emigration. Petrila has turned some of its old mine buildings into a cultural site, and the local mining museum keeps the memories alive.

The mountains are the valley's future. The Parâng mountains, rising just south-east of Petroșani, have a ski resort reached by a chairlift and a road, and in summer the high ridges offer superb hiking with views over glacial lakes. The Retezat National Park, to the west, is one of the wildest mountain areas in Europe, with dozens of glacial lakes and a population of bears, wolves and chamois.

For riders, Petroșani is a crossroads of wonderful roads. The DN66 runs south through the Jiu Gorge, a narrow canyon carved by the river, with tight curves, tunnels and a railway alongside, to Târgu Jiu, home of the sculptures of Constantin Brâncuși. Head east and you can reach the Transalpina, the DN67C, which climbs to over two thousand metres over the Parâng mountains, with stunning views; it is open only in the summer months, usually from late June or July to October, depending on the snow. To the north, the road over the Merișor pass leads to Hațeg.

Petrila, about ten kilometres away, and Petroșani have fuel, shops, guesthouses and restaurants. Try papanași, fried doughnuts with sour cream and jam, for an indulgent dessert, and plan your crossing of the Transalpina for a clear morning, when the views are at their best.
t.capalna dealul hanului@47.3,23.7:
Somewhere above the Someș valley, on a hill the villagers call Dealul Hanului, the inn hill, the Romans kept watch over the northern edge of their province of Dacia. After Trajan's conquest in 106, the new province had to be defended on all sides, and its northern frontier, in what the Romans called Dacia Porolissensis, ran through these hills between the Meseș mountains and the upper Someș. Forts, watchtowers and earthworks controlled the valleys, and Căpâlna, near the village of Gâlgău, is one of the many small sites that formed that network, part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire in Dacia that Romania has put forward for UNESCO listing.

Do not expect stone walls and reconstructed towers. Most sites like this are low earthworks, scatters of stones and traces in the fields that archaeologists can read but most riders will need to imagine. What you get instead is the view the Roman soldiers had: the broad, slow river winding through the valley, villages strung along the road, wooded ridges stretching away to the north toward Maramureș. Not far away, near Dej, lie the remains of the larger Roman fort at Cășeiu, known in antiquity as Samum, which guarded the Someș crossing.

The Someș valley is a quiet, rural corridor between Dej and Jibou, a landscape of hay meadows, orchards, small fields and wooden gates carved with patterns, where horse carts are still a common sight. The road along the river is mostly flat and gently curving, with a decent surface but occasional potholes, and it is a pleasant, unhurried ride. The side roads that climb into the hills are narrower and rougher but give better views and lead to villages where little seems to have changed in decades.

Dej, sixteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel stations, shops and restaurants; it grew rich on salt, mined here since Roman times and probably before, and on the trade along the river. In Gâlgău and the neighbouring villages, you will find small shops and perhaps a bar, but little else.

The best time to ride here is late spring, when the meadows are full of flowers, or early autumn, when the haystacks stand in the fields and the orchards are heavy with plums, some of which will end up as țuică, the fierce plum brandy offered to guests in every village. Sip carefully, and only when the riding is done.
t.historic centre of sighisoara@46.2,24.8:
Sighișoara is a medieval citadel that people still live in, and that is what sets it apart. Founded by German settlers, the Transylvanian Saxons, who were invited by the Hungarian kings in the twelfth century to colonise and defend the region, it grew into a prosperous town of craftsmen's guilds, each of which built and defended its own tower in the walls. Nine towers survive out of the original fourteen, named after the tailors, shoemakers, tinsmiths, butchers, furriers and others, and the old town on its hill above the Târnava Mare river was listed by UNESCO in 1999.

The symbol of the town is the Clock Tower, which guards the main gate and holds a clock with carved figures that change with the days of the week. Climb it for the view over the steep, colourful roofs. A covered wooden staircase, the Scholars' Stairs, leads up from the main square to the Church on the Hill and the old Saxon cemetery, a peaceful place among the trees at the top of the town. Near the clock tower, a house is said to be the birthplace of Vlad III, the prince remembered as Vlad the Impaler and the inspiration for the name of Dracula; the town plays up the connection with enthusiasm.

The citadel's cobbled lanes are steep and narrow, and riding in is neither necessary nor pleasant. Park in the lower town and walk up. Arrive early in the morning or stay for the evening, when the day visitors have left and the streets are quiet. In summer, the town hosts a medieval festival that fills the streets with costumes, music and crowds.

The surrounding countryside is the land of the Saxon fortified churches, villages where the church was enclosed in strong walls and towers to protect the community from raids. The DN13 runs south-east toward Brașov through rolling hills, and from it, side roads lead to Saschiz, with its fortified church and tower on the hill, and to Viscri, Biertan and other villages, several of them also UNESCO sites. The main road carries a lot of trucks; the side roads are quiet but sometimes rough.

Sighișoara, a town of over thirty thousand people, has fuel, shops and plenty of restaurants. Try a hearty Transylvanian meal of sarmale, cabbage rolls with polenta and sour cream, or a pork stew, and toast the day with a glass of wine from the Târnave vineyards, the white wine region that surrounds the town.
t.perisor varful colnicului@47.3,24.3:
The upper valley of the Zagra stream, in the hills of Bistrița-Năsăud county in northern Transylvania, is the sort of place that has produced poets. The village of Hordou, now named Coșbuc, birthplace of the poet George Coșbuc, lies not far away, near Năsăud, and Liviu Rebreanu, one of Romania's great novelists, was born in Târlișua, a little to the west. The hills around Perișor and Zagra, with the summit called Vârful Colnicului, are a landscape of meadows, beech woods and scattered farms that seems to have stepped out of their books.

There is also older history here. The Romans held this northern edge of Dacia from the early second century until the late third, and their frontier through these hills was marked by forts, watchtowers and lookout posts on high points, of which the hilltops around Perișor were part. Little remains to see above ground, but the views explain the choice: from the higher slopes you look north toward the Țibleș and Rodna mountains and south across the valleys of the Someș Mare.

The people of this region, the old Năsăud border district, have a strong sense of identity. In the eighteenth century, the Habsburgs organised the area as a military frontier, with peasants serving as border guards in exchange for privileges, and the pride of that history is still felt. The local costume, with peacock feathers on men's hats, is one of the most distinctive in Romania.

Riding here means small roads. The route through the Zagra valley is narrow, winding and often bumpy, with horses and carts, livestock and the occasional tractor sharing the road. It is not fast riding, but it is beautiful, with wooden houses, carved gates and haystacks in the fields. To the east, the DN17D follows the Someș Mare up past Năsăud toward Rodna and over the Șetref pass into Maramureș, a wonderful road through the mountains, best in summer and early autumn.

Nimigea de Sus, about six kilometres away, and Năsăud have fuel and basic services; Bistrița, the county capital, has everything. In the villages, look for local cheeses and honey sold from farm gates, and if you are offered pălincă, the strong fruit brandy of the north, take a small glass and save the rest for the evening, when the bike is parked and the light is golden over the hills.
t.poieni rambusoi@46.9,22.9:
West of Cluj, the valley of the Crișul Repede cuts through the hills toward the Hungarian plain, and the main road between Transylvania and the west follows it. The village of Poieni and the hill of Râmbușoi lie in this valley, between Huedin and Ciucea, with the forested slopes of the Vlădeasa massif, part of the Apuseni mountains, rising to the south. In Roman times, the frontier of Dacia ran through the hills to the north, along the Meseș mountains, and this corridor was a natural route to watch; hilltop positions in the area formed part of the defensive network, and the larger fort at Bologa guarded the valley nearby.

Ciucea, six kilometres away, is worth a stop. The poet and politician Octavian Goga bought a mansion here in the early twentieth century, which had previously belonged to the Hungarian poet Endre Ady, and it is now a memorial museum with gardens and a mausoleum. Goga was one of the leading voices for the union of Transylvania with Romania in 1918, and his house is a quiet place to learn a little about the region's complicated past.

The main road, the DN1 and E60, is one of the busiest in Romania, carrying heavy truck traffic between Oradea and Cluj, and it is not a pleasant ride. Overtaking is frequent and sometimes reckless, and the surface can be worn. The joy lies in the side roads: south from Huedin, the road climbs into the Apuseni through the Drăgan valley and toward the Vlădeasa, with tight curves, forests and a reservoir, and beyond lie the karst plateaus, caves and gorges of the Apuseni Natural Park, some of the best riding in Romania. North from the valley, smaller roads wind through the hills of Sălaj toward the Meseș.

Huedin, around fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a good range of fuel stations, shops and restaurants, and the region is known for its pottery, especially in the village of Izvoru Crișului, along the main road east toward Cluj. Many villages here have a mixed Romanian and Hungarian population, and you will hear both languages.

Spring and autumn are the best times to ride. In the Apuseni, try a bowl of balmoș, polenta cooked with cheese and butter, or a plate of grilled trout, and look out for the wooden churches that dot the hills.
t.church of the holy archangels@47.6,23.6:
Just outside Baia Mare, where the city gives way to the hills, the countryside of northern Romania begins to show the tradition that made this region famous: churches built entirely of wood, with steep shingled roofs and tall, needle-like spires. Many of them are dedicated to the Holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel, and this dedication is common across the region, from small village churches to some of the eight Wooden Churches of Maramureș listed by UNESCO in 1999. Surdești and Plopiș, both within a short ride of Baia Mare, are among the finest of those, with spires that seem far too tall for the buildings beneath them.

These churches were built by Orthodox and later Greek Catholic communities from the seventeenth to the nineteenth centuries, partly because stone churches were long restricted for Romanians in Habsburg and Hungarian Transylvania, and partly because the forests offered abundant oak and fir. The craftsmen built without nails, using wooden joints, and decorated the interiors with paintings of saints, biblical scenes and the Last Judgement, often in a vivid, naïve style. Many are still in use, and visiting usually means finding the person with the key in the village.

Baia Mare, a city of over a hundred thousand people eight kilometres away, has its own story. Its name means big mine, and gold, silver and other metals were mined here for centuries; the old town centre, with Stephen's Tower and the square, has been restored. The mining legacy also includes serious pollution, notably a cyanide spill in 2000 that contaminated rivers far downstream.

For riders, Baia Mare is a gateway to Maramureș. The DN18 climbs north over the Gutâi pass, with a series of tight hairpins through forest, to the Mara valley and Sighetu Marmației, and the roads beyond lead to the villages of the Iza and Mara valleys, with their carved wooden gates, and to Săpânța, famous for its Merry Cemetery, where the crosses are painted with humorous scenes and verses about the deceased. Road surfaces are mixed, and farm traffic is common, so ride with care.

Fuel and services are easy in Baia Mare. In the villages, look for local specialties like plum brandy, called horincă in Maramureș, homemade cheeses and honey. Sunday morning, when the villagers attend church in their traditional dress, is a special time to visit.
t.calugareni cetate@46.6,24.9:
Călugăreni lies in the Niraj valley in Mureș county, in the heart of the region known as Székely Land, and here the signs, the conversation and the church spires announce that you are in a Hungarian-speaking part of Romania. The Székelys are a Hungarian community who, for centuries, guarded the eastern borders of the kingdom, and their villages, with carved wooden gates and whitewashed churches, are among the most distinctive in Transylvania. In Hungarian, the village is called Mikháza.

Long before the Székelys, the Romans were here. Călugăreni is the site of an auxiliary fort on the eastern frontier of Roman Dacia, which ran along the foothills of the Carpathians in the second and third centuries. Archaeologists have excavated parts of the fort and the civil settlement that grew up around it, and an open-air display with information panels helps visitors understand what is otherwise a grassy field with low banks. It is part of the chain of Roman frontier sites that Romania has nominated for UNESCO listing.

The landscape here is gently hilly, with orchards, hay meadows and forests, and the Gurghiu mountains rising to the east. The area is rich in salt: at nearby Sărățeni, salt springs and salt lakes have been used since ancient times, and further east, Praid has a vast salt mine open to visitors, while Sovata has Lake Ursu, a salt lake where the water layers trap heat and create unusual warm temperatures near the surface. Bathing in these salty waters is a popular local pastime in summer.

The riding is relaxed and pleasant. The roads through the Niraj valley and into the hills are mostly good, with gentle curves and light traffic, and the road east to Sovata and Praid climbs into more forested country. From there, you can head into the Harghita mountains or north toward the volcanic Călimani. Watch out for horse carts and cows on the road, especially in the evenings when herds come home.

Miercurea Nirajului, about eleven kilometres away, has fuel and basic shops; Târgu Mureș, the county capital, has everything. The local cuisine is Hungarian in flavour: try a bowl of goulash soup, or kürtőskalács, a sweet chimney cake roasted over coals and rolled in sugar and cinnamon, best eaten warm from a roadside stall. Autumn, when the orchards are heavy with apples and the forests turn golden, is a lovely time to ride.
t.dumbraveni magura@47.3,23.9:
In the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, a fortress on a hill above the Someș valley near Ciceu belonged not to the rulers of Transylvania but to the princes of Moldavia, on the far side of the Carpathians. Stephen the Great received the castle of Ciceu and its estates as compensation from the Hungarian king, and the Moldavian princes held it for decades, a curious enclave in the middle of Transylvania. The castle was later destroyed, and only ruins remain on the hill above Ciceu-Corabia, but the story gives a sense of how fluid borders and loyalties were in this part of Europe.

The hill of Măgura, near Dumbrăveni, lies in the same part of the Someș valley, between Dej and Beclean, and the Romans had their own reasons for watching it. The northern frontier of their province of Dacia ran through these hills in the second and third centuries, and high points like this were used for lookouts and signal stations. Today, the hilltop is grazing land and woods, and its main attraction is the view: the broad valley of the Someș below, villages scattered along the road, and the hills of northern Transylvania rolling away on every side.

This is deep countryside, and the riding is a slow pleasure. The road along the Someș between Dej and Beclean is generally in decent condition, with gentle curves and a mix of farm and local traffic, and the side roads into the hills are narrower, steeper and more rural, with gravel and potholes in places. Horse carts, flocks of sheep and dogs guarding them are part of the scenery. Spring brings fresh green and flowers, and late summer brings haymaking and fruit.

Dej, about fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a full range of services, including fuel, shops and restaurants. The town is an old salt town with a Gothic Reformed church in its centre and a long history as a market for the surrounding villages. In the villages, small shops can provide basic supplies, and some farms sell honey, cheese and fruit.

At the end of the day, find a guesthouse in the area and ask for a meal of local dishes: ciorbă de perișoare, sour soup with meatballs, or tochitură, a pork stew served with polenta, a fried egg and cheese. And raise a glass to the strange history of a valley where Moldavian princes once held a castle far from home.
t.ilisua tibles@47.2,24.1:
Ilișua is a small village near Uriu in the valley of the Someș Mare, and in Roman times it was the site of a fort guarding the northern frontier of Dacia. The fort, known in antiquity as Arcobara, housed a cavalry unit, and archaeologists have uncovered its walls, gates and buildings, along with inscriptions and finds now displayed in museums in the region. Like the other sites of the Roman frontier in Romania, it is part of a nomination for UNESCO world heritage, and like most of them, it is now largely fields and grassy banks, with little to see above ground but a great deal of history beneath.

From the fort, the frontier line ran north into the hills toward the Țibleș mountains, a volcanic range rising to over eighteen hundred metres on the border between Bistrița-Năsăud and Maramureș. Watchtowers on the heights allowed the garrison to monitor the approaches, and the view from the higher ground shows why: on a clear day you can see far across the hills toward the mountains of the north. The Țibleș are wild and forested, with beech and spruce woods, meadows and rocky summits, and are home to bears, wolves and deer.

The valley of the Someș Mare is a broad, fertile corridor between Beclean and Năsăud, with villages, orchards and fields along the river, and the main road through it is generally in good condition, with gentle curves and moderate traffic. The roads that lead north into the hills, toward the Țibleș, are narrower and more winding, with steep climbs and some poor surfaces, but they are wonderfully quiet and scenic. The village of Reteag, a few kilometres away, has a manor house and an old church, and the area is dotted with traditional wooden houses and gates.

Căianu Mic, around seven kilometres away, and Beclean have fuel and basic services; Bistrița, the county capital, and Dej have everything a rider might need. In the villages, small shops sell basic supplies, and you may find farm produce for sale by the roadside.

The best time to ride here is from late spring to early autumn, when the roads are clear and the hills are green. In winter, the Țibleș are snowy and cold, and the side roads can be impassable. In the evening, find a guesthouse in one of the villages and enjoy a meal of homemade food, often grown or raised by the hosts themselves.
t.orheiu bistritei vatra satului@47.1,24.6:
Bistrița is the town where Jonathan Harker spends his last comfortable night before heading into the mountains in Bram Stoker's Dracula, and the village of Orheiu Bistriței lies just eight kilometres to the south-east, in the hills above the valley of the Bistrița river. In Roman times, this was the site of an auxiliary fort on the north-eastern frontier of Dacia, and the remains lie beneath the village itself, which the locals know as the vatra satului, the village hearth. Excavations have revealed the outline of the fort, and finds are displayed in the county museum in Bistrița.

Bistrița was founded by Saxon settlers in the Middle Ages and became a prosperous trading town, known in German as Bistritz or Nösen. Its tall Evangelical church dominates the central square, and the arcaded merchants' houses of the Sugălete add to the old-town atmosphere. The town has made the most of its literary fame: there is a hotel named after the Golden Krone, where Harker stayed in the novel, though it is a modern building.

From Bistrița, the DN17 heads east toward the Tihuța pass, the Borgo pass of Stoker's novel, and over the mountains to Vatra Dornei in Bukovina. It is a wonderful road, climbing through forests and meadows with long curves and good views, and in summer it is a popular route for riders heading to the painted monasteries of Bukovina. The surface is generally good, but trucks are frequent, and the weather on the pass can change quickly, with fog and rain common even in summer.

The hills around Orheiu Bistriței are gentle and rural, with orchards, meadows and woods, and the smaller roads through the villages are narrow and quiet, perfect for a slower ride. To the south, the road toward Reghin passes through the valley of the Șieu, with more Saxon villages and fortified churches along the way.

Bistrița, a city of over eighty thousand, has fuel, shops, restaurants and accommodation of every kind. In town, try a plate of local sausages or a bowl of ciorbă, and in autumn look out for apples and plums sold at the roadside. And if you head over the pass at dusk, with the mist rising from the forests and the last light fading behind you, you might understand why Stoker chose this landscape for his tale.
t.perra vaara peravaara@66.0,23.9:
Perävaara is a modest hill in the Swedish Tornedalen, a little north of Haparanda, and it is one of the points of the Struve Geodetic Arc. Between 1816 and 1855, the astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve and his teams measured a chain of triangles stretching from Hammerfest on the Arctic Ocean to the Black Sea, over two and a half thousand kilometres, to determine the exact size and shape of the Earth. The survey points were marked on hilltops, church towers and rocks, and the surviving ones in ten countries were listed by UNESCO in 2005. At Perävaara, the station is a small marker on the summit, with a sign explaining its place in the chain. Struve's neighbours on the arc nearby include Jupukka and Pullinki, both a short ride away.

The Tornedalen is a borderland with a character of its own. The Torne river forms the frontier between Sweden and Finland, and the people on both sides speak Meänkieli, a Finnic language recognised as a minority language in Sweden. Haparanda and Tornio, its Finnish twin, are practically one town split by the border, and you can cross back and forth without noticing, except that your watch jumps an hour.

The riding is long, straight and calm, through forests of pine and birch, across bogs and past farms along the river. The road north up the Torne valley towards Övertorneå and Pajala follows the river with long, flowing bends, and the scenery is serene rather than dramatic. Watch for reindeer on the road: they belong to the Sámi herding communities and they stand their ground. Moose are also common.

The Arctic Circle is just to the north, and in June the sun barely sets. The light at midnight is strange and beautiful, soft gold over the river. The mosquitoes, unfortunately, also appreciate the season, so bring repellent and a net if you plan to stop in the forest. Autumn, with the birch woods turning yellow and the first northern lights, is short but spectacular; winter is for snowmobiles, not bikes.

For fuel and food, head to Haparanda or Tornio, which have everything you need, including big supermarkets; Haparanda even has a large IKEA, a slightly surreal sight at the top of the Baltic. Further north, stations are sparse, so fill up before you go.
t.oremus cellars@48.3,21.5:
Tolcsva is a quiet village in the Tokaj wine region of northeastern Hungary, on the slopes of the Zemplén hills above the Bodrog river. The Oremus cellars here are among the most famous in the region: a network of tunnels cut into the volcanic rock over centuries, their walls black with the noble mould that thrives in the damp, steady cold. The estate has been owned since the 1990s by the family behind Vega Sicilia, one of Spain's most celebrated wineries, and it has become a showcase for the revival of Tokaji after the communist decades.

The wine that made Tokaj famous is aszú, a sweet wine made from grapes shrivelled by botrytis, the noble rot, which develops in the autumn mists rising from the Bodrog and the Tisza. The grapes are picked one by one, and the resulting wine is intense, golden and capable of ageing for decades. Louis XIV is said to have called Tokaji the wine of kings and the king of wines. The region has a long history of classifying its vineyards, among the earliest in the world, and in 2002 UNESCO listed it as a cultural landscape. Today Tokaj also produces excellent dry whites from the Furmint and Hárslevelű grapes.

The Zemplén hills are volcanic, with rounded summits covered in oak and beech forests and vineyards on the lower slopes. The roads between Tolcsva, Olaszliszka, Erdőbénye and Sárospatak wind through the hills and along the river, with gentle curves, little traffic and views over the vineyards. The surface varies, and potholes are common on the minor roads, so stay alert.

Sárospatak, eleven kilometres away, has a Renaissance castle associated with the Rákóczi family, leaders of the Hungarian struggle against the Habsburgs, and a famous Reformed college, founded in the sixteenth century, with a historic library. The town has fuel, restaurants and hotels. Tokaj town, at the confluence of the Bodrog and the Tisza, is another good base.

Hungary has a zero-tolerance policy on alcohol for drivers and riders. If you want to taste, plan to stay the night; many wineries offer rooms, and a slow evening in a cellar, with candles and a glass of aszú, is one of the great pleasures of the region. Ride the hills in the morning instead, when the mist lies in the valleys.
t.polonina wetlinska and smerek@49.2,22.5:
In the far southeastern corner of Poland, where the country meets Slovakia and Ukraine, the Bieszczady mountains rise in long, rounded ridges covered with beech forest. Above the tree line, the summits are open meadows called połoniny, and Połonina Wetlińska is one of the most beautiful, a long grassy ridge with views over endless forested hills. Smerek, a peak at its western end, rises to over twelve hundred metres. On the ridge, the Chatka Puchatka, Winnie the Pooh's hut, a small mountain refuge, has been a beloved stop for hikers for decades. The walk up from Wetlina or the Przełęcz Wyżna pass takes a couple of hours, and the view from the top, especially at sunset, is unforgettable.

The Bieszczady were once densely populated by the Boykos and Lemkos, Ukrainian-speaking highlanders with their own wooden churches and traditions. After the Second World War, in 1947, the communist authorities forcibly resettled the remaining population in the operation known as Vistula, and many villages disappeared entirely, leaving only orchards, cemeteries and the foundations of churches in the forest. The landscape you see today, wild and empty, is partly the result of that tragedy. The surviving wooden churches, such as Smolnik, are listed by UNESCO among the wooden tserkvas of the Carpathian region.

The forests are now among the wildest in Poland, home to wolves, lynx, brown bears and European bison, reintroduced after their extinction in the wild. You are unlikely to see them from the road, but signs warn of bears, and locals take them seriously.

The riding is excellent. The Great Bieszczady Loop, the Duża Obwodnica Bieszczadzka, links Lesko, Ustrzyki Dolne, Ustrzyki Górne, Wetlina and Cisna, winding through the valleys and over passes with tight bends, good surfaces and views over the forested ridges. The road between Wetlina and Ustrzyki Górne, passing below the połoniny, is particularly beautiful. Traffic is light outside the summer holidays, but watch for logging trucks, wildlife and tourists stopping suddenly.

Fuel is limited in the mountains; Cisna and Ustrzyki Górne have small stations, but fill up in Ustrzyki Dolne or Lesko to be safe. Try the local pierogi, and a bowl of soup in a mountain inn after the ride.
t.church of the assumption of the blessed:
Haczów, a village in the foothills of the Carpathians in southeastern Poland, has a church that is considered the largest Gothic wooden church in Europe, and one of the oldest. Built in the fifteenth century, probably on the site of an earlier church, the Church of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St Michael the Archangel is a massive structure of larch logs, with a steep shingled roof and a bell tower, standing among old trees. Inside, the walls are covered with polychrome paintings, the oldest from the late fifteenth century, showing saints, biblical scenes and decorative patterns, and the atmosphere is dim, warm and fragrant with old wood. In 2003 the church was listed by UNESCO among the Wooden Churches of Southern Małopolska, along with five others in the region. It is still used for worship, so check visiting times and dress respectfully.

The village lies in the valley of the Wisłok river, between Brzozów and Krosno, in a landscape of rolling hills, fields, orchards and woods. It is a quiet, rural area, with wooden houses, roadside shrines and churches in every village.

Krosno, about fifteen kilometres away, was a prosperous trading town in the Renaissance, with a market square surrounded by arcaded houses, and it is famous for glassmaking, with a glass heritage centre. It is also associated with Ignacy Łukasiewicz, the pharmacist who invented the kerosene lamp in the 1850s and helped found the world's oil industry. At Bóbrka, near Krosno, the oil mine he established in 1854, considered the oldest in the world, is now an open-air museum, with wooden derricks and old equipment among the trees. It is a strange and fascinating place.

The riding is pleasant. The roads between Haczów, Brzozów, Krosno and the villages of the Wisłok valley wind through the hills with gentle curves and views over the countryside. Further south, the Low Beskids rise towards the Slovak border, with forests, wooden churches and quieter roads, and beyond them the Bieszczady. The surface is generally good, but watch for farm vehicles and village speed limits, which are enforced.

Brzozów and Krosno have fuel, shops and restaurants; Korczyna is closer. Try żurek, a sour rye soup with sausage and egg, a Polish classic, in a village inn.
t.synevyr vilshany@48.4,23.7:
Lake Synevyr is the largest mountain lake in the Ukrainian Carpathians, a dark, deep pool surrounded by spruce forest at about a thousand metres, formed thousands of years ago when a landslide blocked a valley. It is called the sea eye, and on a calm day, it reflects the trees and the sky like a mirror. A sad legend tells of a count's daughter, Syn, who fell in love with a shepherd, Vyr; the count had the young man killed, and the girl wept so much that her tears formed the lake. The lake is the centrepiece of the Synevyr National Park, which protects a large area of old forests in Zakarpattia, and nearby there is a rehabilitation centre for brown bears rescued from captivity, where you can see them in large forest enclosures.

Vilshany is a village in the valley of the Tereblia river below the lake, and the area around it, with Kolochava and Synevyrska Polyana, is a world of wooden houses, haystacks, orchards and Orthodox and Greek Catholic churches. Kolochava has turned itself into a village of museums, with an open-air museum of traditional life, a museum of the Soviet era and others, a curious and charming place. The people of these mountains are Ukrainians and Rusyns, and they keep many traditions: woodworking, weaving, folk music and seasonal festivals.

The riding is rough and beautiful. The roads from Mizhhirya to Synevyr and Kolochava climb through narrow valleys along rivers, with forests on both sides, and the surface ranges from decent asphalt to broken, potholed tarmac and gravel. Expect livestock, horse-drawn carts, logging trucks and pedestrians on the road. The scenery is spectacular, with mountains, meadows and villages, and in autumn the colours are intense.

The weather in the Carpathians is changeable, with heavy rain possible at any time and snow in winter. Summer and early autumn are the best seasons.

Mizhhirya, about twenty kilometres away, has fuel, shops and simple restaurants; the villages have small shops. Try banosh, a rich cornmeal porridge cooked with sour cream and served with cheese and crackling. Ukraine is at war, and although Zakarpattia is far from the front lines, check the current official travel advice very carefully before considering any trip, and follow local instructions.
t.stana la oroiesi@47.2,23.1:
On the hills above Zalău, in the county of Sălaj in northwestern Romania, the Roman Empire reached its northern limit in Dacia. After Trajan conquered the Dacian kingdom in 106, the Romans built a frontier system along the edges of the new province, with forts, watchtowers, walls and ditches, and in 2024 UNESCO listed it as the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia. The site at Stâna, La Oroieși, is one of many small elements of that frontier: a watchtower or defensive line on a ridge, where soldiers watched over the approaches from the free Dacian lands beyond. There is little to see on the ground, but the location, with views over the hills, explains why it was chosen.

The greatest Roman site in the area is Porolissum, on the hills near Moigrad, about fifteen kilometres from Zalău. It was a large fortified town and military base, controlling one of the main passes through the Meseș mountains, and it grew into a busy trading centre, where Romans and free Dacians exchanged goods. The excavated ruins include a fort with a reconstructed gate, an amphitheatre, temples and a customs post, spread over a hilltop with wide views. It is one of the most impressive Roman sites in Romania, and it is rarely crowded.

Zalău, the county capital, is a modern town with a county museum displaying finds from Porolissum and other sites. The surrounding countryside is a landscape of rolling hills, orchards, vineyards and villages, with forests on the ridges of the Meseș mountains. The villages of Sălaj are known for their wooden churches, small and beautiful, often hidden among trees on hillsides.

The riding is good. The roads through the Meseș mountains climb over ridges with tight bends and views over the hills, and the minor roads between villages wind through farmland and forests. The surface varies, with good main roads and poorer minor ones, where potholes are common. Watch for horse-drawn carts, livestock and dogs, especially in villages.

Zalău, about seven kilometres away, has fuel, mechanics, shops and restaurants. Try ciorbă, the sour soups of Romania, and a plate of sarmale, stuffed cabbage rolls with polenta and sour cream. Romania requires a road vignette, the rovinieta, for cars, but motorcycles are exempt.
t.bologa gradiste@46.9,22.9:
