The village of Bologa lies in the valley of the Crișul Repede, on the main road between Cluj-Napoca and Oradea, where the river cuts through the hills between the Apuseni mountains and the Meseș. On a hill above the village, known locally as Grădiște, the Romans built the fort of Resculum, which guarded one of the main routes into the province of Dacia from the west. The fort was rebuilt several times, from earth and timber to stone, and archaeologists have uncovered its walls, gates and towers. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia. On another hill above the village stand the ruins of a medieval castle, which controlled the same valley in later centuries. Climbing to either site gives fine views over the valley and the surrounding hills.

A few kilometres west, in the village of Ciucea, the poet and politician Octavian Goga had his estate, and his mansion is now a memorial museum, with a garden and a wooden church brought from another village. Goga was one of the most popular Romanian poets of the early twentieth century, known for his poems about the Transylvanian peasantry.

The Apuseni mountains, rising to the south, are a wild, beautiful region of limestone plateaus, caves, gorges and forests, with scattered villages where traditional life continues. The Drăgan valley, south of Bologa, climbs into the mountains past a reservoir and through forests, a beautiful and quiet road. The Scărișoara ice cave, with an underground glacier thousands of years old, and the Bears' Cave, with fossils of cave bears, are among the highlights of the region.

The main road through the Crișul Repede valley is busy with trucks, as it is one of the main routes between Romania and Hungary, and it demands care. The side roads into the Apuseni are much more pleasant, with tight bends, steep climbs and beautiful scenery, though the surface can be poor and gravel sections are common. Watch for livestock, carts and dogs in the villages.

Huedin, about thirteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. The area is known for its traditional cooking: try balmoș, a rich polenta with sheep's cheese, and the local plum brandy, pălincă, best saved for the evening.
t.hurez sub cornet@47.1,23.0:
The hills of Sălaj between Buciumi, Stârciu and Cizer are a landscape of small villages, orchards, pastures and woods, and like much of this county, they were part of the northwestern frontier of Roman Dacia. Hurez, Sub Cornet, is one of the sites of that frontier listed by UNESCO in 2024, probably a watchtower or a stretch of defensive earthwork on a ridge, part of the chain of military posts that linked the forts. Little is visible on the ground today, and the site is better appreciated as part of a wider landscape of Roman frontier archaeology.

A few kilometres away, at Buciumi, the Romans built a fort to guard a pass through the Meseș mountains, and its excavated remains, with walls and gates, are among the best preserved on this stretch of frontier. The fort held an auxiliary unit, and the soldiers' settlement grew around it, with houses, workshops and a bath house. Walking around the site, among the meadows and orchards, it is easy to imagine the soldiers watching the forested hills to the north and west, where the free Dacians lived.

The villages of Sălaj have another treasure: dozens of wooden churches, built mostly in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, many with tall, slender towers and painted interiors. They are among the finest examples of folk architecture in Romania, though fewer visitors come here than to the more famous churches of Maramureș. Look for them on hillsides above the villages, often surrounded by graves and old trees. Many are locked, but someone in the village usually has the key.

The riding is quiet and rural. The roads between villages wind through the hills with gentle bends and short climbs, and traffic is light. The surface varies from good to poor, with potholes and patched sections, and some minor roads are unpaved. Horse-drawn carts, sheep, cows and dogs are common, and village children wave at passing riders. The Meseș mountains offer a few more challenging roads, with tight bends through forests.

Crasna and Zalău have fuel, shops and restaurants; the villages have small shops where you can buy bread, cheese and cold drinks. Spring, when the orchards are in blossom, and early autumn, when the plums and apples are ripe, are lovely. In late summer, families make pălincă, the strong local fruit brandy.
t.varadia chilii@45.1,21.5:
Vărădia is a village in the Banat, in southwestern Romania, close to the Serbian border, where the hills of the Banat mountains descend towards the Pannonian plain. In Roman times, it was the site of Arcidava, a fort on the road that Trajan's legions built to advance from the Danube into Dacia during the wars of 101 to 106, and later a garrison on the frontier. The site at Chilii, near the village, is part of the UNESCO listing of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia. The fort's earthworks can be traced on a hill above the Caraș river, and the location, controlling the valley, explains why it was chosen.

Oravița, about fourteen kilometres away, is a small town with a remarkable history. In the eighteenth century, under Habsburg rule, it was a mining centre, and in 1817 the townspeople built a small theatre modelled on the Burgtheater in Vienna, the oldest theatre building in Romania, still in use and open for visits. Oravița was also the starting point of the first mountain railway in what is now Romania, opened in 1863 to Anina, a coal mining town in the mountains. The line climbs through tunnels and over viaducts in a dramatic landscape, and it is sometimes called the Semmering of the Banat. Trains still run on it, slowly, and the ride is a delight.

The Banat has a multicultural heritage, with Romanians, Serbs, Germans, Hungarians, Czechs and Croats living side by side for centuries, and the villages reflect this diversity, with Orthodox and Catholic churches and German-style houses.

The riding is excellent. The roads from Oravița into the Banat mountains climb through beech forests with tight bends and steep gradients, and the road to Anina is particularly beautiful. Further south, the Danube gorge, the Iron Gates, is one of the great rides of Europe, where the river squeezes between cliffs on the border with Serbia, and the road follows it for many kilometres, with views of the river and the carved face of the Dacian king Decebalus on a cliff. The surface is generally good on the main roads.

Oravița has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try the Banat cooking, with its Austro-Hungarian influences: goulash, schnitzel and pastries. The region is also known for its wines, especially from Recaș, near Timișoara.
t.galgau casa popii@47.3,23.7:
The Someș river winds through northern Transylvania in a broad valley between rolling hills, and near Gâlgău and Poiana Blenchii, it forms a natural corridor between the Transylvanian plateau and the northwest. In Roman times, this valley marked the northern edge of the province of Dacia, and the frontier ran along the hills above it, with watchtowers and small forts. Casa Popii, the priest's house, near Gâlgău, is one of the sites of that frontier listed by UNESCO in 2024: probably a watchtower position on a ridge overlooking the valley. As with many of these sites, there is little to see above ground, but the views over the valley and the hills explain its purpose.

The valley has a quiet, rural character, with villages of wooden and brick houses, orchards, fields and the river meandering through meadows. Storks nest on electricity poles in the villages, and in summer the hills are covered with hay meadows full of wild flowers.

Dej, about eighteen kilometres away, is an old town at the confluence of the Someș Mare and the Someș Mic, and for centuries it was an important centre of salt mining. Transylvania sits on huge salt deposits, and salt was one of the main sources of wealth for the region, carried down the Someș on rafts. The salt mine at Dej is no longer open to tourists, but the larger salt mine at Turda, south of Cluj-Napoca, has been turned into an extraordinary underground park, with a Ferris wheel, a boating lake and a sports ground in vast caverns hundreds of metres below the surface. The town also has a fine Gothic Reformed church.

The riding is pleasant. The main road along the Someș valley is busy with trucks between Dej and the northwest, but the minor roads through the hills, towards the Lăpuș country and Maramureș, are quieter and more scenic, with bends, climbs and views over the valleys. North of the valley, the Țibleș mountains rise with forests and wild scenery. The surface varies, and potholes are common on minor roads. Watch for carts, livestock and dogs.

Dej has fuel, mechanics, shops and restaurants. Try the local smoked sausages and cheeses, and plăcintă, a pie filled with cheese, cabbage or apples, sold at roadside stalls.
t.negrilesti negru voda@47.3,24.1:
Negrilești is a small village in Bistrița-Năsăud county, in the hills of northern Transylvania, near the valley of the Someș Mare. The name of the site, Negru Vodă, recalls the legendary founder of Wallachia, a figure from the Romanian chronicles who is said to have crossed the Carpathians in the thirteenth century to found the principality; whether he existed at all is still debated, and many places in Romania bear his name. The site itself is part of the UNESCO listing of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia, probably a watchtower or a small fortification on a hill, part of the northern frontier of the province. Little is visible, but the hills offer good views over the surrounding countryside.

The area lies between the Transylvanian plateau and the mountains of the north, and it has a quiet, rural character, with villages, orchards and pastures. Beclean, a small town on the Someș, has fuel and shops. Bistrița, the county capital, about forty kilometres east, is an old Saxon town, founded by German settlers in the Middle Ages, with a Gothic Evangelical church whose tower is one of the tallest in Romania, and a lovely old centre with arcaded houses.

Bistrița has a literary fame that has little to do with its real history. In Bram Stoker's novel Dracula, Jonathan Harker stays in Bistritz before travelling over the Borgo Pass to the count's castle. The pass is real, the Tihuța pass in the mountains east of Bistrița, and a hotel built in the shape of a castle stands near the top, cashing in on the legend. The road over the pass, towards Vatra Dornei and Bucovina, is a beautiful ride, climbing through forests with long bends and views over the mountains.

The riding around Negrilești is quiet. The roads through the hills are narrow and winding, with variable surfaces, potholes and gravel in places, and very little traffic. The main road along the Someș valley is busier. Watch for horse-drawn carts, livestock and dogs, which are common in villages and sometimes chase motorcycles.

Beclean and Căianu Mic have small services; Bistrița has everything. Try the local cheeses, smoked meats and pălincă, and look for the Saxon churches in the villages around Bistrița, some fortified, a legacy of the German communities.
t.church of the holy parasceve@47.7,24.1:
Maramureș is one of the few corners of Europe where wood is still the language of the sacred, and the church of Saint Parascheva at Poienile Izei is a good place to learn it. It stands on a small rise above the Izei valley, a dark timber church with a steep, double-tiered shingled roof and a slender spire, built in the early seventeenth century and moved to its present spot later. Inside, the walls and ceiling carry painted scenes from the eighteenth century, and the one that always gets quoted is a vivid Last Judgment in which sinners get remarkably specific punishments.

The village is tiny, hardly two hundred metres from the church by the map, and the road through it is a lesson in how people here live. The houses have carved gateways, the hayfields are cut by hand in July and stacked in neat cones, and in the evenings you may see women in headscarves walking back from the hills with rakes. UNESCO lists a group of the wooden churches of Maramureș together, and this one belongs among them, which means you may share the yard with a few other visitors but rarely with a crowd. Ask in the village if the church is closed, because someone usually has a key.

The riding is the pleasure of slow, undulating valley roads rather than anything dramatic. From the Iza valley you follow a ribbon of asphalt through Botiza and on toward Rozavlea, passing carved crosses, small shrines and the odd horse-drawn wagon. The surface is mixed, with good stretches and ones that frost has chewed up, and you should expect to slow for sheep, geese, and unlit corners where hay carts have left straw on the tarmac. It is worth riding it on a clear morning when the mist lifts off the Rodna and Gutâi ranges, and summer evenings bring a smell of cut hay and woodsmoke that I still associate with the north of Romania.

For fuel, the realistic choice is Rozavlea, about nine kilometres away, or a larger town on the main valley road; the hamlets between do not have pumps. You will find food at family guesthouses, where plum brandy, smoked meat, and a pot of sour cabbage rolls arrive without much ceremony. A short stop is enough to see the church, but give the valley the afternoon.
t.ciglean varful cigleanului 1@47.2,23.2:
Vârful Cigleanului is a hilltop above the Someș valley in Sălaj, in that mild, folded part of northwestern Romania where the land rises in wooded ridges toward the Meseș mountains. The name simply means the peak of the Ciglean, and like many hill labels in Transylvania it points to an old vantage point more than a famous summit. The ground is orchard and pasture on the lower slopes, oak and beech on the higher, and on a clear day the view runs along the river toward Jibou.

Jibou, about six kilometres away, is the anchor of the district and well worth a stop. It has a baroque-era castle that belonged to the Wesselényi family, and beside it a botanical garden that has grown on the park since the twentieth century, with greenhouses and shaded avenues, the kind of place a rider can wander for an hour in boots without feeling out of place. The Someș river runs through the town, and the old road along its banks was an important route for salt and grain between Transylvania and the north.

The riding is gently engaging. The road out of town climbs through small villages such as Creaca and Mirșid, with curves that are open enough to enjoy without constant braking, and gradients that rarely bite. The surface is a mix of good and tired asphalt, and after rain mud can come off the fields at field gates. Traffic is light apart from the odd timber truck and slow farm vehicles, and you may meet a horse and cart on a corner now and then. Spring brings blossom on the orchards and a green that feels almost aggressively fresh; October is warm gold, and the air smells of apples and woodsmoke.

The local tradition here is plum brandy, called țuică, and small family makers will press a glass on you if you stop long enough; politely decline if you are riding. For fuel and food go to Jibou, which is large enough for pumps, shops, cafés and a couple of places that serve grilled meat and hearty soup. There is no obvious facility at the summit itself, so take what you need before you climb. The place is a quiet reward for the extra ten minutes on a side road.
t.comarnicel ii@45.6,23.4:
The pin sits in the folded country between the Hațeg basin and the coal towns of the Jiu valley, and the closest honest description is high Carpathian hill country: steep, forested, and quieter than the maps suggest. The Retezat range rises to the south, its granite peaks carrying snow into early summer, and the whole area belongs to Hunedoara county, a land of old mining, Dacian history and shepherds who still move flocks through the hills.

Comărnicel is a name that appears on hills and meadows throughout this region, and I cannot pin down exactly what feature this one marks, so I will talk about what surrounds it. The nearest real towns are Petrila and Petroșani, both mining towns of the Jiu valley, where black-coal workings shaped the streets, the apartment blocks and the identity of the people. Petroșani is large enough for everything a rider needs: fuel, food, a pharmacy, and a roof for the night, and Petrila has its own services too. The Jiu valley was a hard place to work and a hard place to close, and you will still see old pit-heads and workers' housing from the communist era.

For riding, this is a rewarding area. The road that links the Jiu valley with the Hațeg country passes through the Băniţa defile, a narrow gorge where the asphalt twists beside a stream and the walls close in with limestone and beech. Corners are tighter than on the plain, the surface is generally good on the main road and uneven on the side roads, and you should expect lorries labouring up the gradients. The weather changes quickly; a bright morning can become fog and rain by afternoon, and the temperature drops noticeably as you climb. Late spring, when the meadows are thick with flowers, and early autumn are the best seasons.

Nature is the real attraction. Chamois, brown bear and lynx live in the Retezat, the national park to the south, and roe deer cross the road at dawn and dusk, so stay alert in the forest sections. Streams run cold and clear, and the air smells of resin and wet stone. The villages in the hills are small, with limited shops and no reliable fuel, so fill the tank in Petroșani or Petrila before you head up, and carry a snack for the long stretches in between.
t.capalna hotroapa@47.3,23.8:
Căpâlna sits in the Someș country northwest of Dej, in a landscape of long, rounded hills that the Transylvanian plateau does so well. Orchards, hayfields and small woods climb the slopes, villages sit where streams meet, and the horizon always seems to hold another soft ridge. "Hotroapă" is a local word that refers to a hole or hollow in the ground, and I cannot say for sure which feature gave this spot its name, so I will leave the mystery as it is and tell you what you can count on.

What you can count on is the sense of rural Transylvania at ordinary speed. The nearest villages, Poiana Blenchii, Gâlgău and Vad, are small, quiet places where life is built around farms, a church and a shop, and you may see a man mowing a steep bank with a scythe even today. The Someș river drains the area and has carried salt, timber and grain for centuries, and nearby Dej, about sixteen kilometres away, grew up as a salt-trading town where the Someșul Mare and Someșul Mic rivers meet. Salt was the region's old wealth, and the whole district carries traces of its mining and carting.

On the bike, the roads here are the enjoyable kind that do not demand attention. They wind through the hills with a succession of gentle bends, short climbs and easy descents, and surfaces vary from smooth to patched. Gravel from field tracks and mud near gates can turn a quiet corner treacherous, so keep a little margin. Traffic is light and mostly local, and dogs and geese can appear from nowhere. The best season is May to June, when the grass is high and the air smells of elderflower, or September, when the light is long and warm and the plum harvest is on.

Fuel and a meal are in Dej, a town of about thirty-eight thousand with several stations, supermarkets and restaurants serving grilled meat, soup and local pastries. The villages have little beyond a shop and perhaps a bar, so do not count on fuel at Căpâlna itself. Take a few minutes to enjoy the hush, because a place like this is gone as soon as you start the engine.
t.hurez la frasin 1@47.0,23.0:
This corner of Sălaj sits along the Roman frontier of Dacia, which makes it a more serious place than its gentle hills suggest. West of Zalău the Meseș mountains rise in a long wooded ridge, and through them runs a natural gate, the Meseș Pass, which the Romans fortified as part of their northern defences. The great site of Porolissum, with its fort, civil settlement and amphitheatre, stands on a ridge nearby, and the watchtowers and small works scattered across the hills belong to the same system.

"La Frasin" means by the ash tree, a perfectly ordinary Romanian farm label, and I would not claim to know what lies at the exact pin; what I can say is that the surrounding hills were watched by Roman patrols for about a century and a half, and that traces of towers, camps and earthworks still appear in forest clearings if you know where to look. The Roman frontier here was not a wall but a chain of lookouts and forts on high ground, linked by tracks, so the best way to read it is to climb a hill and notice how far you can see.

For riding, the roads in the area are a pleasure. They climb in long, open bends through beech and oak woods, drop into small valleys with farms and orchards, and give the occasional view across to the Meseș ridge. The surface changes between good, rough and patched, and gravel collects on corners after rain, so be careful on descents. Traffic is thin on the side roads, though the main route through the pass carries lorries and a steady flow of cars. Spring and autumn are lovely, with blossom or colour, and summer mornings are cool under the trees; winter can bring ice to the shaded corners, so be wary from November.

The nearest towns are small, with Cizer, Stârciu and Buciumi offering little beyond a shop and a bar, and Crasna the biggest at about fifteen kilometres. For reliable fuel, a meal and a bed, Zalău is the answer, a county seat with several stations and restaurants. Fill up there before heading into the hills, bring water, and give yourself time to stop on a ridge and look west toward the line that Rome once drew across these woods.
t.salva modrut@47.3,24.3:
Salva lies where the Someșul Mare valley opens into a broad bowl in Bistrița-Năsăud county, with the Rodna mountains standing to the northeast and a ring of low wooded hills closer in. The town is a railway junction, a lorry stop on the road through the valley, and the kind of place that looks ordinary until you ask about its past. Modruț is a hill name on the edge of the settlement, and I would be inventing if I told you what stands on it, so I will describe the ground instead: pasture, scrub, a few oaks, and a view down onto roofs and the river.

The Năsăud district around here has an unusual history. In the eighteenth century the Habsburg crown raised a border-guard regiment among the local Romanian peasants, who received land and some privileges in return for military service on the frontier, and this produced villages unusually proud of their schools and their literacy. That tradition shaped the region's character, and you still see it in the large village schools and the way people talk about education. The railway line from Salva runs north to the timber country of the Vișeu valley, where a narrow-gauge forest railway has become a tourist attraction.

As a ride, Salva is the doorway rather than the destination. The main road along the Someș is wide, well surfaced and busy with trucks, and it is quicker than it looks, so watch for overtaking on blind bends. Turn off onto the smaller roads and the pace drops, with tight villages, orchards and farm traffic, and surfaces that go from good to ragged in a few hundred metres. Summers are warm without being oppressive, and the best times are May and early autumn, when the slopes are green or gold and the Rodna ridges show snow or the first dusting of winter.

Fuel and food are easy here. Salva and the neighbouring Nimigea de Sus are big enough for stations, shops and cafés, and a plate of sarmale, cabbage rolls, or a grilled mici with mustard comes cheap and quickly. The spot rewards a short stop and a look at the hills, not a long stay, but it is a handy base for the roads into the Rodna foothills.
t.zagra dealul lupului@47.3,24.3:
Zagra is the last farming village before the land begins to climb in earnest toward the Rodna mountains, the highest range in the Eastern Carpathians north of the Prislop pass. Pietrosul Rodnei, at about 2,300 metres, is the summit, and the whole massif is protected as a national park and biosphere reserve, with glacial lakes, rocky ridges and alpine meadows that stay snowy into June. From the Dealul Lupului, the Wolf Hill, you look across a patchwork of hayfields toward those peaks, which look closer than they are.

The name is old and true to the place. Wolves still live in the Carpathians, and shepherds in these valleys keep big white sheepdogs for good reason, so if you walk uphill from the road give any flock a wide berth and do not approach the dogs. Brown bears and lynx are also present in the forested parts of the range, though you are far more likely to meet a cow on a bend than a predator. The air has the particular smell of mountain hay mixed with woodsmoke, which I have never managed to describe to anyone who hasn't been.

Riding here is some of the best in this part of the country. The side road up the Zagra valley has curves that tighten as you climb, passing farms, stream crossings and a few steep ramps where the surface is patched with asphalt of varying age. In wet weather expect mud on the corners and loose gravel, and in spring there may be rockfall after thaw. Higher up, the road becomes a track, so most riders turn back at the last houses. Early morning is clearest, with cool air and sharp light on the ridges, while afternoon thunderstorms can build quickly in July and August.

Zagra itself is small, with a shop and a bar, but nothing you could call a fuel station, so top up in Nimigea de Sus, about four kilometres away, or in Salva. For a meal, ask at a village guesthouse, where homemade bread, sheep's cheese and smoked pork are usually on offer, and where a glass of țuică may arrive unannounced. Dress in layers, because the temperature drops quickly after sunset, and carry water for the climb.
t.prodanesti pe sant@47.2,23.3:
"Pe Șanț" means on the ditch, and in Romanian hill country that word is nearly always a clue. A șanț is an earthwork, a trench or rampart, and the countryside of Sălaj holds many of them, from Roman-era frontier lines to medieval and prehistoric defences. I cannot tell you which this one is without making something up, but I can tell you that you are standing on land where people have been digging in, and fighting over, for a very long time.

The landscape is gentle. Prodănești sits just outside Jibou, close to the Someș river, in low hills of orchard, pasture and scattered oak that fold toward the Meseș range. Jibou itself carries more history than its size suggests. The Wesselényi family built the castle here, and the town was the birthplace of Miklós Wesselényi, a nineteenth-century Hungarian-Transylvanian reformer who campaigned for the abolition of serfdom, and who was much admired and much persecuted in his day. The park by the castle later became a botanical garden, a green and slightly unexpected place that makes a decent break from the saddle.

The roads between Prodănești, Creaca and Jibou run in modest bends through farmland, and the rhythm is relaxed: a short climb, a shallow dip, a village with a church and a few dogs, then back into the fields. The surface changes without warning, so keep your eyes ahead and avoid the temptation to enjoy the view at speed. Traffic is light and mostly local, though tractors and horse carts appear without warning, particularly in harvest season. Spring blossom and golden autumn make the best backdrop, and in summer the heat sits heavily in the valleys by mid-afternoon.

For fuel and a meal, Jibou is the obvious choice, only three kilometres away, with stations, small supermarkets and cafés where you can try the local pastries or a bowl of bean soup in smoked bread. The hamlet has little to offer beyond a shop, so fill up beforehand. Spend a few minutes looking at the fold of the land, and you can begin to read where an old ditch might once have run.
t.church of st philip and st james the apo:
The wooden church in Sękowa is small, dark and quietly astonishing. It stands on a slope in the Beskid Niski, the low and thickly wooded mountains of south-eastern Poland, and dates from the early sixteenth century, with a steep shingled roof, a tower with a pointed top and a gallery running around the walls. The timber has gone almost black with age, and inside the walls and ceiling are painted with colourful flowers, figures and scenes of faith from the seventeenth century. It is one of the wooden churches of southern Małopolska listed by UNESCO in 2003, and unlike a museum piece, it is still used for services.

The craft is the story. These churches were built by village carpenters using only axes and simple tools, without nails in some parts, locking logs together with joints, and covering the roof and walls with split shingles that need replacing every few decades. They have survived fires, wars and neglect because communities kept repairing them, and you see that devotion in the care taken with the surroundings.

The hills around hold a layered and painful history. In May 1915 the Gorlice-Tarnów offensive broke the Russian front here, and the fighting left countless graves in the hills, now tended as small war cemeteries, many designed by the Slovak architect Dušan Jurkovič with wooden crosses and gentle landscaping. Gorlice, the nearest town, with nearly thirty thousand people, is also a birthplace of the oil industry, since the pioneer Ignacy Łukasiewicz worked on oil lamps and wells in this region in the 1850s. Fuel, food and shops are easy in Gorlice, and Sękowa itself is a village of one and a half thousand.

For riders, the Beskid Niski is a joy. The roads wind through beech forest and open meadows, over low passes, with gentle gradients, few cars and decent asphalt, though a few back roads have patches and gravel. Autumn is glorious, with copper beech leaves, mist in the valleys and the smell of smoke, and spring brings blossom. Winters are cold, with snow and ice. Eat pierogi, barszcz and smoked cheese in a roadside inn, and ask whether the church key is available, because a lit interior is worth the stop.
t.moigrad la poiana de sus@47.2,23.1:
The Romans did not build their frontier in Dacia as a single wall. They built it as a chain of forts, watchtowers and signal posts along the crest of the Meseș mountains in what is now north-western Romania, and Moigrad is where the chain had its main fortress. The ancient town was called Porolissum, and it controlled the Meseș Gate, a natural pass through the ridge, where merchants paid customs and soldiers watched for raiders from the north. Walk the site today and you find an amphitheatre, a forum, a temple, stretches of the fort wall and long grassy slopes, all overlooking the green valley below.

La Poiana de Sus is one of the points along that line, and I cannot tell you exactly what stands there, so treat the label as part of the broader frontier landscape. The towers were built of stone and timber, a short walk apart, so that a fire or smoke signal could carry word along the ridge within minutes. Together they form the Roman frontier in Dacia, which is part of the wider UNESCO recognition of Roman limes across Europe.

The country around is soft, hilly farmland, with orchards, hayfields, beech woods and villages where horse carts are still in use. Zalău, a town of about sixty-three thousand, is the main centre, with fuel, supermarkets and a good museum of local archaeology, and small places like Treznea have little more than a shop. Fill up in Zalău before you head into the hills.

The riding is gentle, rolling and quiet, with moderate bends, long views and little traffic outside the main roads. Surfaces vary a lot, from smooth new asphalt to cracked, patched stretches with potholes and gravel on the edge, and in spring, when the snow melts, frost heave is a hazard. Farm animals and slow tractors are the main obstacles, and the occasional horse and cart without lights at dusk. Spring and autumn are lovely, with blossom or colour, and summers are warm without being extreme. Eat a plate of sarmale, cabbage rolls with polenta, or a bowl of hearty bean soup in a village inn, and ask about the local plum brandy, which is strong and honest.
t.hurez poic@47.0,22.9:
Ciucea is the first place to know before you ride into Hurez, because the road from Cluj to Oradea passes through it and the poet Octavian Goga lived and died there. Goga, one of the voices of Transylvanian Romanian nationalism, served briefly as prime minister in 1937 and 1938, and the castle at Ciucea, where he spent his later years, is now a memorial museum. It sits in a small park above the road, with a view of the green hills of the Apuseni mountains, and Goga's grave is nearby.

Hurez and Poic are quieter, small farming places in the folds of the hills south and east of Ciucea, the sort of landscape where most of the human history lies in the soil. The pairing with Românași - Dealul Hențeșu suggests that these are points on the ancient defensive and settlement patterns that crossed the Meseș and Apuseni foothills, from Dacian and Roman times to the Middle Ages. I do not know what exactly is at these coordinates, so the safe description is of the countryside around them: wooded ridges, small meadows with haystacks, orchards of plum and apple and a patchwork of fields.

Ciucea has a few thousand people and some fuel and shops, while Poieni is a smaller village up in the hills. The wise rider tops up at Ciucea or in Huedin, a bigger town on the main road, and takes a snack and water. The main road, the DN1, is busy with trucks and cars, and its curves along the Crișul Repede valley are fast and tiring, so turning off onto the quieter side roads is a relief. These are narrow, with sharp bends, broken edges and gravel on corners, and cows and sheep wander freely, so keep your speed at village level.

Weather in the Apuseni can change in an hour, with mist, rain and cold even in summer. The loveliest months are May and early June, when the fields are bright, and September, when the leaves turn. The smell of woodsmoke, cut hay and wet grass hangs in the air, and at dusk the church bells carry across the valley from one village to the next.
The Năsăud country in northern Transylvania has a history that the rest of Europe barely noticed. In 1762 the Habsburg authorities set up a military frontier here, enrolling local Romanian peasants as border guards in return for land and privileges, and for nearly a century the villages of the region lived under a mix of farm work and army discipline. The result was a surprisingly literate, organised society, with schools and a strong sense of identity, which produced a number of poets and writers. The novelist Liviu Rebreanu was born in the nearby village of Târlișua, and the poet George Coșbuc grew up not far from here.

Dumbrăveni, whose name means oak grove, sits in this soft landscape of rolling hills, orchards and beech woods, in the valley of the Someșul Mare river system. The label Dealul Sflederului, Hill of the Drill, points to a hilltop spot, and the ride list pairs it with a place called Bârsău Mare Cetate, so these are probably points on old hill-forts or defensive sites. I cannot say what exactly lies at these coordinates, so I will describe the country instead and leave the site to you to explore.

Ciceu-Giurgești has about four thousand people, with a shop, a bakery and some fuel, and Negrilești is smaller. The sensible rider fills up in Beclean or Năsăud, both larger towns, before going into the hills. The road network is a mix of main roads with trucks and rough local lanes, so surfaces vary from smooth to gravelled, and the corners can hide mud or manure after rain. Villages have a stray dog or two and a handful of geese that treat the road as theirs.

The Rodna mountains rise to the north, with peaks over two thousand metres and a national park of alpine meadows, a day's ride away if the weather is clear. In late summer and autumn the plums are ripe, and people turn them into țuică, the traditional brandy, so ask if someone offers a sip. Spring brings blossom, and the hills hum with bees. Winters can be cold and snowy, but the roads are usually cleared, and the quiet of a frozen valley is something to remember.
t.brebi dealul mare 4@47.2,23.2:
The Meseș mountains are not high, but they once marked the edge of an empire. In the early second century the Romans conquered Dacia and built a line of defences along the ridge, with a chain of watchtowers, small forts and earthworks, to guard the north-western frontier of the new province. The big fortress at Porolissum, at Moigrad, was the headquarters, and in between were dozens of small posts on hilltops, each in sight of the next. Brebi, a village in Sălaj county, lies on this frontier, and Dealul Mare, the Big Hill, is the kind of name given to the high ground where such a tower would stand.

I can't say what remains at this exact spot, since many towers are now only a low rise in the grass, but the logic of the line is clear when you stand on a ridge and see the next summit in the distance. The sites are not marked like a theme park, and part of the appeal is finding them by following local signs and asking shepherds.

The villages around, Mirșid and Creaca among them, are old Transylvanian places of a mixed Romanian and Hungarian heritage, with small churches, orchards, and farms with big wooden gates. Mirșid has a couple of thousand people and Creaca about three thousand, so you will find a shop, a bar and maybe a pump, but the bigger town of Zalău, not far to the south, is the sure place for fuel and a decent meal.

The roads here are among the quietest in the country. They roll over wooded ridges and open meadows, with broad bends and views that open over valleys, and traffic is mostly tractors and the odd cart. The asphalt can be patchy, with potholes, frost damage and occasional gravel, so keep an eye on the surface and an ear out for dogs. Spring is bright with fruit blossom, summer is warm with haymaking, and autumn burns gold in the beech woods. Evenings are cool, even in July, so bring a layer, and plan lunch around a village inn where soup and bread cost very little.
t.costesti blidaru@45.7,23.2:
Blidaru is the Dacian fortress that makes you rethink what you know about the people Rome conquered. It stands on a steep hill above the village of Costești, in the Orăștie mountains of Transylvania, and its walls are built of precisely cut limestone blocks, laid in the Dacian style called murus dacicus, with timber ties inside to absorb shocks. The builders learned from Greek masonry, and the result is a fortress with strong corner towers and a small square citadel, built on a terrace carved out of the mountain. It was one of the defences guarding Sarmizegetusa Regia, the Dacian capital, a few valleys away, and the group of Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie mountains was listed by UNESCO in 1999.

Getting to the top is a climb. A stone stair of several hundred steps leads up through beech forest from the road, and in summer it is shady and cool. At the top the walls stand taller than a person, the view reaches over wooded ridges, and the silence makes it easy to imagine sentries on the tower. The Romans, under Trajan, fought two wars here in AD 101 to 102 and 105 to 106, and the Dacian king Decebalus took his own life rather than be captured. The Dacian forts were dismantled or burned, but Blidaru survives in good order.

Orăștioara de Sus and Boșorod are small villages with shops and basic services, and you should fill the tank in Orăștie, the nearest real town, before heading up the valley. The road that climbs from the main highway to Costești and on to Grădiștea de Munte is paved, narrow and winding, with farmland, small hamlets and the shape of forested mountains getting closer. Traffic is light, and lorries carrying timber are the main hazard on blind corners.

Come in late spring or early autumn, when the forest is fresh and the air is clear, and avoid the middle of summer weekends, when coaches arrive. Winter brings snow and ice, and the steps can be treacherous. Pack water, because there are no shops at the site, and wear shoes with good grip.
t.gradistea de munte muncel@45.6,23.3:
Grădiștea de Munte is where the Dacian capital stood, and the hills around it hold the remains of Sarmizegetusa Regia, the mountain city that Decebalus ruled from about AD 87 until the Roman legions broke it in 106. The site lies high in the Șureanu mountains, around twelve hundred metres up, on a series of man-made terraces cut into the slope. The most striking remains are the sacred zone, with circular sanctuaries of stone and wood pillars and a large round altar of andesite, often called the sun disc, which may have served as a calendar or a place of sacrifice. Whatever it was, it is a place with presence, set among dark conifers and mountain meadows.

Muncel is a name for one of the nearby terraces, and I do not know precisely what lies at that point, so I will not guess. What is certain is that the whole area is dense with Dacian works, from houses and workshops to water pipes made of fired clay, and that the Dacians managed a mountain city of thousands of people with iron tools, grain stores and strong walls. The complex is part of the UNESCO list of Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie mountains, inscribed in 1999.

Fuel is a real matter. The nearest big town is Orăștie, a fair way down the valley, and Orăștioara de Sus and Boșorod, both small villages, are the last places with a shop. Tank up in Orăștie and carry a little extra if your bike has a small range. The road up from Costești is narrow and winding, with rough patches, damp stretches under trees and occasional livestock, and it ends near the site, where a small car park serves the visitor trail.

The weather at that altitude is cooler and more changeable than in the valley, with fog, sudden rain and cold evenings even in July. The best season runs from late May to early October. The air smells of resin and wet earth, the silence is deep, and in the evening light the stones glow a warm grey. Bring a jacket and a bottle of water, and allow time to sit on the terraces, because that is when the place starts to speak.
t.tarsa platoul tarsa@45.6,23.2:
Târsa sits on a high plateau in the Șureanu mountains, in the same ring of hills that sheltered the Dacian kingdom's heart. The platoul, the plateau, is open grassland and forest edge at roughly a thousand metres or higher, the sort of place where shepherds still bring flocks in summer and the wind carries the sound of bells. Like Grădiștea de Munte, a few kilometres off, it is part of the mountain district where the Dacians built terraces, fortifications and workshops, though I cannot say precisely what survives on this particular plateau.

The pleasure of the spot is the landscape itself. Below the plateau, the valleys of the Orăștie region are a green patchwork of haystacks, orchards and small farms, and above it the ridge lines roll away in layers of blue. Wildflowers fill the meadows in June, with orchids, gentians and big yellow arnica, and deer and wild boar are common in the forest. Bears live in these mountains too, though they keep their distance, and walkers should make some noise.

The ride list pairs this stop with the Monastery of Horezu, in the Wallachian foothills over the mountains, which UNESCO listed in 1993 as a masterpiece of the Brâncoveanu style, founded in 1690s by Prince Constantin Brâncoveanu, with painted porches and a quiet courtyard. A day that takes in both is a good way to see how Romania's history is layered between peoples and centuries.

Boșorod is the nearest place of any size, with about two thousand people, a shop or two and the last pump for some distance, and Bretea Română is a quieter village, so plan fuel in Orăștie or Hațeg. The mountain roads are slow and winding, with surfaces that go from smooth to gravelled, hairpins that look gentler than they are and occasional rockfalls after storms. Do not rush, and leave plenty of time before dark, since the lanes are not lit. Late spring and September are the sweetest months, when the air is clear and the crowds are few. Pack a layer, because a warm valley can turn cold on the plateau, and expect to be passed by a horse cart.
t.purcarete fata carpenului 1 2@47.3,24.1:
Transylvania's northern hills look like a landscape painted by someone who liked orchards and haystacks. Purcărete lies in the folds of the country between the Someș valleys and the Bistrița river, a region that was colonised in the Middle Ages by German-speaking Saxons, who built fortified churches and walled towns, and by Hungarians and Romanians who farmed the slopes. The Saxon town of Bistrița, not far away, still has a tall Lutheran church with a spire that can be seen from miles, and a handsome old centre of arcaded houses.

The label here, Fața Carpenului, Face of the Hornbeam, points to a wooded slope, and the pairing with Salva and Zalău ridings suggests a series of hillside sites that may be archaeological in origin. I do not know what is at these precise coordinates, so rather than invent a monument I will say that this is a place to enjoy a slow ride and an open eye, with the chance that something old is waiting under the grass.

Negrilești, with about fourteen hundred people, and Breaza, with a little over a thousand, are the nearest villages, with a shop and bar each, but fuel is better sought in Beclean, Năsăud or Bistrița. The roads here are old, narrow and quiet, with surfaces that vary from smooth to broken, and bends tighten as they follow the slopes. Farm traffic, wandering dogs and the occasional sheepdog on watch at the roadside call for patience. After rain the edges become muddy and slick, so stay in the middle of your lane.

The seasons are distinct. In April the plum and cherry blossom turns the valley white, in summer the hay is cut by hand in some places, in autumn the beech woods flare orange and the plums become țuică, the clear brandy, and in winter the snow lies deep and the villages are hushed. A late September ride is hard to beat, with warm days, cool nights and the smell of woodsmoke and fruit. Bring cash for village shops, since cards are rare, and accept an offer of a coffee, because hospitality is part of the road.
t.strimbu baiut@47.6,24.1:
Maramureș is a part of Romania where wooden building became an art. The county in the far north, tucked against the Ukrainian border and ringed by forested mountains, has hundreds of timber churches, and eight of them were listed by UNESCO in 1999. The one at Strâmbu, in the Băiuț area, belongs to the Nativity of the Virgin and dates from the eighteenth century, built of oak logs with a steep, double-tiered shingle roof and a tall slender spire. It looks like a church that has learned to float, with a roof that sheds the heavy snow and a tower that reaches for the sky.

The craft is Gothic in feeling, though the builders were village carpenters, and the interior is painted with scenes of judgement, saints and devils in a bold folk style. These churches were often built small and low because, as the usual explanation goes, the authorities in Habsburg times forbade Romanians from building in stone or raising their churches above a certain height, so the people turned to wood and went upwards with the steeple instead. The result is among the most graceful vernacular architecture in Europe.

Băiuț has about two and a half thousand people, Botiza nearly three thousand, and both have shops and cafes, with a pump likely in the larger villages. The bigger towns are Baia Mare to the west and Sighetu Marmației to the north, where fuel is certain. Villages in Maramureș are known for their carved wooden gates, big enough for a hay wagon, and for women in traditional skirts and scarves, who still work in the fields and sell cheese on the roadside.

The riding is a delight. Roads wind through meadows, plum orchards and low forested ridges, with gentle bends, modest gradients and a surface that is usually decent, though patches of gravel and potholes appear after winter. Over the Gutâi pass or the Prislop pass the views are long and the air is cool. Traffic is light, but horse carts and cattle are common, and the evening sees animals driven home along the road. May and June bring flowers, and September is warm and gold. Try the local plum brandy and a plate of smoked cheese and sausage, and take your time.
t.zacharovanyi krai velykyi dil@48.4,23.2:
In Transcarpathia, the westernmost corner of Ukraine, the Carpathians drop down to a plain that feels more Central European than Eastern. The region was part of Hungary for a thousand years, then Czechoslovakia, then briefly independent, then the Soviet Union and finally Ukraine, and the villages carry a mix of languages, churches and foods. Zacharovanyi Krai, the Enchanted Land, is the name of a nature park in the hills of this region, with beech forests, meadows, mineral springs and small rivers.

Velykyi Dil, Great Hill, is the local name for a rise in the landscape, and the pairing with Maramarosh, the historical region that spreads across the border into Romania, shows that this is the same mountain world as Maramureș, with the same wooden churches, haystacks and carved gates. The nearby towns of Kushnytsya and Dovhe are small and quiet, and the larger town of Khust, with its ruined castle on a hill, is a few kilometres away. Spring brings the narcissus meadows near Khust, a valley where wild white narcissus bloom in May, a spectacle people travel to see.

The situation in Ukraine today means that I can offer only general guidance. The country is at war, and travel is subject to restrictions, air raid alerts and fuel shortages. Transcarpathia has been far from the front line, but it is not free from the effects, and anyone thinking of a ride here should check official advice and local conditions first, and be ready to change plans. Take nothing for granted, including fuel, and carry documents at all times.

When the time comes for riding here, the roads will reward you. The old routes climb through villages and forest, with tight bends, poor surfaces and patches of cobble, and the pace is slow. Vineyards around Berehove and Vynohradiv produce good white wine, and in the hills you will find bryndza, sheep's cheese, with bograch, a spicy goulash stew. Autumn is the best season, with mist in the valleys and gold in the forest, and the people have a way of inviting you in for a meal that you will remember longer than any road.
t.hurez cornul vlasinului 1 2@47.0,22.9:
Beyond Ciucea the mountains of Apuseni begin to close in. The Vlădeasa massif, which rises to nearly eighteen hundred metres to the south, is the high point of the range and a place of bare ridges, beech forest and deep valleys, with a mountain lake and cabins for hikers. The road from Cluj to Oradea runs through the valley of the Crișul Repede below it, and the hills on either side are cut with side valleys where small villages cling to the slopes.

Hurez is one of these, a hamlet with small farms and terraced fields, and Cornul Vlășinului, which means the Horn of Vlășin, is a hill name that suggests a pointed rise above the village. The label carries the numbers 1 and 2, which probably mean two separate spots on the same hill, and the pairing with sites at Ciglean and Buciumi suggests that these are old hillside settlements or lookouts, though I cannot say more about them with certainty.

Poieni, a village of about a thousand, and Ciucea, with over four thousand, are the nearest places with shops and fuel, and Huedin is larger still. The valley road is the busiest in the region, with heavy lorries between Cluj and Oradea, and the traffic is a reason to turn away from the main route as soon as you can. The side roads are quiet, but steep, narrow and rough in places, with tight hairpins, wet leaves on shaded bends and unfenced livestock.

In the mountains the weather can turn at any time, with fog rolling in and temperatures dropping, so carry a warm layer and rain gear. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms, and winter brings snow that can close the higher roads. Late May and June, when the meadows are full of flowers and the beech leaves are fresh, are the best times, and September is nearly as good. You may meet shepherds with big white dogs, so stop and let them see you, and ask permission before walking across a field. The smell of cut hay and woodsmoke is the true soundtrack of the ride.
t.component including aggtelek@48.5,20.5:
Under these low wooded hills runs one of the great caves of Europe. The Baradla, a limestone passage about twenty-five kilometres long, starts near Aggtelek in Hungary and crosses the border into Slovakia, where it is called the Domica, so the same cave is entered from two countries. Water has been cutting it for millions of years, and the result is a series of halls and galleries filled with stalactites, stalagmites and dripping curtains of stone, kept at a steady temperature of about ten degrees all year. Guided tours go in through the Aggtelek entrance, and in one big hall called the Concert Hall, musicians perform, because the acoustics are so good. UNESCO listed the caves of the Aggtelek and Slovak Karst in 1995, one of the first cross-border natural sites in Europe.

The land on top is a karst plateau, a limestone upland with sinkholes, small meadows and beech woods, called the Gömör-Torna karst. It is a quiet, rural area of small villages, where farmers still cut hay by hand in some places and storks nest on chimney tops. Aggtelek itself has a few hundred people and a couple of guesthouses. On the Slovak side, Rožňava is a pleasant old mining town with a cathedral, and the cave of Domica is close to the border.

Riding in the Karst is quiet and rolling. The roads are narrow, patched and often empty, with views over wooded ridges and sudden drops into little valleys, and the bends are of the moderate, lazy kind. After heavy rain, mud and leaves can be slippery. The area is not high, with the plateau at about five hundred metres, so winter brings frost but not deep snow. May and June are ideal, with green meadows and flowering orchids, and autumn is golden. Take care in the villages, where geese, dogs and old tractors share the road.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Rudabánya is fifteen kilometres away, Szendrő a little further, and Rožňava, in Slovakia, has fuel, shops and a bigger range of services. Fill the tank before you reach the plateau. Bring a jacket for the cave, since the chill is surprising after the summer sun. A bowl of goulash or a plate of stuffed cabbage at a village inn is the right lunch, and the local plum brandy is strong.
t.franciscan missions in the sierra gorda:
In the 1740s and 1750s, Franciscan friars led by Junipero Serra, the same man who would later found missions in California, arrived in the Sierra Gorda, a rugged range in the state of Queretaro, to bring the Pame and other indigenous peoples into mission communities. The five missions they built, at Jalpan, Landa, Tilaco, Tancoyol and Conca, are among the most extraordinary churches in Mexico. Their facades are covered in vivid, almost wild, baroque decoration, with saints, angels, flowers, and symbols that seem to reflect local indigenous hands as much as European ones. UNESCO listed them in 2003.

Jalpan is the main town and the best base. The church sits on a plaza, its pale tower and richly ornamented front glowing in the afternoon light, and the town is relaxed and friendly, with a good market. The other missions are scattered in the hills, each at the end of a pleasant drive through villages of orchards, maize fields and stone walls. The Sierra Gorda is also a biosphere reserve with remarkable variety, from dry scrub to cloud forest, jaguars in the deeper valleys, and a startling number of bird species.

The riding is excellent. The road from Pinal de Amoles down to Jalpan, the famous Highway 120 through the mountains, is a long run of tight bends and hairpins that drops from pine forest to subtropical valley, and it is one of the best twisty roads in central Mexico. The surface is mostly good, but fog, landslides after rain, and the occasional cow keep you honest. The roads between the missions are quieter, narrower and more varied. Early morning is best, before the heat and the buses.

Jalpan has fuel, food and basic hotels, and a visit is easy to turn into a loop. The best seasons are autumn and spring; summer brings heavy rain and winter can be chilly at altitude. Local specialities include gorditas, and in the villages you may be offered strong coffee grown in the same mountains. Take it, and sit awhile under the church wall.
t.vysokyi zamok and pidzamche@49.8,24.0:
Above Lviv's old town rises a wooded hill that locals simply call the High Castle, Vysokyi Zamok, and below it, tucked against its slopes, lies Pidzamche, whose name means under the castle. For a rider used to the cobbled squares at the centre, this is the quiet back door of the city: older, scruffier and more honest. The castle itself is long gone, a victim of the sieges and demolitions of earlier centuries, and what remains are earthworks and a few fragments of wall. What you climb for is the view. From the top, some four hundred metres above sea level, the red roofs and church spires of Lviv spread out in a patchwork, and on a clear evening the light turns the whole city gold.

Lviv was founded in the thirteenth century by King Danylo of Galicia and named after his son Lev, and the hill is where the first fortress stood. Later, the city passed through Polish, Austrian and Soviet hands, each leaving its architecture in the streets. At the summit stands the Union Mound, a grassy hill raised in 1869 to mark three hundred years of the union of Poland and Lithuania, and now a favourite spot for picnics and photographs. Pidzamche itself holds some of the oldest corners of the city, with the churches and the remains of what was once a thriving Jewish quarter, now mostly gone but remembered in a few ruins and plaques.

Riding here means cobbles, tram lines and tight turns. The streets are narrow, the surface is uneven, and wet stone is slippery, so take it slowly. The city is quieter early in the morning, when bakeries open and the cafes begin to hum. Lviv takes coffee seriously, and a stop at one of the old cellar cafes is part of the experience; chocolate, strudel and strong espresso are the local pleasure.

Fuel is plentiful in and around the city, and there are stations on the ring roads. Be aware that the situation in Ukraine can change quickly, with air raid alerts and travel restrictions, so check official advice and local conditions before you plan anything. The city has a long history of resilience, and its people are warm and direct.
t.l viv the ensemble of the historic centr:
Few city centres in Europe have had as many names as this one. Lviv to Ukrainians, Lwow to the Poles who ruled it for centuries, Lemberg to the Habsburg officials who governed Galicia, and Lvov to the Soviets, it is a city that was built by many hands and still shows every one of them. The old town, a UNESCO listing, is a dense tangle of streets around the Rynok, the market square, where the houses are tall, narrow and ornamented with carved stone, each with its own character and its own story.

The mixture of peoples is the point. Ukrainians, Poles, Jews and Armenians lived side by side, each with their own churches and quarters, and the old town still has a Latin cathedral, an Armenian cathedral with beautiful frescoes, the Dormition Church with its distinctive tower, and the huge baroque Dominican church with its green dome. The Jewish population was largely destroyed in the Second World War, and the city's later history was shaped by wartime losses, border changes and Soviet rule. Today it is among the most lively cities in Ukraine, famous for its cafes, bookshops and sense of humour.

Riding in the centre is slow and a little punishing. The cobblestones are hard on suspension, tram tracks cross the streets at awkward angles, and many central streets are closed to cars or restricted. Park at the edge of the old town and explore on foot, ideally in the morning. Further afield, the roads south toward the Carpathians, through Stryi and into the foothills, become more enjoyable, with forested ridges and wooden churches, including the one at Rohatyn, an example of the region's timber architecture. In spring and autumn, the light on the hills is lovely.

Lviv has fuel at many stations and plenty of food. Try borscht, varenyky, and the honey drinks of the region. As the country is at war, conditions can be difficult and unpredictable, with air raid warnings, curfews and checkpoints, and any plan must be checked against the latest official guidance. The city, for all that, remains one of the most remarkable in Central Europe.
t.church of all saints@49.8,22.0:
Blizne, in the green rolling country of the Subcarpathian region, has one of the oldest wooden churches in Poland, and you can see its age before you step inside. The Church of All Saints dates in its main structure from the late fifteenth century, built of larch and fir logs, with a steep shingled roof that sweeps nearly to the ground and a slender tower that seems to grow out of the nave. It is a classic of the Gothic wooden tradition that spread across the Carpathian foothills, and in 2013 it joined the UNESCO list of wooden churches of the Carpathian region.

The interior is the real marvel. Its walls and ceiling are covered in painted decoration, with patterns of vines and flowers, saints, and scenes from the Bible, applied in the sixteenth century and later restored. The colours are warm and slightly faded, and the effect is more like a cosy family chapel than a cathedral. The church is usually locked, but a key holder lives nearby, and a short phone call or a visit to a neighbour often leads to the door being opened. A modest donation is thanked with real warmth.

The riding in this part of Poland is easy and charming. The roads wander between small villages through hills of meadow, orchard and mixed forest, with the Beskid Niski mountains to the south. Surfaces are good and traffic is light, and the corners are gentle and flowing. Brzozow, the nearest sizeable town, has fuel, cafes and shops, and villages like Jasienica Rosielna and Blizne offer little more than a small grocery shop, so fill up beforehand. Summer is warm, and September, when the mist lies in the valleys, is lovely.

Nearby, you may pass roadside shrines, wayside crosses and small cemeteries. Local food tends to be hearty: pierogi, sour rye soup and good dark bread. A wooden church is the kind of place that rewards a slow visit, and if you get the chance to sit inside in silence for a moment, the smell of old wood and wax will stay with you for a long time.
t.bosorod@45.6,23.2:
South of the Mures and west of the Retezat massif, the Hateg country is an oddly self-contained basin, ringed by mountains and full of old stories. Bosorod lies on its eastern side, near the town of Pui, in a landscape of meadows, small farms and wooded slopes that rise gradually toward the Orastie Mountains. This is where the Dacians built their strongholds, and the fortress at Banita, which shares the label with Jigoru Mare, is one of six that make up the UNESCO World Heritage listing of the Dacian Fortresses of the Orastie Mountains.

The Dacians, who lived in what is now Romania, had a powerful kingdom under Burebista and later Decebalus, and in the early second century AD they fought two wars against the Roman emperor Trajan. They lost, and the fortresses were destroyed or occupied, but the stonework survives, laid in the distinctive style known as murus dacicus, a mix of dressed blocks and timber ties. The Hateg basin was also the setting for the Roman provincial capital, Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, whose ruins lie nearby. The area has more surprises: Hateg is a famous site of dwarf dinosaurs, which lived on an island here in the Cretaceous, and the little church of Densus nearby is built partly from Roman stone.

The riding is varied and rewarding. The main road through the basin, the DN66 between Petrosani and Deva, has decent surfaces and gentle bends, while the lanes up toward the hills are narrower, steeper and sometimes unpaved. Sheep appear without warning, and in summer, afternoon thunderstorms are common. Fresh air and long views make up for the slow progress. The best time is May to October, and mornings are the most atmospheric.

Pui is a small town with a shop and a few places to eat, but the real fuel stop is Hateg, a town of over ten thousand about seventeen kilometres away. Carry some cash for village shops. If you are offered homemade plum brandy, called tuica, take only a sip if you are riding, and accept the hospitality with a smile.
t.titesti dealul cazanului@45.4,24.4:
The Olt is one of Romania's great rivers, and where it cuts through the Southern Carpathians, between Brezoi and Calimanesti, it does so in a long, narrow gorge that has been a corridor for armies and traders for two thousand years. Titesti and Perisani lie just off this corridor, in the hill country that rises on its western side, where the road leaves the traffic behind and climbs through orchards, hay meadows and beech woods. Dealul Cazanului, the Cauldron Hill, is one of those names that points at the shape of the land more than any particular monument.

The Romans knew the value of the valley. After conquering Dacia in the early second century, they built a line of forts and watchtowers along the Olt, known as the Limes Alutanus, to guard the province's southern edge, and the gorge itself was the gateway. Boita, to the north, was the site of a fort called Caput Stenarum, the head of the narrows, a name that says it all. Little remains above ground in most places, since the stone was reused for churches and farms, but the placement of the sites shows how well the Romans read a landscape.

The modern main road, the DN7, runs through the gorge and is busy, with heavy lorries and long queues in summer, so most riders find the side roads far more enjoyable. The lanes around Titesti and Perisani are narrow, with tight curves and patchy asphalt, and the views of the Capatanii and Cozia mountains are splendid, particularly in autumn. Farm tractors, horse carts and wandering sheep are part of the traffic. Weather in the hills can change quickly, with mist in the morning and storms in the afternoon.

Both villages are small, with a shop at most. Brezoi, about twelve kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and a market, and Calimanesti, a spa town on the river, has cafes and hotels. If you are lucky, a local will offer you home-made cheese, plum jam or a glass of the region's wine, which is made in small quantities and tastes of the hills.
t.poieni horhis@46.9,22.9:
The Crisul Repede is the river that cuts through the Apuseni Mountains in north-western Romania, and it carries the main road and the railway between Cluj and Oradea along its valley. Poieni and Horhis lie on the hills just above this corridor, in the zone where the great bulk of the Apuseni gives way to lower, rolling farmland. Ciucea, down in the valley, is the nearest village of any size, and is known for a small castle that once belonged to Octavian Goga, a Romanian poet who briefly served as prime minister in the 1930s. He is buried there, and the house is now a museum.

The road through the valley is the E60, and it can be hard riding: heavy with trucks, narrow in places and slow behind farm vehicles. Most riders will want to leave it for the roads that climb into the hills, where the traffic vanishes and the villages become small clusters of wooden houses, orchards and meadows. The corners are tighter, the surface variable, and the hay in summer smells wonderful. Sheep and cattle are common on the road, and farmers wave at passing bikes.

The label here includes Brusturi and a reference to ruins, which suggests the Roman and medieval remnants scattered across this part of Transylvania. The Roman province of Dacia's northwestern frontier lay not far from here, and small watchtowers and fortlets were built along the ridges. The area is also steeped in Romanian folk culture, with traditional costumes, carved gates and painted wooden churches in the villages of the Huedin region, famous for their folk art and their embroidered blouses.

Huedin, a town of about nine thousand, is the place to buy fuel and supplies, and it has a cluster of cafes and a Saturday market. Ciucea has a petrol station and a small shop, but the smaller villages are thin on services, so carry cash. Early summer and early autumn are the best times for riding here, and the hills are especially lovely when the mist lifts in the morning.
t.luncani piatra rosie@45.6,23.2:
Piatra Rosie, the Red Rock, is one of the six Dacian fortresses of the Orastie Mountains and, arguably, the most awkward to reach, which is exactly how its builders wanted it. The fortress stands on a steep hill above the village of Luncani, with its walls stepping up the slope in terraces, built in the characteristic Dacian way, from dressed stone blocks laid with timber beams. It was part of a defensive chain that protected the Dacian capital, Sarmizegetusa Regia, which lies higher in the mountains. UNESCO listed the group in 1999.

The Dacian kingdom reached its height under King Decebalus, who for years held off the Romans, and the fortresses are the physical record of that struggle. When Trajan's legions attacked in AD 101 and again in 105 and 106, the Dacians fell back to these hilltop strongholds one by one. Piatra Rosie fell in the second war, and its defenders were killed or taken, but the stone footings and the commanding view remain. At the top, you can see in several directions, which was the whole idea. The walk from the road is steep and can be slippery after rain, so wear proper boots.

The riding is mostly on narrow lanes through the foothills, with beech and oak forest closing in around the road and glimpses of the high Retezat peaks on clear days. Beyond the villages, forest roads can be rough, with loose stones and washouts, and not all of them are suitable for fully loaded touring bikes. Weather is changeable, with fog at dawn and thunder in the afternoon. A visit in late spring, when the meadows are full of wildflowers, or in autumn, when the beech leaves turn orange, is a delight.

The nearest town of any size is Hateg, sixteen kilometres away, and smaller places like Bosorod and Pui have shops and a few places to eat. Take water, a snack and a spare layer. Villagers are generally friendly and curious, and a polite greeting in Romanian will earn you a smile and sometimes a free glass of milk or a shot of homemade palinca.
t.huta dealul cozlii@47.0,22.9:
Huta is the sort of name that appears in dozens of places in Romania, from the old word for a glassworks or a forge, and it hints at an older economy, when these hills supplied charcoal, timber and metal to the towns of Transylvania. This Huta lies in the rolling country between Ciucea and the Crasna valley, in the hills where Salaj county meets Cluj, and the Dealul Cozlii, the hill named in the label, is one of the many wooded ridges that fold across the horizon. I cannot point you to one specific monument here, and that is a fair description of the pleasure: it is a landscape for wandering rather than ticking boxes.

The countryside is gentle and old. Villages string along valley floors, their houses fronted by wooden gates, their gardens full of plum trees and beans on poles, and the slopes above are a patchwork of hayfields, pasture and beech forest. In summer, haystacks sit in the meadows like small thatched houses, and the smell of cut grass and woodsmoke follows you from village to village. The Church of the Holy Archangels in the ride name is a reminder that many of these villages have small wooden churches with steep shingle roofs, some of them centuries old, and a couple of minutes inside is generally rewarded with a smell of wax and old timber.

The roads are narrow, with moderate gradients and a lot of blind bends, and the asphalt can be broken. Cows, geese and the occasional horse cart use the road as their own, and you will probably find yourself slowing to a walk behind a farmer and a flock of sheep. It is best taken at an easy pace. In wet weather, clay and mud can make the unpaved lanes treacherous.

Services are scarce. Cizer and Ciucea have shops and a basic petrol station in the latter, but for anything more substantial, you want Crasna, a town of about six thousand, or Huedin, which is bigger. Bring cash, fill up before you leave the main road, and be prepared to ask for directions, which will be given with enthusiasm and not always with accuracy.
t.cozia lotrisor@45.3,24.3:
Brezoi is where two rivers meet and the mountains lean in. The Lotru comes down from the high ridges of the Parang and Lotru ranges, the Olt arrives from the north through its famous gorge, and below the confluence the valley opens just enough for a town of about seven thousand people to settle. Cozia and Lotrisor sit on either side of this junction, and the great pyramid of the Cozia massif stands over the road to the east, a dark wall of beech and spruce that glows copper in October.

Cozia is the name most Romanians know, because of the monastery on the riverbank a few kilometres downstream. It was founded in 1388 by Mircea the Elder, the Wallachian prince, who is buried inside, and its proportions and carved stone are among the finest of the medieval Wallachian style. Tourists crowd the car park in summer, but the courtyard has a cool, slightly austere calm. The monks sell honey, icons and small jars of jam, and the Olt, quick and green, runs just below the walls. The Romans also valued this corridor and kept watchtowers along the river on the line of the Limes Alutanus, which is where the Cozia and Lotrisor label comes from, but you will need a guide or a good map to find them.

The riding here is rewarding. Heading up the Lotru valley, the road climbs past a large reservoir and eventually joins the Transalpina, the high mountain road that crosses the Parang range, though its upper sections are closed by snow for much of the year and usually open only in summer. The lower valley is a pleasure, with long, flowing curves, forest shade and the sound of water. The main road along the Olt, the DN7, is a different animal: the busy route to Sibiu, shared with trucks, and sometimes slow.

Brezoi has fuel, a supermarket and a handful of cafes and restaurants, and Calimanesti and Caciulata, a few minutes down the valley, are old spa towns with bakeries and terraces. Try the grilled trout, which is usually excellent, and a bowl of ciorba, the local sour soup. Come in late spring or early autumn to avoid the crowds.
t.frontiers of the roman empire dacia@47.2:
Above the town of Zalau, where the Meses mountains form a long, wooded ridge across northern Transylvania, the Roman Empire built one of its most remote defences. The mountains separated the province of Dacia from the free tribes to the north, and the ridge was fortified with a line of watchtowers and forts, the western part of what is now called the Frontiers of the Roman Empire in Dacia. The greatest of them was Porolissum, a garrison town and customs post on the Meses Gate, the pass through the ridge, near the village of Moigrad.

Porolissum was a busy place. It had a fort on a hilltop, a town below, an amphitheatre where soldiers watched gladiators fight, and a customs post where merchants paid duties on goods crossing the frontier. Today, the stones of the gate, the walls and the arena can still be seen, lying in meadows with a long view over the hills. It feels astonishingly remote for a place that once held thousands of people. The museum in Zalau houses the best finds, and it is worth a visit if you want to understand the scale of the operation.

For riders, the approach is the highlight. The road from Zalau climbs through orchards and beech woods to the pass, with decent asphalt, gentle gradients and a sequence of easy bends. Heavy traffic is rare outside harvest time, though trucks and farm vehicles do use it. The ridgeline itself is best explored by smaller lanes, many of which are rough, with gravel and potholes. Autumn is outstanding, with the beech woods turning bronze and the fields misty in the mornings.

Zalau, only nine kilometres away, is a town of more than sixty thousand people, with all the fuel, shops and restaurants you could want. Villages on the ridge, such as Mirsid and Creaca, are small, with a basic shop and perhaps a bar. If you stop for lunch, look out for local specialities, such as smoked sausages, polenta with cheese and sour cream, and plum brandy distilled in backyards. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.
t.mirsid dealul mare 1@47.2,23.2:
Mirsid is the kind of village you pass on the way somewhere else, until you notice that it sits at the foot of the greatest Roman frontier in Transylvania. The ridge of the Meses mountains rises behind it in a long, dark line of beech and oak, and the Romans built a series of watchtowers along the crest, looking north across the border into the lands of the free Dacians. The name Dealul Mare, Big Hill, with the number one attached, suggests the first in a sequence of those lookout points, and in a few of them you can still make out the square footprint of a tower in the grass.

The landscape itself tells you why this was a good place for a frontier. The ridge is steep on both sides, with long views across a patchwork of fields and orchards, and it is easy to imagine a sentry watching for smoke from the next tower along. The area is farmed, with small plots and haystacks, and in summer the air is thick with the smell of cut hay. In autumn, plum harvests fill the villages with the sweet, fermenting smell of tuica in the making.

The riding is relaxed and sociable. The roads around Mirsid wind over low hills, through orchards and past tidy farms, and the surface is variable, with smooth stretches and rough patches. Gradients are moderate and bends are mostly gentle, with a few sharper ones where the road drops into a valley. Sheep and cattle are common, and tractors are slow, so there is little point in hurrying. The tracks leading up to the ridge are rough, and best taken on foot unless you have a light bike and good boots.

The village has a shop and a couple of bars. For fuel and anything more serious, Zalau, a town of over sixty thousand people, lies about eight kilometres away, and has supermarkets, cafes and workshops. Late spring and early autumn are the best times to visit, with clear air and comfortable temperatures, and views stretching to the Apuseni mountains on a good day. Bring a jacket, since the ridge can be breezy even in summer.
t.sangeorgiu de meses@47.0,22.9:
The village of Sangeorgiu de Meses lies on the southern flank of the Meses mountains, in the old Hungarian-Romanian borderland of Salaj, and its name carries the saint of horsemen, George, and the mountain that gives the area its character.
