It is a place that rides begin and end, which suits it well: a quiet village with a church, a shop, a couple of bars, and an easy exit onto roads that climb in several directions. A few kilometres away is Cizer, and a little further, the small settlements of Starciu and Mal, each with its own cluster of orchards and farm tracks.

The Meses range is a low, forested ridge, but it has a big history. In Roman times it was the northern limit of the province of Dacia, and the line of watchtowers on its crest looked out over the lands beyond. Later, it separated Transylvania from the Hungarian plain, and the region was a mix of peoples: Romanians, Hungarians and some Germans, each with their own church. In the villages, you can often see both Orthodox and Reformed churches within a few hundred metres of each other. The rural architecture is charming, with steep roofs, carved gates and long gardens.

The riding around the village is exactly what you want after a long day. The roads are narrow, curving over gentle hills with small climbs and descents, through meadows and woodland. The surface is a mix, some of it excellent and some of it patched and bumpy, and speeds are low. It is a pleasure to ride slowly in the evening, when the light turns the hills gold and the smell of woodsmoke drifts across the road. In winter the area is cold and snowy, and the minor roads can be icy.

As for supplies, the village has the basics, but fuel and supermarkets are fifteen kilometres away in Crasna, a town of around six thousand. Carry some cash for the village shops, and expect a friendly welcome. If someone invites you in for coffee or a shot of palinca, accept the coffee at least. The best season for riding is from May to October, and September, with the plums and the first mist, is hard to beat.
t.fildu de sus greban@46.9,22.9:
Fildu de Sus is strung along a valley in the hills between Ciucea and the Crasna country, where the Apuseni mountains soften into rounded, grassy ridges, and Greban, the hill in the label, is one of those ridges. The valley is small and green, with a stream, a line of houses, and orchards climbing the slopes, and it feels a long way from the main road that carries the traffic between Cluj and Oradea. Poieni and Ciucea are the nearest villages, and Negreni lies a short distance to the east.

It is a landscape of ordinary rural life, and that is its charm. People here make hay with scythes and pitchforks, store it in conical stacks, and carry it home on horse-drawn carts, and in the evening the cows walk home on their own along the road. Houses are low and whitewashed, and some of the older ones still have shingled roofs and carved wooden porches. You may see women in headscarves tending vegetable gardens, and men chatting at the gate. The church, often a small one, stands on a rise above the village and is worth a quiet minute.

The roads are narrow and winding, and the surface is a lottery, but the bends are mostly gentle and the gradients short. Expect some patches of gravel, cattle, and the occasional pothole you could lose a wheel in, especially after winter. The pleasure is in the slow pace, the smell of hay, and the long views from the ridges, which on a clear day reach the high peaks of the Vladeasa massif. Fog can fill the valleys in the morning, and thunderstorms roll in quickly in summer afternoons.

Nothing much in the way of services is available in the village, aside from perhaps a small shop. Ciucea, five kilometres away, has a petrol station and shops, and Huedin, fifteen kilometres to the east, has supermarkets, restaurants and a weekly market. A thermos of coffee and some bread and cheese in the saddlebag are worth carrying. Early autumn, when the mist burns off and the leaves turn, is the best time to come.
t.san francisco del valle de tilaco@21.2,-:
In the middle of the eighteenth century, a group of Franciscan friars led by Junipero Serra, later famous for his missions in California, set about building five churches in the Sierra Gorda of Queretaro, one of the roughest, most remote parts of central Mexico. The mission of San Francisco del Valle de Tilaco is one of the five, along with Jalpan, Landa, Concá and Tancoyol, and together they were inscribed as World Heritage in 2003 as the Franciscan Missions in the Sierra Gorda. The church at Tilaco stands in a small village, and its facade is covered with stucco decoration in a style that mixes European baroque with local imagery, with saints, flowers, and symbols that might have been designed by the indigenous workers who built it.

The Sierra Gorda is a surprising landscape. It lies at the northeast edge of Queretaro state, where the mountains of the Sierra Madre Oriental fall away towards the Gulf of Mexico, and in a few kilometres you pass from dry scrub to cloud forest, oak woods and tropical canyons. The area is a biosphere reserve, home to jaguars, ocelots, parrots and over a hundred species of butterfly, and it is one of the most biodiverse parts of central Mexico. In the missions, locals still keep up a calendar of fiestas, and the plaza in front of each church is the centre of village life.

Riding here is serious fun. The roads from Queretaro to the Sierra Gorda, notably Highway 120 through Jalpan, are twisting mountain roads with endless bends, steep climbs, sudden drops and wonderful views, and the surface is generally good but with patches of loose stone and occasional landslides after heavy rain. Traffic is light, but trucks and buses take the middle of the road on blind corners, and cattle may wander. Late autumn and spring offer clear weather, while the summer rains bring mist and slippery surfaces. The route is a big and rewarding day out.

Tilaco is a small village, and nearby Agua Zarca and Landa de Matamoros each have only a thousand or two people, so supplies are modest. Jalpan, the main town of the mission circuit, is the place for fuel, food and a bed, and it is wise to fill up there before heading out on the smaller roads. Try the local zacahuil, a giant tamal, and the strong coffee that grows in the hills.
t.stuor oivi stuorrahanoaivi@68.7,22.7:
There is a point on a bare hill in the far north of Norway that the world once used to measure itself. Stuor-Oivi is one of the stations of the Struve Geodetic Arc, a chain of triangulation points that stretches about 2,800 kilometres from Hammerfest on the Arctic coast to the Black Sea. Between 1816 and 1855 the astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve and his teams measured the arc with astonishing care, and the result was one of the first accurate calculations of the size and shape of the Earth. Thirty-four of the points, in ten countries, were inscribed as a World Heritage site in 2005, and this is one of the Norwegian ones.

What you find on top is modest, a small cairn or a marked rock, a drill hole in the stone and a view across a rolling plateau. The point of the place is the landscape. This is the Finnmarksvidda, the great high plateau of Arctic Norway, a country of low rounded hills, birch scrub, lakes and open tundra that stretches out in all directions. It is the home of the Sami reindeer herders, whose main centre, Kautokeino, lies about forty kilometres away, and in spring and autumn you may see herds moving over the hills and along the roads.

The riding here is another matter. The main road from Alta to Kautokeino is a wide, quiet, well-surfaced route with long open views, little traffic, and reindeer that wander across at will. Treat them with respect and slow right down, especially in autumn and winter, when they come to the road to lick salt. The north Norwegian summer is short, with the midnight sun in June and July and a lot of mosquitoes. The roads can have frost in the shoulders of the season, and winter is no season for a motorbike, with temperatures that can drop below minus thirty.

The station itself is not on a road, so expect a walk across rough ground, with boggy patches, so wear good boots, carry a map and keep an eye on the weather, which can change quickly. Kautokeino has fuel, a shop and basic lodging, and distances between services are long, so fill up whenever you can. The Sami culture is strong here, with the Sami parliament's cultural events, craftwork, and the Easter festival with its reindeer races.
t.terebowiec stream valley@49.1,22.7:
The far south-east corner of Poland is a place where the map runs out of road. The Terebowiec flows through the Bieszczady, the lowest and loneliest range of the Polish Carpathians, a land of wide grassy ridges called poloniny, deep beech forests and a few scattered villages, and the border with Ukraine is never far. The nearest settlements are Lutowiska, a village of a few hundred people, and across the frontier the town of Turka, so this is not a place with services. The nearest town where you can count on fuel and shops is Ustrzyki Dolne, a good half hour back along the valley road.

The Bieszczady were not always empty. Before the Second World War this was home to Boyko and Lemko communities, who herded sheep and cattle and built wooden churches. After the war the villages were emptied, first by the changing borders and then by the forced resettlement of Operation Vistula in 1947, and the forests and meadows took over. What remains are fruit trees standing in the woods where gardens once were, old graveyards and the footprints of cellars, and a sense of absence that sticks with you.

That emptiness is also why the nature here is so rich. The beech forests of the Bieszczady, with their old trees and fallen logs, form part of the Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians, a World Heritage site that stretches across several countries. Brown bears, wolves and lynx live here in numbers that are rare in Europe, and the herds of European bison, reintroduced in the 1960s, are a famous attraction. In autumn the stags roar on the high meadows, and the beeches turn gold and copper.

The riding is excellent in a quiet way. The Bieszczady loop road runs for about a hundred and fifty kilometres through the hills, with gentle climbs, smooth surfaces and long views across the poloniny, and traffic is light except on summer weekends. It passes Wolosate, the highest village in Poland, and the road toward the border at Ustrzyki Gorne, where the pavement ends and the mountains begin. Fog can fill the valleys in the mornings, and in winter snow closes some of the minor roads. Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Carry cash and some food, as shops are few, and keep your speed down at dusk, when deer step out on to the tarmac.
t.zacharovanyi krai irshavka@48.5,23.1:
Transcarpathia is the tucked-away corner of Ukraine, on the far side of the mountains from the rest of the country, and it feels like it. The region, known in Ukrainian as Zakarpattia, was part of Hungary for a thousand years, and later of Czechoslovakia, before the Soviet Union took it in 1945, so the villages mix Ukrainian, Hungarian, Romanian and Rusyn traditions. The Zacharovanyi Krai, the Enchanted Land, is a nature park in the hills near the town of Irshava, a country of beech and oak forest, orchards, and folds of low mountains on the edge of the Carpathian foothills.

The name is deserved. In spring the orchards bloom, in summer the hillsides are thick with wild flowers and herbs, and in autumn the forests turn gold and rust. Villages are strung along stream valleys, with wooden houses, plum trees, and small churches with shingled roofs. This is plum brandy country, called palinka or slyvovytsia, and almost every household distils its own. A strong flavour of the borderlands lingers in the food, with bograch, a spicy paprika stew similar to Hungarian goulash, and banosh, a cornmeal dish served with sheep's cheese.

The Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians, a World Heritage site that stretches across several countries, lie close by, and the Havesova forest in neighbouring Slovakia, named in the ride, is one of its jewels. Old beeches, some of them centuries old, stand beside fallen trunks in a forest left alone.

I have to be frank about the present situation. Since Russia's invasion in 2022, Ukraine has been a war zone, and although Transcarpathia has been far from the front, it is not entirely safe, with air raid alerts and shortages, and foreign travel advisories advise against travel. A rider should check the current situation carefully before thinking of coming here. In peacetime the roads of the region are winding and pretty in a modest way, with the surfaces ranging from good main roads to broken minor ones. Bereznyky and Kushnytsya are villages of several thousand people, and the nearby town of Irshava has fuel and shops.
t.synevyr kvasovets@48.4,23.7:
Up in the Carpathians of Transcarpathia lies the largest lake in the Ukrainian mountains, and a legend that explains it. Synevyr, set in a bowl of spruce forest at just under a thousand metres, is said to have been born from the tears of a count's daughter, Syn, who fell in love with a herdsman, Vyr, and was parted from him. Her father killed the young man, and she wept so much that the tears made the lake, which is why its name is Syn-Vyr. Whatever the truth, the lake is beautiful, dark and still, with a small island and a wooden pavilion on its shore, and the National Park around it is among the finest in the Carpathians.

The wildlife is a big part of the draw. The forests hold brown bears, lynx, wild boar and deer, and a rehabilitation centre for bears that were once kept in poor conditions lies close to the lake, a rare place where you can watch them in large enclosures in the woods. The mountains here belong to the Gorgany range, a rough, boulder-strewn group of peaks with dense, trackless forests and screes, among the wildest in Ukraine. The Kolochava valley, a few kilometres away, is a long village of wooden houses stretched along a river, with a small museum devoted to the narrow-gauge railway that once carried timber from these woods.

The road to the lake climbs from the Tereblya valley through steep spruce woods with a slow, winding surface that varies from decent to rough, and in wet weather it can be slippery with mud and gravel. Fog drifts through the trees and summer thunderstorms are sudden and fierce. The best weather comes from June to September, though the mountains can be cold at night even in July. Autumn has strong colours, and winter brings heavy snow.

Practical matters are difficult at present. Since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, Ukraine has been a war zone, and travellers should check official advice before considering any visit. In normal times, Synevyr, with about four and a half thousand people, and Kolochava, with nearly the same, have basic shops and fuel, and the nearby town of Mizhhirya has more. Local cooking is hearty, with mushroom soups, potato dumplings and sheep's cheese, and a pot of herbal tea is a good ending to a cold evening.
t.copaceni praetorium i cetate@45.4,24.3:
The Olt is the only river that cuts straight through the Carpathians, and the Romans knew it. Between Copaceni and Brezoi, the Olt runs in a deep gorge through the mountains between Transylvania and Wallachia, and the Roman army, after conquering Dacia in 106 AD, built a line of forts and watchtowers along its western bank to guard this key corridor. The Limes Alutanus, as it is known, ran from the Danube northwards along the river, and sites such as Praetorium and Arutela were links in the chain. Some are little more than grassy ramparts today, but they sit on strategic hills with views along the valley.

The gorge itself is spectacular. Forested slopes climb steeply from the river, with limestone crags, tunnels, and the narrow gap known as Turnu Rosu, the Red Tower Pass, which has been a route between Sibiu and southern Romania since ancient times. Cozia Monastery, a Byzantine-style church of white and red stone built in 1388 under the Wallachian prince Mircea the Elder, stands on the river bank and holds his tomb. The hills hold bears, wolves and wild boar, and a scattering of thermal spa towns, such as Calimanesti and Caciulata, use the mineral springs.

For motorcyclists, the valley road, DN7, is a mixed blessing. It is a major route between Bucharest and Sibiu, and it is crowded with heavy lorries, slow vehicles and impatient overtakers, so the gorge section demands care and patience. The road is generally well surfaced, with sweeping bends and good views, but accidents are frequent. Choose a weekday morning if you can, avoid Friday evenings and Sunday afternoons, and take care in the tunnels, which can be damp. Quieter side roads climb into the hills, and the Transfagarasan, one of Europe's best-known mountain roads, is an easy detour from the same corner of Romania. Fog and cold nights are common in autumn, and snow in winter.

Brezoi, with nearly seven thousand people, is the largest nearby town and has fuel, shops and food, and Ramnicu Valcea, to the south, is bigger still. Romanian roadside stalls sell honey, cheese and forest fruits in summer, and a hot corn porridge with cheese and sour cream is a typical lunch. Note that the site names are sometimes marked only by small signs, so a map is useful.
t.gradistea de munte dealul sesului@45.6,2:
High in the Orastie mountains, at around twelve hundred metres, a ring of stone terraces climbs out of the beech forest, and it was once the heart of an empire. This is Sarmizegetusa Regia, the capital of the Dacian kingdom, the people who lived in what is now Romania and who fought two bitter wars against the Roman emperor Trajan in 101-102 and 105-106 AD. The site at Gradistea de Munte was a fortress, a religious centre and a town in one, with workshops, houses on artificial terraces, and a sacred precinct with round and rectangular temples marked out by stone bases and by pillars of andesite. Together with five other Dacian fortresses in the same hills, it was inscribed as a World Heritage site in 1999.

The sanctuary is the strangest part. A large circular platform of stone discs, nearly thirty metres across, stands beside a ring of wooden posts on stone bases that has been nicknamed the Dacian Calendar, though experts still debate its purpose. A great stone disc, usually called the Andesite Sun, lies close by. The Dacians were skilled builders, and their fortresses were made of cut limestone blocks in a style called murus Dacicus, with timber lacing inside to resist battering rams. The Romans took the capital in 106, after the king Decebalus took his own life, and Trajan's Column in Rome shows the war in a spiral of carved scenes.

The road is half of the experience. A narrow, winding asphalt road climbs from Orastie into the mountains, with a lot of bends and a patchy surface, and it runs through beech and fir forest with sudden clearings and views of misty valleys. It is a lovely ride on a dry morning, and slippery on a wet one. Traffic is light, but cars and trucks sometimes squeeze through, and cattle may be on the road. Fog is common, and the weather at this altitude can turn cold and wet in a few minutes, so carry a layer.

Take water and a snack, since there are few places to eat. Spring and autumn are the best times, and the site is quietest in early morning. Wear shoes with a good grip, because the stones can be slick.
t.church of the presentation of the virgin:
In Maramures, they build in wood as if wood were stone. The valley of the Iza, in the north of Romania, near the Ukrainian border, is a country of green hills, haystacks, carved gates and tall, steep-roofed churches of dark oak and spruce, and eight of the wooden churches here, built between the seventeenth and nineteenth centuries, are on the World Heritage list. The church of the Presentation of the Virgin at Barsana, dated to 1720, is one of them. It stands in the cemetery of the village, slender and dark, with a high, shingle-covered roof and a tower that rises like a pencil. Inside, the walls and ceiling are covered with paintings of saints and biblical stories in a naive and moving style.

The reason for all this wood is partly history. After the Mongol invasions of the thirteenth century, and again under Habsburg and Hungarian rule, Romanian Orthodox villagers were not allowed to build in stone, so they used the material they had in abundance, and perfected a style with a double-pitched roof to shed snow and a tall, slim tower that signalled their faith. A newer monastery at Barsana, built in the 1990s, has one of the tallest wooden churches in Europe, and its gardens are popular with visitors.

The ride into Maramures is a delight. From Sighet, the road runs through the Iza valley past village after village, each with its own wooden gate, with the Rodna mountains on one side and the Gutai on the other. Further east, the road climbs over the Prislop Pass, about 1,400 metres, to Moldavia, with bends, long views and cold, wet weather that can change quickly. Surfaces are generally fair, although some stretches have patches and potholes, and you will often be sharing the road with horse carts, tractors and sheep. Haymaking time in July is lovely, with haystacks everywhere, and autumn brings the plum harvest.

Barsana, with about six thousand people, has a few shops and small guesthouses, and fuel is available in larger towns such as Sighetu Marmatiei, so top up when you can. The Merry Cemetery at Sapanta, with its brightly painted crosses, and the steam train, the Mocanita, at Viseu de Sus are among the region's other sights. The hospitality of the farmhouses is famous, and a plate of stuffed cabbage with polenta is the proper reward.
t.starciu dealul secuiului@47.1,23.0:
Between the Apuseni mountains and the Meses range, in the north-west of Transylvania, the Romanian landscape folds into low, wooded hills and farming valleys, and the village of Starciu sits among them in Salaj county. The name Dealul Secuiului, the Szekler's Hill, is a local one that I cannot match to a particular monument, so I would rather be straightforward and talk about the country around. The nearest places are Cizer, a small village a few kilometres away, and Starciu itself, each of about a thousand or two people.

The hills have a long history. This was the northern edge of Roman Dacia, and the pass at Meses, a few kilometres to the north, was guarded by the fort and town of Porolissum, a border garrison with an amphitheatre, a customs post and watchtowers along the ridge. Long before the Romans, people mined gold in the Apuseni mountains to the south, and the Roman mine workings at Rosia Montana, in the same highlands, were so extensive that the whole area was inscribed on the World Heritage list in 2021 as the Rosia Montana Mining Landscape. Tunnels dug by Roman miners can still be walked, and wax tablets recording their contracts were found there.

For riders, this is a quiet corner. The roads in Salaj county wind between woods and meadows, passing villages of low houses with fruit trees, and the surfaces vary from decent to rough. Traffic is light and the pace is slow, with horse carts and the occasional herd of cows on the road. The area is at its best in May, when the hills are green and the orchards are in bloom, and in early October, with the beech woods in colour. Summer thunderstorms can be fierce, and winter brings snow.

For fuel, shops and a meal, head to a bigger town, such as Zalau or Jibou, since the villages offer little more than a corner shop. Local cooking is hearty, with sour soups, smoked sausages, and plum jam, and there is a tradition of home-distilled plum brandy. Make sure you bring a map, since signs are sparse and phone coverage can be patchy in the valleys.
t.tokaj wine region@48.2,21.4:
Tokaj is the place where the world's first classified wine region was drawn on a map, in 1737, long before Burgundy or Bordeaux got round to the idea. The wine country of Tokaj-Hegyalja lies in the far north-east of Hungary, where the Zemplén hills, old volcanoes worn down into rounded cones, fall away to the plain at the meeting of the Tisza and Bodrog rivers. Tarcal and Tokaj sit at the foot of the slope, and the vines climb the south-facing hills above them, in a patchwork of terraces, stone walls and small plots.

What makes the wine is a combination of volcanic soil, long warm autumns, river mists and a fungus. In good years the grapes, mostly Furmint and Hárslevelű, are attacked by noble rot, which shrivels them and concentrates their sugar. Pickers collect the withered berries one by one to make aszú, the sweet wine that Louis XIV called the wine of kings and the king of wines. Cellars are cut deep into the soft volcanic rock, and their walls are covered in a black, velvety mould that thrives on the alcohol fumes. Tasting in one, with a cold stone floor under your boots, is part of the point.

The riding is a slow pleasure rather than a thrill. Roads climb gently from the plain among the vineyards, with tight little turns through villages of low whitewashed houses and cellar doors, and the hillsides give wide views over the river flats toward Slovakia. Traffic is light outside the harvest and festival season, but tractors come out in September and October, and summer afternoons are hot. Surfaces are mixed, with patched asphalt in the villages, so watch for rough edges.

Tokaj has about five thousand people and both fuel and cafes; Tarcal is smaller but has several wine cellars. Remember that tasting and riding do not go together in Hungary, where the legal alcohol limit for drivers is zero. Buy a bottle for the evening instead, and ride up in the late afternoon when the light turns the vines gold.
t.stuzhytsia uzhok@49.1,22.6:
Where the Bieszczady mountains of Poland meet Slovakia and Ukraine, there is a stretch of forest that has hardly been touched. The Stuzhytsia-Uzhok area, on the Ukrainian side of the watershed near the Uzhok pass, is one component of the Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians, a World Heritage group that spans several countries and continues into the Polish Bieszczady and the Slovak Poloniny. The trees here are mostly beech, with fir and sycamore, and in the oldest stands, some of the trunks are huge, with fallen logs lying where they dropped and rotting into the soil, a kind of forest that has almost vanished from Europe. The wildlife is what you might expect from such a place: brown bears, wolves, lynx, and the European bison, which was reintroduced to the Bieszczady in the 1960s.

The landscape is very different from the Polish plain. Long grassy ridges called poloniny rise above the tree line, with views over wave after wave of forested hills, and the villages in the valleys are few and small. Before the Second World War many of them were home to Lemko and Boyko people, who were resettled after the war, leaving old orthodox churches, overgrown orchards and cemeteries in the woods. Today the Bieszczady is known as a wild, quiet corner for hikers and riders.

The roads here are some of the best in Poland for riding. The Bieszczady loop, from Lesko to Ustrzyki Dolne and Wetlina and back, has twisting roads through beech woods, with climbs to viewpoints and views across the poloniny. The road toward Ustrzyki Górne climbs to open ridges with big views. In summer, tourist traffic and tractors can slow things down, and in autumn the leaves are slippery. Winters are long and snowy.

The border region carries constraints. The site itself lies in Ukraine, and since the war began in 2022 travel across the frontier here is not advisable, so treat this stop as a view of the forest from the Polish side. Check which crossings are open, and respect the national park rules. Fuel is available in Lesko and Ustrzyki Dolne, but Lutowiska, the nearest listed village, has little. Carry food and water, bring bear awareness, and aim for September and October when the colours are at their best.
t.pausa turnul lui teofil@45.3,24.3:
The Olt river cuts through the Carpathians in a gorge a few kilometres from Păuşa, one of the few natural gateways between Transylvania and the southern plains, and the Romans knew its value. After Trajan conquered Dacia in AD 106, the frontier of the new province ran along the Olt, a line known as the Limes Alutanus, and a chain of watchtowers and small forts guarded the river, the roads and the passes against raiders from the lands to the east. Turnul lui Teofil, Teofil's Tower, is one of those lookouts, standing on a height over the valley, in a place chosen so that a signal fire or a trumpet call could be passed on from tower to tower.

Today the remains are slight, mostly a rectangle of stone foundations in a clearing, but the setting says it all. The gorge is narrow and green, and the river flows fast between steep, wooded slopes, with a railway and a road squeezed along the bank. The Dacian frontier reached the UNESCO list in 2024, with the Limes Alutanus among its sections. Nearby, the medieval monastery of Cozia, founded in the fourteenth century by Mircea the Elder, stands on the river bank, with a fine painted church.

Riding the Olt valley is a pleasure. The road, DN7, follows the river through the gorge for dozens of kilometres, with curves, tunnels and views of forested slopes and sheer rock, a main artery between Sibiu and Bucharest. Traffic, especially lorries, can be heavy, and overtaking is dangerous, so choose weekdays outside holiday periods or start early. Speed cameras and police checks are common. Fog and rain can cut visibility in the gorge, and in winter ice persists in the shaded stretches.

Călimănești, a spa town about six kilometres away, has fuel stations, restaurants and guesthouses, and its mineral springs have drawn visitors for centuries. Local food includes grilled meats, polenta and cheese, plus plum brandy. Autumn is a fine season, with the forest turning to copper, but early summer is also lovely. Remember that Romania requires a road tax sticker called a rovinieta, which is easy to buy online or at the border.
t.dobricel rangoita@47.3,24.1:
North of the Someș river, in the rolling hills of Transylvania, the Romans built a different kind of frontier. The Limes Porolissensis was a line of forts and watchtowers running along the crest of the Meseș mountains and the hills beyond, which guarded the northern edge of the province of Dacia against the free Dacians and the peoples to the north. The section of the Dacia frontier on the World Heritage list, inscribed in 2024, includes many of these small posts, each set on a hilltop with a view for miles. Dobricel and Rângoița are two of those place names, hills in a countryside of villages, orchards and hay meadows, where a ruined stone tower would stand among sheep.

I cannot describe the particular remains at this spot, which are probably modest, but the landscape is the real subject. The hills around Spermezeu are gently folded, wooded with beech and oak and opened up into pastures, with farms scattered on the slopes. Horse carts are still a common sight, haystacks stand in conical piles, and village churches have tall wooden or tin-clad steeples. The air smells of hay and wood smoke.

Riding is quiet and rewarding if you like minor roads. Narrow county roads follow the valleys and climb over ridges, with sudden changes in surface, gravel patches and potholes, so a robust bike and a slow pace help. Livestock, carts and dogs share the road, and village speed limits are strict. In spring, mud and rain can make side roads slippery, and in winter snow comes early on the hills. Navigation by phone can fail, so carry a paper map.

Spermezeu is a village of about two and a half thousand, with a shop and perhaps a bar, and the nearest larger town, Căianu Mic, about eight kilometres off, has fuel and basic shops. Bistrița is the closest big town for supplies. In farm villages you may be offered homemade plum brandy and fresh cheese, and it is polite to accept a small taste. Late spring and early autumn give the best light.
t.dumbraveni dealul dealul rapelor@47.3,24:
Dej is the town where the Someșul Mare and Someșul Mic meet, a river city with a long history of salt and trade, and the hills above it are the setting for Dealul Râpelor, the Hill of Gullies. The name describes a landscape of badlands, where soft clays and marls have been cut into steep ravines by rain, leaving bare slopes, crumbling edges and odd shapes. On the heights above, the Roman army set up a watchtower as part of the northern frontier of Dacia, the Limes Porolissensis, which is now part of the World Heritage listing of the Dacian frontier.

From a height like this, a sentry could watch the valley of the Someș, one of the main routes across Transylvania, and pass signals to the next tower along the ridge. Few ruins show above ground, but the earthworks and stones are there, and the outlook shows why the spot was chosen. The area belongs to the Transylvanian plain, a landscape of hills and valleys that is far greener and more varied than the name suggests, with orchards, vineyards and old villages.

For riders, the road network in this part of Cluj county is a pleasant mixture. The DN1C links Dej to Gherla and Cluj-Napoca, and quieter county roads climb through the hills, past villages with plum orchards and stone churches. Surfaces vary, with some freshly paved sections and some broken ones, and horse carts and tractors are normal. Rain turns clay roads slick, and in summer the heat shimmers over the fields. Take the minor roads slowly, and keep an eye out for dogs.

Dej has around thirty-eight thousand people, so fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants are easy, and the nearest listed village, Ciceu-Giurgești, is small. Salt was once mined near here, and Ocna Dej, nearby, has a salt lake used for bathing. Traditional Transylvanian dishes include sarmale, cabbage rolls, and mămăligă, a cornmeal porridge served with sour cream and cheese. Spring brings blossom and autumn brings the harvest.
t.lozna curmaturita 2@47.3,23.5:
Lozna is a village on the southern edge of the Meseș mountains, and the pass above it, Curmătura, has been a gateway for thousands of years. Further up the range, near Moigrad, lay Porolissum, the largest Roman town in northern Dacia, with an amphitheatre, a customs post and a fort. The pass at the Porta Mesești, the Meseș Gate, was the road that led from the interior of Transylvania toward the plains of the north, and Roman watchtowers stood on the heights on either side, linked by a wall and ditch. The section is part of the World Heritage listing for the Dacian frontier.

What you see at a point like Curmăturița is probably modest, a mound of stones or a faint platform among trees, but with a little imagination the choice of site makes sense. Every watchtower has a view of the one before it and the one after. The mountains here are low, rounded and forested, rising to about eight hundred metres, with beech woods, meadows and farms. Wolves and bears live in the forest, though you are unlikely to meet them.

Riders will like the roads here. The DN1H runs from Jibou through the hills toward Zalău, and the county roads over the Meseș ridge wind through woods with some tight bends and good views. Surfaces vary, and sudden potholes appear, so ride at a measured pace. Summer weekends bring modest traffic, and the weather can turn stormy in the afternoon. Cattle and sheep, and the occasional horse-drawn cart, share the road. Fog in the mountains makes autumn mornings tricky.

Lozna is a small village, and the nearest town of any size is Jibou, about seventeen kilometres away, with a good botanical garden and fuel and shops. Zalău, further on, has everything you need. Try the local plum brandy, called țuică, and a plate of grilled meat with polenta. Early summer, with wildflowers in the meadows, and September, with mellow light, suit riding best.
t.budacu de jos dealul cetatii 2@47.1,24.5:
Bistrița is a Saxon town, founded by German settlers in the twelfth century, and its medieval centre still has a market square lined with arcaded houses and a tall Lutheran church with a green spire. The Transylvanian Saxons were invited by the Hungarian kings to settle and defend this frontier, and they built fortified towns and villages across the region, with their own laws and guilds. Bram Stoker placed the start of Jonathan Harker's journey in Dracula here, at the Golden Krone Hotel, which makes the town a small pilgrimage stop for the curious.

Budacu de Jos lies a short way south, a village in the hills above the Bistrița valley, and Dealul Cetății, Fortress Hill, is the name of its height. A hill with such a name is a sign of an old fortification, and the listing associates it with the Roman frontier of Dacia, added to the World Heritage roll in 2024. I cannot say what stands on the hill today, and like many of these sites it may be little more than grassy ramparts, but the view over the valley explains the choice. The Roman watchers could see up and down a stretch of the river and the roads that followed it.

The countryside is gently hilly, with orchards, meadows and woodland, and the riding is relaxed. The roads follow the valleys, with long, easy curves and few other vehicles, and the DN17 from Bistrița toward the Bârgău mountains and the Tihuța Pass, known as the Borgo Pass in the Dracula story, is one of the most popular rides in the region. Surfaces are variable, and the pass can be foggy and wet, with trucks on the climb.

Bistrița is a town of over eighty thousand, so fuel, hotels and restaurants are easy, and it is the best base for exploring. Try the local pastries, and the Transylvanian stews that go with strong country bread. Late spring and September, when the hills are green or gold, are the best times to ride.
t.gradistea de munte sarmizegetusa regia@4:
Sarmizegetusa Regia was the capital of the Dacian kings, built high in the Orăștie mountains in the first century BC and the first century AD, and it is one of the most atmospheric ruins in Europe. A fortress of stone blocks, a sacred precinct of circular and rectangular temples, and terraces for houses and workshops were laid out on a series of platforms among beech forest, at an altitude of around 1,200 metres. The sanctuary is the star, with rings of stone bases and wooden posts, and a large circular platform of andesite stones that may have worked as a calendar or a place for ritual. Cut stones and finely made tiles show Greek and Roman influence.

King Decebalus made the Dacian kingdom a serious rival to Rome, and Trajan fought two wars against him, in 101 to 102 and 105 to 106. In the second war the Romans besieged and took the fortress, and Decebalus took his own life rather than be paraded in triumph. The scenes are shown in spiralling relief on Trajan's Column in Rome, which is the best record of the war. The Romans then built a new capital, Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, in the Hațeg basin, and the mountain stronghold was abandoned. The site is part of the Dacian Fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains, a World Heritage group since 1999.

The road is the adventure. From Orăștie, you wind up the valley through Costești and Grădiștea de Munte, into steep forested hills, on narrow asphalt that gets rougher near the top. There are tight bends, sudden gravel patches and plenty of cattle. Rain brings mud and fog, and winter can close the upper section with snow. It is a slow, pretty ride, and the last stretch, near the ruins, is a car park with walking paths.

Food is limited, so bring a picnic. Come on a clear day in late spring or early autumn, and expect the temperature to be much cooler than in the valley. A short walk from the car park leads up to the sanctuary.
t.oudtshoorn@-33.6,22.2:
Oudtshoorn owes its elegant sandstone buildings to the feathers of a very large and bad-tempered bird. In the years before the First World War, ostrich feathers were fashionable in Europe and America, and farmers in the Little Karoo made fortunes supplying them. Merchants built grand houses known as feather palaces, with fine stonework and ornate interiors, and some of them still stand. The boom collapsed around 1914, when fashion changed and the war disrupted trade, but ostrich farming continues, now for meat, leather and tourism.

The town lies in a dry valley between two mountain ranges, the Swartberg to the north and the Outeniqua to the south, and the climate is hot and dry, with cold winter nights. It has a population of about sixty thousand and is the main hub of the Little Karoo, with fuel, supermarkets, hotels and restaurants. The CP Nel Museum tells the story of the feather era, and several farms offer tours where you can see the birds up close. They are strong, fast and not as friendly as they appear, so keep your distance.

For riders, Oudtshoorn is a gateway. Route 62 runs through the town, and from here the Cango Caves, a limestone cave system about thirty kilometres north, are an easy day trip. Beyond lies the Swartberg Pass, a gravel road built by the engineer Thomas Bain in the 1880s, which climbs in tight hairpins over the mountains to Prince Albert. It is a spectacular ride, but the surface is loose and the road is narrow, so check conditions and take it slowly.

The best seasons are spring and autumn, with clear skies and moderate temperatures. Summer afternoons can be extremely hot, and winter nights can be near freezing. Try ostrich meat, which is lean and tastes a little like beef, or a plate of Karoo lamb. Early morning is a good time to leave town, when the mountains glow and the air is cool.
t.kerrojupukka jupukka@67.3,23.2:
Somewhere on a rocky hilltop above the Torne river, a small mark in the stone once helped answer a very old question: how big, and what shape, is the Earth? Kerrojupukka is one of the points of the Struve Geodetic Arc, a chain of triangulation stations that stretches roughly 2,800 kilometres from Hammerfest in Norway to the Black Sea. Between 1816 and 1855, the Baltic German astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve and his teams measured it, hilltop by hilltop, working with tripods, signal towers and an extraordinary patience, and the result was one of the most accurate measurements of the Earth's size and flattening made up to that time. Thirty-four of the surviving points, spread across ten countries, were listed as a World Heritage site in 2005. Sweden's share lies up here in the Torne valley.

The setting is Tornedalen, the Torne river valley, which runs along the border between Sweden and Finland, a land of birch and spruce forest, bogs, low rounded hills and slow wide water. Pajala is the nearest village, with about two thousand inhabitants and the fuel and food you will need, because the next services are a long way off. The Arctic Circle lies about seventy kilometres south, and in summer the sun hardly sets, while in winter the northern lights dance over the snow. The people speak Swedish, Finnish and Meankieli, the local Finnish dialect, and Pajala was home to the preacher and botanist Lars Levi Laestadius, whose revivalist movement spread across Lapland.

Riding here is about distance and emptiness. Roads are straight and good, usually quiet, with long views across bogs and forest. The danger is wildlife: reindeer and elk wander onto the tarmac, especially at dusk and dawn, and a collision with an elk can be fatal. Keep speed down, watch the verges and carry a warm layer even in July. Mosquitoes are legendary in midsummer, so bring repellent.

Local specialities include whitefish from the river, cloudberries in late summer, and leipajuusto, a squeaky baked bread cheese, served warm with jam.

The best season is June to August for the endless light, or September for autumn colours and quiet roads. Winters are brutally cold, with temperatures below minus thirty, and are for ice-roads and specialists. Climb the hill, find the marker if you can and imagine surveyors carrying brass instruments up here two centuries ago.
t.hjemmeluft@69.9,23.2:
Six thousand years ago, someone stood on a polished rock slab beside the head of the Alta fjord and began to peck a reindeer into the stone. Then they did it again, and so did their descendants for the next four thousand years. The result, at Hjemmeluft and the other carving fields around Alta, is the biggest collection of prehistoric rock art in northern Europe, thousands of figures of elk, reindeer, bears, fish, boats and people, and some in curious shamanic poses, drumming or dancing. It was listed by UNESCO in 1985. The carvings were made by hunter-gatherers whose world was the shore, the ice and the seasonal movement of animals, and many show hunting scenes, with the line of a reindeer fence or a figure drawing a bow.

A boardwalk loops over the rock slabs near the Alta Museum, which stands right at the site, so you can walk among the carvings in the open, with the fjord glittering on one side. Some of the figures have been painted red so they can be seen in the flat light, a modern aid, and the museum explains how the old carvers worked. The best time to look is at low sun, when the shadows pick out every groove; in summer the midnight sun makes that the quiet hours, and in spring and autumn it comes early and long.

Alta itself, with about twelve thousand people, is the biggest town in Finnmark, a spread-out place known for the northern lights and for the river that bears its name, a famous salmon water that runs through Europe's biggest canyon, Sautso. It also has a recent place in Sami history, because the fight against the Alta dam in the early 1980s was a turning point for Sami rights in Norway. Fuel, food and repairs are all easy here, and it makes a natural base for the northern leg of a long journey.

The riding is classic Arctic. The E6 runs north along the shore of the fjord and across the Finnmark plateau, with bare mountains, lakes and vast skies, and reindeer wandering onto the road in summer, which makes careful riding essential. The North Cape is around two hundred kilometres further on. Summer brings the midnight sun, but also wind and cold rain, so layers are essential. Winter riding is for specialists only.

Try the local salmon or reindeer stew, and a cup of strong coffee.
There is a church in the Polish foothills that has a ceiling like a field of flowers. The Church of the Archangel Michael at Binarowa, near Gorlice in Lesser Poland, was built around the year 1500 from larch and fir logs, in the Gothic style, with a steep shingled roof and a tower covered in wooden scales. From the outside it is a modest, dark country church. Inside it opens into an explosion of painted decoration, with vines, flowers and ornaments on the ceiling, scenes from the Bible and the saints on the walls, and a rich Baroque altar. The paintings date from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The church was listed by UNESCO in 2013 as one of the wooden churches of the Carpathian region, and it is one of the finest in Poland.

Wooden church building was a way of life in these hills. Timber was cheap, carpenters were skilled, and communities, Catholic in this village and Orthodox and Greek Catholic further east, built beautiful churches without stone. Many were destroyed by fire, war and neglect, and the survivors are precious. A marked route, the Wooden Architecture Route of Lesser Poland, links dozens of churches across the region, and you can ride it in a week, picking up a new village and a new roof every few kilometres.

The setting is gentle: green hills, orchards, streams and farms with long barns and haystacks, with the low wooded ridges of the Beskid Niski, the Low Beskids, to the south. Gorlice, the nearest town at around twenty-eight thousand people, has fuel, food and shops. It also has a place in the history of oil: in the mid-nineteenth century, Ignacy Lukasiewicz and his partners drilled some of the first oil wells in the world in this part of Galicia, and a kerosene lamp is a point of local pride. In 1915, the Gorlice-Tarnow offensive broke the Russian front, and many wartime cemeteries dot the hills, designed by Dusan Jurkovic.

The roads are small, curving and quiet, with some rough surfaces, but they make a delightful ride, particularly in May and June when the orchards bloom and again in September. Be sure to check opening times: churches are often locked, and a caretaker will open them on request.

Try a plate of pierogi ruskie, filled with potato and cheese, in a local inn.
t.dacian fortresses of the orastie mountai:
Two thousand years ago, on a ridge in the Orastie Mountains, a king built a capital whose walls were a puzzle that Roman engineers had to solve with blood. The Dacians were a people of the Carpathians, farmers, shepherds and ironworkers, who under their king Burebista and later Decebalus built a powerful state that frightened Rome. To protect it, they built a ring of stone fortresses on hilltops in these mountains, using a technique called murus dacicus, a wall of dressed stone blocks with a core of rubble and timber ties, which could stand up to attack. The six fortresses, including Sarmizegetusa Regia at the heart, Costesti and Blidaru, Luncani-Piatra Rosie and others, were listed by UNESCO in 1999.

Sarmizegetusa Regia stands at about twelve hundred metres in a clearing in the beech forest, with big terraces, a ruined fortress and the sacred area, where circles of stone pillars and a large round platform of andesite suggest religious rites, perhaps astronomical ones. Emperor Trajan took two wars, in AD 101 to 102 and 105 to 106, to defeat Decebalus, who killed himself rather than be taken to Rome. The story is told in spiral on Trajan's Column in Rome, and the Romans blew up the capital and garrisoned it, but the stones remained.

The ride is a pleasure. From Orastie, a small town on the Mures valley with fuel and food, a narrow road climbs up the valley of the Gradiste river, through villages, past Costesti, and into the mountains, with forest on both sides and the road getting steeper and narrower toward the top. Surfaces vary, with potholes and gravel patches, and in winter the road can be closed by snow. The fortresses are in remote spots, so go prepared, with water, rain gear and a spare layer.

The forest has bears, wolves and lynx, though you are unlikely to meet them on the road. In summer, the meadows are full of flowers and the air smells of hay and pine.

The best months are May to October. Local cooking is simple and filling: mamaliga, polenta, with sheep cheese and smoked sausage, and a glass of plum brandy, tuica, for those not riding. Allow a full day, as the site is spread out and the scenery deserves time.
t.cozia masivul cozia@45.3,24.3:
The Olt is one of the few rivers in Romania that cut straight through the Carpathians instead of going around them, and one of the places where it does it is the foot of the Cozia massif. A narrow gorge, a few kilometres long, runs between steep wooded walls, with the river dark and fast at the bottom, a railway and a road squeezed in beside it, and the ridge of Cozia towering on one side. The mountain itself is a rounded, forested block of crystalline rock, high enough to hold snow into spring, and much of it is protected as a national park, with beech, fir and oak, chamois on the high crags, bears in the forest and a good scattering of rare plants.

The riding is tied to that gorge. The national road DN7, the old main route from Sibiu south to Ramnicu Valcea and Bucharest, follows the Olt through the mountains, and it is a famous road for good reasons: wooded slopes, river views, tunnels and long open bends, though it is also one of the busiest roads in the country, full of trucks that make overtaking a gamble. Early morning on a weekday is the answer. The small town of Brezoi, with about six and a half thousand people, has fuel and supplies, and so do the spa villages down the valley at Calimanesti and Caciulata, where hot springs have attracted visitors for generations. From Brezoi a road turns west up the Lotru valley, a quiet climb along reservoirs toward the Transalpina, the great high road across the Parang mountains.

The Cozia monastery, which lies down the valley beside the river, is among the oldest and most important in Wallachia. Prince Mircea the Elder founded it in 1388, and he is buried in its church, a fine stone building with carved doors, painted interiors and a pronaos that is a landmark of medieval Romanian architecture. The monastery was a centre of manuscript copying, and its setting in a bend of the river, against the forested slope, is memorable.

Summer brings crowds and heat in the valley, and the best times are May and June or September, when the forest is green or golden. Winters bring snow and ice on the high bends.

Try trout from a mountain stream, and a bowl of ciorba de burta, the sour tripe soup, in a roadside inn.
t.sangeorgiu de meses dealul la frasini 1@:
The Romans came into the western Carpathian foothills in AD 106, after Trajan's second war against the Dacians, and they decided to keep what they had won. They turned it into the province of Dacia, and on its northwestern edge they drew a frontier along the crest of the Mes mountains, a long, low, forested ridge that runs across northern Transylvania. Along that ridge they built a line of timber towers and small forts, each within sight of the next, so that a watchman could light a fire or wave a signal and the message would run along the whole line in minutes. The frontier zone of Dacia Porolissensis was added to the UNESCO list in 2024 as part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire.

The point labelled Dealul La Frasini 1 belongs to that chain, and the name means the hill at the ash trees. From the coordinates, I believe it is one of the watchtowers, which today survive only as a low square platform of earth and stone in the woods, a place you would not notice without a signboard. I would rather admit that than make up a detail. What I can say is the landscape: rolling, wooded hills, meadows cut for hay, and villages of Romanian and Hungarian speakers, with long views across the Sălaj country.

The nearest village on the map is Starciu, small and quiet, so fuel and food are best found at larger towns. The nearest sizeable place is Crasna, about fourteen kilometres away, with some six thousand people, and Zalău, the county capital, is not far off with every service. The roads here are small, often with rough patches and the occasional hole, climbing and falling over the ridges, with horse carts and cattle on them in summer. The pleasure is in the quiet.

The Mes mountains are low, about six hundred or seven hundred metres at the crest, but they feel like a wall when you cross them. Late spring brings meadows full of flowers, and autumn brings beech colours. Winter can bring snow and black ice.

Local food is generous: sheep cheese, smoked bacon, plum brandy and bread baked in a wood oven. Stop at a farm gate and ask.
t.comarnicel iii@45.6,23.4:
Not every ruin in the Orastie Mountains is a famous one. Comarnicel III sits on the same forested massif as the great Dacian capital of Sarmizegetusa Regia, a few kilometres east of it as the crow flies, and the number in its name tells you that archaeologists have found several sites by that name, each a patch of terrace, wall or platform on a ridge. I cannot say what this particular one held, and I will not guess. What I can say is that the Dacians, before the Roman conquest in the early second century, shaped these mountains with terraces cut into the slopes, with houses, workshops, shrines and defensive walls, and that the remains are scattered across many hillsides.

The land is rugged, steep, forested and cut by narrow valleys, with rushing streams and clearings where shepherds still graze flocks in summer. To the south, beyond the ridge, lies the Jiu valley, a mining country around Petrosani, where Petrila, the nearest large town on the map, was a coal town for more than a century. The contrast is striking: a high green mountain on one side and a landscape of mines and colliery villages on the other. Both are real Romania.

The roads are small and demanding. Forest tracks, gravel and potholed asphalt lead up into the mountains, with steep gradients, tight bends and the occasional stream crossing. After rain they can be slippery, and in winter they are often closed. This is a place for a lightweight bike, a careful rider and a day without hurry. Fuel is to be found in Petrila and the neighbouring towns of the Jiu valley, and in Orastie on the other side, and nowhere in between, so fill the tank beforehand.

Wildlife is rich. The forests hold bears, wolves, lynx, red deer and capercaillie, and the meadows hold orchids. Bears are usually shy, but never leave food in a tent or beside your bike.

The best months are June to September. Even then the weather can turn quickly, with fog and hail, so pack a waterproof. Local shepherds make smoked cheese, burduf, packed in pine bark, and will sometimes sell a piece to a polite visitor.
t.sangeorgiu de meses dealul la frasini 2@:
A watchman on a Roman tower had a simple job and a lonely one. He stood on a wooden platform on a hill, looked along the frontier and waited. If he saw a raiding party coming, he lit a signal fire or beat an alarm, and the next tower along the line repeated it. The men who did this were not Romans from Italy but auxiliaries, soldiers recruited in the provinces, from Gaul, Syria, Thrace or Britain, who served twenty-five years and received citizenship at the end. The second of the two sites at Dealul La Frasini in the Mes hills belongs to that system on the Dacian frontier, and it was recognised by UNESCO in 2024 as part of the Dacia Porolissensis frontier.

I believe the site is a watchtower, but I have no guidebook detail to offer, so let me give you the landscape. The hill sits among low forested ridges and pastures near the village of Starciu, in the county of Salaj, in north-western Romania, in a country where Romanian and Hungarian villages lie side by side. Hay is still cut by hand in many meadows, and haystacks stand in the fields on poles until the winter. In the woods are oak, hornbeam and beech, with hazel scrub at the edges and plenty of mushrooms in autumn.

The roads are minor, narrow and not always well surfaced. They wind over the ridges, and in places the asphalt gives out to gravel. Expect a horse cart or a flock of sheep around any corner. Fuel is available in Crasna and Zalau, and you should not count on any in the villages. Phone signal can drop in the valleys.

Winters are cold and snowy, summers are warm with thunderstorms, and the best times to ride are May to June and September to October. Early morning mist hangs in the hollows, and the whole country has a pastoral calm.

It is worth stopping at the first village shop to buy bread, cheese and a bottle of local water, since the hills do not offer much else. If someone invites you in for a glass of palinca, the strong plum brandy, accept with grace and then ride slowly.
t.falcusa dealul muncelului@47.3,23.8:
Dej sits where two rivers meet, the Somes and the Somesul Mic, and it has been a salt town for as long as anyone remembers. The Romans knew salt here, and so did the medieval Hungarian kings, who taxed it. A few kilometres north-west of the town, on a hill called Dealul Muncelului near the village of Falcusa, the Roman frontier of Dacia Porolissensis left a trace. As far as I can tell from the label, it is one of the watchtowers or small installations of the limes, and it was included in the 2024 UNESCO listing. There is little to see but earth banks and a clearing. What interests me is the line of sight: from here the Romans could watch the road along the Somes valley, a corridor that ran from Napoca, today's Cluj, to the frontier fort at Porolissum.

The surrounding country is the Transylvanian Plain, but not the flat kind. It is a rolling landscape of low hills, clay ridges and shallow valleys, with fields of wheat, maize and sunflowers, plum orchards, and villages of long, low houses. Sheep and cattle graze the slopes, and old wells with wooden sweeps stand beside the road. In summer the hills turn golden, and in autumn there are bonfires of stubble and the smell of woodsmoke.

Dej is a town of about thirty-eight thousand with all you need: fuel, food, repairs. The main road from Cluj to Baia Mare passes nearby and is busy with trucks, so I would use the smaller roads. They are quiet but patched, with potholes in places, and cattle and carts have right of way as a matter of custom. Distances are modest and you can build a gentle day around the hills.

Look at the villages: the churches are often wooden or stone, with tall spires, and cemeteries have carved wooden crosses. Some villages near here have both Orthodox and Reformed churches within sight of each other, a record of the region's mixed history.

Late spring and early autumn are the best times. Midsummer can be hot, and winter can bring fog and ice. Try a plate of sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with pork and rice, with a spoonful of sour cream.
t.dabaceni coama pietrar 2@47.3,23.6:
Coama Pietrar means stone crest, and the name is accurate in a modest way: a stony ridge among pastures and woodland in the hills of northern Transylvania. The site, listed as Dabaceni Coama Pietrar 2, is one of the numbered installations of the Roman frontier of Dacia Porolissensis, and the 2 suggests there is a neighbour. I believe it is a watchtower, though I cannot give you a plan of it, and the visible remains are probably no more than a low mound or square platform in the grass.

What is worth thinking about is why the frontier was here. Beyond the line of towers lay territory not under Roman rule, inhabited by peoples the Romans called free Dacians and Carpi, and the frontier was a place of trade as well as defence. At Porolissum, the big fort and town on the Mes ridge, there was a customs station where goods crossing the line were taxed, and soldiers on the towers were part of a system that managed movement, not only fighting. The frontier was a filter. The system was added to the World Heritage list in 2024.

The country around is gentle upland. Pastures, hay meadows, patches of oak and beech woodland, and small villages tucked into folds in the hills. The village of Rus is the closest on the map, and larger towns are some distance away, with Copalnic-Manastur the nearest one over five thousand. Plan your fuel at a bigger town, and do not expect much in the villages. The roads can be rough, narrow and sometimes steep, with rain turning clay surfaces slick, and the signage is not always clear, so a good map or offline navigation helps.

At haymaking time the air smells sweet, and in autumn the woods are full of mushroom pickers. Weather is changeable, and thunderstorms in summer can be violent. Spring is a delight, with fruit blossom in the orchards.

If you stop in a village, a shop will sell you fresh bread, cheese and cold drinks, and people are generally curious and friendly. A few words of Romanian go a long way, and so does a smile. The hills are quiet and there is little traffic, which is its own reward.
t.buciumi groapa mare@47.1,23.0:
At Buciumi the Romans built a proper fort, not just a tower. It was an auxiliary fort on the frontier of Dacia Porolissensis, a rectangle of earth and stone walls with corner towers and gates, big enough to house a unit of a few hundred men, and it stood on a spur overlooking the approaches from the north. Excavations in the twentieth century found barracks, a headquarters building and a bathhouse. The fort was part of the chain of installations along the Mes ridge, and in 2024 it was recognised by UNESCO as one of the sites of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire in Romania.

The label, Groapa Mare, means big pit, a local name for a hollow near the site, and I cannot tell you what it refers to. But the landscape is clear. This is the northern edge of the Transylvanian hills, where the ridges of the Mes mountains rise in forested steps above the plain of the Salaj. Meadows are mowed by hand, haystacks stand in autumn, and orchards of plums and apples cover the lower slopes. Villages are scattered and small, with wooden barns and tall wells.

A fort like this had a long working life. Troops were stationed here for generations, and with them came traders, craftsmen and families, building a small civilian settlement outside the walls. Archaeologists find coins, pottery, tools and tombstones, which tell of soldiers from many parts of the empire, who married local women and settled down. The frontier was a mixing zone, much as it is today in this part of Romania, with Romanian, Hungarian and Roma communities living close together.

The nearest town of size is Crasna, where you will find fuel, shops and a bank, and the county town of Zalau is a short ride further. The roads are small and winding, with patchy surfaces and sudden holes. Cattle and horse-drawn carts are everyday hazards. A relaxed pace suits the countryside. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with golden light in October and the smell of woodsmoke.

If you see an old man leaning on a gate, ask him about the fort: local people usually know where the stones came from.
t.stana la balize@47.2,23.1:
Zalau is the sort of Romanian city that few foreigners visit, a county capital of some sixty thousand people at the foot of the Mes mountains, with communist-era apartment blocks, a pleasant old centre and a surprisingly rich past. The point called Stana La Balize lies in the hills about five kilometres away, on the edge of the town. Stana means a sheepfold, a summer shepherd's camp, and the word tells you what these slopes were used for: pasture. The second part of the label may refer to markers or boundary posts, but I cannot be sure. As part of the group of sites on the Roman frontier of Dacia Porolissensis, it likely marks a watchtower or a related feature on the ridge above Zalau.

The reason the Romans cared about this place is the gap. North of Zalau the Mes mountains are crossed by a pass, the Mes Gate, a natural doorway between the Transylvanian basin and the plains to the north-west. Whoever controlled the pass controlled the traffic of people, animals and goods. The Romans built Porolissum, a fortress, town and customs post, just above the gate at what is now Moigrad, and the towers and forts along the ridges on either side were part of its web. Today the pass is crossed by a road, and Porolissum is an open-air archaeological park with an amphitheatre, a temple area and the foundations of the fort.

Zalau has all the services a rider needs: fuel stations at every entrance, restaurants, hotels and garages. It is also the best base for visiting this part of the frontier, as the roads fan out to the sites. The ride north over the Mes Gate is a pleasant climb through beech forest, with moderate gradients and a view from the top.

Spring and autumn are the best seasons. Summer can be hot, and winter brings fog and snow. In the villages around, the haystacks, the wells and the sheepfolds look as they have for generations.

Try the Salaj speciality, the sheep cheese called telemea, and a glass of local wine from the hills toward Simleu.
t.hurez dealul mare@47.0,22.9:
Hurez is a village that sits where the foothills of the Apuseni Mountains run out into the Transylvanian basin, and the hill called Dealul Mare, the big hill, is among the sites that make up the Roman frontier of Dacia Porolissensis. The line of towers and forts began near here and ran north-east along the ridges. I believe this one is a watchtower or a related installation, though I cannot supply details, and there is little to see beyond banks and a clearing. It joined the UNESCO list in 2024 with the other Romanian parts of the frontier of the Roman Empire.

The closest town on the map is Huedin, a small place of about nine thousand on the main road from Cluj-Napoca to Oradea, an old crossroads with a long history. Huedin has fuel, food and repair shops, and it is the gateway to the Apuseni, a range of limestone plateaus, caves and forested valleys. The ride from Cluj to Huedin on the old E60 road goes along the valley of the Somesul Rece, with views of the mountains rising to the south, though the road is busy and often slow behind lorries. A far better way to see the country is to turn off into the hills and take the smaller roads, which are quiet and patchy.

The villages around Huedin are known for their folk culture. Calata, in the hills, is famous for its embroidery, a black and red pattern on white cloth, and the villagers still wear traditional costume on feast days. Houses have steep roofs and carved wooden gates, and shepherds bring sheep down from the high pastures in autumn.

Weather can be changeable, with fog in the valleys in autumn and snow from November. The best season is late spring, when the meadows are bright with flowers, and early autumn, when the beeches turn orange.

If you are staying, look for a guesthouse in one of the villages and take the opportunity to eat a home-cooked meal. Typical dishes are tochitura, a pork stew, and papanasi, doughnuts with sour cream and jam, a dessert worth the detour.
t.ciceu poieni varful osoiului@47.3,24.1:
Hay is still cut by hand in the hills of northern Transylvania, and the slopes near Ciceu-Poieni are as good a place as any to see why that matters. This is a country of steep meadows above small villages, with clumps of forest, plum trees along the lanes and the stone-and-wood houses of farmers who still keep a few cows and sheep. Vârful Osoiului is a hilltop name rather than a signed attraction, about four kilometres from Negrilești, and it works best as a way to understand the landscape between the Someș valley and the hills of the north.

In late June and July the meadows are mown with scythes and, increasingly, small mowers, and the cut grass dries in rows and is built into haystacks around a central pole, a shape that varies from village to village. The meadows are rich in flowers, orchids, sage, clover and campanulas, and this sort of traditional hay country is among the most species-diverse farmland in Europe, because it has never been ploughed or sprayed. Butterflies fill the air in summer, and corncrakes, once common across the continent, still rasp from the grass at night in some places.

The roads here wind along ridges and valleys with tight bends, short steep climbs and limited visibility. Surfaces vary a great deal. Main roads are mostly decent, but local ones can be patched or broken, and gravel and mud wash across after rain. Horses and carts, cattle, dogs and slow farm vehicles are common, and nobody is in a hurry, so match the pace. Dusk brings deer and wild boar to the verges.

Fuel is the limiting factor. Negrilești, with fewer than fifteen hundred people, is small, and the more reliable stations are in larger towns in the valley. Fill up beforehand and bring water. Food, when you find it, is hearty and unfussy: stuffed cabbage, polenta with sour cream and cheese, smoked sausages and sweet cheese pastries. A homestay in a village is often the best option for a meal.

Aim for late June or early July if you want the haymaking, or September for clear air and the first colour in the woods.
t.hurez la frasin 2@47.0,23.0:
Frasin is the Romanian word for ash tree, and a place called La Frasin simply means by the ash. Toponyms like this are the real map of rural Romania. Hurez, a commune in the county of Sălaj, and the hills around it are scattered with names that describe a landscape in a few words: a spring, a clearing, a saddle, a lonely tree that once marked a boundary or a meeting place. You can read the countryside by them.

The hills here belong to the Meseș range, a long, low and forested ridge that runs across the north-west of Transylvania and, for centuries, marked the gateway between the Transylvanian plateau and the plain to the west. Cizer, the nearest village of any size, lies about six kilometres away, and Zalău, the county capital, is a reasonable ride beyond. The country is gentle by Carpathian standards, with summits under a thousand metres, but steep enough that the roads wind and the views change at every turn. Forests of beech and oak give way to open pasture and plum orchards in the valleys.

This is also mining country of a quieter kind. Not far south, in the Apuseni Mountains, the Roșia Montană mining landscape, a UNESCO site since 2021, preserves the underground galleries the Romans dug for gold, and the whole region has long been tied to metal and salt. Those histories do not show on the surface here, but they explain why so many tracks and old roads cross these hills.

Riding is a mix of modest tarmac and rough surfaces. Expect narrow roads, tight bends, loose gravel and occasional potholes, with the odd horse and cart, and shepherd dogs that come out of nowhere to inspect a passing bike. Speed limits in villages are fifty and are enforced. Be careful on gravel descents, especially in wet weather when the clay becomes slick.

Fuel is available in the larger towns, and Zalău has everything, but small villages may have only a pump at a shop. A village shop or crossroads bar will sell coffee, beer and a basic sandwich, and often a friendly conversation if your Romanian is better than the barman's English.

Come in autumn, when the beech leaves turn rust and gold, and the plums are picked.
t.bozna osoiul ciontului 1@47.1,23.0:
Sheep run the economy of these hills, and the shepherds have a rhythm that has barely changed. In spring the flocks move up from the villages to the hill pastures around Bozna, in the Sălaj county of north-west Romania, and stay until autumn, with dogs, a few helpers and a hut where the milk is turned into cheese. Osoiul Ciontului is a hilltop name, about six kilometres from Meseșenii de Jos, and it is an invitation to think about this old pastoral life.

The cheeses are simple and good. Caș is the fresh, soft cheese made right after the milking, telemea is a salty, brined cheese similar to feta, and urdă is a ricotta-like curd made from the whey. Smoked cheese is wrapped in spruce bark in some regions, and mămăligă, the polenta that is the national staple, comes with sour cream and cheese. Bring an empty stomach if a shepherd offers you a bite. Refusing can offend.

The dogs deserve a word. Romanian shepherd dogs are big, rough-coated and serious, and they will protect their flock against wolves and strangers. On a motorcycle, you may find yourself being escorted along the road by a pack with no friendly intent, so slow down, do not stop in their midst and keep your speed steady until you pass. They almost never pursue beyond the edge of their pasture.

The riding itself is gentle country-lane stuff. The roads follow valley floors and cross low ridges, with bends tight enough to keep you busy and gradients that are rarely severe. Surfaces vary from smooth asphalt to broken patches, and there is gravel at junctions. Traffic is light, and the main hazards are animals, slow tractors and horse-drawn wagons. In summer, thunderstorms build quickly in the afternoon, and the sky can go dark in minutes.

Fuel is in the larger towns, and Meseșenii de Jos, with a few thousand people, is the nearest sizeable place. Small shops sell basics, and bread, cheese and sausage make a decent roadside lunch.

Spring brings green slopes and the first lambs; autumn, with its mist and woodsmoke, is calmer.
t.treznea varful obarsiei@47.1,23.0:
Treznea is a small village that appears in Romanian history books for a bad reason. In August 1940, the Second Vienna Award, imposed by Germany and Italy, handed northern Transylvania to Hungary, and in the weeks that followed, Hungarian troops entered the area. On 9 September, in Treznea and the neighbouring village of Ip, dozens of Romanian civilians were killed in reprisals, and a memorial in Treznea recalls them. The territory returned to Romania in 1944, but the memory of those years still shapes local life.

The landscape is not dramatic, which is part of the contrast. The village lies on the southern flank of the Meseș Mountains, in the county of Sălaj, among rolling hills of pasture, orchard and beech wood, and Vârful Obârșiei, the hilltop that gives this point its name, is a quiet summit about six kilometres from Meseșenii de Jos. The word obârșie means source or origin, and in Romanian usage it can mean the head of a stream. Clear small streams run off the ridges here and feed the rivers of the Crasna valley below.

Mixed communities of Romanians, Hungarians and Roma live across this region, and the older houses and churches reflect all three traditions, with Orthodox, Greek Catholic and Reformed churches sometimes in the same valley. That makes the area a lesson in how complicated borders can be, and a reminder to be respectful and curious when you talk to the people you meet.

For riders the roads are quiet and winding, with plenty of bends, short climbs and views from the ridges. Surfaces range from decent asphalt to rough patches and gravel, so ride within your sight, and watch for horses, carts, geese and stray dogs. Weather in the Meseș is changeable, with fog in cooler months and heavy summer storms. Fuel is limited in the villages, so fill up in larger towns, and Zalău is the reliable choice. Small shops in the villages sell coffee, bread and simple food.

An unhurried visit in spring or autumn, with an hour spent at the memorial, adds a sober but meaningful layer to the ride.
t.buciumi coasta ograzii 2@47.1,23.0:
Plums are the quiet crop of Sălaj, and in the hills around Buciumi the orchards tell you so in every direction. In September, branches bend under purple fruit, the verges are littered with windfalls, and the smell of fermenting mash drifts from backyard stills, because this is where țuică is made. Țuică is the plum brandy of Romania, usually distilled twice, and served in small glasses with food. In Transylvania, the stronger, double-distilled version is often called pălincă.

Coasta Ogrăzii, a hillside name that roughly means the slope of the garden or yard, is one of several points around Buciumi, a village about six kilometres from Stârciu, and it sits among smallholdings where families keep an orchard, a pig, some hens and a kitchen garden. Distilling is a social ritual, with neighbours sharing a licensed still, and a tour of the villages in autumn would be incomplete without a sip offered by somebody's grandfather. Politeness suggests you accept a small glass and hold it for a toast, but with a bike waiting outside, a sip is enough, and nobody will be offended if you say you are riding.

The riding is quiet and varied. Lanes snake along the hillsides between the orchards, with short steep rises and bends that suit a light bike. The surface is variable, with smooth patches, rough ones and a lot of grit. Autumn adds wet leaves, squashed plums and mud on the road, a slippery combination, so slow down in the orchards. Traffic is rare, mostly small tractors, horse wagons and the occasional car.

Fuel is the practical constraint. Stârciu, with just over a thousand people, is too small to count on, and larger towns such as Zalău have stations and shops. Pack water and a snack, and ask at a village shop before heading up a track.

In late April, when the plum blossom turns the slopes white and the first warm day brings out the bees, it is just as good as autumn.
t.mesesenii de sus coasta ciungii 1@47.1,2:
