Poarta Meseșană, the Meseș Gate, is the narrow pass through the Meseș Mountains that has carried travellers between Transylvania and the Hungarian plain for two thousand years. The Romans knew it, and watched it. Not far north of Zalău, on the heights above the pass, the Roman town and fort of Porolissum guarded this entrance to the province of Dacia, and its amphitheatre, customs post and the remains of the frontier wall can still be seen on the hill at Moigrad. The ridge to the south, where Meseșenii de Sus lies, was part of the same defensive landscape, with watchtowers on the high points.

Coasta Ciungii, the slope of the crippled one, if you take the old word literally, is one of several hill names near the village, and the point lies about six kilometres from Meseșenii de Jos. The Meseș range is a long, low backbone, thickly forested, rarely rising above a thousand metres, and its slopes are a patchwork of beech wood, pasture and orchard. From its crest, on a clear day, the plain opens to the west and the Carpathians rise to the east.

Geologically, the Meseș is a mix of crystalline rock and limestone, with small caves and rock outcrops, and a few springs that rise at its foot. Wildlife includes roe deer, wild boar and foxes, with wolves and lynx in the wilder woods further east, and the bird life in summer ranges from buzzards and honey buzzards to hoopoes in the open farmland.

Riding the minor roads here means narrow strips of tarmac, steep short gradients and many blind bends, with patched or gravel surfaces at times. Take care in the hills when it rains, since the clay turns greasy, and watch for animals on the road, especially at dusk. In winter, snow and ice make some of the smaller roads impassable for a motorcycle. A visit to Porolissum is a good detour, and its site museum helps with the layers.

Fuel is easy in Zalău, a city of over sixty thousand, a short ride away, and basic supplies are available in the larger villages. Try a village shop for bread, sausage and cheese, and a roadside bar for coffee.

Spring and early autumn have the best light and the least mud.
t.buciumi dosul sigaului@47.1,23.0:
Wooden churches are the signature of this part of Romania, and Sălaj has some of the finest outside Maramureș. In the hills around Buciumi, tall shingled steeples rise above hay meadows, and inside the dark timber interiors the walls are covered with faded paintings of saints, angels and devils. Many were built in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries by village carpenters who had no architect, only a feel for proportion, and the best of them seem to grow out of the ground.

Dosul Șigăului, one of several hill points around Buciumi, about six kilometres from Stârciu, is a ridge name rather than a landmark, and the church story belongs to the whole district. Transylvanian villages here often have a Greek Catholic history. In 1700, many Romanian Orthodox in Transylvania accepted union with Rome in exchange for rights under Habsburg rule, and this Greek Catholic Church became a pillar of Romanian national awakening. It was banned by the communist government in 1948, its property was given to the Orthodox Church, and many congregations met secretly until 1989. Today, in many villages, two churches stand close together, one old and wooden, one new and concrete, which can lead to disputes but also to some very lovely architecture.

If a church is open, step in quietly and ask permission to look around, and respect the rule that women cover their heads and men remove hats. Often a key is kept by a neighbour, and a small tip is welcome. Look at the paintings, which usually include a Last Judgement, and at the carved doors.

Riding here is on small hilly roads with plenty of bends, loose stones and potholes, and a lot of agricultural traffic. The main road through the valleys is decent, but the lanes up to the hill villages can be rough. Fog in the early morning and storms in the afternoon are common in summer. Fuel is hard to come by locally, because Stârciu is tiny, so fill up in Zalău or another larger town before you go. Basic shops stock water, bread and sweets.

Early morning, when the church bells ring and the hay smells sweet, is the best time to arrive.
t.alba iulia apulum ravelinul capistrano@4:
Alba Iulia is the town that Romanians think of as the birthplace of their country. On 1 December 1918, a great national assembly met here and voted for the union of Transylvania with the Kingdom of Romania, an event celebrated every year as the national day. Four years later, in 1922, King Ferdinand and Queen Marie were crowned in a cathedral built for the purpose, and the fortress became a symbol of the modern Romanian state.

The fortress itself is older and more intricate. Built between 1715 and 1738 by the Habsburgs, in the style of the French engineer Vauban, it is a huge star-shaped citadel with seven bastions, ramparts, gates and ditches, one of the largest fortifications of its kind in southeastern Europe. A ravelin is a triangular outwork set before a curtain wall to cover the gate, and Capistrano is one of several such works, with grassy banks and stone walls that now serve as a park. The gates are ornamented with Baroque sculpture, and on summer mornings, guards in period uniform march along the walls.

Underneath the star lie older layers. The Romans founded Apulum here, a major legionary base, and the Dacian predecessors, the medieval Transylvanian princes and Michael the Brave, who briefly united Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania in 1600, all left their mark. Michael is remembered in the town by a monument near the fortress.

For riders, Alba Iulia is an easy base, with a calm centre and a ring of quiet roads along the Mureș river and into the surrounding wine hills. The citadel streets are partly cobbled, with limited vehicle access, so park outside and walk. Fuel and services are plentiful in a town of some sixty-five thousand people, and cafés and restaurants line the streets near the main gate. Try the local wines, including fresh whites from the Alba vineyards, or a bowl of ciorbă, a sour soup, in one of the cellars.

The fortress is open from morning to evening, and evenings in summer have a pleasant crowd.
t.saratel cetate 2@47.1,24.4:
Bistrița, the main town of this northern corner of Transylvania, was a Saxon stronghold, and the villages around Sărățel still carry traces of the German settlers who came in the twelfth century at the invitation of the Hungarian kings. Sărățel itself, near the Șieu river, takes its name from a word for salty, and this part of the Transylvanian plain lies over salt-bearing rock, which has produced salty springs and mud for centuries. Cetate means citadel in Romanian, and the second of two hilltops with that name lies about four kilometres from Șieu-Măgheruș.

The hills here are low and open, a patchwork of cultivated fields, grazing land and small woodlots, with soft ridges that run across the horizon. Their shapes explain why defenders built forts on the ridges: they have a clear view for miles. Which period the cetate is from is something an archaeologist would want to tell you, since hillforts in this region range from prehistoric times to the Middle Ages, and I would not like to guess.

The Saxon towns and fortified churches of the region make a rewarding detour. Bistrița has a medieval town centre with a Gothic Evangelical church and an arcaded main square. It also has a literary claim: Bram Stoker, who never visited, sent his hero Jonathan Harker through Bistrița on the way to Count Dracula's castle in Dracula, and a hotel in town still bears the name of the Golden Krone he described.

For riders the roads in the plain are broad and gently rolling, with a few steeper climbs, and surfaces that vary from newish asphalt to potholed patches. Traffic is moderate, with trucks on the main routes, and the minor roads are quieter. Watch for horse-drawn carts and animals. In summer, heat can be strong, and storms can form fast. Fuel is easy in Bistrița and in larger villages along the main roads; carry cash for small shops.

Late summer, when the sunflowers and maize are high and the stubble fields are golden, gives the area its best colour.
t.zalau dealul celor sase cai@47.2,23.1:
Zalău is the kind of county town that most visitors drive straight through, which is a pity, because it has more history than its blocks of communist-era flats suggest. It is the capital of Sălaj, a county that long went by the Latin-flavoured name Silvania, the land of forests, and it sits in a green basin below the Meseș Mountains with a population of about sixty-three thousand. The hill called Dealul Celor Șase Cai, the Hill of the Six Horses, lies a few kilometres outside the centre, and what exactly the horses were nobody on the map will tell you.

The town's cultural weight comes from the Reformed college founded here in the seventeenth century, named after the Wesselényi family who patronised it, and from the teenager who went to school in its classrooms: the Hungarian poet Endre Ady, who studied at the college in the late 1880s and early 1890s and is remembered with a statue. The county museum in town looks after finds from Porolissum, the Roman frontier city on the heights to the north, and it is a good place to start if you want to know what the Romans were doing in these hills.

For the rider, Zalău is the useful end of the day. It has every kind of fuel station, supermarkets, tyre shops and a few hotels, and the roads that leave it climb quickly into the hills in several directions, with bends, short steep rises and views over orchards and pasture. Those back roads are narrow and a little rough in patches, and in many villages the road surface gives way to gravel at the edges. Traffic on the main roads includes lorries, so overtaking needs care, and speed limits drop sharply in the villages.

Eat plainly and well. A lunch menu in a town restaurant will usually offer a clear soup, a pork or chicken main with potatoes or polenta, and a pancake with jam, for what an English traveller would think a startlingly modest sum. The coffee is strong and served with a small glass of water.

If you have time, the Roman ruins at Moigrad are a short run north, and the wooded ridge behind them gives a feel for how remote this frontier once was.
t.sita casa uriesilor@47.3,24.2:
Giants appear in the place names of the northern Carpathian hills, and Casa Urieșilor, the House of the Giants, is one of them. Sita, a hill name rather than a village stop, lies about four kilometres from Spermezeu in the county of Bistrița-Năsăud, in a country of forest, hay meadows and scattered farms between the Someș valley and the first ridges of the Țibleș range. I cannot tell you what the giants did, and neither, I suspect, can most of the people who live nearby; the name is a piece of folk memory attached to a rock or a clearing, and it is better left a mystery.

Romanian folklore is full of such beings, huge ancestors who lived before the present race and moved boulders, dug lakes or threw stones at each other across valleys. Where a field of loose rocks or a strange outcrop catches the eye, someone has usually said that a giant left it. Alongside them there are fairies, the iele, whom you must not name after dark, and the strigoi, the restless dead, and a good deal of local life is still shaped by saints' days and the old agricultural calendar, with bonfires on the eve of St John in June.

For the rider the area is a collection of narrow valley roads linked by steep ridge crossings. The main road through Spermezeu is decent, but the side roads that climb toward the hill farms are patched and sometimes gravelled, and a sharp rain shower turns the clay to grease. Corners are tight, visibility is limited by hedges and hay, and you may meet a horse cart or a herd of cows in the middle of the road. A relaxed pace, plenty of space to stop, and a light touch on the brakes will see you through.

Spermezeu has some two and a half thousand people and a few shops, and you can find coffee and basic food, but fuel is better sought in larger towns such as Năsăud or Bistrița, so start the day with a full tank. Mobile signal can fade in the valleys, so carry a paper map or an offline one.

Autumn mornings, with mist in the hollows and smoke rising from chimneys, make the legends feel closer.
t.popeni voievodeasa 3@47.2,23.2:
Voievodeasa means the voivode's wife, and the hill that carries the name is one of several summits that rise around Popeni, in the north-west of Sălaj. Who she was and which voivode she belonged to is not on any signpost, and local stories differ, so it is safest to say that the name belongs to the long age of Transylvanian princes and nobles whose estates, castles and quarrels once shaped these hills. The point lies about four kilometres from Creaca, a village of nearly three thousand.

What you can see for yourself is the birdlife, which is remarkable for a district that rarely appears in a bird guide. The mixture of hay meadow, hedgerow, scrub and woodland supports species that have vanished from much of western Europe. Red-backed shrikes impale their prey on thorns along the lanes, hoopoes probe the short grass near farmyards, and in spring cuckoos and golden orioles call from the oak woods. Honey buzzards and short-toed eagles wheel above the ridges on warm days, and storks nest on utility poles in the villages, often in the same spot for decades.

The Meseș hills are not high, but they run in long folds, so a ride across them is a succession of short climbs and descents with quick changes of view. The road surface varies. Some stretches have been resurfaced, while others are broken by frost and spring floods, and loose gravel collects on the outside of bends. Slow tractors are the commonest obstacle, followed by dogs and ducks. Dusk brings wild boar and roe deer, so avoid riding after dark if you can.

Fuel is a question of planning. Creaca has a few shops and a place to eat, but a proper filling station is more likely in Zalău, a half-hour away. Carry water, since the villages may not have a convenient tap, and take a layer for the evening, when the air cools quickly after sunset.

Early summer is the time for birdsong, and a quiet pause on a verge, with the engine off and binoculars in hand, is rewarded.
t.buciumi poiana seredanilor@47.1,23.0:
Bees do well in the hills around Buciumi, where acacia, linden, wildflower meadows and fruit orchards flower in turn from April to August, and in many gardens a few painted hives sit under the plum trees. Poiana Șeredanilor, which one might loosely translate as the glade of the Șeredan family or people, is a clearing name near the village, about five kilometres from Stârciu. It is a place on a map more than a viewpoint, but it gives you the right country for talking about honey.

Romania is one of Europe's major honey producers, and acacia honey, pale and clear and slow to crystallise, is the national favourite, with linden, sunflower and mixed forest honey close behind. Many villagers keep a handful of hives and sell jars at the roadside, usually with a hand-lettered sign and no attendant, just a bucket for money. Look for a table at a gate with jars of honey, jam, pickled vegetables and a bottle of something stronger. The bees are gentle enough, but when the hives are being worked, a dark leather jacket can excite them, so keep moving.

The area's riding is sociable rather than demanding. Lanes meander between meadows and orchards, with gentle bends and short hills, and most of the surface is acceptable, though there are rough sections where heavy trucks have broken the edges. Villages come with sudden speed bumps and children on bicycles. In hot weather, the smell of mown hay and of wild thyme drifts across the road, and swallows skim the tarmac. Sudden summer storms are common in the afternoon, and the forecast can change fast.

Fuel is not available at Stârciu, a village of just over a thousand, so plan a stop in a larger place such as Zalău before heading up into the hills. A village shop will sell basics, and if you strike up a conversation the owner may offer a spoonful of the latest harvest.

Late May, when the acacia blooms and the air is heavy with scent, is as good as it gets.
t.ortelec dealul magurice 1@47.2,23.1:
Măgurice is a small măgură, and a măgură in Romanian is a rounded hill, usually isolated, often with a tuft of trees at the top. Ortelec, the village the point belongs to, sits in the western foothills of the Meseș range in Sălaj, about four kilometres from Mirșid, and Dealul Măgurice rises among a series of such low, smooth summits above a landscape of hay meadows and plum orchards. The landscape here was never rugged. It was shaped by water and by centuries of grazing, and the soil is a heavy clay that holds moisture.

That clay explains a good deal about the riding. In dry spells the lanes are firm and pleasant, with little dust, but after rain they become slick and sticky, and a thin film of mud coats the tarmac wherever a tractor has turned in from a field. The bends here come in clusters, short, tight and often blind because of hedges and tall grass, and hills are short but steep. A bike with decent tyres and a rider with patience will do well. Autumn and spring bring the greatest variation, with fog in the morning and sun in the afternoon, and winter often means ice on shaded corners.

Ortelec is a quiet place, and the sound you will most often hear is a cowbell or a distant chainsaw. Houses are painted in pastel colours with tall wooden gates, and elderly women in headscarves sit on benches in the evening watching the road. Greetings matter. A nod or a raised hand is returned, and a rider who stops to ask the way is usually met with curiosity and directions that include landmarks like the old school and the third plum tree. Mirșid, the nearest town, has a few thousand inhabitants, with shops and a bakery.

Fuel is the one shortage. Mirșid has little, and the surest supply is in Zalău, so fill up there before you leave. Bring cash, because smaller shops may not take cards.

On a clear morning in June, with the haymaking just begun and the swallows low over the fields, you will see the country at its most generous.
t.zalau dealul dojii 2@47.2,23.1:
Winter changes the character of the hills around Zalău completely. The town sits at the foot of the Meseș Mountains, in a basin that traps cold air, and from December to February the hills are often grey and fogbound, with snow lying on the shaded slopes and ice in the hollows. Dealul Dojii, one of the summits on the town's edge, about five kilometres from the centre, is an ordinary hill name, and it gives you a good excuse to talk about the seasons.

Spring comes late and quickly. By April the plum and cherry trees are in blossom, the hay meadows turn green, and the first storks return to their nests, clacking from chimney tops in the villages. May and June are the finest months for riding, with warm, clear days, wildflowers on every bank and long evenings. Midsummer can be hot, often over thirty degrees in the valley, and the afternoon often ends with a thunderstorm, sometimes with hail. Late September and October bring clear, cool days and a long procession of colour as the beech woods turn.

The roads follow the weather. In spring, frost heave and the meltwater from the snow leave potholes, and the local council patches them slowly. In summer, road edges crumble in the heat, and tar can soften on the sunniest slopes. Autumn leaves make bends slippery. And in winter, the hill roads may be iced or covered with packed snow for days, which suits tractors and not motorcycles. If you are planning a longer route, check the forecast the night before and be ready to turn back.

Zalău itself is a good base year-round, with fuel stations, a cluster of hotels and guesthouses, bakeries and supermarkets. There are also a number of garages that can fix a punctured tyre or a loose chain. The pedestrian streets in the centre have cafés and terraces that fill when the sun comes out.

Choose May or October, and pack both a warm layer and a waterproof.
t.perisor ponoara in varf@47.3,24.2:
A ponoară, in the Romanian of these hills, is a sinkhole or swallow hole, a place where a stream vanishes into the ground. Ponoară în Vârf, which translates roughly as the sinkhole at the top, is a name that suggests limestone, and limestone country has its own character: dry ridges, hidden springs, small caves and sudden depressions in the meadows where the soil has collapsed. The point lies near Perișor, about four kilometres from Spermezeu, in the north of Bistrița-Năsăud county, and I have not seen the sinkhole itself, but it fits the geology of the region.

Karst country has a way of confusing the water. Streams dry up in summer and reappear lower down the valley as springs, wells run low in drought, and old people can tell you exactly which spring never fails. Many villages are built around a single dependable source with a stone trough and a carved wooden spout, where passers-by stop to drink and fill bottles. If you find one beside the road, the water is usually cold and good, though in an uncertain place it is wise to ask a local before drinking.

The ride here is slow and varied. Roads follow the valley floors and then climb steeply up and over spurs, with some hairpins on the steepest sections and gravel on others. Rain in the hills can bring mud and small rockfalls, and in winter the shaded bends are treacherous. In summer, expect farm traffic, horses and cattle, and beware of dogs that guard the flocks. Light on the descents is dappled and changes fast, so slow down for the shadows.

Spermezeu, with some two and a half thousand people, has a few shops and cafés, but fuel is scarce, and the safest plan is to fill up in a larger town before heading into the hills. Phone signal can drop out in the valleys.

Spring, when the streams are full and the beech leaves are fresh, is the best moment for this country.
t.ortelec dealul magurice la stramtura 1@4:
Strâmtură means a narrow place, a gap or defile, and La Strâmtură is a spot where the Măgurice hills pinch a stream and a lane into a tight corridor. The point lies near Ortelec, about four kilometres from Mirșid in the western Meseș, and the narrowness gives the whole valley a sense of enclosure that you can feel on a bike: the road shrinks, the trees close in and the sound of the engine bounces off the banks.

In places like this, water has always been a source of power and food. Small streams in these hills once turned the wheels of mills, grinding maize and wheat for whole villages, and many mill sites survive as overgrown stone foundations beside the water. Some of the streams hold trout and grayling, and villagers still fish them on summer evenings. Crayfish, which need clean water, were once common and are making a modest comeback in some places. The Meseș is a quiet corner of Romania, and the quietness shows in the water.

Another reality is that many of the people who built the houses are no longer here. Since the 1990s, many families from Sălaj have worked abroad, in Italy, Spain, Germany and elsewhere, and money sent home has paid for large new houses, some of which stand empty for most of the year. They are often built in a showy style with tall columns and tiled roofs, beside older farmhouses of timber and daub. The result is a countryside in which new and old stand cheek by jowl, and in which the population is older than it once was.

The riding is narrow and technical, with short sections of damp, shaded road and little room for error. Slow down for the blind bends, and give cyclists and walkers plenty of space. Mirșid has a few shops, but fuel is better found in Zalău, so arrive with a full tank. In the summer holidays, the villages briefly fill with returning families and the roads are busier.

Visit in late summer, around the time of the village festivals, when the diaspora comes home.
t.buciumi coasta ograzii 1@47.1,23.0:
Coasta Ogrăzii, the slope of the yard, is a hill name that recurs around Buciumi, and the first of the two points sits on the side of a ridge about five kilometres from Stârciu. Hillside names like this describe the old pattern of farming here: a garden or paddock on a slope close to the house, kept for fruit, vegetables or a cow, with the forest above and the stream below. It is a landscape of small scale, in which a family might own a dozen scattered plots of a few hundred square metres each.

That pattern comes from land reform and its reversal. After the Second World War, the communist government collectivised farmland, and in the early 1990s the land was returned in small parcels to the heirs of former owners, often with no clear boundaries. The result is a patchwork, with hay cut in strips of different lengths and a good deal of abandoned land that is turning into scrub and birch. Some farmers have gone, and others have stayed and kept a few cows. The change is visible from the road, and it is one reason the hay meadows are so rich in flowers: the traditional, low-intensity farming that created them still goes on in many places.

For the rider, the lanes on this slope are among the better ones in the area, with a recent patch of asphalt in places and a firm, if narrow, gravel track in others. The bends are smooth, the gradients modest, and the views across the hills are wide. Even so, the usual rural hazards apply: a cow in the road, a tractor around a blind corner, a dog asleep in the middle of a bridge. Slow down at the entrances to farms, where mud and straw often cover the surface, and keep an eye out for children playing near the roadside.

Fuel is available in Zalău rather than in Stârciu, which is a small village with a shop and little else, so plan a stop in town. Carry water, a spare layer and some cash.

A weekday afternoon in mid-June, when the hay is down and the air smells of cut grass, shows the place at its best.
t.negrilesti cornul malului 1@47.3,24.1:
Sunday is the day to see Negrilești as it wants to be seen. The village, a few kilometres from the hill known as Cornul Malului, the horn of the bank, lies in the northern part of Bistrița-Năsăud county, and on a Sunday morning the lanes fill with people in their best clothes walking to the church, the older women in headscarves and dark skirts, the men in waistcoats, the children scrubbed and unhappy. After the service, groups gather outside, the bells keep ringing for a while, and the village eats late.

Traditional costume in this region has its own logic. Women's blouses, called ii, are white linen embroidered at the sleeves and neck with geometric patterns, and every region has its own motifs and colours; the Romanian blouse became an emblem of national identity in the twentieth century and has a way of turning up on fashion catwalks. Men wear a sheepskin vest, a wide leather belt and a black hat. In some villages you will still see the costume on feast days, at weddings and at the Sunday hora, the village dance, and young people have started wearing pieces again as a point of pride.

Weddings in the countryside are a big affair, with a band of fiddle, accordion and drums, three days of eating, and a long procession through the village. If you hear music drifting from a field or a yard in summer, it is likely a wedding or a christening, and it is quite acceptable to wave and walk on rather than stop. The same goes for funerals, which are held at home and followed by a meal.

The road to Cornul Malului is a narrow and winding country lane with tight bends and patched asphalt. Take care at Sunday church times, when pedestrians crowd the road and cars park along the verges. Negrilești has barely fifteen hundred people and no reliable fuel, so the bigger towns, such as Năsăud or Bistrița, are where to fill the tank. A village shop sells water, bread and snacks, and often a few simple pastries on Sunday.

A summer Sunday in the early afternoon, when the village slows to a nap, is a good moment to pass quietly through.
t.zalau poienita@47.2,23.1:
Poieniță is a small poiană, which is the Romanian word for a clearing in the forest, and a clearing is a good place to begin talking about mushrooms. Around Zalău, from late summer to the first frosts, the woods are full of people with baskets and plastic bags, wandering slowly between the beech trunks with their eyes on the ground. The Poieniță point lies a few kilometres outside the town, on the wooded edge of the Meseș foothills, and it belongs to a tradition of foraging that has not died out with the arrival of supermarkets.

Chanterelles, known here as gălbiori, are the favourite, sold by the roadside in tubs and mixed into omelettes, stews and soups. Porcini, or hribi, appear after warm autumn rain, and a few foragers know good places they would never share. Wild raspberries and blueberries ripen in summer, and elderflower and acacia blossom are turned into syrup and fritters in spring. Every household seems to have a jar of forest jam or pickled mushrooms in the cellar. It is a good rule never to eat anything you cannot identify, and to buy mushrooms from a seller who can tell you what they are.

The forest roads are the quiet pleasure of the ride. Beech and hornbeam arch overhead and filter the light into a soft green, which is lovely on a hot day. The surface is sometimes smooth and sometimes broken, with branches, mud and leaves, and logging lorries use some of the tracks, so expect mud from their tyres and a short stretch of tarmac wrecked by their weight. Do not go deep into the woods on a road bike after rain, since clay roads can become impassable, and do not leave your bike on a track used by timber trucks.

Zalău has everything a rider needs, from fuel to repairs, and it is close enough that a day out in the forest is easy to turn around. Small cafés in the town serve strong coffee and plum pastries.

Early morning in September, with mist in the beech wood and a chill on the air, is the ideal hour.
t.zalau langa masa craiului@47.2,23.1:
Masa Craiului means the King's Table, and the name is borrowed here for a hill or a flat rock near Zalău, but it brings to mind the great limestone ridge of Piatra Craiului far to the south, the King's Rock, where the idea of a royal table in the mountains started. Lângă Masa Craiului, beside the King's Table, is the sort of name that must once have pointed to a flat boulder or a table-topped crag. I do not know which, but the hills here have plenty of such features.

What I can tell you is what the Romans left. Just north of Zalău, on a ridge above the village of Moigrad, lie the ruins of Porolissum, the frontier town of Roman Dacia. Founded after the conquest of Dacia in the early second century, it grew into a customs station and a garrison town of some importance, with forts on the neighbouring hills, a forum, temples, an amphitheatre and the remains of a wall that ran along the ridge. Soldiers from across the empire served here, and the inscriptions they left include dedications to the gods of far-off homelands. The setting, on a long wooded ridge looking out to the pass, is remarkable, and the site museum explains the layout.

The ride from Zalău to Moigrad is short and pleasant, with a road that winds up through the villages and then through beech woods to the ridge. Bends are tight, surfaces are decent in most places, and traffic is light, apart from the occasional bus or farm vehicle. On the site itself, the tracks are gravel and grassy, so leave the bike at the car park and walk. Wear sturdy shoes, since the hill is steep and the stones are uneven. In the rain, the clay path becomes slippery.

Zalău is a city of more than sixty thousand, with several fuel stations and many places to eat. There are also a few simple cafés near the ruins, and local families sell honey and plum brandy from stalls at weekends.

Go on a clear spring day, when the grass is green and the view reaches far over the plain.
t.alba iulia palatul guvernatorului@46.1,2:
The Habsburgs rebuilt Alba Iulia in the early eighteenth century as a fortress, and the buildings inside the walls still bear the mark of imperial administration. After the Habsburgs took control of Transylvania at the end of the seventeenth century, they chose this old princely seat as a military and administrative base, and a succession of governors and garrison commanders lived and worked in the barracks, arsenals and offices that fill the citadel. The Governor's Palace takes its name from that period. Oarda, a village now almost a suburb, lies just to the south, along the Mureș river.

That river is the thread of the place. The Mureș rises in the eastern Carpathians and runs west across Transylvania to the Hungarian plain, and for two thousand years it has carried traffic and people. The Romans built their military base on its bank, in what is now the Partoș district, and later the Roman town grew up in the area of Oarda and Alba Iulia. Gold from the Apuseni Mountains, which lie to the west, came down this valley, and the wealth it brought explains why Apulum was among the largest cities in Roman Dacia.

Inside the walls, today's visitor finds a restored and car-free town of cobbled streets, cafés, shops and museums. The Batthyaneum library, founded by a Catholic bishop, preserves a rare collection of manuscripts and has an astronomical observatory that was once one of the best in the region. The Union Hall, where the 1918 assembly met, is a short walk away. Outside the walls, the town has broad modern avenues, with plenty of space to park.

Riding in and out of Alba Iulia is easy. The main roads run along the Mureș valley with long gentle bends and moderate traffic, with lorries and buses on the busier stretches. The quieter roads along the foothills to the west pass through vineyards and orchards and are good for a relaxed morning. Fuel and everything else are easy in a town of some sixty-five thousand people. Many guesthouses are tucked into the old streets.

Autumn, with the harvest of grapes and the smell of new wine in the cellars, is a good time to visit.
t.negrilesti cornul malului 2@47.3,24.1:
Two points carry the name Cornul Malului, and the second of them belongs to the same ridge as the first, just over a kilometre from Negrilești, a village of fewer than fifteen hundred people in the north of Bistrița-Năsăud county. The name means the horn of the bank, and in the language of these hills a mal is a steep bank, a slope above a stream or a field boundary, so the horn must be a spur or a corner that juts out from the hillside. It is another quiet high field in a country made of them.

Look north and east from the ridges of this part of Transylvania and the land begins to rise toward the mountains. The Țibleș and Rodna ranges lie in that direction, the latter a long crest of crystalline rock that peaks at Pietrosul Rodnei, at 2,303 metres, and has glacial lakes, alpine meadows and a national park. Chamois, marmots and, in the forests, brown bears live there. On the hills around Negrilești you are in the foothills of that world, where the climate is a little cooler and wetter than on the plain.

Weather matters here. The hills catch the westerly rain and the winter snow comes early, so autumn and spring can be wet and muddy. Mist forms in the valleys at dawn and slowly burns off, and thunderstorms in summer roll in quickly. For a motorcyclist, this means a rain jacket is not optional, and a morning that starts in sunshine may need a layer by noon. Road surfaces in the hills are mixed, with decent asphalt on the main roads and potholes or gravel on the side lanes, so check ahead before taking a lane you do not know.

The nearest fuel is in a larger town, and Năsăud or Bistrița are the safer places to fill up. Negrilești has a couple of shops for water and bread. Keep an eye on the fuel gauge, since the distances feel short on the map but the winding roads use more petrol than you expect.

Visit on a day with good visibility in spring or autumn, when the snow still sits on the high ranges.
t.sangeorgiu de meses@47.0,23.0:
Saint George is the patron of this village, and on 23 April, his feast day, Sângeorgiu de Meseș comes to life. Romanians call the day Sângeorz or Sfântul Gheorghe, and in rural Transylvania it has long marked the start of the pastoral year, the day when sheep are taken to the hills and the shepherds make their contracts for the season. Green branches are hung on gates, fires are lit, and people make sure to eat lamb. The village sits in the western Meseș, about six kilometres from Cizer, a village of some two and a half thousand.

Villages named after saints are common in Transylvania, and the church usually keeps the name alive. Sângeorgiu de Meseș, Saint George of the Meseș, tells you it belongs to the range, which separates it from the many other Sângeorgiu villages elsewhere, and from its Hungarian neighbours who gave the saint a different name. It is a reminder that in this part of Romania, many places have two or three names in different languages, and the road signs sometimes show them side by side.

The ride into the village is gentle. The road follows a valley with orchards and hay meadows on either side, turning gently through a few bends and up a short rise to the church. The surface is decent in most places, with some patches of damage and loose gravel at the edges. Watch for livestock, because cows are brought home along the road in the evening, and for horse carts, which have the right of way in practice if not in law. Dogs run out of gates, so keep a steady line and do not swerve.

Fuel is not available in the village, and Cizer has only a small shop, so fill up in Zalău or another larger town. The village shop sells basics, and in spring a few households offer homemade cheese and eggs. If you stop in front of a house, someone may come out to ask where you are going, and the conversation usually ends with an invitation to come in for coffee.

Spring, around the feast day, is a good moment, and so is the first week of May, when the orchards are in bloom.
t.popeni dealul racova@47.2,23.2:
Timber is the economy of the forest villages of Sălaj, and the roads show it. Popeni, in the north-west of the county, is among the hills that supply beech, oak and spruce to sawmills in the valleys, and the lane to Dealul Racova, about three kilometres from Mirșid, is one of the routes along which logging trucks run. You will see stacks of cut trunks beside the road waiting for collection, with bark and sawdust smells and big tyre marks in the mud.

Forestry in Romania is a matter of national debate. The country holds some of the largest remaining areas of old-growth forest in Europe, in the Carpathians, and illegal logging has been a scandal for years, with activists and rangers attacked in some regions. Closer to home, in the low hills of Sălaj, the forests are mostly managed second-growth beech and oak, and the work is mostly ordinary, with local firms and small crews. Still, the roads carry the weight of heavy trucks, which break up the edges and leave deep ruts.

For the rider, that means caution. Logging roads may be very muddy after rain, and wet clay is as slippery as ice. Trucks come around blind bends in the middle of the road, so keep right and listen for engines. After a storm, branches and trunks sometimes lie across the lane. In the high season for cutting, which runs from autumn through winter, you may find roads partly blocked and flagged with branches. If you meet a loaded truck on a narrow stretch, pull over and let it pass, and give it a wave.

In summer, the forest road is a pleasure. The air under the beech canopy is cool and smells of leaf mould, the light is green, and the silence is broken only by birdsong and the distant whine of a saw. Mirșid, a village of a couple of thousand, has a shop and a bar, but fuel must come from larger towns, and Zalău has the best choice.

A weekend morning, when the trucks are idle and the roads are empty, is the best time to ride here.
t.alba iulia apulum cetate@46.1,23.6:
Apulum was a metropolis on the Mureș, and today it is mostly under Alba Iulia's streets and fields. In Roman Dacia, which was conquered by Trajan in 106 AD, the legion XIII Gemina was stationed here, and around the camp grew two towns, one for the soldiers' families and traders and a second, grander one that gained the rank of colony. Apulum was the wealthiest city of the province, and probably its capital for a time, thanks in part to the gold mines of the nearby Apuseni Mountains.

The Romans left in the 270s, abandoning Dacia to the Goths and other peoples, but the site continued to be used, and the later Alba Iulia, with its medieval cathedral and its princely court, grew out of it. Roman stones are visible all over the modern town. Inscriptions are built into church walls, columns stand in courtyards, and a Roman gate has been reconstructed at the entrance to the Habsburg citadel, which is a good place to see how the layers fit together. Cetate is the Romanian word for the citadel, the star-shaped fortress that dominates the town today.

The Principia, the headquarters building of the legion, has been excavated and conserved, and the National Museum of the Union displays Roman finds alongside the later history. It is a fascinating place for anyone interested in how Rome ran a frontier province.

For motorcyclists, Alba Iulia is an easy stopover on the road across Transylvania. The main roads that pass through it are generally good, with busy sections and some road works. Inside the citadel, streets are partly cobbled, so park outside and walk. Parking is straightforward, and fuel stations and workshops are found on the outskirts of a town of some sixty-five thousand. Cafés and restaurants inside the walls tend to be a little more expensive than those outside.

The evening, when the walls are floodlit and the day trippers have left, is the best hour for a stroll.
t.galgau saua dealul arsurei@47.3,23.7:
A șa, in the language of the Carpathians, is a saddle, a low point between two summits that allows a road or a path to cross a ridge. Șaua Dealul Arsurei, the saddle of the burnt hill, lies near Gâlgău, a village of fewer than nine hundred people in the hills of Sălaj, and the name is a good example of how such crossings are remembered. Arsură means a burn or a scorched place. It might refer to a fire in the forest, or to the old practice of clearing woodland for pasture by burning it, which left a hillside bare and blackened.

Saddles matter to a rider. They are where the road lifts out of one valley and drops into the next, and the sudden change of view, from a green hollow into an open sweep of hills, can be one of the quiet pleasures of a day. Here the saddle gives you a long look over a landscape of hay meadows, scattered farms and low ridges that fold away to the horizon, with the Meseș range behind. On a clear day the light picks out every field boundary and haystack.

The roads are lively. Climbs to the saddle are short but can be steep, with a few tight bends where the surface is patchy. In wet weather the clay on the descent can be treacherous, and in winter ice may linger on the shaded side long after the sun has melted it elsewhere. Livestock graze near the road, and dogs from nearby farms may bark and chase. A gentle throttle and a steady line will keep everyone calm.

Gâlgău lies in the valley of a small river and has a shop or two. Fuel, however, is not available in the village, so plan to fill up in a larger town before you start. Keep a few small notes and some water in your pocket, and you will manage.

Come in early summer, when the meadows are in flower and the air is warm and still.
t.spissky hrad and the its associated cult:
Spiš Castle is huge, and from a distance it looks like a long white crown laid on top of a hill. It stands above the small town of Spišské Podhradie in eastern Slovakia, on a travertine outcrop about two hundred metres above the plain, and it is one of the largest castle complexes in Central Europe, with the ruined walls and towers covering some four hectares. It was first recorded in the early thirteenth century, was rebuilt and extended by Hungarian kings and noble families such as the Zápolya and the Thurzo, and fell into ruin after a fire in 1780. UNESCO lists the castle together with the nearby church, town and village of Žehra.

The setting makes it. The hill rises out of the Hornád valley, with the High Tatras in the north and the Slovak Paradise to the south, and the castle appears from many miles away as you cross the plain. Inside, rooms, chapels and a Romanesque palace have been consolidated, and from the top of the tower you can look across a landscape of fields, red roofs and church spires. The film Dragonheart used the castle as a backdrop in the 1990s, and the ruins have a cinematic air.

Close to the castle, Spišská Kapitula is a small walled ecclesiastical town with a Romanesque-Gothic cathedral, St Martin's, and a street of canons' houses that has hardly changed in centuries. A short ride away, Levoča preserves a ring of medieval walls and a church of St Jacob that holds the tallest Gothic wooden altar in the world, carved by Master Paul in the early sixteenth century, standing about eighteen metres high.

The roads of the Spiš region are pleasant: gentle hills, farmland and views of the Tatras, with moderate traffic and good surfaces. Villages are tidy, with painted houses and village churches with onion domes. Spišské Podhradie has fuel, cafés and guesthouses, and Levoča and Poprad are close for anything more. Weather can change rapidly at this altitude, with cool nights even in summer and snow from November.

Take a warm layer for the castle's windy ramparts, and allow at least two hours inside the walls.
t.plettenberg bay@-34.1,23.4:
The Portuguese called this bend of the coast Bahia Formosa, the beautiful bay, and nobody has seriously disagreed since. Plettenberg Bay, or Plett as everyone calls it, sits near the eastern end of South Africa's Garden Route, with a curved beach below forested hills and the dark rocky peninsula of Robberg standing out to sea. The Dutch governor Joachim van Plettenberg gave the town its present name in 1778, and the place grew through timber, whaling and later tourism.

The ride to it is a good one. Coming from Knysna, about thirty kilometres to the west, the N2 crosses a series of river gorges and green hills, with the sea sometimes glimpsed through the milkwood trees. Heading east, the road drops into the Keurbooms river valley, then climbs again toward the Tsitsikamma coast, where it passes the Bloukrans bridge, famous for the highest commercial bungee jump from a bridge in the world, at some two hundred metres. The road is well maintained, but trucks use it heavily, and it can be busy at Christmas and Easter, so mid-week outside school holidays is calmer. Wind off the sea, especially a sharp south-easter, can be fierce.

Nature is the real draw around here. Robberg Nature Reserve has a clifftop trail, a colony of Cape fur seals and fishing boats working the swell. Between June and November, southern right whales come close to shore to calve, and you can often spot them from the beach or headlands, while dolphins are around all year. The inland forests, part of the Garden Route's famous evergreen belt, are home to the Knysna turaco and, with a lot of luck, elusive leopards.

Plett has fuel, restaurants and plenty of places to stay, though prices in December and January climb quickly. Seafood is good, with oysters from nearby Knysna a regional favourite. Take a morning to walk Robberg, give the afternoon to the beach, and save the evening for watching the light go pink over the bay.
t.kareedouw@-34.0,24.3:
Kareedouw is a farm town in the folds of the Eastern Cape, and its quiet is the first thing a rider notices after the long road. It lies on Route 62, the scenic alternative to the N2 coastal highway, in a valley between the Tsitsikamma and Kouga mountains, about forty kilometres inland from the coast near Humansdorp. The surrounding land is a patchwork of orchards, with apples and pears grown in the long valley called the Langkloof, and in spring the white and pink blossom turns the slopes into a soft cloud. In late summer and autumn the fruit is picked, and trucks carry it down to the packhouses.

The town itself is small and functional, with a few shops, a garage, a church and some roadside stalls selling fruit and biltong, South Africa's air-dried meat. It is not a place of famous sights, and it makes no attempt to be. What it offers is a pause on one of the world's longest wine and farming routes, since Route 62 runs for hundreds of kilometres from Cape Town through the Little Karoo, past Barrydale, Calitzdorp and Oudtshoorn, to the Eastern Cape. The towns along it have developed a reputation for quirky roadside cafés, art studios and pubs, and it has become a favourite among motorcyclists.

The riding in this section is good. The road follows the valley, with gentle curves between orchards and hills, then climbs over low passes with views across the mountains. The surface is generally paved and in decent condition, though heavy farm trucks and the occasional tractor slow the pace, and there are sections where the tarmac is rough or patched. Sheep, cattle and the odd baboon might appear on the road, so keep an eye out. Weather can be changeable, with cold mornings in winter and hot afternoons in summer, and thunderstorms in the mountains.

Fuel is available in Kareedouw, but it is wise to top up whenever you pass a station on Route 62, because villages are far apart. Simple cafés serve toasted sandwiches, pies and coffee, and farm stalls sell fresh fruit in season. The best months are spring and autumn.
t.outeniqua pass@-33.9,22.4:
The Outeniqua Pass is the quick way from the coast to the Karoo, and a motorcyclist's first lesson that South Africa's mountains come in a hurry. On the coast, George sits among green hills with the Indian Ocean on the horizon. Twenty minutes inland, the N12 climbs the face of the Outeniqua range in a series of well-engineered bends, crests at roughly eight hundred metres, and drops into the dry, rocky country of the Little Karoo toward Oudtshoorn. The pass was opened in the early 1950s, replacing the older Montagu Pass, which still exists as a gravel road a short distance away.

The riding is a joy. The surface is smooth, the bends are broad and well banked, and the views, back to the sea or forward over the brown folds of the interior, are wide. In the morning the coastal side is often wrapped in mist, while the northern slopes are bright and dry. The climate changes with the altitude: the coast is humid and mild, and the top of the pass can be cool and windy. Look out for heavy trucks crawling uphill, and for baboons near the roadside, which are best left alone. Rain turns the surface slick, and fog on the upper slopes reduces visibility without warning.

The mountains are a wall for weather as well as for traffic. The Outeniquas catch the moisture off the sea, so the coastal side supports forests of yellowwood and stinkwood, while the northern side, in the rain shadow, is semi-desert with aloes and succulents. This is the border between the Garden Route and the Karoo, and crossing it in a few minutes is a real pleasure. The old Montagu Pass, built in the 1840s by the engineer Henry Fancourt White, is worth a detour for those with a bike that suits gravel, a fine example of Victorian road building with dry-stone walls and a gentle gradient.

George, just six kilometres away, is the place for fuel, a decent lunch and supplies. It is the largest town on this part of the coast, with petrol stations on its main roads, and in South Africa an attendant will fill the tank for you. On the way up, there is a viewpoint with space to stop and look. Once over the top, Oudtshoorn, the ostrich-farming capital, is about sixty kilometres on, with the Cango Caves nearby, and a cold drink is welcome after the climb.
t.wilderness beach@-34.0,22.6:
Wilderness beach is a wide, pale curve of sand that runs east from the mouth of the Touw River toward Sedgefield, backed by dunes, lakes and wooded hills, and on a calm morning it is among the loveliest places on the Garden Route. The Indian Ocean rolls in with long, slow breakers, and the horizon is clean and blue, with the dark green flank of the Outeniqua mountains behind. The beach stretches for many kilometres, so you can walk for as long as you like and meet nobody but a few dog walkers and the odd fisherman casting a line from the shore.

It is also a place to take care. The surf here can be powerful, and rip currents are common along this coast, so swim only where lifeguards are on duty, in the busy summer season from about December to January, and stay in sight of the flags. At other times, the water is cold and the surf unpredictable. Walking along the beach is safer, and low tide reveals shells, rock pools and the long, curved lines of the dunes. The lagoon at the Touw river mouth is calmer and good for paddling, though the water can be brackish and tea-coloured from the forest.

The wildlife is a main attraction. Between July and November, southern right whales come into the bays here to calve, and you can often see them from the dunes, with their broad backs breaking the surface and their huge tails slapping the water. Dolphins patrol the surf line throughout the year, and in the lakes behind the beach, kingfishers, herons and fish eagles hunt in the reeds. The coastal forest and fynbos behind the dunes are full of birds and sunbirds, with the scent of wild sage and sea air.

Riding to the beach is easy, along the N2 and the quiet road down to the sand, with only a small stretch of loose sand at the parking area, so be careful with a heavy bike. The weather changes quickly, with morning mist often burning away to hot sunshine, and sudden showers are normal. The best months are February to April, when the sea is warm and the crowds have gone. George, about eleven kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and every service, while the village has a few cafes and a small shop, so bring water and sun protection.
t.knysna lagoon@-34.0,23.0:
Knysna sits on the edge of a lagoon, a broad, sheltered stretch of water that almost seems like a lake until you notice the tide running in and out through a narrow gap in the sandstone cliffs. These are the Knysna Heads, two great cliffs that guard the entrance, and the passage between them is one of the most dangerous harbour mouths in South Africa, with many ships lost over the years. A viewpoint on the eastern Head offers a spectacular look at the channel and the surf breaking on the rocks. The lagoon itself is a protected estuary, home to the rare Knysna seahorse, found nowhere else, and a variety of fish and birds.

The town has a long and colourful history. It was founded in the early nineteenth century by George Rex, a settler of mysterious origins whom local legend claimed to be the illegitimate son of King George III, and who built up a timber and shipbuilding business here. Timber from the surrounding forests, yellowwood and stinkwood, built the town's wealth, and the great Knysna forest still stands in the hills behind, a remnant of the ancient forest with a handful of shy elephants, the last in the region. The Knysna loerie, a bright green forest bird, flashes crimson wings among the trees.

The waterfront is lively, with restaurants, boat tours and craft shops, and the town is known for oysters, grown in the lagoon and celebrated in the Knysna Oyster Festival each July. Eat them fresh with lemon, with a glass of local white wine. A few kilometres outside town, the Featherbed nature reserve on the western Head can be reached by a ferry across the lagoon and offers walks and views.

For riders, the N2 here is a spectacular road, running along the coast and across the lagoon on a causeway and bridge, with the forest-covered hills on one side and the sea on the other. The surface is excellent, the curves long and sweeping, but traffic can be heavy, particularly in the holiday season from December to January, with trucks, buses and tourists. Rain falls throughout the year, so be ready for showers and wet roads. Knysna is a town of nearly seventy thousand people, with fuel, supermarkets, motorcycle shops and a wide range of accommodation. Plettenberg Bay, thirty kilometres east, is the next larger stop along the coast.
t.zakopane@49.3,20.0:
Zakopane is the winter capital of Poland, and in summer it is the hiking capital too. The town lies at the foot of the Tatra Mountains, the highest range in the Carpathians, with the peak of Giewont, topped by a metal cross, looming above it. Nearly thirty thousand people live here, and many millions visit each year, so the main street, Krupówki, is crowded with souvenir stalls, grill restaurants and walkers. It is lively rather than quiet, but the mountains behind it are real.

The place has its own culture, that of the Górale, the highlanders, who have lived in the Tatra foothills for centuries. Their wooden houses, with steep roofs and carved decoration, formed the basis of the Zakopane style at the end of the nineteenth century, and the music, with fast fiddle tunes, and the costume, with embroidered felt trousers, are still a living tradition. Oscypek, a smoked sheep's cheese, is sold everywhere, grilled and served with cranberry jam, and a glass of hot mulled wine or beer is a good way to warm up in the evening.

The roads around town are narrower than you might hope. Traffic into Zakopane can be heavy at weekends and holidays, with queues on the approach from Nowy Targ, and the surrounding roads are busy with coaches and cars. The route along the foothills toward Kościelisko and Poronin, and further east toward the Slovak border, has long views of the ridge on clear days, with meadows and dark spruce forest. Some sections have bumpy asphalt or ruts left by heavy trucks, and speed limits in villages are enforced. Early mornings give you quiet roads, and the high Tatras in autumn light are very fine.

Zakopane is large enough to offer fuel, repairs and every kind of food, with stations on the main roads in and out. Kościelisko and Poronin have services too. Weather in the mountains can change quickly, with cold rain and mist even in summer, and snow possible from October. The warm föhn wind, the halny, can blow hard at times.

Spend an hour on Gubałówka, the hill north of town, if time allows. The view across the roofs to the whole wall of the Tatras is the best overview of what you have come for.
t.lesko@49.5,22.3:
Lesko is the quiet gatekeeper of the Bieszczady, a small town of around five and a half thousand on the River San, where the flat farmland of the Carpathian foothills starts to crumple into forested ridges. Its market square is wonderfully unhurried, with an old town hall in the middle, and the town carries a deeper past than its size suggests: before the Second World War a large share of the population was Jewish, and the stone synagogue from the seventeenth century survives, now a gallery, while a Jewish cemetery on a hillside above the town still draws visitors. The castle, rebuilt after fires, belonged for a long time to powerful noble families.

For a rider, Lesko is the place where you decide how serious the day will be. Beyond it the Great Bieszczady Loop heads south through Ustrzyki Dolne, Wetlina and Cisna, a road of rolling, well-surfaced bends through beech and fir forest, past mountain meadows called połoniny that turn gold in autumn. Traffic is light except on summer weekends, and the roads are patrolled, so keep to the limits. Wildlife is the main surprise: bison have been reintroduced to these hills, and brown bears, wolves and lynx live in the forests, though you are far more likely to meet a deer on the tarmac at dusk.

Fuel is easy in Lesko, which has several petrol stations and supermarkets, and nearby Zagórz, with its ruined Carmelite monastery on a hill, is useful for supplies as well. Beyond Cisna, services thin out rapidly, so fill the tank before heading deeper. Local cafes serve pierogi, bigos and a strong coffee, and in the villages you will find smoked trout from the clear streams and homemade bread.

The Bieszczady were emptied of people after the war, when many Ukrainian-speaking villages were cleared, and the forest has quietly reclaimed the sites of old farms, with orchards and church foundations standing in the woods. It gives the area a haunted, peaceful feel. Come in late September or October, when the beech leaves turn copper and the mist hangs in the valleys, and the whole range seems to glow.
t.nowy targ@49.5,20.0:
Nowy Targ is the main town of Podhale, the highland district at the foot of the Tatras, and it feels as if it had always been a place where mountain farmers came down to trade. About thirty-four thousand people live here, in a broad, windswept basin about six hundred metres above sea level where the Czarny and Biały Dunajec rivers meet, and the weekly market, held on Thursdays, is a long-standing tradition where highlanders in embroidered waistcoats still sell sheep, cheese, wool and wooden goods. The cheese to look for is oscypek, a smoked, spindle-shaped sheep's-milk cheese pressed in carved wooden moulds, and you will find it on stalls throughout the region.

The basin is known for its cold. Winter air collects here under the surrounding hills, and Nowy Targ has long been counted among the coldest places in Poland on clear, still nights. Summer, by contrast, is mild and green, and the view of the Tatra wall to the south, a jagged line of grey peaks, is the reason most riders come. On a clear day it fills the whole horizon.

The riding is a pleasant mix of straight, fast road and gently rolling country. Roads run between wooden highland houses with steeply pitched shingle roofs, past roadside crosses and chapels, and toward the foothills, where the bends tighten. The main road to Zakopane is heavy with traffic, particularly on summer weekends and in the ski season, and slow lorries make overtaking tiring, so use the smaller roads when you can. Police patrols and speed cameras are common in the villages.

You will not struggle for fuel or food. Nowy Targ has several petrol stations, supermarkets and cafes, and the market square has restaurants serving regional dishes like kwaśnica, a sour cabbage soup, and potato pancakes with goulash. A short ride east leads to Czorsztyn and the Pieniny, where the Dunajec cuts through a limestone gorge that visitors raft in wooden boats. Take time to stand in the square and look south. The Tatras do not look real from here, and no photo does them justice.
t.balea lake@45.6,24.6:
Bâlea Lake sits at 2,042 metres in the heart of the Făgăraș mountains, a small, cold glacial lake in a bowl of bare rock, and it is the high point of the Transfăgărășan, the road that Romanians say is the best in the world. It was built between 1970 and 1974 on the orders of Nicolae Ceaușescu, who wanted a military route across the Carpathians after the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968. Thousands of soldiers and labourers blasted it out of the rock, and the cost in lives is said to have been high, so every hairpin has a story attached.

The road itself is magnificent. From the north, it climbs from the forest through a succession of bends and switchbacks, sweeping up beside waterfalls and cliffs until it reaches the long Bâlea tunnel, which opens onto the lake at the highest point. From the south, it follows the huge Vidraru Dam and then climbs in tight hairpins through a green valley. The surface is mostly good but can be patched, and cold rain and thick fog are common even in July. Be cautious on the descent, as cars stop suddenly for photos. It is a road that wants a slow pace and a long day.

The pass is open only in summer, usually from early July to late October, depending on the snow, and the rest of the year it is shut by drifts and avalanches. In the winter, an ice hotel is built beside the lake, and a cable car runs from the waterfall below. Around the lake in summer you will find small stalls selling grilled sausages, cheese, honey and hot drinks, along with a few chalets. Prices are high, and the quality varies, but the view is hard to beat.

Chamois and marmots live on the slopes, and bears are in the forests below. Go early, before the traffic builds, and carry on in the evening, when the crowd has gone and the peaks turn pink.
t.lille reipas raipas@69.9,23.4:
Some of the most important monuments in the world are very small. Lille-Reipas, on a hill above the town of Alta in far northern Norway, is one of them. It is one of the points of the Struve Geodetic Arc, a chain of survey stations running from Hammerfest on the Arctic Ocean to the Black Sea, about 2,800 kilometres, that was used in the nineteenth century to measure the size and shape of the Earth. UNESCO listed the surviving points in 2005, and a simple marker is all that stands at most of them.

The survey, led by the astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve, took decades, from 1816 to 1855, and relied on triangulation, with observers on hilltops looking across forests and lakes to the next point. The work crossed what are now ten countries and several empires, and it gave one of the first accurate measurements of the Earth's curvature. Standing here, on a hill in the Arctic, you are on the northern end of that chain, and the view across the fjord and birch scrub shows why the site was chosen.

Alta itself is worth the visit. It is the largest town in Finnmark, with about twelve thousand people, a cathedral clad in titanium that is known as the Northern Lights Cathedral, and a long tradition of Sami culture. Its most famous treasure is the rock carvings at Hjemmeluft, listed by UNESCO in 1985, thousands of years old, showing reindeer, boats and people. The Alta river runs through the Sautso canyon, often described as Europe's largest, and is renowned for its salmon. In the late 1970s a fight over a dam on the river became a landmark in the history of Sami rights.

Riding around Alta is open and relaxed. The E6 runs through town with long, straight stretches, wide views and few vehicles outside summer, and side roads lead to quiet fjord shores. Reindeer are common, and wind can be strong. The ground is bare of trees in places, and the midnight sun lasts from late May to late July. Mosquitoes can be a trial in summer, so keep the visor closed.

Fuel is easy in Alta, with stations and shops, and it is the sensible place to fill up and eat. Beyond, the Finnmark distances are long, and services are far apart.
t.sanok@49.6,22.2:
Sanok is the last proper town before the Bieszczady, the wild, empty corner of south-eastern Poland where the country runs into Ukraine and Slovakia. About forty thousand people live on the banks of the San River, in a valley of wooded hills, and the town has a calm, dignified feel, with a castle on a rise, an old market square and a river that is wide and clear in summer.

The open-air museum on the hillside is the one stop to make. It is among the largest of its kind in Poland, with wooden houses, churches and farm buildings brought from villages across the region, including those of the Lemko and Boyko mountain peoples, whose communities were largely uprooted after the Second World War. Walking between the old timber churches, with their onion domes and shingled roofs, is a gentle way to understand the cultural mix that once covered these hills. The castle holds a remarkable collection of icons from Orthodox and Greek Catholic churches, and also the largest collection of works by Zdzisław Beksiński, the painter born in Sanok in 1929, whose dark, dreamlike canvases are sometimes called hallucinatory. The town also builds buses, as it has for generations.

The Bieszczady Loop, which starts here, is the reason riders come. The road climbs south through beech forests and open mountain meadows, the połoniny, where grass ridges run above the tree line, then drops to the huge lake at Solina, the largest artificial lake in Poland, with its great curved dam. Bends are gentle and varied, the surface mostly good, and traffic is light outside the summer weekends. The forests hold brown bears, wolves, lynx and a herd of European bison, though you are far more likely to see deer, and sheep crossing the road. Early mornings can be misty, and fog in the valleys is common.

Fuel is plentiful in Sanok, which has many stations, so fill up before going south, since the villages in the mountains have few. Zagórz, about six kilometres away, has a ruined Carmelite monastery on a hill and a small supply of services. Pierogi, potato pancakes and fresh trout from mountain streams are the local meals to look for.

Start early, take layers because the weather changes quickly, and plan time to stop in the villages. September, when the grasses turn gold and the crowds thin, may be the best month.
t.cisna@49.2,22.3:
Cisna lies in the far south-east of Poland, where the Carpathians push up against the borders of Slovakia and Ukraine, and the land turns wild and empty. This is the Bieszczady, a range of rounded, grassy ridges called połoniny rising above dense beech forest, and it is among the least populated parts of the country. Cisna itself is a hamlet of a few hundred people, with a scattering of wooden guesthouses, a handful of cafes and one famous bar. The nearest large town is Snina, across the Slovak border, and on the Polish side, Lesko and Ustrzyki Dolne are the places to stock up.

The emptiness has a history. Before the Second World War these valleys were home to Lemko and Boyko villagers, who lived in wooden houses and worshipped in small timber churches. After the war, the villages were emptied by forced resettlement in the late 1940s, and many were abandoned and left to the forest. Today you can still find orchards gone wild, old stone crosses and ruined foundations among the trees, and a few restored wooden churches that hint at what was lost. It gives the landscape a quiet, haunted beauty.

The riding is delightful. The roads wind through beech woods, over passes and along the edges of broad meadows, past little wooden buildings and herds of sheep. The surface is mostly good, the traffic is light except on summer weekends, and the bends are medium-paced and open. In autumn the forest burns red and gold, and in the early morning mist lies in the valleys like smoke. The forest is the home of bison, bears, wolves and lynx, and while you will almost certainly not see them, animals on the road are a possibility.

Cisna also has a narrow-gauge forest railway at nearby Majdan, which runs on summer days and gives a slow ride through the woods. The famous bar, Siekierezada, with its heavy timbers and its tradition of folk music, is the traditional place to end a day in the hills. Fuel can be hard to find in the high villages, so fill the tank in Lesko or Ustrzyki Dolne. The weather can change quickly, so pack a rain jacket. In winter, the road is often icy and the high passes closed to the unprepared.
t.novaci@45.2,23.7:
Novaci is the southern gate of the Transalpina, and for a town of fewer than three thousand people it has a good deal of mountain on its doorstep. It sits in Gorj county, on the southern edge of the Parâng range, where the Oltenian foothills fold up into the high Carpathians, and the air smells of sheep, hay and woodsmoke. Sheep farming has been the livelihood of the district for centuries, and the shepherds still drive their flocks up to the high pastures in summer, living in simple huts and making cheese.

The road that starts here is the Transalpina, the DN67C, the highest paved road in the Romanian Carpathians, which reaches about 2,100 metres at the Urdele Pass. Its origins are disputed, with legends about Roman legions and medieval traders, but the modern road was built in the 1930s under King Carol II and was long known as the King's Road. It was used by German troops during the Second World War, then fell into decline, and after a lengthy renovation, it reopened as one of the great mountain roads of Europe. It is usually closed to traffic by snow from late autumn to early summer.

Close by, the Tismana Monastery, one of the oldest in the country, stands in a wooded gorge, and the village of Hobița, a short drive away, is the birthplace of the sculptor Constantin Brâncuși, whose Endless Column stands in Târgu Jiu, the county capital, about sixty kilometres away. The Gorj region is a place where folk traditions are strong, with painted houses, carved gates and a robust cuisine of grilled meats, polenta, cheese and plum brandy, the țuică.

Riding up from Novaci, the road climbs through spruce forest in long bends and then breaks out onto bare, grassy ridges, with views over a sea of peaks. Weather can change very quickly, with fog and cold wind at the top, even in July. Sheep, cattle and dogs wander over the road, and gravel and potholes can appear after the thaw. Fill up here, since services on the high road are very limited, and the nearest bigger centre is Crasna, about thirteen kilometres away.

Come in June or September for the best weather, and carry layers for the cold at the top.
t.sebes@46.0,23.6:
Sebeş is where the Transalpina comes down to earth, a town of about twenty-seven thousand people on the Sebeş River in Transylvania, and the northern end of the great mountain road. It belongs to the world of the Transylvanian Saxons, German settlers who were invited here in the twelfth century by the Hungarian kings to defend the frontier and develop the land. They built fortified churches and walled towns, and Sebeş, which they called Mühlbach, grew into one of the seven fortified cities that gave Transylvania its German name, Siebenbürgen.

The Evangelical church in the centre, a large Gothic building with a high roof and fortified tower, dates from the thirteenth century onwards and is among the finest in the region. Parts of the old town walls and towers survive, and the old streets near the main square have a quiet charm. Not far away, the village of Lancrăm was the birthplace of Lucian Blaga, one of Romania's leading twentieth-century poets and philosophers, and the local wine, a crisp white, is often drunk with his lines in mind.

The Sebeş Gorge and the mountains behind the town are a wild area, with bears, wolves and lynx, and the Transalpina climbs into this country through pastures and forest. Coming down from the pass, the road drops through dense spruce and beech forest with a series of bends, then crosses the valley floor. The surface, now well maintained, is smooth, though frost heave and slides can cause patches of damage, and the lower stretches carry trucks.

Sebeş is a practical stop. Fuel stations and shops line the main road, and there are cafes, bakeries and restaurants in the centre, so it is a good place to eat after a long day in the mountains. Local dishes include grilled meats, stuffed cabbage and a sweet pastry called cozonac. Fill up here before the climb if you are going the other way, since stations on the pass are almost non-existent.

Arrive in the evening, when the light is low on the church walls, and the long descent from the mountains is behind you. The high road, with its clear air and sheep bells, will feel like a different country.
t.baia mare@47.7,23.6:
Baia Mare means the big mine, and the town has earned it. For centuries, gold, silver, lead and copper were dug from the hills around it, and the city grew rich on metal, with medieval Hungarian kings granting it privileges and encouraging German miners to settle. A hundred and thirty-six thousand people live here now, in a bustling northern city with a lively centre, and the mining past is visible in the old buildings, the museum and the scarred hills around.

The old centre has a few good surprises. Stephen's Tower, a Gothic bell tower from the fifteenth century, is the best-known landmark, and the Butchers' Tower is a remnant of the old defences. The main square has colourful baroque houses, and the Mining Museum tells the story of the trade. In the late nineteenth century, the town became a magnet for painters, who set up a colony, the Baia Mare School, that produced much of the country's modern landscape painting.

There is a darker chapter too. In January 2000, a dam holding the waste from a gold-processing plant near the town burst, and cyanide-laden water flowed into the Lăpuș and then the Someș and Tisza rivers, killing fish for hundreds of kilometres, one of the worst environmental accidents in Europe at the time. The rivers recovered, but the memory lingers, and mining remains a sensitive issue here.

Baia Mare is the gateway to Maramureș, a remote, deeply traditional region of valleys and wooden churches. Eight of the churches, tall and narrow with shingle-covered roofs and slender spires, are listed by UNESCO, and the ride leads through villages where carved gates, haystacks and horse carts are an ordinary sight. The roads wind up and down the valleys, with bends and short climbs, and surfaces can be uneven, with potholes after winter. Heavy traffic on the main roads includes lorries and slow vehicles, and animals wander across the road.

Fuel and services are plentiful in Baia Mare, with stations on the outskirts and shops in the centre. It is a good place to fill up and eat, since villages in the valleys have fewer options. A bowl of sour soup, ciorbă, and a plate of grilled meat will see you through the day.

Start early, take time to talk to people, and bring a scarf if you intend to enter a church.
t.barsana@47.8,24.1:
Maramureș is the corner of Romania where the twentieth century arrived late and politely, and Bârsana is a fine place to see what it left alone. The village strings itself along the Izei valley under forested hills, with high carved wooden gates in front of the farmhouses, haystacks built round tall poles in the meadows, and women in headscarves going about their business as if no coach had ever stopped. Sighetu Marmației, the nearest real town, lies about fifteen kilometres to the north-west, and the Ukrainian border is not far beyond it.

The wooden churches are the reason for coming. Several of them in this district are on the UNESCO list, and the old church of Bârsana, dating from the early eighteenth century, is one of them, a dark, steep-roofed building with a shingled spire whose walls are painted inside with saints and sinners. Higher up the slope stands a much younger monastery, built in the 1990s in the same timber tradition, whose great wooden church is among the tallest of its kind in Europe. It is a strange and gentle sight to find a new building made with the old skills, in oak and shingle, and it gives you a sense that the tradition is alive rather than preserved.

The roads in the valley are narrow but mostly sound, running through villages where horse carts are still a common sight, so keep your speed down and stay alert for animals, children and carts coming round the bends. Potholes appear after winter. The valley is at its best in late spring, when the meadows are full of flowers, and again in September, when the hay is stacked and the mist hangs in the hollows. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms, and the road gets slick fast.
