Food here is simple and good. Ask for bulz, a hearty dish of polenta with cheese and sour cream, and a glass of țuică or pălincă, the local plum brandy, which is stronger than it looks. Fuel is available in Sighet or Vișeu de Sus, so fill the tank beforehand, and do not count on card machines in the village shops. Many families offer rooms in their own houses, and breakfast comes with homemade jam, cheese, and sometimes a lecture on the gate in the yard.
t.sighetu marmatiei@47.9,23.9:
Sighetu Marmației sits where the Iza meets the Tisa, and across the Tisa is Ukraine, so the whole town has the slightly watchful air of a border place that has changed hands more than once. It was Hungarian for centuries, Czechoslovak for a short while, then Romanian, and in the early twentieth century it had one of the largest Jewish communities in the region. Elie Wiesel was born here in 1928, and his childhood home is now a small museum. The town is the biggest in Maramureș, with about forty thousand people, and it has every service you could want, including plenty of fuel.

Two places in town are worth the time. The Memorial of the Victims of Communism and of the Resistance occupies a former prison where, in the early 1950s, the communist regime locked up political figures, academics, priests and others who had stood in its way, and many died in the cells. It is a stark, serious museum, and few visitors leave it unmoved. Outside the town, the open-air village museum has gathered old houses, barns and churches from around the region, which gives a good summary of the carpentry traditions you will see in the villages that follow.

For the rider, Sighet is a hub. Roads lead east along the Iza valley toward the wooden churches at Bârsana, Ieud and Șurdești, north to the border at the Tisa, and west to Săpânța, where the Merry Cemetery, with its painted wooden crosses carrying jokes and portraits of the dead, is the single most famous sight in the region. The surfaces on the main roads are patchy but passable, and truck traffic is heavy on the national road. Keep your speed down in villages, where children, dogs and horse carts share the tarmac.

Eat well here. Markets in the town sell cheese, smoked meats, honey and pickles, and the local restaurants serve cabbage rolls, grilled sausage, and soup in bread. Pălincă, the plum brandy, is offered with every meal, and refusing it too often is thought slightly rude. Come in September if you can, when the hay is in, the plums are ripe and the light over the hills has an autumn softness, and the wood smoke from village chimneys drifts across the valley.
t.lviv@49.8,24.0:
Lviv's old centre is a tight puzzle of cobbled lanes, courtyards, domes and spires, laid out around a market square where the town hall tower looks over rows of tall townhouses in pastel colours. It was founded in the thirteenth century by Prince Danylo of Galicia, who named it after his son Lev, and it has been ruled over the centuries by Poles, Austrians, Soviets and now Ukrainians, which explains why the city has been known as Lwów, Lemberg and Lviv. UNESCO listed the historic centre in 1998, and the mix of Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and Habsburg architecture is one of the best preserved in central Europe.

Lviv is also a city of coffee. The Habsburg tradition of cafes survived everything, and small places tucked into cellars serve strong espresso, hot chocolate and cheesecake, sometimes with a theme, from chocolate shops to cafes decorated like mines. The Armenian Cathedral, the opera house, the Lychakiv Cemetery with its sculpted tombs and the bell towers of the Dominican church all lie within a short walk of each other. In the evening the streets fill with students and musicians, and trams rattle along the cobbles.

Ride out in the afternoon and you cross green farmland toward the Polish border. Roads are in mixed condition, with patches of broken asphalt, potholes and cobbles in older streets, and trams can be hazardous when the rails are wet. The wooden church of Saint Paraskeva at Radruż, on the other side of the border in Poland, is one of the surviving wooden churches of the Carpathian region, inscribed by UNESCO, with a steep shingled roof and painted interior. Border waits can be long, and anyone planning to cross should check current rules.

It is essential to say that Ukraine has been at war since 2022, and Lviv, although far from the front, has suffered missile and drone attacks. Air raid alerts happen, and travel advice from most governments cautions against non-essential travel. Anyone thinking about visiting should follow official guidance. For people living here, the city carries on with remarkable resilience, and the same cafes stay open.
t.ciudad valles@22.0,-99.0:
Ciudad Valles is the commercial capital of the Huasteca Potosina, the lush, tropical eastern part of San Luis Potosí where the dry highlands of central Mexico fall toward the Gulf coast. It is a hot, busy city of over a hundred thousand people on the Río Valles, with sugar cane, citrus and cattle country around it, and a marked change in climate and culture from the desert plateau a few hours west. The air is humid and the vegetation thick, with palms and banana plants.

The Huasteca is known for its water. Turquoise rivers drop over limestone steps in places such as Tamasopo and the Cascadas de Micos, where you can swim in warm pools beneath waterfalls, and the Tamul waterfall, one of the tallest in Mexico, plunges from a wide ledge into a river canyon. In Aquismón, the Sótano de las Golondrinas, a huge cave pit hundreds of meters deep, swallows flocks of swifts at dawn. Farther south, in Xilitla, the English poet Edward James built Las Pozas, a surreal garden of concrete sculptures and staircases among the jungle.

Local food is its own tradition. Zacahuil, a giant tamale baked for hours in a pit and served in huge slabs, is the Huastecan classic, along with enchiladas huastecas and bocoles, thick corn cakes. Music in the region is the son huasteco, with fiddle and guitar and a falsetto singing style. The Teenek people, who have lived here for centuries, keep their language and distinct dress in the highland villages.

For riders, the roads through the Huasteca are curving, hilly and green, climbing through coffee and orange groves and dropping into river valleys. Highways 70 and 85 link the main towns, and the surface is mostly fair, though potholes, topes (speed bumps) and animals on the road are common, so slow down in villages. Ciudad Valles has fuel, supermarkets and hotels, so stock up. The best months are November to April, with warm, dry weather, while summer is very hot and humid, and the rainy season brings heavy storms. Avoid riding at night.
t.campeni@46.4,23.1:
Câmpeni lies in the Apuseni Mountains of western Transylvania, in a high, wooded valley cut by the river Arieș. This is Țara Moților, the land of the Moți, a highland people known for their woodcraft, their wooden buckets and troughs, and a long history of rugged independence. The town is small, about eight thousand people, but it is the capital of the area, and it carries more history than its size suggests.

In 1848, during the Transylvanian revolution, a young lawyer named Avram Iancu led a force of Romanian peasants in these mountains, defending them against Hungarian troops, and he remains a national hero. Câmpeni was his base, and a memorial and a small museum recall him. The region also has gold in its story: Roman miners dug into these hills, and the mining villages around Roșia Montană, not far away, have been worked for two millennia.

The riding is the draw. From Câmpeni the main road runs up the Arieș valley toward Arieșeni, climbing through spruce forest and pastures with a sequence of twisty bends, sometimes with a broken edge or a patch of loose gravel, and passes little farms with haystacks stacked on poles. Beyond lies the Bihor massif, with karst plateaus, sinkholes and caves, including the Scărișoara ice cave, one of the largest underground glaciers in Europe. Bring a warm layer; it can feel cold even in summer when the clouds close in.

Fuel is available in town, and since service stations in the mountains are few, tank up before heading higher. The local food is simple and filling: smoked sausages, polenta with sheep cheese and sour cream, and homemade plum brandy, which hosts may press on you with great generosity.

Traffic is light, apart from the occasional horse cart and trucks hauling timber. Late spring has wildflowers and waterfalls full from the melt, while autumn brings gold in the beech woods. Winter snow can close high stretches for a while.
t.borsa@47.7,24.7:
Borșa spreads along the Vișeu valley in northern Maramureș, a long straggling town of twenty-seven thousand with the high, bare ridge of the Rodna Mountains rising to the south. Pietrosul Rodnei, the highest summit, tops two thousand three hundred metres, and the range is a national park with alpine meadows, glacial lakes and a population of chamois. In winter the town becomes a ski resort, with a lift climbing the slopes above the spa suburb of Băile Borșa, where mineral springs rise in the woods.

Maramureș has a distinctive culture that feels older than the rest of Romania. In the villages nearby, wooden churches with slender, steep spires, some of them centuries old, hold painted interiors, and the carved wooden gates are marks of pride. Here, people wear traditional dress to church on Sundays without any thought of putting it on for visitors, and haymaking is still done by hand with pitchforks in the steeper fields.

For the rider, Borșa is the foot of one of the great Carpathian crossings. The road east climbs to the Prislop Pass, at roughly fourteen hundred metres, and drops into Bukovina and its painted monasteries. The ascent is long and well-surfaced with broad bends, and the view back across the green ridges is superb. At the top there is a market of stalls selling honey, cheese and woolly socks, and a small monastery. Fog and cloud come quickly, and in winter snow can close the road, so check conditions outside summer.

Fuel is no problem in Borșa, which has several stations, but there are fewer on the empty stretches beyond the pass. The town also serves local specialties such as sheep's cheese, smoked meats, and the sweet, strong plum brandy known as țuică.

The best months are June to September. Evenings are cool, even in July, and thunderstorms roll across the ridge in the afternoon, so aim to cross the pass in the morning light and be back in the valley before the clouds build.
t.oravita@45.0,21.7:
Oravița lies at the south-western edge of Romania, in the Banat hills where the land begins to fold up toward the Anina Mountains. It is a small town, twelve thousand people or so, and yet it holds a handful of distinctions that would suit a city ten times its size. The little theatre here, opened in 1817, is regarded as the oldest in Romania, a neat neoclassical hall with a horseshoe auditorium that has been restored and still hosts performances.

The industrial story is stranger still. The Habsburg empire mined copper, iron and coal across this part of the Banat, and in 1854 the first railway in what is now Romania opened here, linking Oravița with Baziaș on the Danube. A few years later, the mountain line from Oravița to Anina, built to carry coal, climbed through tunnels and over viaducts in a series of spirals and was nicknamed the Semmering of the Banat after the Alpine railway. Parts of it are still in use, and the cuttings and stone arches are worth finding in the woods.

The riding around Oravița is unhurried and rural. From town you can climb to Anina on a winding road through beech forest, then continue to the Nera Gorge, where the river has carved a deep canyon with waterfalls and one of the wildest corners of the Carpathians. Surfaces vary, and potholes appear in some villages, so give yourself time. South, the road to the Danube leads to the Iron Gates region, which is one of Europe's great river gorges.

The local population includes Romanians, Serbs, Czechs and Germans, who settled here over the centuries, and the cooking blends Banat and Central European traditions, with sausages, goulash, and rich cakes. Fuel is available in Oravița, though stations in the mountains are few.

The best seasons are late spring and early autumn. Summers are hot on the lower roads, while winter can bring ice on the high stretches.
t.humenne@48.9,21.9:
Humenné lies in the far east of Slovakia, along the Laborec river, with the green hills of the Vihorlat range rising to the east and the long wooded border with Poland and Ukraine not far beyond. It is a small industrial town of about thirty-five thousand people, and the main sight is the manor house in the centre, a Renaissance residence rebuilt by the Drugeth family, who were powerful landowners in this part of the old Kingdom of Hungary. It now houses a museum and sits in a pleasant park.

What draws riders is the country around it. Vihorlat is a volcanic mountain range covered in beech woods, and at its heart lies Morské oko, the Sea Eye, a still green lake in a crater-like hollow, one of the most photographed beauty spots in the east. Beyond Snina, the Poloniny National Park shelters some of the last primeval beech forests in Europe, recognised by UNESCO, with brown bears, wolves and lynx in the deep woods. Visitors are most likely to see roe deer at dusk, or the odd wild boar crossing the road, so keep your speed down after sunset.

The roads here are quiet, sometimes narrow, and the surfaces vary from smooth to patched, with potholes after winter. Villages along the way often have wooden churches in the Greek Catholic and Orthodox traditions, with onion domes and painted icons. About thirty-five kilometres north-west, the small town of Medzilaborce has a museum dedicated to Andy Warhol, whose parents came from a village nearby, which is a surreal and pleasing find in the middle of the hills.

Fuel is available in Humenné, and Snina has stations too, but the mountain roads have none, so fill up. Local cooking is simple, with halušky, pierogi, and hearty soups, and prices are low.

Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons, with clear air and good colour. Summer is warm, and in winter the high roads can see heavy snow.
t.miskolc@48.1,20.8:
Miskolc is the great industrial city of northern Hungary, wedged into a valley where the foothills of the Bükk mountains come down to the plain. For a century its blast furnaces and steelworks at Diósgyőr defined it, and when that industry shrank the city had to find another face. It has found a gentler one, with thermal baths, parks and cultural festivals, though the mood remains plain and working-class, with block-built estates and stout, friendly people.

A few sights stand out. The castle at Diósgyőr, a Gothic stronghold built in the fourteenth century, was a favourite royal residence under Louis the Great, and its restored towers are now used for medieval festivals. At Miskolctapolca, a spa suburb, you can bathe in warm water inside natural caves, a curious and relaxing experience after a long ride. In the hills to the west lies Lillafüred, a small resort around a lake with a grand palace-hotel and a waterfall tumbling beside it, reached by a narrow-gauge forest railway or a winding road.

For motorcyclists the Bükk is the draw. The plateau and its beech forest are cut by roads with sweeping bends, steep climbs and sudden views across the valleys, lightly trafficked by Hungarian standards and surfaced reasonably well, though some stretches are patchy. The sinuous road toward Szilvásvárad, where Lipizzaner horses are bred, is among the finest rides in the country. To the east, the Tokaj wine region lies about an hour away, with vineyards on volcanic slopes famous for sweet golden wine.

Hungary uses an electronic vignette for motorways, and fuel is available at stations throughout the city and along the main roads. Local dishes include stuffed cabbage, goulash cooked in a cauldron and langos, fried dough with sour cream and cheese.

Late spring and early autumn are best, with cool nights in the hills.
t.storms river@-34.0,23.9:
Storms River is a village of a few houses and a petrol station tucked in a clearing of the Tsitsikamma forest, a place that would be easy to overlook if the setting were not so extraordinary. The Garden Route here runs along a narrow strip of land between the Indian Ocean and the mountains, with ancient indigenous forest, towering yellowwood trees, ferns and mist, and every river cutting a deep gorge on its way to the sea. The Khoi name Tsitsikamma is usually translated as place of much water, and the name is earned.

The N2 highway crosses the gorge on a high concrete arch, the Paul Sauer Bridge, completed in 1956, which hangs about a hundred metres above the river. A little to the west, the Bloukrans Bridge is higher still, and hosts a commercial bungee jump that claims the title of the highest in the world. Even if you do not jump, the view down into the gorge is dizzying. The Storms River Mouth, in the national park, is reached by a side road that drops steeply to the coast, where a rope suspension bridge crosses the river just where it meets the sea. The rocks and the waves are impressive, and the Otter Trail, South Africa's famous coastal hiking route, starts nearby.

On the bike, the N2 through this area is a good road rather than a thrilling one: wide, well-surfaced, with long gentle curves, forested slopes, and a fair amount of lorry traffic. A toll is charged at the Tsitsikamma plaza, and cash or card is usual. Weather is the wild card. The coast gets rain throughout the year, and mist can drift into the forest, so pack a waterproof layer, and be careful on wet tar under the trees. Summer, December to February, is busy, while spring and autumn are quieter and mild.

Fuel is available in the village, and there are cafes, a few places to sleep and a good selection of local trout, seafood and rooibos tea. For larger stocks, Plettenberg Bay to the west and Humansdorp to the east are the main towns.

The forest here feels almost prehistoric, with Knysna loeries calling in the canopy, and, if you are lucky, a troop of vervet monkeys on the roadside. Ride slowly, and take the side road down to the river mouth.
t.kaaimans river pass@-34.0,22.5:
Kaaimans River Pass is the opening movement of the Seven Passes Road, a route that the great Cape road builder Thomas Bain laid out in the nineteenth century to link George with Knysna by way of a sequence of river gorges. It is only about a hundred metres above sea level here, but the road descends and climbs through a deep, wooded valley with a character all of its own. The river itself is dark, tea-coloured from the tannins in the fynbos and forest, and winds toward the Indian Ocean through a landscape of green slopes and shadowy gullies.

The gorge is lush with indigenous forest, thick with yellowwood, stinkwood, and tree ferns, and the air is damp and cool even on a hot day. The most famous feature is the railway viaduct across the river mouth near Wilderness, built for the line that once carried the Outeniqua Choo-Tjoe steam train along the coast. The line is a part of local memory, and the old bridge still stands against the sea. The lagoons and beaches nearby are among the loveliest on the Garden Route.

For a rider, the pass is a gentle introduction. The road dips into the gorge with a series of bends, crosses the river on an old bridge, and climbs the far side, with the forest closing in. The surface is generally good, but the damp can leave patches slick, especially under trees, and leaf litter and the occasional fallen branch can be hazards. Traffic is steady, with trucks and tourists, and there are cyclists as well. Early morning light through the canopy is lovely, and the sound of birdsong is constant.

Fuel is easy: George, about eight kilometres to the north-west, is the biggest town on the Garden Route's western end and has stations, supermarkets, and restaurants. Wilderness, a short distance south, has cafes and a beautiful beach, and the whole stretch is well served. Rain can arrive at any time of year, and the Garden Route is greener for it. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable seasons, and winter days can be crisp and clear. Keep an eye on the weather over the mountains, and a spare layer in the bag.
t.hoekwil@-34.0,22.6:
Hoekwil is the kind of village that artists and retreat-seekers find and then try not to tell anyone about. It sits in a fold of green hills on the Seven Passes Road, a few kilometres inland from the Wilderness lakes, where the Garden Route's coastal tourist rush thins out into forest, smallholdings, and cattle grazing under tall trees.

The landscape around it is made of deep, wooded river gorges that the Cape road builder Thomas Bain had to find a way across in the nineteenth century, one after another, which is how the Seven Passes got its name. Hoekwil lies on the plateau between the Kaaimans and Touws gorges, and a short walk or ride from the village will bring you to a lookout over the Kaaimans River gorge, where the winding river and the forest have a shape that people say resembles the outline of Africa. Whether you see the continent or not, the drop into the dark, tea-coloured water is impressive.

For a rider, Hoekwil is a breathing space on a road that rewards slow, attentive riding. The road is narrow, tree-lined, and bendy, with dappled light that makes the surface hard to read, so go gently on entering shade. Gradients are modest between the passes and steeper where the road drops into a gorge. Traffic is mixed: farm vehicles, cyclists, and tourists in hire cars who stop without warning. The surface is generally paved, but patches and rain-washed gravel can appear, and on a damp day the forest floor leaves a greasy film.

There is not much in the way of fuel here, and the sensible plan is to fill the tank in George, about ten kilometres to the north-west, before turning onto the Seven Passes. The village has a handful of cafes, craft shops, and a few farm stalls, usually with good coffee and home baking. The forest is wet, and mist hangs in the trees on cool mornings, with a smell of leaf mould and woodsmoke. Rain can arrive at any time of year on this coast, so keep a waterproof layer within reach.
t.karatara@-33.9,22.8:
Karatara is a forest village that exists because of timber. It lies deep in the Knysna-Tsitsikamma forest belt, on the road that Thomas Bain pushed through the Outeniqua foothills, and for years its people worked the great yellowwood and stinkwood forests that surround it. The sawmills have quietened, and the community has shifted toward crafts and the careful use of the forest, but the sense of a settlement built around the trees is still strong.

The surroundings are among the most remarkable forests in South Africa. The indigenous Knysna forest, with its towering yellowwoods, its tangled lianas, and its cool, green gloom, covers the lower slopes and hides one of the country's most elusive animals, the Knysna elephant. Only a tiny number survive, and sightings are rare. Birdlife is easier: Knysna turacos flash crimson in the canopy, and Cape parrots, rarer, are sometimes heard rather than seen. After rain the forest steams, and the whole road smells of damp earth and bark.

The ride through Karatara is a quiet, rural one. This is the less-visited stretch of the Seven Passes, where the road leaves the polished tourist belt and becomes narrower, rougher, and more remote. Some sections are gravel, and the surface can be loose, corrugated, or muddy after rain, so a road bike with thin tyres should proceed with care, and an adventure bike will be more comfortable. Speeds are low, and the corners are tight, with wooded drops beside the road. There is little traffic, and the silence in the forest is deep.

Do not count on fuel or a full meal. Knysna, about twenty-five kilometres away, is the sensible place to fill up, and George, a bit farther, is the larger town. The village has basic shops, and it is a good place to stop and buy water, but it is not a tourist stop in the usual sense. Mist and rain are frequent, and the light under the trees fades early, so aim to be through the forest before dusk. A warm layer is helpful, because the air is cool and damp even in summer, and the quiet makes it easy to linger.
t.prince alfreds pass@-33.7,23.2:
Prince Alfred's Pass is one of the great gravel roads of the Cape, and it is wonderfully unhurried. It runs for around seventy kilometres from the forests of Knysna north to Avontuur, climbing through the Outeniqua Mountains to just over a thousand metres, and it is the sort of road where the journey is more important than the destination. The pass was designed by Thomas Bain and built in the 1860s, and it is named for Queen Victoria's son Prince Alfred, who visited the Cape in 1860.

The first stretch from Knysna runs through indigenous forest, with tall yellowwoods, ferns, and mossy trunks. As the road climbs, the forest gives way to fynbos and then to a drier, more open landscape of the Langkloof, a long valley known for its apple orchards. The contrast is dramatic, and so is the geology: the road is cut into sandstone and quartzite, and the scenery changes every few kilometres. There are old picnic spots, a few river crossings, and a very strong sense of remoteness.

It is a road for adventure bikes, or at least for riders who are comfortable on gravel. The surface is graded dirt, with corrugations, stones, and patches of deep, loose material. After heavy rain it can become muddy, and sections are narrow, with drops at the edge. Allow plenty of time, since the speed is low and the road is long. Mobile coverage is patchy.

The nearest towns with proper supplies are Knysna to the south and Uniondale beyond the northern end. Avontuur, which means adventure, is the tiny railhead at the top and it lives up to the name with its stillness. Spring and autumn are good seasons, with mild temperatures and clear skies, while winter can bring cold, rain, and even snow on the high ground. It is best to start early, since the light fades fast in the forest and a gravel pass is not something to tackle in the dark.
t.havesova primeval forest@49.0,22.3:
In the far north-east of Slovakia, in the hills where Slovakia, Poland and Ukraine meet, the beech forests have never been cut. Havešová is one of these primeval forests, a steep slope of giant beech trees, some over forty metres tall and hundreds of years old, with fallen trunks decaying slowly on the forest floor and new trees rising in the gaps. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, inscribed in 2007 and extended since, and it lies within Poloniny National Park, one of the least visited and most remote national parks in Central Europe.

The forest is strictly protected, and access is limited to a marked trail, which climbs steeply from the road. The atmosphere is extraordinary: dim, quiet, cool, with moss, ferns and fungi everywhere, and the sounds of woodpeckers and owls. Wolves, bears, lynx and European bison live in the area, though you are unlikely to see them.

The region is sparsely populated, with small villages, wooden churches and Rusyn culture. Several wooden churches in the area, such as those at Topoľa, Uličské Krivé and Ruský Potok, are worth a visit. The Starina reservoir, built in the 1980s to supply drinking water, flooded several villages, whose inhabitants were resettled.

The roads are narrow and winding, with little traffic, through forests and valleys, and they are a pleasure to ride, though surfaces can be rough. Snina, fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel, shops and services. The border with Ukraine is close but there is no crossing point in the immediate area, and the Polish Bieszczady mountains, across the border to the north, are reached by longer routes. Spring, when the forest is fresh green, and autumn, when the beeches turn gold and copper, are the best times.
t.bardejov town conservation reserve@49.3,:
Bardejov's main square is a long, gently sloping rectangle lined with Gothic and Renaissance burgher houses, their tall gables painted in pastel colours, with the Gothic Basilica of St Giles at the top and the old town hall standing alone in the middle. The town grew rich in the Middle Ages on trade between Hungary and Poland, and its walls, bastions and moat largely survive. Bardejov was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 2000, along with its Jewish suburb, with a synagogue and ritual bath from the eighteenth century, a reminder of the community that lived here until the Holocaust.

The basilica holds eleven Gothic winged altars, a remarkable collection, and the town hall, one of the first Renaissance buildings in Slovakia, houses a museum. In summer, the square fills with café terraces and the town feels lively but relaxed.

A few kilometres north, Bardejovské Kúpele is a spa town in a forested valley, with mineral springs, a colonnade, and an open-air museum of folk architecture, with wooden houses and churches brought from villages in the region. Empress Elisabeth of Austria, known as Sisi, stayed here in 1895, and a statue commemorates her visit.

The region around Bardejov is hilly and green, with wooden churches, forests and small villages, close to the Polish border. To the east, the Dukla pass was the scene of a terrible battle in 1944, when Soviet and Czechoslovak forces fought to break through German lines, with huge losses; a memorial and military museum at Svidník commemorate it. For riders, the roads are winding, with little traffic, and they cross into Poland toward the wooden churches of the Beskid Niski. Bardejov has fuel, shops and restaurants. Try bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese, and the local beer. Late spring and early autumn are lovely seasons here.
t.sarmizegetusa colonia ulpia traiana augu:
After conquering Dacia in AD 106, the emperor Trajan founded a new capital for the province in the Hațeg basin, and named it Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa, borrowing the name of the Dacian royal capital in the Orăștie mountains to the north-east. The city grew into a prosperous centre, with a forum, temples, baths, and an amphitheatre that could seat thousands, and its ruins, partly excavated, lie in fields beside the modern village of Sarmizegetusa. The site has a museum, and you can walk around the forum and the amphitheatre, imagining the gladiatorial games that once filled it.

The Hațeg basin is a beautiful landscape, a flat valley surrounded by mountains, with the Retezat to the south, one of the wildest ranges in the Carpathians, with glacial lakes and peaks over 2,500 metres. The Hațeg Country is also a UNESCO Global Geopark, known for its dinosaur fossils, including dwarf dinosaurs that lived on an island here at the end of the Cretaceous period.

The area is full of historical sites: the church of Densuș, built partly from Roman stones, one of the oldest churches in Romania; the Prislop monastery, in a peaceful valley; the ruined castles of Colț and Mălăiești; and, further north, Corvin Castle in Hunedoara, a Gothic fortress with towers and a drawbridge.

For riders, the roads around Hațeg are pleasant, with gentle curves through the valley and steeper climbs into the mountains. The road from Hațeg over the Merișor pass to Petroșani is a good ride, and from there you can reach the Transalpina and the Jiu gorge. Weather can change quickly in the mountains, and the high roads close in winter. Hațeg, eighteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants. The villages of the basin sell sheep cheese and smoked bacon from the farm gate, and a glass of plum brandy is often offered before you can refuse. Late afternoon is the time to be in the ruins, when the Retezat turns blue behind the amphitheatre and the fields go quiet.
t.lozna curmaturita 1@47.3,23.5:
Lozna is a village in the northern hills of Sălaj county, close to the Someș river, a place of small farms, orchards and wooden houses, and Curmăturița is a saddle in the hills above it, where a Roman watchtower is thought to have stood. The northern frontier of Roman Dacia ran through this area, following ridges and river valleys, and small towers and forts were placed to watch over the approaches. Today there is little to see, but the view from the saddle, over the rolling hills and the Someș valley, is lovely, and it explains why the Romans chose the spot.

The countryside around Lozna is quiet and traditional, with hay meadows, plum orchards and patches of forest. The villages have wooden churches, some of them old, and the people are welcoming to visitors. In autumn, the smell of plum brandy, țuică, being distilled in the yards fills the air.

Jibou, seventeen kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel, shops and services. It is home to the Wesselényi castle, a Baroque palace of a Hungarian noble family, and a botanical garden, one of the largest in Romania, with greenhouses and gardens. The Someș valley, between Jibou and Dej, is a winding river road through wooded hills, with a railway line alongside.

The roads in the hills are narrow, winding and often in poor condition, with potholes, gravel and dirt sections, so ride carefully, especially in wet weather. Watch out for horse carts, animals and farm vehicles. The main road along the Someș is better, with gentle curves and good views. May is lovely, with orchards in blossom and meadows full of flowers, and September brings the plum harvest and long, soft evenings. Whatever the month, carry water and something to eat, since village shops keep irregular hours, and allow time to talk: in places like Lozna, a stranger on a motorcycle is still an event, and the conversation that follows is often the best part of the day.
t.monastery of horezu@45.2,24.0:
Constantin Brâncoveanu, prince of Wallachia at the end of the seventeenth century, was a wealthy, cultured ruler who built churches, palaces and monasteries across his principality, and Horezu was his masterpiece. Founded in 1690, the monastery sits in a quiet valley in the foothills of the Căpățânii mountains, surrounded by walls, with a church at the centre of a courtyard lined with arcaded cells. It is the finest example of the Brâncovenesc style, a blend of Byzantine, Renaissance and Baroque, with carved stone, painted interiors and elegant porches, and it was inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1993. In 1714, Brâncoveanu and his four sons were executed by the Ottomans in Istanbul; the Romanian Orthodox Church later canonised them as martyrs.

The church is richly painted inside, with portraits of the founder and his family, and the monastery is home to a community of nuns, so dress modestly and keep quiet.

The town of Horezu, a couple of kilometres away, is famous for its pottery, with red, brown and cream glazes decorated with roosters, fish, spirals and flowers. The craft of Horezu ceramics is listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage, and potters sell their work in workshops and roadside stalls. Horezu has fuel, shops and restaurants.

The region of northern Oltenia is excellent for riding. The road along the foothills, from Râmnicu Vâlcea to Târgu Jiu, passes through villages, orchards and forests, with monasteries along the way, such as Bistrița, Arnota and Polovragi. To the north, the mountains rise, and the Transalpina, one of the highest roads in Romania, starts at Novaci, not far to the west, climbing to over 2,100 metres. The Olt valley, to the east, offers a gorge road toward Sibiu. The Transalpina opens only in the warmer months, usually from early summer to mid autumn, so check before planning a crossing. Back in Horezu, a plate of sarmale, cabbage rolls with polenta and sour cream, makes a fine end to the day, eaten off a local plate if the restaurant has any sense.
t.porolissum@47.2,23.2:
On a hill above the village of Moigrad, the Roman town of Porolissum guarded a key pass through the Meseș mountains, the gateway to Roman Dacia from the north-west. Founded as a military camp after the conquest in 106, it grew into a town of thousands, with a large fort, an amphitheatre, temples, baths and a customs post, and it became a municipium, a self-governing city, under the emperor Septimius Severus. The ruins are among the most impressive Roman remains in Romania, with a reconstructed fort gate, walls and parts of the town, and they are part of the frontier sites of Roman Dacia.

The site covers a large area on the hilltop, with views over the Meseș mountains and the Transylvanian plain. Walking around it, you can see the outlines of buildings, roads, the amphitheatre and the fort, and imagine the bustle of a frontier town, with soldiers, merchants and travellers coming and going.

Zalău, eight kilometres away, is the county capital, a town of over sixty thousand, with fuel, shops and restaurants. The county museum has a good collection of finds from Porolissum. The Meseș mountains, a low ridge of forests and pastures, are pleasant for walking and riding, with winding roads through villages and woods.

The roads around Porolissum are narrow and winding, with some potholes and gravel, and the climb up to the site from Moigrad is steep. The main road from Zalău to Cluj crosses the Meseș pass, with curves and climbs, but also heavy traffic. The best time to visit is spring or autumn, when the hills are green or golden and the weather mild. Visit in the morning, when the hilltop is cool and empty, and the wind brings the smell of cut hay up from the fields. Several villages around the Meseș keep small wooden churches with shingled spires, worth a detour on the way back down, and Zalău has the cafés and the full tank you will want afterwards.
t.banita@45.5,23.2:
The Dacians, before the Romans conquered them, built a ring of fortresses in the mountains around their capital Sarmizegetusa Regia, and Banița is one of them, perched on a limestone peak, Piatra Cetii, above the village of the same name. It guarded the southern approach to the Dacian heartland, controlling the route from the Jiu valley, and it was taken by the Romans during Trajan's wars at the beginning of the second century. The Dacian Fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains, including Banița, were inscribed on the UNESCO list in 1999.

The remains are modest, with stone walls and terraces, but the setting is dramatic, on a rocky summit with views over the mountains and valleys. The climb from the village is steep, and the path can be slippery, so wear good shoes.

The village of Banița lies in a valley between the Șureanu and Retezat mountains, close to the Jiu valley, the coal-mining region of Romania. Petroșani, Vulcan and Lupeni were mining towns, and the miners played a dramatic role in Romanian politics in the 1990s, with violent marches on Bucharest known as the mineriade. Many mines have closed, and the region is trying to reinvent itself through tourism.

For riders, the area offers excellent roads. The DN66 runs from Hațeg over the Merișor pass to Petroșani, a winding road through forests, and from Petroșani, the Transalpina climbs south over the mountains to Novaci, one of the highest roads in Romania, while the Jiu gorge road heads south toward Târgu Jiu. Weather can change quickly in the mountains, and high roads close in winter. Vulcan, ten kilometres away, has fuel and shops. In the guesthouses of the Jiu valley, the food is miners’ food: big bowls of sour soup, polenta with cheese and sour cream, grilled meat. After a day on the high roads, nothing could be better, and the evenings at this altitude are cool even in July.
t.yasynia tserkva of our lord s ascension@:
High in the Ukrainian Carpathians, in the valley of the Black Tisa, the village of Yasinia stretches along the river beneath steep spruce-clad slopes. On a rise near its centre stands a small wooden church, the Church of the Ascension, sometimes called the Strukivska church, built in the early nineteenth century by Hutsul craftsmen without nails. Its stepped roofs, covered in wooden shingles, and its small domes give it a cosy, fairytale shape, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of wooden tserkvas of the Carpathian region in Poland and Ukraine.

The Hutsuls are the highlanders of these mountains, known for their colourful embroidery, woodcarving, music and the long wooden trembita horns that once carried messages across the valleys. Yasinia is surrounded by some of the finest mountain scenery in Ukraine. To the east rises the Chornohora ridge with Hoverla, the country's highest peak at just over two thousand metres, and to the west the Svydovets range, both partly protected in the Carpathian Biosphere Reserve with ancient beech forests also on the UNESCO list. In summer the high pastures, the polonyny, are dotted with shepherds' huts and the smell of wood smoke and cheese.

The road through Yasinia climbs over the Yablunytsia pass towards Ivano-Frankivsk, with long bends through forest and open views towards the peaks. The surface ranges from new asphalt to deep potholes, and logging trucks, livestock and horse-drawn carts are all part of the traffic. Weather in the mountains can change quickly, with heavy rain and fog in summer and deep snow in winter.

Ukraine has been at war since the full-scale Russian invasion of 2022, and all of the country is under travel warnings from most governments, so check the current situation, entry rules and insurance carefully before considering a visit. Yasinia, with several thousand residents, has fuel, shops and small cafés, though supplies can be irregular. Hutsul cuisine includes banosh, a rich cornmeal porridge cooked with sour cream and topped with brynza cheese and crackling, as well as mushrooms and berries picked from the surrounding forests.
t.barsau mare cetate@47.3,23.7:
In the north of Transylvania, the Someș river winds through a valley of green hills, woods and villages with wooden churches and haystacks, and on a hilltop near the village of Bârsău Mare, the faint remains of a Roman fortification overlook the valley. This was part of the northern frontier of Roman Dacia, the province created after Trajan's conquest in the early second century, and it is one of the sites included in the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia, listed by UNESCO in 2024.

The northern frontier of Dacia ran along the hills and valleys of this region, guarding the province against the free Dacians and other peoples beyond. Fortlets and watchtowers like the one at Bârsău Mare were linked to larger forts, such as Porolissum, near Zalău, one of the largest Roman sites in Romania. The Romans withdrew from Dacia in the 270s, but the region kept its Latin-based language, and the debate about the continuity of Romanians in Transylvania remains a lively topic. The landscape here is rural and traditional, with horse-drawn carts, orchards and meadows full of flowers in spring.

The roads in this part of Romania vary greatly. Main routes are generally paved and in reasonable condition, while smaller roads can be potholed or unpaved, especially in villages. Traffic is light, but watch for horse carts, livestock and pedestrians, especially at dusk. The valley of the Someș offers pleasant riding, with gentle curves and views, while the hills to the north and west, towards Maramureș, have more challenging and scenic routes, through forests and over passes.

Fuel is available in Dej, a town of almost forty thousand, and in larger villages, while small villages may have no services. Dej is known for its salt mine, now open to visitors. Romanian cuisine is hearty: try sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with meat and rice, served with polenta and sour cream, or ciorbă, a sour soup with vegetables and meat. Village shops and restaurants are simple but welcoming, and locals are often curious about travellers.
t.treznea dealul manastirii@47.1,23.0:
The Meseș mountains, a low, wooded range in north-western Romania, formed a natural barrier for the Roman province of Dacia, and the Romans fortified it with a line of watchtowers, walls and fortlets. Near the village of Treznea, on a hill known as Dealul Mănăstirii, the Monastery Hill, the remains of one of these defences overlook the valleys. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia, listed by UNESCO in 2024, and a short distance away lies Porolissum, one of the largest Roman settlements in Dacia, with a reconstructed gate and an amphitheatre.

Treznea has a darker, more recent history. In September 1940, after northern Transylvania was transferred to Hungary, Hungarian troops killed dozens of villagers here, and a memorial commemorates the victims. The surrounding hills are covered in beech and oak forests, with meadows and orchards around the villages, and the area is known for its traditional wooden architecture and rural life. In spring, the meadows bloom with wildflowers, and in autumn, the forests turn gold and red.

The riding in this area is varied and often challenging. The roads over the Meseș mountains climb through forests, with tight bends and steep gradients, while the valleys have gentler, flowing routes through villages and farmland. Road surfaces vary from good asphalt to potholed and gravel, and horse carts, livestock and pedestrians are common. The main road between Zalău and Cluj-Napoca is busy with trucks, so it pays to explore the smaller roads.

Zalău, a town of over sixty thousand, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and is the capital of Sălaj county. The county museum in Zalău has a good collection of Roman finds from Porolissum. Local cuisine includes dishes such as tocană, a meat stew, and papanași, fried dough with sour cream and jam, as well as pălincă, a strong fruit brandy, offered as a welcome in many homes. Take time to talk with locals, who are often generous with stories and hospitality.
t.uzhok tserkva of the synaxis of the arch:
Just below the pass that carries the road and railway from Uzhhorod into Galicia, the village of Uzhok keeps one of the finest wooden churches of the Carpathians. The tserkva of the Synaxis of the Archangel Michael was built in the middle of the eighteenth century in the Boyko style, with three log chambers each topped by a tiered roof, rising in stages like a set of stacked hats, all covered in wooden shingles. It stands on a slope among old trees, with a separate bell tower nearby, and it is one of the sixteen wooden tserkvas of the Carpathian region in Poland and Ukraine listed by UNESCO in 2013.

The Uzhok Pass itself, at 852 metres, has been a crossing point since medieval times, linking the Hungarian lowlands with Galicia, and it saw heavy fighting in the First World War, when the Russian and Austro-Hungarian armies battled for control of the Carpathian passes in the winter of 1914 and 1915. Military cemeteries from that war lie scattered through these mountains. The pass also marks the boundary between the Zakarpattia and Lviv regions, and nearby the borders of Ukraine, Poland and Slovakia meet, with the protected beech forests of the region stretching across all three countries.

The road over the pass is one of the quieter routes through the Ukrainian Carpathians, with long climbs through beech and spruce forests, gentle hairpins and views over rolling ridges. The surface has historically been uneven, with potholes and patched sections, and conditions change from year to year, so it is worth asking locally. Snow covers the pass in winter, and fog and rain are common in spring and autumn.

It has to be said plainly: Ukraine is at war, and the situation affects travel throughout the country, including the western regions, even though they are far from the front line. Martial law is in force, there are restrictions on movement, and border crossings may be busy or limited. Anyone thinking of riding here should check the latest official travel advice. When peace allows, this is a beautiful and welcoming region, with villages where wooden churches, old traditions and simple mountain food, mushrooms, cheese, potatoes and smoked meats, are still part of daily life. The nearest larger towns are Turka on the Galician side and Velykyi Bereznyi in Zakarpattia.
t.matkiv tserkva of the synaxis of the ble:
Matkiv is a small village in the upper valley of the Stryi river, in the Turka district of the Lviv region, high in the Ukrainian Carpathians. Its wooden church, the tserkva of the Synaxis of the Blessed Virgin Mary, was built in the first half of the nineteenth century, and it is a fine example of the Boyko tradition, named after the highland people who have lived in these mountains for centuries. The church has three log frames topped by tiered pyramidal roofs, each level slightly smaller than the one below, and the whole building is covered in wooden shingles that have weathered to a silver grey. It is part of the UNESCO listing of wooden tserkvas of the Carpathian region in Poland and Ukraine.

What makes these churches remarkable is their construction. They were built by local carpenters using techniques passed down through generations, often without nails, with logs carefully notched and fitted together. Inside, the walls are often painted with religious scenes, and the iconostasis, the wall of icons separating the altar from the nave, is the centrepiece. Each church reflects the faith, the skills and the resources of its community, and many are still used for worship today.

The Boyko country around Matkiv is a land of rolling ridges, forests, meadows and small villages strung out along the river valleys. Haymaking is still done by hand in many places, and the haystacks, built around wooden poles, dot the hillsides in summer. Volovets, about twenty three kilometres away, sits on the other side of the main ridge in Zakarpattia, while Slavske, a ski resort, is a similar distance away to the east. The roads are narrow, winding and often in poor condition, with potholes, gravel and mud after rain, and they pass through forests where bears and wolves still live, though they are rarely seen.

The war in Ukraine affects any plan to visit. Even in the west of the country, far from the front, there are restrictions, air raid alerts and changing rules for foreigners, and official travel advice must be checked before setting out. In calmer times, this is a region of great beauty and quiet hospitality, where a traveller can still find a bed in a village house and a meal of banosh, a dish of cornmeal cooked with sour cream, topped with cheese and crackling.
t.church of the holy archangels@47.6,23.8:
Șurdești is a small village in the hills of Maramureș, in the north of Romania, and its wooden church of the Holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel is famous for its spire. Built in the eighteenth century from oak logs, the church has a steep double roof covered in shingles and a slender tower that rises far above the trees, among the tallest wooden church towers in the region. It is one of eight wooden churches of Maramureș listed by UNESCO in 1999, each a masterpiece of local carpentry, built by village craftsmen using traditional techniques.

The churches of Maramureș were built in wood partly because the Orthodox Romanian communities were not allowed, under Hungarian rule, to build in stone, and partly because wood was abundant in the surrounding forests. Inside, the walls are covered in painted scenes from the Bible, often with local touches, such as saints in peasant costume or devils with the faces of unpopular officials. The church at Șurdești is still used for services, and visitors are welcome when it is open, though it is polite to dress modestly.

Maramureș is one of the most traditional regions of Europe, where many people still live by farming, with horse-drawn carts on the roads, haystacks in the fields and carved wooden gates in front of the houses. The riding is superb, with roads winding through green hills, forests and villages. The best road in the area is the climb over the Gutâi Pass, between Baia Mare and Sighetu Marmației, a twisting mountain road through beech forests, with tight bends, steep sections and views over the hills. The surface has improved in recent years, but potholes and gravel can still catch you out, and horse-drawn carts appear around blind bends.

Baia Sprie, about eight kilometres away, is an old mining town with fuel and shops, while Baia Mare, the regional capital, is a larger city with everything you could need. The local food is simple and filling: sour soups, polenta with cheese and sour cream, stuffed cabbage rolls and the strong plum brandy, palincă, offered to visitors as a sign of welcome. Accept a small glass if you must, but only at the end of the day's ride. Winters are cold and snowy, and the best riding season runs from late spring to early autumn.
t.dobricel varful lazului@47.3,24.1:
Spermezeu is the kind of place a road atlas barely notices: a commune of scattered villages in the hills of Bistrița-Năsăud, in northern Transylvania, between the upper Someș valley and the Țibleș mountains. The site of Dobricel, on the hilltop known as Vârful Lazului, is one of the many archaeological places recorded in the area, a high point above the valleys where traces of earlier inhabitants have been noted. There is not much to see without an archaeologist's eye, but the hilltop and the country around it are a good excuse for a ride through a region few foreigners ever visit.

This is a landscape of rounded hills, orchards, hay meadows and beech woods, with villages strung along the streams. Life still follows the seasons, with haymaking in summer, plum picking in autumn and pig slaughtering before Christmas. Many houses have carved wooden gates and verandas, and the churches range from old wooden buildings to newer, larger ones built with money sent home by villagers working abroad. Spermezeu, Dobric and Negrilești are small communities, each with a church, a shop and perhaps a bar.

The roads in this part of Transylvania are a mix of tarmac and gravel, with the main roads generally in decent condition and the side roads narrow, rough and sometimes muddy. Climbing to the hilltops brings wide views over the hills, towards the mountains of Rodna and Țibleș to the north and east. The riding is slow but rewarding, with little traffic, apart from tractors, carts and the occasional flock of sheep. Dogs guarding the sheep can be aggressive, so ride past them slowly and calmly.

Fuel is not available in every village, so fill up in a larger town before heading into the hills. Căianu Mic, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest town of over five thousand people, and Beclean and Bistrița are the larger centres in the area. The food in village guesthouses is home cooked and generous, with soups, stews, cheese and fresh bread, and the plum brandy flows freely. The weather is continental, with hot summers, cold winters and frequent thunderstorms in the afternoons in summer, which can turn dirt roads into mud in minutes.
t.bologa magura bologii@46.9,22.9:
Bologa is a village in the valley of the Crișul Repede, the swift river that flows west from the hills of Cluj county towards Oradea and the Hungarian plain. On the hill above it, known as Măgura Bologii, lie the remains of a castle that once guarded the valley, and in the fields nearby are the traces of a Roman fort, built to protect the north western edge of the province of Dacia. The fort, known in antiquity as Resculum, is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia, listed by UNESCO in 2024, a line of forts, watchtowers and walls that ran along the edge of the Roman province from the second to the third century.

The Crișul Repede valley has always been a corridor, and today it carries the main road from Cluj-Napoca to Oradea, as well as the railway. Ciucea, a few kilometres downstream, was the home of the poet and politician Octavian Goga, whose house and gardens are now a museum. Further down, the river cuts a gorge through the mountains, with rock walls, tunnels and the railway weaving in and out along the river.

The main road through the valley is busy, especially with trucks, and it is not much fun to ride. But the roads that branch off into the Apuseni mountains to the south are a different story. They climb through forests and meadows, past villages and farms, to high plateaus with wide views, caves and karst landscapes. The Apuseni are one of the best riding areas in Romania, with quiet roads, varied scenery and friendly people. The surface quality varies, and some roads are unpaved, but that is part of the adventure.

Huedin, about fifteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, shops and restaurants. The area around Huedin, known as Țara Călatei, is home to a Hungarian minority with its own traditions, including colourful costumes and painted wooden ceilings in the churches. The food is a mix of Romanian and Hungarian, with goulash, stuffed cabbage and sweet pastries. The weather is changeable, with rain likely at any time, and the mountains can be cold even in summer, so pack layers and waterproofs.
t.surducu mare centum putea rovina@45.3,21:
A hundred wells: that is the meaning of Centum Putea, the Latin name of a Roman fort in the hills of the Banat, near the village of Surducu Mare in Caraș-Severin county. It was one of the forts that guarded the road from the Danube to the heart of Roman Dacia after the emperor Trajan conquered the region in the early second century, and it is part of the line of sites listed by UNESCO as the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia. Little survives above ground, just traces of earthworks in the fields, but the name alone conjures a picture of a well-watered camp on the road north.

The Banat is a region with a complex history, ruled in turn by Hungarians, Ottomans and Habsburgs, and settled by Romanians, Serbs, Germans, Hungarians, Czechs, Slovaks and others. In the eighteenth century, the Habsburgs brought in settlers from all over their empire to farm the land, and the villages still reflect that mix, with churches of different faiths, and sometimes different languages spoken in neighbouring villages. Many of the German communities left after the Second World War or emigrated in later decades, leaving empty houses behind.

The landscape around Surducu Mare is a mix of low hills, fields, orchards and woods, between the Banat plain to the west and the mountains to the east. The roads are mostly quiet, with gentle bends and short climbs, and they link small villages and towns. The surface can be rough, with potholes and patched sections, and some roads are unpaved. Further south, the Danube Gorges, where the river cuts through the Carpathians at the Iron Gates, offer some of the most spectacular riding in Romania, with the road running along the river beneath towering cliffs.

Bocșa, about fifteen kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel and shops, and Reșița, an old industrial city with a long tradition of iron and steel making, is a little further east. Timișoara, the largest city in the Banat, is a lively, cosmopolitan place, and the starting point of the revolution of 1989 that brought down the communist regime. The summers are hot and dry, so carry plenty of water, and the winters can be cold, with snow in the hills.
t.santioana varful mortila@47.0,24.6:
Sântioana sits in rolling country on the edge of the Transylvanian Plain, in Bistrița-Năsăud county, a gentle landscape of low hills, fields, orchards and scattered woods. The hilltop of Vârful Mortila, above the village, is one of the many archaeological places recorded in this part of Transylvania, a high point that would have made a natural lookout or settlement site for earlier peoples. There is little to see on the surface, but the view from the top gives a fine sense of the landscape, with the Transylvanian hills rolling away in every direction and the mountains rising on the horizon.

The area has a strong Saxon heritage. Teaca, a small town about eight kilometres away, was founded by German settlers in the Middle Ages and has a large Gothic church, and the surrounding villages were once home to Saxon farmers, many of whom left for Germany in the late twentieth century. Bistrița, the county capital, is an old Saxon town with a tall church spire, arcaded houses and fragments of its medieval walls, and it is also the town where Jonathan Harker stops on his way to Count Dracula's castle in Bram Stoker's novel. The Borgo Pass of the novel, now the Tihuța Pass, lies to the north east, and its road towards Bukovina is one of the classic rides of the region.

The riding around Sântioana is easy going, with roads winding through the hills, linking villages and small towns. The surfaces vary, with some good stretches and some rough patches, and the side roads may be gravel or dirt. Traffic is light, except near the towns and on the main roads. In summer, the fields are full of sunflowers and maize, and in autumn the woods turn gold and red. Watch out for horse-drawn carts, which are still common in rural Romania, especially on minor roads and in the evening.

Fuel is available in Teaca and the larger towns, but not in every village, so plan your stops. Mărișelu and Șieu are small communities with basic shops. The food in this part of Transylvania is hearty, with sour soups, stews, sausages and pastries, and the local wines from the hills around Teaca have a long tradition. The weather is continental, with warm summers, cold winters and afternoon storms that can be sudden and heavy.
t.brancovenesti castel@46.9,24.8:
Upstream from Reghin, where the Mureș leaves the mountains and widens into the Transylvanian hill country, the village of Brâncovenești stands beside a castle with round corner towers and a long, plain facade overlooking the river. Known in Hungarian as Marosvécs, it was rebuilt several times over the centuries, and in the twentieth century it belonged to the Kemény family. Between the two world wars, Baron János Kemény opened its doors to a circle of Hungarian writers from Transylvania, the Helikon group, who met here every summer to read, debate and plan their literary work. Those gatherings made a remote country house one of the liveliest literary addresses in the region for almost two decades.

The castle stands on a site with much older roots. A Roman fort guarded the Mureș valley here, at the north eastern edge of the province of Dacia, and its remains are part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia, added to the UNESCO list in 2024. The fort controlled the route up the valley into the Carpathians, the same route that the modern road and railway follow today.

For riders, the valley of the upper Mureș is a fine introduction to the Carpathians. North of Brâncovenești, the river enters the Mureș Defile between Deda and Toplița, a narrow, wooded gorge about thirty kilometres long, where the road follows the river through a series of bends, with forested slopes rising steeply on both sides. It is a beautiful ride, though the road can be busy with trucks, and the surface varies. Beyond Toplița, the road climbs towards the high basins of Harghita and the eastern Carpathians.

Reghin, about eight kilometres away, is the main town of the area, with fuel, shops and restaurants, and it has a long tradition of making musical instruments, especially violins, from the resonant spruce wood of the surrounding mountains. The area is ethnically mixed, with Romanian and Hungarian communities living side by side, each with its own churches and traditions. The food reflects that mix, with goulash and chimney cake alongside sarmale and polenta. The weather is continental, with warm summers and cold winters, and the river valley can be foggy in the mornings in spring and autumn.
t.levoca@49.0,20.8:
Spread across a ridge in eastern Slovakia, with the jagged peaks of the High Tatras rising on the northern horizon, the Spiš region holds one of Europe's great clusters of medieval monuments. The town of Levoča, the old regional capital, was a wealthy royal free town, and its walls, burgher houses and Renaissance town hall still surround a long central square. Inside the church of St James stands Master Paul of Levoča's carved Gothic altarpiece, finished in the early sixteenth century and the tallest of its kind in the world, an astonishing tower of limewood saints and filigree.

Close by, above Spišské Podhradie, Spiš Castle sprawls across a travertine hill: one of the largest castle complexes in Central Europe, its ruined walls covering a whole summit and visible for miles. Opposite it, on another hill, Spišská Kapitula is a small walled church town with a cathedral and canons' houses, little changed in centuries. Levoča, the castle, the Kapitula and the Gothic church at Žehra, with its remarkable medieval frescoes, are listed together by UNESCO, and riding between them gives you a day of shifting perspectives on the same few hills.

The riding is easy-going and scenic, across rolling farmland, rapeseed fields and woods, with the castle appearing and disappearing on its hill as you approach. The main road between Prešov and Poprad passes through the area and can be busy with trucks; the minor roads to Žehra and towards the Slovenský raj national park are quieter and more fun, with gentle curves and occasional rough patches. Weather can turn quickly, especially with the Tatras so close, and on clear autumn evenings the castle glows orange in the last light.

Spišské Podhradie and Levoča both have fuel and places to eat; Krompachy is another option. Try bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese and bacon, and a cold Slovak beer once the riding is done. The castle is a steep walk up from the car park, worth every step for the view over the Spiš basin. In summer the castle hosts historical events, and if you are around in early July, Levoča's pilgrimage to the hill above town draws huge crowds.
t.rozok@49.0,22.5:
Rožok is a small patch of very old forest on the eastern edge of Slovakia, close to the borders with Poland and Ukraine, and it is one of the components of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a World Heritage Site that stretches across many countries. Here, on a steep slope above the Starina reservoir, beech trees have grown undisturbed for centuries, some of them huge, with smooth grey trunks and wide canopies, and fallen trees lie rotting on the forest floor, feeding fungi, insects and birds.

It is part of the Poloniny national park, the most remote and least populated corner of Slovakia, where the mountains roll away in long, forested ridges and meadows called poloniny open up on the summits. Wolves, bears and lynx live in the forests, and European bison have been reintroduced. The area is also rich in wooden churches, built by the Rusyn communities who lived here for centuries, and many villages were abandoned when the Starina reservoir was built in the 1980s to supply drinking water to eastern Slovakia.

The roads here are narrow, quiet and winding, following valleys between the forested hills. From Snina, the road leads past the reservoir towards Stakčín and the villages near the Ukrainian border, with little traffic apart from the occasional truck carrying timber. The surfaces can be rough, with potholes and gravel, and the roads become narrower and steeper in the hills. The forest is beautiful in autumn, when the beech trees turn golden, and spring brings a carpet of wildflowers.

Snina, roughly twenty kilometres back towards the west, is the last place with a proper filling station and supermarket; beyond it the villages offer a shop, a pub and a lot of silence, so arrive with a full tank. The forest itself can be visited on a marked trail, which is steep in places but rewarding. Remember that this is a protected area, and stick to the marked trails and respect the rules of the park.
t.ladomirova@49.3,21.6:
In the village of Ladomirová, just north of Svidník in north-eastern Slovakia, a small wooden church dedicated to the Archangel Michael stands on a gentle rise among trees. Built in the eighteenth century by the Greek Catholic community without using a single nail, it has three wooden towers with onion-shaped tops, rising in height from east to west, and its interior holds an iconostasis of painted icons. It is one of the eight wooden churches of the Slovak Carpathians inscribed together by UNESCO in 2008, and its simplicity and craftsmanship are deeply moving.

The surrounding region is the land of the Rusyns, an East Slavic people with their own language and culture, and Svidník has an open-air museum of folk architecture and a museum of Ukrainian and Rusyn culture. The hills around here saw some of the fiercest fighting of the Second World War in central Europe, during the Battle of the Dukla Pass in the autumn of 1944, when Soviet and Czechoslovak troops tried to break through German defences. A large memorial and military cemetery stand near Svidník, and tanks and aircraft are displayed in the so-called Valley of Death north of town.

The riding around Ladomirová is gentle and rural, through rolling hills, forests and small villages. The main road from Svidník to the Dukla Pass and the Polish border carries some trucks, but the side roads are quiet, with gentle bends and a few rough patches. The landscape is green and peaceful, and the wooden churches dotted around the villages make for a rewarding tour. May, with fresh green on every slope, and October, when the woods go russet, are the months to aim for.

Svidník is five minutes down the road for petrol, a supermarket and a plate of halušky. The church at Ladomirová is usually locked, but the key can often be obtained from a local caretaker, and a visit is well worth the effort. Respect the church as a place of worship, and dress modestly.
t.kwiaton tserkva of saint paraskeva@49.5,:
The little wooden church at Kwiatoń is often called the most beautiful of its kind in Poland, and when you see it you understand why. Built in the seventeenth century by the Lemko community, it has three parts, each topped by a tower with a bulbous cupola, rising in height from the sanctuary at the east to the bell tower at the west, all clad in wooden shingles and set in a green churchyard among old trees. Inside, painted walls and an iconostasis of icons glow in the dim light. It is one of the wooden tserkvas of the Carpathian region in Poland and Ukraine inscribed by UNESCO in 2013.

The Lemkos, a Rusyn people, lived in these hills of the Beskid Niski for centuries, until most of them were deported in 1947 in Operation Vistula, when the communist authorities forcibly resettled Ukrainian and Lemko populations to western Poland. Many of their churches were taken over by Roman Catholic parishes, and the landscape still bears the scars of abandoned villages and overgrown orchards. In 1915 the First World War swept through too, with the great Gorlice offensive, and many small war cemeteries, some designed by the Slovak architect Dušan Jurkovič, are scattered through the hills.

The roads of the Beskid Niski are quiet, narrow and winding, through forests and valleys and over low passes, with little traffic and lovely views. The surfaces can be rough, especially on the smaller roads, and the weather can change quickly. The area is perfect for relaxed touring, with plenty of wooden churches to explore, and it is beautiful in all seasons, especially in autumn when the forests change colour.

For fuel and a proper meal, ride the seventeen kilometres to Gorlice, which is also known as the place where the world's first street lamp fuelled by kerosene was lit, by Ignacy Łukasiewicz, in 1854. The villages around Kwiatoń have little more than a shop, so plan ahead. The church is usually locked, but it can be visited on certain days, and there is information at the entrance.
t.wolosatka stream valley@49.1,22.7:
The Wołosatka is a mountain stream in the far south-eastern corner of Poland, draining the slopes below Tarnica, at 1,346 metres the highest summit of the Polish Bieszczady. Its valley is part of Bieszczady National Park and of the World Heritage listing of primeval Carpathian beech forests: dark, mossy woods of beech and fir where dead trunks are left to fall and rot, and where bears, wolves, lynx and wildcats still move freely. Above the treeline the ridges open into the połoniny, high grass meadows that turn tawny in autumn and give the range its rolling, almost Scottish silhouette.

This was once a lively corner of the old Polish-Ukrainian borderland, home to Boyko villages, Orthodox churches and Jewish townsfolk. War and the forced resettlements of the 1940s emptied it almost completely, and nature crept back over orchards, cemeteries and foundations. At Wołosate, at the head of the valley, a stud farm breeds the sturdy Hucul mountain horses, and the trailheads up to Tarnica fill with hikers on summer weekends. Turka and the Ukrainian villages over the ridge look close on the map, but the frontier here is closed to casual crossing; this is a dead end in the best sense.

For riders the draw is the Wielka Pętla Bieszczadzka, the big Bieszczady loop through Lesko, Ustrzyki Dolne, Ustrzyki Górne, Wetlina and Cisna, which has become a classic Polish motorcycle tour. The road down to Wołosate branches off it near Ustrzyki Górne, a narrow ribbon along the valley floor with forest pressing in on both sides. Surfaces have improved a lot over the years, but expect frost damage, gravel in corners, logging trucks and walkers on the verge. Late September and October, when the beeches blaze copper against blue sky, are glorious; winter is long and snowy.

Fuel is the thing to plan here. Lutowiska is the nearest village of any size, but for a reliable fill and a supermarket think of Ustrzyki Dolne or Lesko, and do not run the tank low on the loop. Ustrzyki Górne has a few eateries serving pierogi, trout and żurek sour soup to hungry hikers, and simple guesthouses dot the valleys. The phone signal comes and goes, which some people regard as a feature.
Roman Dacia's north-western frontier ran along the crest of the Meseș mountains, and the hill country around Mirșid, east of Zalău, is laced with its traces: watchtowers, earthworks and small forts placed so that each could see the next. In 2024 these remains became part of the World Heritage listing for the Frontiers of the Roman Empire in Dacia. The name of the spot, La Strâmtură by the wolves' brook, gives a fair idea of its character: a narrow place in the hills, wooded and quiet, where the eye has to work to pick out a low mound or a ditch in the grass.

A few kilometres away lies the reason for all this watchfulness. Porolissum, near the village of Moigrad, was the great Roman stronghold of the region, a fort and town that controlled a key pass and the trade that flowed through it from the free Dacian lands beyond. Its rebuilt stone gate and walls stand on a hilltop, and walking among the foundations of the amphitheatre and the customs post, looking north over the Someș plain, you feel very much at the edge of the empire.

The roads here are a pleasure for anyone who likes quiet, rolling country. Minor roads loop between villages of houses with wooden gates and orchards, climbing over low ridges and dropping into valleys, with views of the Meseș hills and the plain. Surfaces range from new tarmac to patched and potholed, and horse-drawn carts are still a normal part of the traffic, as are dogs who take their guarding duties seriously. Autumn, with the beech woods turning and plum brandy being distilled in the villages, is a lovely time.

Zalău, the county town, is only about seven kilometres away and has fuel, supermarkets, mechanics and restaurants. Mirșid itself is a village with a shop or two. Sălaj cooking is hearty: sour soups, sarmale cabbage rolls, polenta with cheese and cream, and of course pálinka or țuică offered with enthusiasm. Ask before stepping onto field paths to reach the remains, and give grazing animals and their shepherd dogs plenty of room.
t.dumbraveni dealul podului 2@47.3,24.0:
Above the valley of the Someș Mare in Bistrița-Năsăud county, the hill called Dealul Podului carries the faint remains of a Roman watch post, one of a string of small installations that kept an eye on the northern edge of the province of Dacia. Like many points on this frontier, inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2024, it is less a monument than a viewpoint with a story, a place where soldiers once scanned the horizon for movement in the free lands to the north. Today the horizon holds forested ridges, orchards and villages strung along the river.

Just to the west stands a ruin with a very different tale. The castle of Ciceu, above the village of Ciceu-Mihăiești, was for a time a possession of the princes of Moldavia inside Transylvania, granted to Stephen the Great in the late fifteenth century, which shows how tangled the politics of this region were. The castle was later destroyed, and only fragments remain on a volcanic hill, but the view is worth the climb. The Someș valley here is a broad, fertile corridor, used for millennia by people moving between the Transylvanian basin and the north.

The roads are a mixture: the main road along the Someș between Dej and Beclean is busy with trucks and fast traffic, while the side roads up into the hills are narrow, steep and rough, sometimes turning to gravel near the top. The villages are spread out along the roads, with traditional houses, wells and gardens, and you share the tarmac with carts, cattle and tractors. Spring brings blossom in the orchards, and early autumn the harvest, with colours deepening on the hills.

For a full tank and a choice of food, Dej, about fourteen kilometres away, is the obvious town, a former salt-mining centre with a fine Gothic Reformed church. Ciceu-Giurgești and the nearby villages have small shops. If you are hunting the actual frontier remains, a local farmer may well point the way, and a few words of Romanian, or Hungarian in some villages, go a long way.
t.brebu caput bubali cetatuie@45.4,22.1:
Caput Bubali, the head of the buffalo, is a wonderfully odd Roman name, and it belongs to a station on the road that carried troops and supplies north from the Danube into the heart of Dacia after Trajan's conquest. The hill known as Cetățuie, near the villages of Brebu and Cornuțel in the Banat, holds the earthworks of a fort that guarded this route as it threaded through the hills towards Tibiscum, the important Roman centre near Caransebeș. It is part of the Dacian frontier group listed by UNESCO in 2024, and like much of it, it needs a little imagination and a good eye for ditches and banks.

The landscape is the gentle edge of the Banat mountains, where the Timiș river and its tributaries flow out of the high ground towards the plain. To the east rise the Țarcu and Godeanu ranges, often snow-capped into late spring, and to the west the Semenic mountains, with their beech forests and the high plateau above Reșița. The Banat was a frontier for centuries after the Romans too, between the Ottoman and Habsburg empires, and it remains one of the most ethnically mixed regions of Romania, with Romanian, Serbian, German and Hungarian heritage visible in its villages.

For riders, the area offers a fine variety.
