The main road from Caransebeș to Reșița crosses rolling hills with good curves, and from there routes climb into the Semenic mountains with steep hairpins and forest roads. The Timiș valley road south towards Orșova and the Danube, through the Teregova pass, is a lovely run. Surfaces vary from good to bumpy, and traffic is moderate. Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons.

Caransebeș, ten kilometres away, is a small town with fuel, mechanics and restaurants, and a good place to stop. Try the local specialities: grilled meats, polenta, and the sausages of the Banat, which are famous. The fort itself is on private land, so be respectful and ask permission if you want to explore.
t.dumbraveni varful runcului@47.3,24.0:
The countryside around Vârful Runcului is the landscape that two of Romania's best-loved writers came from, and it shows in their work. Liviu Rebreanu, born in the Năsăud area in 1885, set his novel Ion, about a peasant's hunger for land, in villages very like these, and the poet George Coșbuc grew up not far away in the valleys north of Năsăud. The hill itself, a rounded summit above the Someș valley, carries traces of the Roman watch system that once guarded the northern frontier of Dacia, part of the World Heritage listing since 2024, but its real charm is the view of the farmland Rebreanu wrote about.

Fields of maize and wheat, hay meadows and orchards patch the slopes, and the villages, Negrilești, Ciceu-Giurgești and Reteag among them, keep a slower pace. Haystacks still stand in the meadows in late summer, built around a central pole, and storks nest on the electricity poles. The Someș Mare flows through the valley below, lined with willows and poplars, and in the evening the light turns gold on the hills.

The riding here is quiet and rural. The main road along the valley is straightforward and fast, while the tracks climbing to the hilltop villages wind and buck, with loose gravel and potholes. Traffic is light, but watch for carts, livestock and village dogs. The landscape is gentle rather than dramatic, and the pleasure lies in the slow rhythm of the villages and the wide views across the valley. It is gentlest of all in late May, when the meadows are full of flowers and the cuckoo calls from every wood.

Căianu Mic, about thirteen kilometres away, and Beclean, a little further, are the places to find fuel and shops. In the villages, you might be offered home-made bread, cheese and plum brandy, and hospitality is generous. The Rebreanu memorial house and museums dedicated to both writers can be visited in the area, and they offer an insight into the culture and history of this corner of Transylvania.
t.romanasi largiana cetate@47.1,23.2:
At Românași, in the valley of the Agrij in Sălaj county, the outline of a Roman fort called Largiana can still be traced on a low rise above the village, its rectangle of ramparts and ditches softened by centuries of ploughing. It stood on the road that ran from Porolissum, the great frontier stronghold to the north, down towards Napoca, today's Cluj, and it housed an auxiliary unit guarding the approach to the Meseș mountains. Archaeologists have found inscriptions, coins and pottery here, and the site is part of the Dacian frontier listed by UNESCO in 2024.

Sălaj is a county of low hills, woods and small villages, often overlooked by travellers rushing between Cluj and the Hungarian border. Its wooden churches, built by Romanian communities in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, are tall and slender with steep shingled roofs, and several survive in the villages around Românași. The Meseș ridge, forested with beech and oak, separates the county from the Transylvanian basin, and the pass across it on the road between Zalău and Cluj offers broad views.

For riders, the main road between Zalău and Cluj over the Meseș pass is a good run, with curves and climbs and generally decent surfaces, though trucks are common. The side roads through the Agrij valley and the villages are narrower and quieter, with gentle bends, patched tarmac and the usual village hazards of dogs, carts and chickens. The countryside is green and peaceful, at its best in spring and early autumn.

The county town of Zalău is a quarter of an hour away and handles petrol, cash machines and repairs; in the villages, expect a small shop and, if you are lucky, a bar with a bench outside. Look for local specialities such as sour soups, cabbage rolls and home-made cheese, and enjoy the slower pace of life in this quiet corner of Transylvania.
t.hurez intre dealul mare si arsura@47.0,2:
Somewhere between Dealul Mare and Arsură, two wooded hills above the village of Hurez in Sălaj county, the Roman frontier of Dacia ran along the heights, marked by watchtowers and small earthworks that are now almost hidden by forest. Together with the towers further north on the Meseș ridge, they formed a line that looked west towards the lands beyond the empire, and they were included in the World Heritage listing of the Dacian frontier in 2024. Finding the remains requires a map and some determination; the reward is a sense of how thinly Rome stretched its soldiers across these hills.

A short ride south, the village of Ciucea sits on the Crișul Repede river at the edge of the Apuseni mountains. Its small castle belonged first to the Hungarian poet Endre Ady and later to the Romanian poet and politician Octavian Goga, who is buried nearby in a striking mausoleum, and the estate is now a memorial museum. Two poets of two nations in the same house says a lot about the history of this region, where Hungarian and Romanian cultures have lived side by side for centuries.

The main road between Cluj and Oradea, part of the E60, runs through Ciucea along the Crișul Repede valley, and it is busy, with heavy trucks and fast cars, so take care. The lanes that climb towards Hurez and Cizer are quiet, narrow and winding, through forests and small villages, with rough patches and occasional gravel. The Crișul Repede gorge, west of Ciucea, is a dramatic stretch, with the river cutting through limestone cliffs.

Huedin, a market town seventeen kilometres east, is where to refuel; Ciucea has a few small shops and places to eat. The area is known for its traditional crafts, including pottery and weaving, and for its hearty food. Enjoy a hot bowl of soup and some polenta before heading back into the hills.
t.negrilesti dealul muncelului@47.3,24.0:
Bram Stoker never came to Transylvania, but he sent Jonathan Harker through Bistrița, and the town still enjoys the connection. Dealul Muncelului, a hill above the village of Negrilești, sits west of Bistrița in the Someș valley, and from here the road east leads through the Saxon town to the Tihuța pass, the Borgo Pass of the novel, where Count Dracula's carriage is supposed to have met his English visitor. It is a fine excuse for a ride, even if the vampire is fiction and the real history more interesting.

The hill itself carries traces of the Roman frontier watch system, part of the Dacian limes inscribed by UNESCO in 2024, and the countryside around is gentle farmland and orchards. Bistrița was founded by German settlers, the Transylvanian Saxons, in the twelfth century, and its Gothic church, arcaded houses and fortified walls show their wealth and skill. South of the town, the Lechința area produces white wines that have been made since Saxon times, and the vineyards spread over the sunny slopes.

The road over the Tihuța pass to Vatra Dornei is a superb ride, climbing through forests and meadows with curves, hairpins and views of the Călimani mountains, and it is generally well surfaced, though busy in places with trucks. Around Negrilești, the roads are quieter and more rural, winding through villages and hills, with patched surfaces and the occasional cart or herd of sheep. In high summer the pass is a cool escape from the baking valley floor.

Căianu Mic, about ten kilometres away, has fuel and shops, and Bistrița has everything you need, including hotels and restaurants. Stoker gave Harker a night at an inn in Bistrița called the Golden Krone, and the town has happily leaned into the joke ever since. Out in the villages, try the local cheese, the cabbage rolls and the plum brandy, and enjoy the hospitality.
t.church of the holy paraskeva@47.8,23.9:
In 1780 a painter named Radu Munteanu covered the inside of the wooden church at Desești with scenes that still shock and delight: a Last Judgment in which sinners are marched off to a hell full of grinning devils, alongside saints, prophets and lively village figures. The church, dedicated to the Holy Paraskeva and built in 1770 from oak logs, rises above the village with a tall, slender tower and a steep double roof of shingles. It is one of the eight wooden churches of Maramureș inscribed by UNESCO in 1999, and its paintings are among the best preserved of them all.

Maramureș is a land apart, cut off from the rest of Romania by mountains and long isolated, so that traditions survived here that have vanished elsewhere. Carved wooden gates stand in front of houses, women still wear traditional dress on Sundays, and haystacks dot the meadows in summer. The Mara valley, where Desești lies, is one of the most beautiful parts of the region, with villages strung along the river, orchards and hay meadows. Nearby are the salt lakes of Ocna Șugatag, popular for bathing, and the village of Breb, famous for its traditional way of life.

The road over the Gutâi pass, from Baia Mare into Maramureș, is a superb ride, with a long series of hairpins climbing through beech forests to the top and then descending into the Mara valley. The surface is generally good, though trucks and buses use the road, and the corners need care. In the valley, the roads are quieter, winding along the river through villages, with carts and livestock to watch out for. Summer brings village festivals and fairs, and in October the beech woods on the Gutâi glow like embers.

Cavnic, a small ski town about twelve kilometres away, has fuel, and Baia Mare and Sighetu Marmației have everything. The villages have small shops and guesthouses offering home-cooked food. The church at Desești is usually open, or the key can be obtained from the priest or a caretaker; dress respectfully and leave a donation if you can.
t.varful lui patru@45.6,23.5:
Roman soldiers rarely chose to live above two thousand metres, but on Vârful lui Pătru, a broad grassy summit of the Șureanu mountains in southern Transylvania, they did. A small fortification on the top, part of the network that watched over the passes after Trajan conquered Dacia, is often described as one of the highest Roman military posts anywhere, and it now belongs to the World Heritage listing of the Dacian frontier. Imagine a winter up here in a wool cloak, with the wind coming straight off the Carpathians, and the posting suddenly sounds like a punishment.

The Șureanu are rounded, open mountains, with alpine meadows, juniper and dwarf pine on the tops, glacial lakes in the hollows and dense spruce forests below. Shepherds bring their flocks up for the summer, and their dogs are large and serious. Just to the north-west, deep in the beech forests of the Orăștie mountains, lie the Dacian fortresses that the Romans came to destroy, including Sarmizegetusa Regia, the old royal capital, with its sanctuaries and stone calendar circle. Standing on the summit, you can trace the long story of conquest across the ridges.

The riding reason to come is the Transalpina, Romania's highest paved road, which crosses the Parâng and Șureanu mountains between Novaci in the south and Sebeș in the north and passes not far east of the peak. It climbs to above 2,100 metres near the Urdele pass, with long, open sequences of bends over bare ridges, views that seem to go on forever and very changeable weather. The high section is normally closed by snow from late autumn until early summer, so check before planning. Fog can arrive in minutes, livestock wander onto the road, and the north side through the Oașa and Tău Bistra reservoirs has its own share of twisty forest riding.

Fill up in Petroșani or Petrila in the Jiu valley, in Novaci, or in Sebeș, depending on your direction, and carry water and warm layers even in August. Simple cabanas and guesthouses around Obârșia Lotrului and Rânca serve grilled meat, polenta and sour soups, and roadside shepherds sometimes sell cheese, which is worth stopping for.
t.stolniceni buridava romana@45.0,24.3:
South of Râmnicu Vâlcea the Olt river leaves the mountains and broadens across a valley of orchards and villages, and on the terraces above it at Stolniceni lie the remains of Buridava, a Roman military settlement whose name the Romans borrowed from an older Dacian centre nearby. It sat on the Limes Alutanus, the frontier road along the Olt that guarded the eastern edge of Roman Dacia, and soldiers stationed here left inscriptions, bricks stamped with unit marks and the foundations of baths. The site is part of the Dacian frontier listing inscribed by UNESCO in 2024.

The attraction of Buridava for both Dacians and Romans was salt. At Ocnele Mari, just a few kilometres away, salt has been mined since antiquity, and the deposits are still worked today; there are salt lakes and a visitable mine. Upriver, where the Olt cuts through the Carpathians in a narrow gorge, the monastery of Cozia, founded in the fourteenth century by Prince Mircea the Elder, stands on the riverbank with its banded stone and brick church, and Mircea himself is buried there.

The riding around here is rich. North of Râmnicu Vâlcea, the Olt gorge road through the Carpathians is fast and scenic but busy with trucks heading for Sibiu. West, the road to Horezu runs along the foothills through villages famous for their glazed pottery, and from there you can reach the Transalpina at Novaci. East, the Transfăgărășan begins near Curtea de Argeș. The local roads around Stolniceni are smaller and quieter, with orchards and vineyards on the slopes, patched surfaces and village traffic. Summer can be hot in the valley, so early starts pay off.

Petrol is never a worry here: Mihăești, four kilometres off, has a station, and Râmnicu Vâlcea on the Olt has a dozen more, plus tyre shops and supermarkets. The monastery at Horezu, a masterpiece of the Brâncovenesc style with carved stone porches and painted walls, and the potters' workshops along the main street are well worth a detour west. When the day ends, papanași, fried cheese doughnuts drowned in sour cream and jam, are the traditional Oltenian reward, and the plum brandy offered with them is rarely optional.
t.lunca la bolovani@47.0,24.7:
La Bolovani means at the boulders, which tells you most of what a local would have said about this spot on the hills near the village of Lunca, between Monor and Șieuț on the eastern edge of the Transylvanian basin. Archaeologists know it as one of the sites along the Roman frontier of Dacia, a small watch post on a ridge commanding views east towards the Călimani and Gurghiu mountains, beyond which lay lands Rome never controlled. In 2024 it joined the World Heritage listing of the Dacian limes, though in the field you will find a quiet hill, sheep and very few signs.

This is the meeting point of Transylvania's Romanian, Hungarian and Saxon worlds. To the south, the town of Reghin is famous for violin making, with workshops that have supplied orchestras across Europe, and its Saxon church and old houses hint at the town's past. Along the Mureș valley, the castle at Brâncovenești, a Renaissance stronghold rebuilt many times, stands above the river. The Călimani, an extinct volcanic range with a vast caldera, rise in the north-east, wild and forested, home to bears and capercaillie.

For riders, the countryside here offers quiet, rolling roads between villages, with long views and patched tarmac. The main road from Reghin to Bistrița cuts across it, and from Reghin you can follow the upper Mureș through the gorge between the Călimani and Gurghiu mountains towards Toplița, a fine, winding valley ride with forest on both sides and the river beside you. Watch out for horse carts, especially at dusk when they often have no lights, and for potholes after winter. Late spring and early autumn are ideal.

For a tank of petrol, Teaca is nineteen kilometres away, and Reghin or Bistrița have a wider choice of stations, garages and supermarkets. The villages themselves offer a shop, perhaps a terrace bar, and a lot of curious looks at a loaded motorcycle. Watch for carved wooden gates outside the houses, often dated and decorated with sun symbols, and in late summer for tables by the roadside piled with honey jars, plums and baskets of forest mushrooms. A conversation in sign language with a farmer leaning on his gate is part of the experience.
t.brebi comoraste@47.2,23.2:
The hill of Comorâște, above the village of Brebi in Sălaj county, overlooks the Someș valley as it turns north towards Jibou, and its name hints at buried treasure, comoară, which is how villagers often explained odd mounds and old stones on their land. Archaeologists explain it more prosaically as a Roman watch site on the north-western frontier of Dacia, part of the line of towers and forts strung along the Meseș hills and inscribed by UNESCO in 2024. From the top you can see across the valley to the forested ridges that once marked the edge of the empire.

Jibou, seven kilometres away, is a small town with an unexpected treasure of its own: the Wesselényi castle, a Baroque palace of the Hungarian noble family who owned these lands, and next to it one of the largest botanical gardens in Romania, created in the twentieth century with greenhouses, a Japanese garden and plants from around the world. The Someș river flows through the valley, and the countryside around is a mix of farmland, orchards and forest, with villages of traditional houses and wooden churches.

The roads around Brebi are typical of rural Sălaj: narrow, winding and sometimes rough, with gentle climbs and descents, and views across the valley. The main road along the Someș from Jibou to Dej carries trucks and cars, but the side roads are quiet, and the pleasure lies in exploring the villages and hills at a gentle pace. Look out for animals on the road, and for the occasional pothole. The landscape is green and lush in spring and early summer, and golden in autumn.

Jibou, seven kilometres off, is the practical stop, with a filling station, a couple of supermarkets and simple restaurants where ciorbă, sour soup, arrives in generous bowls. Out in the villages, life moves at the pace of the horse cart, and a stranger who stops to admire a wooden church may well end up being offered a glass of țuică and a long chat in mixed languages. On a hot afternoon, the shade of the botanical garden's old trees in Jibou is a welcome refuge, and the castle beside it has been undergoing restoration.
t.component of szendro rudabanya hill@48.4:
The Szendrő-Rudabánya hills are a modest ridge of low wooded hills in northeastern Hungary, between the Bódva and Sajó valleys, and they are not on any tourist itinerary. That is a large part of their charm. This is the quiet borderland near Slovakia, with small villages, orchards, vineyards and forests of oak and hornbeam, where the roads are empty and the pace slows to that of a cart.

Rudabánya, the little town at the heart of it, has a remarkable past. Its name means ore mine, and iron, copper and silver were dug here from medieval times into the twentieth century; the old open-pit workings left a deep hole that has since filled with an emerald lake. In the same pits, in the late 1960s, miners came across fossils of a Miocene ape now called Rudapithecus hungaricus, about ten million years old, an important find for understanding the evolution of the great apes. A small museum in the town tells both stories, and the rust-coloured rocks around the pit hint at why people dug here at all.

The riding is gentle and undemanding, with roads looping through the hills between Rudabánya, Szendrő and Edelény. They are narrow, often patched and sometimes broken at the edges, so leave a margin and keep an eye out for horse-drawn carts, tractors and children on bikes in the villages. Corners are friendly, gradients mild, and the views from the ridgetops over the Bódva valley towards the Slovak karst hills are lovely in late afternoon light. Wine cellars cut into the hillsides, like the ones around Szendrő, hint at a long tradition of small-scale winemaking.

Szendrő has the remains of a hilltop castle and a few basic shops; Edelény, about eleven kilometres away, is the nearest town of any size, with fuel, groceries and the restored L'Huillier-Coburg mansion, one of the largest Baroque country houses in Hungary. Miskolc, the regional city, is further south for anything else. Bring cash for small places, expect limited English, and enjoy being somewhere few riders ever reach. The Aggtelek caves, on the karst plateau to the north, make an excellent next stop.
t.bodruzal@49.4,21.7:
Bodružal is a tiny Rusyn village in the far northeast of Slovakia, close to the Polish border, with a few dozen houses scattered along a valley among the forested hills of the Low Beskids. What brings people here is its wooden church of St Nicholas, built in 1658, a three-domed Greek Catholic church with shingled walls and onion-shaped towers stepping up from east to west. It is one of the eight churches in the UNESCO listing of the wooden churches of the Slovak part of the Carpathian mountain area, and it is a perfect example of the Lemko style: compact, harmonious and rooted in its landscape. Inside, the iconostasis glows with painted saints.

This is a borderland with a complicated history. The Rusyns, or Lemkos, an Eastern Slavic people who have lived in these hills for centuries, have seen borders, empires and nations shift around them. In the autumn of 1944, the Dukla Pass, just a few kilometres away, saw one of the bloodiest battles on the Eastern Front, as Soviet and Czechoslovak forces fought to break through German defences into Slovakia. Tens of thousands died, and the area around Svidník is full of memorials, military cemeteries and old tanks left in the fields.

The landscape is gentle and green: rolling hills, beech and fir forests, meadows full of wildflowers in summer and small villages with wooden houses. Wildlife includes deer, wild boar, and even bears and wolves in the deeper forests. The roads are narrow and quiet, mostly asphalt but often patched, with some lovely flowing curves through the valleys and over the low passes. Traffic is light, though tractors and gravel on the corners keep you honest.

Bodružal itself has no services. Svidník, eleven kilometres down the valley, does, with fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and the Museum of Ukrainian Culture with an open-air village of wooden buildings. Medzilaborce, to the east, is home to the Andy Warhol museum, since his parents emigrated from a Rusyn village nearby. Try bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese, and in autumn, the region's mushrooms. The church is usually locked; look for a phone number on the gate or ask in the village for the key.
t.sita varful sitii@47.3,24.2:
On a hilltop near the village of Spermezeu, in the Someș hills of Bistrița-Năsăud county in northern Romania, a small watchtower once stood guard over the northern edge of the Roman Empire. When the emperor Trajan conquered Dacia in the early second century, the Romans built a frontier around their new province, the Dacian limes, a chain of forts, watchtowers and earthworks running along the Carpathians and through the hills. Vârful Sitii, the summit of Sita, was one of the observation points, chosen because from here soldiers could watch the valleys to the north and send signals to the forts behind them.

What survives on the ground is modest, low earthworks and traces of foundations, but the view explains everything. From the summit you look across a landscape of rolling hills, forests and small fields, with the mountains of Maramureș and the Rodna range on the northern horizon. In the time of the Romans, the free Dacians and other tribes lived beyond this line, and the watchtowers were the eyes of the empire.

This is a quiet corner of Transylvania, far from the tourist trail, where life still follows the seasons. Haystacks dot the meadows in summer, villagers work the fields by hand or with horses, and wooden gates and churches decorate the villages. The forests are home to deer, foxes and wild boar, and storks nest on the electricity poles in the villages.

The roads are rural, often narrow, patched or unpaved, winding through the hills and valleys between Spermezeu, Zagra and Răpănașu. The final approach to the summit is likely on foot or along a farm track. Riding here is slow and peaceful, with little traffic other than tractors, horse carts and the occasional flock of sheep. Spermezeu and the neighbouring villages have small shops; for fuel and supplies, Căianu Mic, about ten kilometres away, or the larger towns of Beclean and Bistrița are your best bets. Weather can change quickly in the hills, with summer thunderstorms and cold, snowy winters, and dirt roads become muddy after rain. Take your time, greet people as you pass, and you will often be met with curiosity and kindness.
t.domnesti@47.0,24.5:
Domnești sits in the hills just south of Bistrița, the old Saxon town in northeastern Transylvania, and like several places in this region it marks a point on the Roman frontier of Dacia, where watchtowers once looked out from the ridgetops over the province's edge. Nothing dramatic remains here, but the location is perfect for exploring a corner of Romania that mixes Roman, Saxon, Hungarian and Romanian history in a single valley.

Bistrița, about eleven kilometres away, was founded by German settlers in the twelfth century, the Transylvanian Saxons, who built fortified towns and churches across the region. The town's Evangelical church, with its tall Gothic tower, dominates the central square, and the arcaded merchants' houses of the Sugalete are a reminder of the town's medieval prosperity. Bram Stoker sent Jonathan Harker through Bistrița on his way to Count Dracula's castle, and the Borgo Pass, the Tihuța, which crosses the mountains to the east towards Bucovina, has become famous through the novel.

The riding around here is excellent. The Tihuța pass road climbs through forests and meadows to a high pass, with good curves and views, and continues into the Bârgău mountains and on to Vatra Dornei. Shorter rides through the hills around Domnești, Mărișelu and Budacu de Jos take you along quiet country roads with farms, orchards and wooden churches. Surfaces vary, with some smooth stretches and some potholed ones, so stay alert. Stray dogs and slow trucks are the usual hazards.

Domnești and the nearby villages have small shops, but for fuel and a proper meal head into Bistrița, which has everything you need. Transylvanian food is hearty: try sarmale, cabbage rolls filled with meat and rice, mămăligă, polenta often served with cheese and sour cream, and the local plum brandy, țuică or pălincă, which is offered generously and should be treated with respect, especially if you are riding. Autumn is a beautiful time to visit, when the forests turn gold and red, and the harvest brings markets and festivals to the villages.
t.vanatori dealul cocinilor@47.0,22.9:
The hill of Dealul Cocinilor rises above the valley of the Crișul Repede near Ciucea, on the western edge of Cluj county, and it marks another point on the Roman frontier of Dacia, this time in the Meseș mountains, where the limes ran along the hills protecting the province of Dacia Porolissensis. The watchtowers here guarded the approaches from the west and north, and from the hilltop you can still see why: the valley below is a natural corridor, used by traders, armies and travellers for thousands of years.

Today that corridor carries the E60, the main road from Oradea to Cluj-Napoca, and it is one of the busiest roads in Romania, heavy with trucks and cars. Riding it is not much fun, but leaving it, even for a few kilometres, opens up a different world. The Crișul Repede cuts a narrow gorge between Ciucea and Bucea, with railway, river and road squeezed together in the forest, and the Apuseni mountains to the south offer some of the best riding in the country, with roads climbing to high plateaus, karst landscapes, caves and villages that seem lost in time.

Ciucea itself is known for its connection to two poets. Octavian Goga, the Romanian poet and politician, had his manor here, now a memorial museum with a lovely wooden church brought from another village. Before him, the house belonged to Endre Ady, one of the greatest Hungarian poets. That two national poets of rival traditions are tied to one small village says something about the layered history of Transylvania.

Nature here is a mix of beech and oak forests, meadows and rocky slopes. In spring the hills are full of wildflowers, and in autumn the forests turn every shade of orange. The roads are generally paved but narrow and sometimes in poor condition, with sharp bends in the gorge. Watch for speeding trucks on the main road and slow-moving farm vehicles on the minor roads. Ciucea can sell you petrol and groceries; for a wider choice, carry on sixteen kilometres east to Huedin. Try the local cheese, smoked meats and fresh bread from village bakeries, and enjoy the quiet once you leave the main road behind.
Warm water has drawn people to this corner of the Mureș valley for at least two thousand years. Below the hill of Dealul Urie, near the spa town of Geoagiu-Băi, the Romans built Germisara, a fort on the hill at Cigmău and a bath settlement around the hot springs a few kilometres away, and soldiers and settlers from across the empire came to soak their aches in the thermal pools. Excavations in one of the old spring basins brought up a remarkable hoard of votive offerings, including small gold plaques dedicated to the healing gods and the nymphs, thrown into the water by grateful bathers. The ruins of the fort on Dealul Urie are low and grassy, but the setting, above a broad river plain with mountains on both sides, makes the climb worthwhile.

Before the Romans, this was the heartland of the Dacians. A short ride south, the Orăștie Mountains hide the remains of their great fortresses, Sarmizegetusa Regia, Costești and Blidaru among them, built of carefully dressed limestone blocks in the forests, and now on the World Heritage list. Trajan's wars of the early second century ended with their destruction and the creation of the Roman province of Dacia, which is why Romanian is a Latin language today.

Geoagiu-Băi is still a spa, a little old-fashioned, with thermal pools fed by the springs and a holiday atmosphere in summer. Geoagiu town, four kilometres away, and Orăștie, a pleasant small city with a medieval fortified church at its centre, both have fuel, shops and places to eat. The A1 motorway runs along the Mureș valley nearby, which makes this an easy stop on a long day.

The better riding is away from the motorway. Climb south from Orăștie on the road towards Costești and the Grădiștea valley and you are into forested hills on narrow, winding asphalt that eventually turns to gravel near the fortresses. North of the Mureș, the roads into the Metaliferi mountains around Geoagiu and towards Balșa climb through quiet villages and orchards. Surfaces are inconsistent, and in the villages you will share the road with horse carts and geese. Spring and autumn are lovely; summer afternoons can be hot in the valley, which is exactly when a thermal pool is less appealing than a cold drink in the shade.
t.zavoi agnaviae balta neagra fanete@45.5,:
Zăvoi lies in the valley of the Bistra, a river running east to west between the Poiana Ruscă mountains to the north and the Țarcu range to the south, and for most riders it is a waypoint on one of the best roads in western Romania: the old route from Caransebeș in the Banat over the Iron Gate of Transylvania to Hațeg and the Roman capital of Dacia at Sarmizegetusa. The Romans used this corridor too. The road between their fort at Tibiscum, near Caransebeș, and the colony of Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa passed through the valley, and Agnaviae was a station along it, where travellers and couriers stopped to rest. Today little remains above ground, but the line of the valley is unchanged.

Oțelu Roșu, the small town just down the road, has a name that means red steel, after the steelworks that dominated its economy for more than a century. Under the Habsburgs it was called Ferdinandsberg. The mill has had a hard time since the end of communism, and the town has the slightly worn look of many former industrial centres, but it has fuel, shops and simple places to eat.

The riding is the main reward here. Heading east from Zăvoi, the road follows the Bistra and then climbs to the Iron Gate of Transylvania, a low pass of about seven hundred metres where a monument marks a battle against the Ottomans in the fifteenth century. The road is well graded, with flowing curves through beech forest and meadows, and on the far side it drops into the Hațeg basin, one of the most beautiful valleys in the country, ringed by the Retezat mountains. Traffic is generally light, though logging trucks and the occasional bus need watching on the bends.

The wetlands at Balta Neagră near Zăvoi are a quiet place where the river meadows are still mown by hand, home to frogs, storks and dragonflies on summer afternoons. If you want to go higher, the Muntele Mic ski area above Borlova has a road climbing to around fifteen hundred metres with sweeping views over the Banat. Weather in the valley can be warm and sticky in summer; in the mountains, thunderstorms build quickly in the afternoon.
t.component of koniar plateau@48.7,20.3:
The Koniar plateau is a slab of limestone lifted above the surrounding valleys in southern Slovakia, one of the high karst tablelands that together make up the Slovak Karst. From the road it looks like nothing much: open grassland, scattered trees, a few pastures, steep wooded edges falling to the valleys of the Slaná and its tributaries. The interest is underneath. Rain soaks straight through the limestone, carving caves, shafts and swallow holes, and the whole cave system of the Slovak Karst and Hungary's Aggtelek, just over the border, is protected as a single World Heritage site. Nearby you will find the Ochtinská aragonite cave, filled with white needle-like crystals, the Gombasecká cave with its thin straw stalactites and, further north, the Dobšinská ice cave.

Up on the plateau the vegetation is unusual for Slovakia, with steppe grasses, orchids and warmth-loving shrubs on the dry, thin soil, and in early summer the meadows are full of butterflies. Raptors circle over the edges. The views from the rim are long and wide, over gentle hills and villages with red roofs and church spires, and in autumn the beech woods on the slopes turn bronze.

The riding around Rožňava, Plešivec and Štítnik is relaxed and pleasant. Roads are mostly quiet two-lane routes threading along valleys and over low ridges, with a few properly entertaining climbs where the road leaves the valley floor and switchbacks up through forest. Surfaces vary, from fresh asphalt to patched and broken tarmac in the villages, and you will meet horse carts and slow farm traffic in places. North of here the roads into the Slovak Paradise and the Low Tatras become steeper and more alpine in character.

This area is rich in castles and manors. Krásna Hôrka, above the village of the same name near Rožňava, was gutted by a fire in 2012 and has been under restoration since, and the Andrássy manor at Betliar, with its big English park, is a lovely place to walk. Rožňava itself grew rich on mining and has a handsome square. It and Revúca are the towns for fuel, food and lodging; Dobšiná is smaller but useful too. On the plateau itself there are no services at all, so bring water.
t.wooden churches of southern ma opolska@4:
The church of St Michael the Archangel in Binarowa looks, from the outside, like a simple barn with a tower: dark shingled walls, a steep roof and a small onion-topped belfry. Step inside and the walls and ceiling explode with colour, covered with painted decoration of saints, scenes from the Bible and floral patterns, some of them centuries old. Built around 1500 of larch and fir, without nails in the traditional joinery, it is one of the Wooden Churches of Southern Małopolska, a group of Gothic churches inscribed as a World Heritage site. The local story is that it was built from timber left over from another church, but whatever its origins, the result is one of the finest wooden interiors in Poland.

The surroundings are the rolling foothills of the Low Beskids, the Beskid Niski, a landscape of meadows, woods and small villages that feels much more remote than its distance from Kraków suggests. Further south and east, the Orthodox and Greek Catholic wooden churches of the Lemkos, a Ruthenian people expelled from the region after the Second World War, dot the hills with their characteristic stepped roofs and domes, and many are also listed by UNESCO.

Biecz, a few kilometres away, is a small town with a big past. In the Middle Ages, it was an important royal town on the trade routes to Hungary, and it is sometimes called little Kraków for its town hall tower, churches and old houses. It also had a notorious reputation for its executioners. Gorlice, a little further on, was the scene of a major battle in 1915, when German and Austro-Hungarian forces broke through the Russian lines, and the area is dotted with the military cemeteries of the First World War. Nearby, at Bóbrka, the world's first oil mine was established in 1854 by Ignacy Łukasiewicz, inventor of the kerosene lamp, and it is now a museum.

The roads here are lovely: quiet, gently winding through the hills, with good surfaces on the main roads and some rougher stretches on the smaller ones. Watch out for horse carts and tractors. Biecz has fuel and a few restaurants, and Gorlice is a larger town with everything you need. Try pierogi in a village inn, and if you are lucky, a bowl of żurek, sour rye soup with sausage and egg.
Ieud is a long village strung along a side valley of the Iza river in Maramureș, in Romania's far north, and it has not one but two wooden churches. The one on the hill, the Church of the Nativity of the Virgin, is one of the eight Wooden Churches of Maramureș listed by UNESCO, and it is one of the oldest, with a tall, slender bell tower and a double roof of wooden shingles that reaches almost to the ground. Inside, the walls are covered with eighteenth-century paintings on wood and cloth, with scenes from the Last Judgement in which the damned are dressed in the clothes of the local enemies of the time. The church is also known for the Ieud Codex, a manuscript found here, one of the oldest texts written in the Romanian language.

Maramureș is one of the places in Europe where traditional rural life has survived most strongly. You will see haystacks shaped by hand, horse-drawn carts, carved wooden gates at the entrances to farmyards and, on Sundays and holidays, people in traditional dress going to church. The villages are built almost entirely of wood, though new houses are spreading. The hills around are covered in beech and spruce forests and the meadows are full of flowers in early summer, hay-making in July and August.

The road along the Iza valley, from Dragomirești through Bogdan Vodă to the junction with the Vișeu valley, is a pleasant, winding road with good asphalt in most places, but you need to watch out for carts, livestock and children in the villages. To the east, the road climbs to the Prislop pass and continues into Bucovina, a spectacular mountain route with views of the Rodna mountains. To the north, the narrow-gauge forest railway from Vișeu de Sus, still pulled by steam engines, runs up the Vaser valley and makes a great day out. Beyond Sighetu Marmației, near the Ukrainian border, the village of Săpânța has the Merry Cemetery, with its brightly painted wooden crosses and humorous epitaphs.

Fuel is available in the larger villages along the main roads, such as Dragomirești and Rozavlea, and in Vișeu de Sus. Guesthouses in Ieud and other villages offer simple rooms and home cooking: sour soups, polenta with cheese and sour cream, and pălincă, the strong plum brandy that every household seems to make.
t.pui dealul robului 1 and 2@45.6,23.1:
On a hill above the Strei valley near the village of Pui, in south-western Transylvania, faint earthworks mark one of the many small Roman military posts that guarded the province of Dacia after Trajan conquered it in AD 106. The Romans held Dacia for about a hundred and seventy years, and they ringed it with forts, watchtowers and roads; in 2024 a long series of these sites was added to the World Heritage list as the Frontiers of the Roman Empire in Dacia. At Dealul Robului there is nothing grand to see, just the shape of the ground under grass and trees, but the position tells you everything: a clear view down the valley, which was one of the routes into the heart of the province.

That heart was close by. A short ride west lies Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, the Roman capital of Dacia, with the remains of its forum and amphitheatre in a quiet field, and up in the Orăștie mountains to the north-east are the fortresses of the Dacian kings who fought Rome. The Hațeg Country around Pui is also a UNESCO Global Geopark, thanks to its dinosaurs. In the early twentieth century Baron Franz Nopcsa, a brilliant and eccentric local aristocrat, found that the dinosaurs here were unusually small and proposed that they had evolved on an island, an idea now widely accepted. In the village of Densuș, the little stone church, built partly of Roman stones, is one of the oldest in Romania still in use.

The main road, DN66, runs through Pui on its way from Hațeg to Petroșani and the Jiu valley, with a good surface and steady truck traffic. South of the valley the Retezat mountains rise steeply, a national park since 1935, with more than fifty glacial lakes; side roads lead up into their valleys, narrowing to gravel as they go. East of Petroșani the Transalpina, the highest road in Romania, climbs over the Parâng mountains, but that is a high-summer adventure, closed for much of the year.

Hațeg, about fifteen kilometres away, is the town for fuel, shops and restaurants. Pui itself has basic shops and guesthouses offer home cooking: soups, grilled meat, polenta and fresh cheese. The land around is farmland and orchards, and in late summer roadside stalls sell plums and apples straight from the trees.
t.cormenis rapa malului 1@47.3,23.5:
The Someș river cuts through the low hills of north-western Transylvania in a series of wide loops, and at Cormeniș, a small village in Sălaj county, it passes below a bank where the Romans placed one of their watchtowers. This was the northern edge of the province of Dacia Porolissensis, the frontier facing the free Dacian tribes beyond, and a line of towers and small forts ran along the hills, linked by signals and patrols. The site at Râpa Malului, the riverbank cliff, is one of the many components of the Dacian frontier listed by UNESCO in 2024. As so often on the Dacian limes, there is little to see apart from a slight rise in a field, but standing up there with the river below, you can easily imagine a small garrison watching the valley.

The Someș valley here is beautiful in a quiet way: willows and poplars along the water, steep hillsides of meadows and woods, and villages with small churches. North of the river, the hills of Țicău and the Lăpuș country lead into Maramureș, and several villages in the area have old wooden churches, simpler than the famous ones further north but often in lovely settings on a hill above the houses. In autumn the colours are wonderful, and in winter the valley can be wrapped in fog for days.

The road along the Someș, from Jibou towards Dej, follows the river through the narrow section of the valley with gentle, flowing bends, light traffic and a few rough patches. The railway runs alongside, sometimes crossing the river on old bridges. Side roads into the villages are narrow, sometimes unpaved, and you will meet horse carts, cattle and geese. Roads in this part of Romania have improved a lot in recent years, but surfaces can still change from smooth to broken without warning.

Jibou, about twenty kilometres away, is the town for fuel, shops and food, and it has a surprise: the Wesselényi castle, a baroque mansion of the Hungarian noble family, with a large botanical garden behind it, one of the best in the country, with greenhouses and a Japanese garden. Village shops along the Someș sell basics, and if you are offered a glass of homemade pălincă, it is polite to accept, though not before riding.
t.saratel cetate 1@47.1,24.4:
The name Sărățel means the little salty place, and this corner of Bistrița-Năsăud has salt underground: springs of brine rise here and there in the hills, and for centuries people used them for cooking, curing meat and treating animals. Salt was one of the reasons the Romans wanted Dacia, along with gold, and on a hill near the village they placed a fort, Cetate, meaning the citadel, at the north-eastern corner of their province. Behind it lay the valley of the Șieu and the road towards the interior; in front, the hills where the free Dacians lived. The site is now part of the Roman frontier of Dacia on the World Heritage list, though, like most of these places, it is visible mainly as an outline of banks and ditches.

The landscape is gentle and open. The hills are covered in meadows, orchards and patches of oak and beech forest, and the villages along the Șieu are a mix of Romanian and, historically, Saxon and Hungarian communities, each with its own church. To the south, the Lechința area is known for its vineyards, a reminder that Transylvania was wine country long before the modern era, and local white wines are still made there. In spring, the orchards bloom white and pink, and the hills are a fresh green.

Riding here is relaxed. The roads between Șieu-Măgheruș, Lechința and the villages around follow the valleys and climb over low ridges in wide bends, with little traffic and decent surfaces on the main routes. The main road from Bistrița towards Reghin and Târgu Mureș is busier, with trucks, but has some pleasant sections over the hills. Watch out for horse carts, which are still common, and dogs that like to chase motorcycles. After rain, mud from the fields can make the village roads slippery.

Lechința, about six kilometres away, has a fuel station and basic shops, and Bistrița, a little further north, is the main town of the county, with everything you could need. In the villages, small shops and bars offer coffee, cold drinks and simple snacks. Look out for fresh cheese and honey sold at the roadside, and, if you are lucky, a plate of sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with meat and rice, at a local guesthouse.
t.alba iulia apulum domus 1@46.1,23.6:
Alba Iulia wears its history in layers, and the bottom layer is Roman. The Legio XIII Gemina, the legion that held the heart of Dacia, was based here for over a century and a half, and around its fortress grew Apulum, one of the largest cities of the province. Excavations inside the modern citadel have revealed parts of the legionary fortress, and a Roman house, a domus, with its foundations, rooms and heating system, has been uncovered nearby, showing how the wealthier inhabitants lived. Together with the rest of the Dacian limes, these remains are now on the World Heritage list.

The second layer is the one you see first: the huge star-shaped citadel of Alba Carolina, built by the Habsburgs in the early eighteenth century in the style of Vauban, with seven bastions, deep ditches and monumental gates covered with carvings. Inside are the Roman Catholic cathedral of St Michael, one of the oldest in Transylvania, the tomb of the great fifteenth-century commander John Hunyadi, and the Orthodox coronation cathedral, where King Ferdinand and Queen Marie were crowned in 1922. Alba Iulia is a symbolic city for Romanians: in 1600 Michael the Brave briefly united the three Romanian principalities here, and on 1 December 1918 the assembly that proclaimed the union of Transylvania with Romania met here, which is why 1 December is the national day.

The riding around is varied. To the south, the Sebeș valley leads to the start of the Transalpina, the highest road in Romania, crossing the Parâng mountains at over two thousand metres, a spectacular ride that is open only in the summer months. To the east, the Saxon villages such as Câlnic, with its fortified keep, are reached along quiet country roads through the vineyards and hills. North and west, the Apuseni mountains offer forested valleys and winding roads. The A1 motorway passes close to the city and requires a vignette, the rovinieta.

Alba Iulia is a city of about seventy thousand people with fuel, hotels, restaurants and workshops. The citadel has many cafés and terraces, especially beautiful in the evening when the walls are lit up. The changing of the guard ceremony takes place at the citadel gates at midday. Try the local wines from the vineyards of Alba and Jidvei, which produce some of the best whites in Romania.
t.budacu de jos dealul cetatii 1@47.1,24.5:
Bram Stoker sent Jonathan Harker to Bistritz, and the town of Bistrița, just a few kilometres from here, has never quite escaped the vampire. In the novel, Harker spends a night at the Golden Krone hotel before setting off towards the Borgo Pass and Count Dracula's castle, and today the town has a hotel of that name and the pass a hotel built to look like a castle. The real history is more interesting. Bistrița was one of the seven Saxon cities that gave Transylvania its German name, Siebenbürgen, a rich trading town with a big Gothic church, arcaded merchants' houses and a ring of walls, much of which has been lost.

Long before the Saxons, the Romans were here. On Dealul Cetății, the citadel hill above the village of Budacu de Jos, a fortification marked the north-eastern corner of Roman Dacia, overlooking the Bistrița valley and the routes to the passes into Moldavia. It is now one of the components of the Dacian frontier on the World Heritage list. The site itself is a wooded hill with traces of earthworks; the reward for walking up is a view over the valley, the town and the mountains beyond.

The great riding road here is the DN17 east from Bistrița over the Tihuța pass, Stoker's Borgo Pass, to Vatra Dornei and Bucovina. It climbs gradually through villages and forest to the top, at around twelve hundred metres, with long, flowing bends and wide views of the Bârgău mountains, then descends towards the Dorna depression. The surface is generally good, but trucks are frequent, and in winter snow and ice can make the pass difficult. To the north, smaller roads lead into the Năsăud area and towards the Rodna mountains.

Bistrița is a city of about eighty thousand people with fuel, hotels, restaurants and workshops, and the old town centre is pleasant for a stroll and a coffee. Budacu de Jos is a small village with a shop or two. Try the local dishes in Bistrița, such as balmoș, a rich polenta with cheese and butter from the mountain areas, and look out for the Saxon pastries that are still baked here, a sweet legacy of the German community.
t.ciceu poieni podul milcoaiei@47.3,24.1:
Ciceu-Poieni is a tiny village in the hills north of the Someș, the kind of place that rarely appears on a map, and near it, at a spot called Podul Milcoaiei, the Romans placed a watchtower on the northern border of Dacia. It is part of the Dacian frontier on the World Heritage list, and today it is just a slight hump in the ground among fields and woods, but its position on the high ground gives a wide view over the valleys, which is exactly why it was chosen. The towers were placed so that each could see its neighbours and pass signals along the frontier with fire and smoke.

The area around was later known as the land of Ciceu, after a medieval fortress on a rocky hill near the village of Ciceu-Corabia, south of here. In the late fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, the fortress and its estates were held by the princes of Moldavia, starting with Stephen the Great, who received them from the Hungarian king, so this little corner of Transylvania was for a time an outpost of a neighbouring state. The castle was destroyed in the sixteenth century, and only a few traces remain on the hill, but the story says a lot about how fluid borders were in this region.

The hills here are covered with meadows, orchards and oak woods, and the villages are spread out along the valleys with wooden houses and small Orthodox churches. In early summer the meadows are full of wild flowers, and the scythe is still used for hay on the steeper slopes. The roads are narrow and winding, mostly asphalted but with potholes, gravel and the occasional stretch of dirt, and you will share them with horse carts, cows and the occasional tractor. Take it slowly and enjoy the rhythm of village life.

There are no services at the site and very few in the villages around, so plan ahead. Beclean and Dej, on the main road along the Someș, have fuel, shops and restaurants, and Dej also has one of the old salt mines of Transylvania, now used for treatment and tourism. Village shops sell bread, cheese and drinks, and you will often be greeted with curiosity and friendliness. Ask for directions if you get lost; people will usually go out of their way to help.
t.popeni dumbrava@47.2,23.2:
Think of the frontier of Roman Dacia not as a wall but as a net. In the hills of Sălaj, north of the town of Zalău, the Romans stretched a fine mesh of watchtowers, small forts and earthen barriers across the ridges, all centred on the great fortress of Porolissum, which controlled the most important pass from the province into the lands of the free Dacians. Popeni, a village near Jibou, sits near one of the outer strands of that net: at Dumbravă, a spot on the edge of a wood, the remains of a tower are part of the Dacian frontier on the World Heritage list. You will see a bump in the ground and a lot of grass, and that is all the more reason to use your imagination.

Porolissum itself, at Moigrad, about half an hour south, is the place to go to see what the frontier really looked like. The stone fort has been partly rebuilt, with its main gate, walls and towers, and around it lie the remains of the town, an amphitheatre and the customs post where goods entering the province were taxed. The site sits on a hilltop with sweeping views, and it is one of the best Roman sites in Romania.

The area around Popeni is classic Sălaj countryside: low hills, meadows and woods, plum orchards and small villages. In late summer, the plums are harvested and many of them end up being distilled into țuică or pălincă, the plum brandy that is the drink of hospitality throughout Transylvania. The roads are quiet and narrow, winding over the hills between villages, with asphalt of varying quality. The main road from Zalău to Jibou and on to Baia Mare is busier and faster, with long bends and a few overtaking opportunities. As always in rural Romania, carts, cattle and dogs are part of the scenery.

Jibou, about six kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel, shops and restaurants. Zalău, the county capital, is a little further south and has everything you need, including a good county museum with finds from Porolissum. Try a plate of fresh cheese with polenta and sour cream, and enjoy the slow pace of the countryside, where time seems to move a little more gently than in the city.
The Meseș mountains rise to the west of Zalău like a long green wall, and they formed the natural western boundary of Roman Dacia in this region. Along their crest and on the slopes above the plains, the Romans built a line of watchtowers, and the site above the fields with the evocative name of Șesurile Tâlhăroasei, roughly the robbers' flats, near the villages of Treznea and Aghireș, is one of them. It is part of the Dacian frontier on the World Heritage list. Up in the forest the remains are modest, but the position, high on a slope with a view over the valley, shows how the frontier used every advantage of the terrain.

Zalău, a few kilometres away, is the capital of Sălaj county, a modest industrial town with a pleasant centre, a county museum full of Roman finds from Porolissum and the surrounding sites, and an art museum. The village of Treznea has a darker place in history: in September 1940, after northern Transylvania was transferred to Hungary, Hungarian troops killed dozens of villagers there, and a memorial commemorates the victims. The countryside today is peaceful, with meadows, beech woods and small villages, but these hills have seen many conflicts.

The road over the Meseș mountains, from Zalău towards Cluj-Napoca, climbs through forest in a series of bends, with good views of the hills and valleys, and it is one of the more enjoyable stretches in the area. It is a main road, however, with heavy truck traffic, so overtaking needs care. Smaller roads along the foot of the mountains, through Treznea, Agrij and Hurez, are quieter and narrower, sometimes rough, with steep sections and sharp turns. The forests here are home to deer, wild boar and the occasional bear, so be careful at dusk.

Zalău, about eight kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets, hotels and restaurants. The villages have small shops, and some guesthouses offer home-cooked meals. In the autumn, the beech forests of the Meseș turn gold and red and the light is soft, the most beautiful season to ride here. Try a bowl of ciorbă, sour soup, with fresh bread, and look out for the honey from the mountain villages, which is sold at the roadside in summer.
t.pullinki pullinki@66.6,23.8:
Just north of the Arctic Circle, in the valley of the Torne river that forms the border between Finland and Sweden, stand some of the stations of the Struve Geodetic Arc. Between 1816 and 1855, the astronomer Friedrich Georg Wilhelm Struve and his teams measured a chain of triangles from the Arctic coast of Norway to the Black Sea, more than two thousand eight hundred kilometres, to determine the exact shape of the Earth. The arc is now a World Heritage Site spread over ten countries, and the points in the Torne valley, with names like Pullinki, Perävaara and Jupukka, are marked by drill holes and cairns on the hilltops.

The Torne valley is wide and wooded, with the river flowing broad and fast between the two countries, and villages scattered along both banks. Pello, on the Finnish side, is the nearest town, with around four and a half thousand people. In summer, the midnight sun shines all night, and in winter the northern lights dance across the sky. Reindeer are common on the roads, and you need to ride carefully, especially at dusk and dawn, when they wander onto the tarmac.

The riding here is long and lonely, with straight roads through endless forest, broken by lakes, rivers and hills. Surfaces are generally good, but frost heave can make them bumpy, and gravel roads lead to remote places. Traffic is minimal, and distances between services are long. The riding season is short, roughly June to September, and mosquitoes can be ferocious in midsummer.

Pello has fuel, shops and a few places to eat, and Övertorneå, across the river in Sweden, is another option. Ylitornio, further south, is the nearest town of five thousand. The bridges across the Torne make it easy to switch between countries, and the Swedish and Finnish sides of the valley share a common language heritage in Meänkieli, the Torne valley Finnish. Bring a good mosquito repellent and plan fuel carefully.
t.santa maria del agua de landa@21.2,-99.3:
High in the Sierra Gorda of Querétaro, Franciscan missionaries led by Junípero Serra in the mid eighteenth century built five mission churches, and their facades are an explosion of carved and painted plaster: angels, saints, flowers, fruit, mermaids and symbols that blend Catholic imagery with the local indigenous world. The mission of Santa María del Agua de Landa, in the village of Landa de Matamoros, has one of the most elaborate facades, glowing in pink and ochre. The five missions were listed together as a World Heritage Site in 2003. Serra went on to found the missions of California.

The Sierra Gorda is a biosphere reserve and one of the most ecologically diverse regions of Mexico, ranging from semi desert to cloud forest within a few kilometres. Deep canyons, pine forests, waterfalls and rivers make it a beautiful and wild landscape, home to jaguars, bears and many birds.

For riders, Route 120 through the Sierra Gorda is one of the great roads of Mexico. From San Juan del Río and Cadereyta it climbs through cactus and desert, over the pass near Pinal de Amoles at over two thousand five hundred metres, with countless curves, then plunges down to Jalpan in the warm valley. The section around Pinal de Amoles is known for its hairpins and for fog that can close in suddenly. Surfaces are generally good, but landslides, trucks and livestock require attention.

Look closely at the Landa facade and you start to pick out the details: mermaids holding instruments, the Virgin of the Immaculate Conception in the centre, saints of the Franciscan order, and plant forms that seem to grow out of the stone. The local Pame people, who did much of the work, brought their own vision to it, and the colours, once restored, are surprisingly vivid against the green hills. In the evening, when the plaza fills with families and the light turns warm, it is a fine place to sit.

Jalpan, sixteen kilometres away, is the main town of the region, with the largest of the missions, fuel and services. Landa de Matamoros is a small village with basic shops. The other missions, at Concá, Tilaco and Tancoyol, are reached on side roads. Local food includes enchiladas serranas and fresh fish from the rivers. Ride in daylight and keep fuel topped up in the mountains.
t.owczary tserkva of our lady s protection:
The Lemkos, a mountain people of the Carpathians, built their churches of wood, with onion domes and steep shingle roofs stepping up in tiers toward the west tower, and the one at Owczary, in the Low Beskids south of Gorlice, is one of the finest. Built in the mid seventeenth century as a Greek Catholic church, it was later enlarged and painted inside with a rich polychrome decoration. After the Second World War the Lemkos were deported from this region in Operation Vistula, and the church was taken over by the Roman Catholic parish, while the Greek Catholic community has also returned to use it. It is part of the World Heritage listing of the Wooden Tserkvas of the Carpathian Region in Poland and Ukraine, inscribed in 2013.

The Low Beskids are a gentle range of forested hills, with valleys of meadow and small villages, and the region is full of wooden churches, Catholic and Orthodox, as well as First World War cemeteries. The Battle of Gorlice in May 1915, when German and Austro-Hungarian forces broke through the Russian lines, was one of the great battles of the Eastern Front, and some four hundred military cemeteries were built in the region, a good number of them designed by the Slovak architect Dušan Jurkovič in wood and stone.

Gorlice also has a place in industrial history: Ignacy Łukasiewicz, the pharmacist who invented the kerosene lamp, lit the first street lamp here in the 1850s, and the region was an early centre of the oil industry, with old wells still visible.

The riding in the Low Beskids is lovely: quiet, winding roads through forests and valleys, with little traffic and good views. The roads toward the Slovak border, over passes such as the Dukla, are a pleasure. Surfaces vary, and winter is cold and snowy.

Gorlice, eight kilometres away, has the fuel and food you need, and Sękowa, nearer, has its own wooden church on the UNESCO list. Local food includes pierogi, żurek, a sour rye soup, and Lemko dishes.
t.ruska bystra@48.9,22.3:
Hidden in a fold of the Vihorlat hills near the Ukrainian border, the little village of Ruská Bystrá has a wooden church built in the early eighteenth century, dedicated to Saint Nicholas, with a tower and a roof of wooden shingles and an iconostasis of painted icons inside. It is one of the Greek Catholic churches included in the World Heritage listing of the Wooden Churches of the Slovak Part of the Carpathian Mountain Area, inscribed in 2008, along with Catholic, Protestant and Orthodox churches across the country.

The Vihorlat hills are a volcanic range covered with beech forest, part of which is included in the World Heritage listing of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians. Morské oko, a lake in the Vihorlat formed when a landslide of volcanic rock dammed a valley, is a beautiful spot reached by a short walk from the road. Zemplínska šírava, a large reservoir to the southwest, is a popular summer resort with beaches and water sports, known locally as the Slovak sea.

This is a quiet, rural corner of eastern Slovakia, with small villages, many of them home to Rusyn communities, a Slavic people with their own language and Greek Catholic or Orthodox traditions. The area is poor by Slovak standards, and many young people have left, but the landscape is beautiful.

The riding here is relaxed and empty: winding roads through forests and villages, with little traffic and good views. Surfaces can be rough, and wildlife, including deer and wild boar, crosses the roads. The border with Ukraine is close; the Ubľa crossing is the nearest, but travel to Ukraine is not advisable at present because of the war.

Sobrance, fifteen kilometres away, sells fuel and feeds travellers, and Snina, eighteen kilometres away, is a larger town. Try halušky, potato dumplings with sheep cheese, and the local plum brandy, slivovica, after the bike is parked.
t.synevyr strymba@48.4,23.8:
In the Carpathian mountains of Transcarpathia, in western Ukraine, the forests around Synevyr include some of the last remaining primeval beech forests in Europe, part of the transnational World Heritage Site of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe. Strymba is one of the protected forest areas, in the hills near the village of Kolochava, where beech trees grow old and die without human interference, creating a rich habitat for fungi, insects, birds and animals.

Lake Synevyr, the largest mountain lake in the Ukrainian Carpathians, sits at nearly a thousand metres in a forested valley, its dark waters fed by streams. Legend says it was formed by the tears of a noble girl, Syn, grieving for her lover Vyr, a shepherd killed by her father's men. The Synevyr National Park also has a brown bear rehabilitation centre, where bears rescued from captivity live in large enclosures.

Kolochava, a long village in the valley of the Teresva tributaries, has several open air museums showing the history of the region under different rulers: Austro-Hungarian, Czechoslovak, Hungarian, Soviet and Ukrainian. The region's people include Ukrainians, Rusyns and Hungarians, and the villages have wooden churches and traditional houses.

The roads here are narrow, winding and often rough, with potholes and gravel, climbing over passes and through valleys. The scenery is wonderful, with mountains, forests and rivers.

Transcarpathia has long been a place where borders moved over people rather than people over borders. An old local joke tells of a man born in Austria-Hungary, schooled in Czechoslovakia, married in Hungary, retired in the Soviet Union and buried in Ukraine, all without leaving his village. Kolochava's museums play on exactly that story, and the region's food, from Hungarian style stews to Rusyn dumplings and smoked sheep cheese, reflects it too. However, Ukraine is at war, and most governments advise against all travel to the country, though Transcarpathia has been less directly affected than the east. Martial law, curfews and restrictions apply, and travel insurance is generally invalid. Mizhhirya, twenty two kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and shops, but supplies can be disrupted. Check the current situation very carefully before considering any trip.
t.treznea@47.1,23.1:
The northern frontier of Roman Dacia ran through the hills of Sălaj county, near Zalău, and Treznea is one of the places where its watchtowers, ramparts and forts left traces. The Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia, were listed as a World Heritage Site in 2024, covering hundreds of sites across Romania. Nearby, on a ridge above the valley, Porolissum was the largest Roman town and military complex on this frontier, with a reconstructed gate, an amphitheatre and walls, and it is one of the most impressive Roman sites in Romania.

Treznea itself is a small village with a tragic history. In September 1940, after northern Transylvania was transferred to Hungary, Hungarian troops killed dozens of Romanian and Jewish villagers here, and a memorial commemorates the victims. The region has a complex history of shifting borders and mixed communities, Romanian and Hungarian.

The landscape of Sălaj is a land of rolling hills, orchards and forests, between the Meseș mountains and the plain. It is quiet and rural, with villages, wooden churches and farmland, and the roads are winding and pleasant.

The riding here is gentle and enjoyable, with country roads through hills and villages, little traffic and good views. Surfaces vary, with potholes and patched sections, and horse carts and livestock are common. The road over the Meseș pass toward Cluj, the DN1F, is busier but scenic. Weather is continental, with hot summers and cold winters.

Porolissum deserves a proper stop if you have the time. The site spreads over a hilltop at Moigrad, a short ride north of Zalău, and its reconstructed stone gate, the foundations of the camp and the remains of temples, a customs post and the amphitheatre give a real sense of how large this frontier town once was. Trade with the free Dacians beyond the line passed through here, and the views from the ridge over the hills of Sălaj explain why the Romans chose it. Excavations still go on most summers, and on a quiet weekday you may have the hill almost to yourself, with only skylarks and grazing sheep for company. Zalău, eight kilometres away, is the county capital, with fuel, services and a museum displaying finds from Porolissum. Local food includes sarmale, cabbage rolls, mici, grilled sausages, and the plum brandy, țuică, offered as a welcome in every home.
t.razboieni cetate grajduri cap@46.4,23.9:
In the Mureș valley near Ocna Mureș, the village of Războieni-Cetate takes the second half of its name, cetate, fortress, from the Roman fort that once stood here, guarding the road and the river in central Dacia. The fort was a base for a cavalry unit, and its remains, close to the farm buildings of the communist era collective, the CAP, whose stables give the site its odd label, are part of the World Heritage listing of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia. Little is visible above ground, but the outline of the fort can be traced in the fields.

Ocna Mureș, two kilometres away, is a town built on salt. Salt has been mined here since Roman times, and the town's salt lakes, formed in collapsed mines, are used for bathing in summer. The salt was carried down the Mureș by boat, and the river was a major trade route through Transylvania. Turda, a short ride north, has one of the most spectacular salt mines in the world, turned into an underground park with a Ferris wheel and a lake.

The landscape of the Mureș valley is wide and agricultural, with hills on either side, orchards, vineyards and villages. The Trascău mountains to the west offer dramatic limestone gorges, such as the Turda Gorge and the Râmeț monastery valley, and quiet roads.

The riding here is pleasant, with the main road along the Mureș busy with trucks, but the minor roads into the hills and mountains quieter and more scenic. Surfaces vary, and horse carts are common. The road through the Trascău mountains is narrow and winding, a lovely ride.

Ocna Mureș has pumps, a few shops and a guesthouse or two, and Aiud and Alba Iulia, to the south, are larger towns. Alba Iulia has a huge star fortress and is where the union of Transylvania with Romania was proclaimed in 1918. Try the local wines of the Târnave region and the hearty food of Transylvania.
t.geoagiu drumul romanilor@45.9,23.2:
The Romans loved hot water, and at Geoagiu-Băi, in the hills above the Mureș valley, they found it: thermal springs that fed baths at the settlement of Germisara, where soldiers and officials came to bathe and dedicated altars to the nymphs and gods of the waters. The Roman pools carved into the travertine are still visible, and the modern spa uses the same springs. Drumul Romanilor, the Romans' road, recalls the routes that linked the forts and towns of Dacia, and the area is part of the World Heritage listing of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire, Dacia.

Geoagiu itself lies on the Mureș, between Orăștie and Deva, at the foot of the Metaliferi mountains, rich in gold, which was one of the reasons the Romans conquered Dacia. To the south, the Orăștie mountains hold the Dacian fortresses of the kingdom that Trajan defeated in AD 106, including Sarmizegetusa Regia, the Dacian capital, and Costești, listed together as a World Heritage Site.

The landscape here is a mix of the wide Mureș valley, with farmland and villages, and the hills and mountains on either side, covered with forest. The Geoagiu valley, north of the town, is green and quiet, with small villages and pastures.

The riding here is very good: winding roads into the mountains, with good views, little traffic and dramatic scenery. The road to Sarmizegetusa Regia is narrow and climbs through forest, and the Transalpina, one of the highest roads in Romania, starts south of Sebeș, not far east. Surfaces on minor roads vary, and horse carts are common. The main road along the Mureș is busy with trucks.

Geoagiu has a filling station and places to eat, and Orăștie and Deva are larger towns. Deva has a castle on a volcanic hill above the town, reached by a funicular. Try the local food of Hunedoara county, including bulz, polenta balls stuffed with cheese, and the thermal pools of Geoagiu-Băi after a long day on the bike.
t.radacinesti cetate@45.3,24.4:
Rădăcinești is a quiet village belonging to Berislăvești, tucked into the hills on the east side of the Olt valley in Vâlcea county. The word cetate on the label means fortress, and like many such names in Romania it points to an old fortified height above the village, the kind of place where earthworks and a few stones are all that is left of people who once watched this valley closely. You come for the setting rather than for ruins you can walk through.

The setting is good. Down below, the Olt forces its way south through the Carpathians in one of the great river gorges of the country, and the DN7 follows it. That main road is beautiful and tiresome in equal measure: cliffs, river and monasteries on one side, a steady stream of lorries on the other. Climbing away from it towards Berislăvești and Sălătrucel brings instant relief, with narrow lanes through orchards and plum trees, small bridges over side streams and views back to the forested ridges of the Cozia massif. The surface on these local roads is often rough and the corners blind, so treat them gently.

This corner of Wallachia is thick with history. Cozia Monastery, founded by Mircea the Elder in the late fourteenth century, sits on the Olt a short ride away, and Mircea himself lies buried there. Further west, Horezu Monastery, built for Constantin Brâncoveanu, is a World Heritage site and the reason for the name on one of these rides; the village of Horezu is also known for its pottery, glazed in brown, cream and green with roosters and spirals. Gorge, fortress hill, monastery: the Olt has always been a highway as well as a barrier.

The nature here is mid-mountain Romania at its gentlest. Beech and oak woods, meadows full of flowers in June, and in autumn the smell of plum brandy being distilled in back yards. The Cozia massif rising above the gorge is a national park with steep, broken cliffs.

For fuel and food, Călimănești, about nine kilometres away on the Olt, is the practical choice: it is a spa town with stations, shops and plenty of guesthouses around Căciulata. Fill up there before wandering into the side valleys, where shops are small and fuel non-existent.
t.villages with fortified churches in tran:
South of Sighișoara the hills fold into long, grassy valleys, and almost every one of them hides a village built around a church that was also a castle. This marker sits among them, close to Șaeș and Apold, two of the old Saxon settlements whose German names, Schaas and Trappold, still turn up on church plaques and in the memories of the few families who stayed.

The Transylvanian Saxons arrived from the Rhine and Moselle lands from the twelfth century onwards, invited by Hungarian kings to farm and defend the frontier. Through the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, with Ottoman and Tatar raids sweeping in from the south and east, each village turned its church into a refuge: thick ring walls, towers for each family's stores, a well, and a hall where everyone could hold out while the raiders burned the fields. Seven of these villages are on the World Heritage list, but dozens more look much the same, and Apold's church, with its walls still standing above the houses, is a good example of the type.

The riding is calm and pastoral. Lanes wander from village to village over low ridges, past sheepfolds, haystacks shaped like loaves and lines of walnut trees. Tarmac comes and goes; some of the links between villages are gravel or dirt, and after rain they turn into slippery clay that will humble a heavy bike. In dry weather, though, these are some of the most rewarding back roads in Romania, and on a weekday you might meet more buffalo than cars.

Most Saxons left for Germany after 1990, and the villages are now home mainly to Romanian and Roma families. Many churches are locked, but a phone number on the gate or a neighbour with a key often solves that. Some villages have small guesthouses that serve home cooking: soup, smoked meats, cheese, and something with plums or apricots afterwards.

Sighișoara, ten kilometres north, is your base for fuel, cash and supplies, and its walled hilltop citadel, birthplace by tradition of Vlad the Impaler, is worth an evening stroll once the tour coaches have gone. Out here among the villages there is nothing to buy fuel from, so set off with a full tank.
t.monor dealul braniste@46.9,24.7:
This is the Transylvanian Plain at its northern edge, a land of soft hills rather than mountains, and Dealul Braniște is one of the rounded rises between the villages of Monor and Batoș in Mureș and Bistrița-Năsăud country. Braniște usually means a protected wood or reserved pasture, and the hill still carries patches of oak among the fields.
