From the top the view runs out over a rumpled carpet of meadows, orchards and strip fields, with the Călimani mountains a blue line far to the east.

Riding here is about small roads and slow pleasures. The county lanes link village to village over gentle climbs, the corners are mostly open and well sighted, and the traffic is a tractor, a horse cart and somebody's cows walking themselves home. Surfaces are uneven, with patched sections and the odd pothole deep enough to matter, and some links become gravel without much warning. It is lovely in late spring when the meadows are full of flowers, and in early autumn when the haystacks are up and the light turns gold.

Much of this area was Saxon, settled by German-speaking colonists in the Middle Ages, and the old names linger: Batoș was Botsch, nearby Teaca was Tekendorf. Their churches, many now quiet, still stand above the villages. Romanian and Hungarian communities have lived alongside them for centuries, and you will notice the mix in the church styles and the shapes of the gates. A short ride south brings you to Reghin, a town long known for its violin makers, who use the spruce of the nearby mountains for their soundboards.

The region also sits on salt. Sărățel and Sărățeni, places on these rides, take their names from salt springs and outcrops, and in the old days salt was carried from Transylvania down the rivers and over the passes as one of the province's main sources of wealth.

There is nothing to buy on the hill itself. Batoș, about four kilometres away, is a large village with a shop. For a reliable fuel stop, Teaca is the nearest town of any size, about fourteen kilometres off, and Reghin and Bistrița offer everything you could want. Carry water in summer, because shade is scarce once you leave the woods.
t.ileanda la casoi@47.3,23.6:
Ileanda is a village on the Someș, the big river of north-western Transylvania, at a point where the valley narrows between wooded hills on its way from Dej towards Jibou. The railway runs alongside the water, the road keeps company with both, and the hills on either side rise in long slopes of beech, hornbeam and pasture. La Căsoi is a local name for a spot among those hills; you will not find a monument here, just the landscape and whatever the season is doing to it.

As riding goes, the Someș corridor is an easy, flowing valley road with river views, broad bends and the occasional village slowing you down. The real fun starts when you turn off it. Side roads climb north towards the Lăpuș country and Maramureș, or south into the Sălaj hills, and they get narrower, steeper and rougher with every kilometre. Expect blind crests, sudden gravel, dogs and the occasional herd crossing. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; high summer can be hot and hazy in the valley, and winter turns the side roads muddy.

This is a border land in more ways than one. The Someș valley has long been the route between the Transylvanian basin and the plains of the north-west, and the villages are a mix of Romanian and Hungarian communities with wooden and stone churches side by side. North of here, Maramureș is famous for its tall wooden churches with needle spires, several of them on the World Heritage list, and some of the villages around Ileanda have older, smaller cousins of that style.

The river is the dominant presence. In spring the Someș runs high and brown with snowmelt from the Rodna mountains; by late summer it slows and clears, and herons stand in the shallows. Storks nest on poles in the villages, and the fields along the river are full of maize and sunflowers.

Ileanda is a village of a couple of thousand people, which usually means a shop and a bar but not much else, so do not count on fuel here. The nearest town of five thousand or more is Copalnic Mănăștur, about twenty kilometres away, and Dej is the safer bet for a full tank, cash and a proper meal. Fill up before you leave the main valley.
t.brancusi monumental ensemble of targu ji:
Three sculptures, one straight line, and a city that grew up around them: that is the Brâncuși ensemble in Târgu Jiu. The Table of Silence stands near the Jiu river, the Gate of the Kiss marks the entrance to the park, and the Endless Column rises at the far end of the Avenue of Heroes, a stack of rhomboid modules in coppery cast iron climbing nearly thirty metres into the sky. Walk the whole axis from river to column and you will cover about a kilometre and a half.

Constantin Brâncuși was born in Hobița, a village not far from here, walked to Paris as a young man and became one of the founders of modern sculpture. In the late 1930s the women's league of Gorj commissioned him to make a memorial to the local soldiers who died defending the Jiu crossing against the German advance in 1916. He gave them something no one expected: no generals, no bayonets, just pure form, a sequence meant to be walked through as a meditation on sacrifice and memory. The communists later neglected it, and at one point there was talk of pulling the column down, but it survived and is now a World Heritage site.

Târgu Jiu is a pleasant mid-sized city with all the services you need, and a sensible place to start or end a ride. North of town the land climbs fast into the Parâng and Vâlcan mountains. The Transalpina, one of the highest roads in Romania, starts its climb at Novaci, east of here, and the road over Polovragi and the gorges of the Olteț and Galbenul are within easy reach. Heading west, the route towards Baia de Aramă and the Cerna valley, where these rides end up, runs through limestone country with gorges and caves.

The riding in the immediate area is flatter than you might expect, with farmland and orchards in the Jiu valley, but give it half an hour and you will be climbing through beech forest. Summer days can be very hot in the valley, so an early start pays.

There is plenty of fuel in town, and the restaurants around the centre serve Oltenian staples: grilled mici, sour soups, and polenta with cheese. Park the bike, walk the axis slowly, and sit for a moment at the Table of Silence; the stone stools around it are cold even on a warm day.
t.village of valea viilor@46.1,24.3:
Valea Viilor means Valley of the Vineyards, and the name is honest: the slopes around the village were planted with vines long before anyone thought of mapping them. The Saxons called it Wurmloch, and its fortified church, a tall Gothic hall with a defensive storey built over the choir and a ring wall around it, is one of the seven on the World Heritage list.

The village lies a few kilometres off the Târnava Mare valley, between Mediaș and Copșa Mică, in a side valley that feels a world away from the main road. The church dominates the centre. Its massive walls and the battlemented upper level, where defenders could drop stones and fire through slits, tell you everything about life on this frontier in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, when raiding armies came often enough that every village needed a castle of its own. Inside it is plain and whitewashed, Lutheran since the Reformation, with a carved altar and the faded paint of older decoration on the walls.

Riding in is short and pleasant, a narrow lane winding up between orchards and old vineyard terraces, some tended, many gone wild. It is the kind of road where you let the bike roll and look around. Back on the main valley road, traffic picks up and the surface is mostly good. The ride to Saschiz goes east through more Saxon country, past rolling hills and villages that each have their own church-fortress.

Copșa Mică, four kilometres away, deserves a mention for different reasons. Under communism it was home to a carbon black plant and a non-ferrous metals smelter that left it one of the most polluted towns in Europe, with soot so thick that sheep were said to turn grey. The factories have mostly closed and the landscape is slowly recovering, but it is a sobering contrast to the pastoral calm of Valea Viilor just up the road.

For practical matters, Copșa Mică and Mediaș have fuel and shops; Mediaș is the bigger and better stocked of the two, with a handsome old centre of its own. Valea Viilor has a small shop and sometimes someone at the church to let you in. In late summer the air in the village smells of ripe plums, and the vineyards above it turn bronze by October.
t.rakoczi wine cellar@48.3,21.6:
Sárospatak is an old town on the Bodrog river, right where the foothills of the Zemplén range run out into the plain, and in Hungarian history it carries more weight than its size suggests. It was a seat of the Rákóczi family, and the castle in town was one of their strongholds in the long wars against the Habsburgs. Local tradition also claims it as the birthplace of Saint Elisabeth of Hungary, in 1207, and the Reformed College here, founded in the sixteenth century, once counted the Czech educator Comenius among its teachers. Not bad for a small place at the edge of the map.

The cellar is part of the same story, because this is the Tokaj wine region, where wine and the Rákóczi name have been connected for centuries. Tokaj wine, and above all Tokaji Aszú, the sweet wine made from grapes shrivelled by noble rot, was famous across Europe in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, and it was said to be a favourite of kings. The region was listed as a World Heritage cultural landscape in 2002. The cellars in this area are cut into the soft volcanic tuff, cool and damp all year, and the dark mould on their walls is part of the process.

The riding here is gentle and pleasant rather than dramatic. The approach roads are quiet and mostly well surfaced, rolling through small villages with press houses and cellar rows on the slopes, and the Zemplén hills to the north give you some gentle bends and the odd viewpoint. Autumn is the best time, when the vineyards go yellow and the harvest is on, though spring is good too, and the summer heat can feel heavy on the plain.

Sárospatak is a proper town of about fourteen thousand people, so you will find fuel, food and cafes without trouble, and Sátoraljaújhely, ten kilometres away, sits on the Slovak border and is just as practical. A word of sense: if you visit a cellar and taste, a rider should taste only a sip, or leave the bike and go on foot. The wine is good, but the road home is long.
t.hortobagy national park the puszta@47.6,:
The Hortobágy is Hungary's great grassland, the puszta, a flat, wide, open plain in the east of the country, and it is unlike anything else in central Europe. Nearly eight hundred square kilometres of it is protected as a national park, which was the first in Hungary, and it is on the World Heritage list too. What you see from the road is grass, sky, horizon, and then, if the light is right, something odd shimmering on the horizon, which locals will tell you is the fata morgana, a mirage that has fooled travellers for centuries.

It looks wild, but it is an old working landscape. Shepherds and cowherds have grazed the puszta for hundreds of years, and the animals are still here: long-horned grey cattle, curly-horned racka sheep, and horses of the Nonius breed. You will see the tall wooden well sweeps that were once used to draw water, standing alone like crooked cranes. In the village of Hortobágy, the nine-arched stone bridge, completed in the 1830s, is the longest in Hungary, and beside it stands an old inn, the csárda, where you can try the local speciality of savoury meat-filled pancakes, which are filling and cheap.

For a rider the plain is easy but not entirely relaxing. The roads are straight, flat and long, with very few bends, and the main challenge is the wind, which comes across the grass without anything to stop it, and can push a bike sideways. Watch for farm vehicles and for wildlife, especially at dusk, when hares and the occasional deer cross the road. The best seasons are spring, when the grass is green and birds are everywhere, and autumn, when tens of thousands of common cranes stop here on their way south, and their calls fill the air at dawn.

Hortobágy village is small and its services are limited, so for fuel and a wider choice of food the best bet is Balmazújváros, about fifteen kilometres away, or Tiszacsege. Bring water in summer, because there is almost no shade, and sun cream, because the sky is bigger than you expect.
t.santiago de jalpan@21.2,-99.5:
Fray Junípero Serra, later famous for his missions in California, started his career in the Sierra Gorda, a rugged, forested range in northern Querétaro, and the church at Jalpan is where it began. Built in the mid-eighteenth century by Franciscan friars and the local Pame people, it is the central one of five missions in the region, and the facade is covered with colourful stucco figures of saints, flowers and angels, a mix of baroque tradition and indigenous imagination. UNESCO listed the five missions in 2003.

The mission of Santiago is on the main square of Jalpan, a small, lively town that is also the base for the Sierra Gorda Biosphere Reserve, one of the most biodiverse protected areas in Mexico, with a mix of desert, cloud forest, pine and tropical habitats packed into a short distance. Orchids, jaguars, ocelots, parrots and black bears are all said to live here. Jalpan feels very different from the dry, high plateau to the west, because it lies in a warm, humid valley, with fruit orchards and the smell of wet earth.

This is some of the best motorcycle country in central Mexico. Highway 120 climbs from the plain at San Juan del Río, through Pinal de Amoles and its hairpins, and descends into the Jalpan valley with long, sweeping bends, hairpin after hairpin, through pine forest and then into tropical vegetation. Fog and rain can come in quickly, and rockfall is a risk, particularly after storms. Keep an eye out for livestock and slow trucks, and take the corners cautiously, because some are blind. The road continues to the Huasteca region, falling steeply to the tropical lowlands.

Jalpan has fuel, small hotels and restaurants around the plaza, and it is the best place to fill up before exploring the other missions, which lie along quiet country roads. The best time to ride is the dry season, from November to April, though summer storms freshen the forest. Try the local fruit and the zacahuil, a giant tamale from the Huasteca, if you find it on a market stall.
t.bridge of atongo@20.0,-99.4:
Silver came out of the mountains of the north, and everything else came back the other way: wine, cloth, tools, tobacco and soldiers. The Camino Real de Tierra Adentro was the road that carried it all, running from Mexico City to Santa Fe, and it opened in the late sixteenth century and remained in use for roughly three hundred years. It crossed rivers and ravines, and where it did, the Spanish built bridges, a number of which have survived. The bridge of Atongo is one of the stone bridges along the road in the state of Mexico, close to Jilotepec.

Jilotepec was an important place long before the Spanish came, a centre of the Otomí people, and the Spanish used Otomí allies to push the frontier northwards, founding settlements among the hills. The old road passed through this country of dry hills, maguey fields and small farms, then headed on toward Querétaro and the silver towns. UNESCO listed the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro in 2010, including bridges and towns along the way, and these structures are a reminder that the road was a piece of infrastructure as much as a route.

Today the country north-west of Mexico City is crossed by fast modern highways, and the old road survives as quiet lanes and village streets. Riding on them can be pleasant, with little traffic, gentle hills and the smell of dust and wood smoke, but surfaces vary and speed bumps appear in every village. Stone bridges are narrow, and some have uneven or slippery paving, so cross them slowly. The dry months, from November to April, are the most comfortable, while summer brings heavy afternoon rain.

Fuel is available in Jilotepec, about ten kilometres away, and the town has cafes and small restaurants, and the main highway to Querétaro has plenty of service stations. I cannot tell you exactly what stands at the coordinates beyond the bridge itself, so allow time to ask a local, because people tend to know exactly where the old bridge is.
Tancoyol is one of the last of the Sierra Gorda missions to be built, and it is perhaps the one that feels most remote. The church of Nuestra Señora de la Luz stands in a small village in the valley of the Santa María river, in the north of Querétaro, with a tall, intricate facade covered with plaster figures, flowers and symbols, a combination of European baroque and the imagination of the Pame people who helped to build it. UNESCO listed the five Sierra Gorda missions together in 2003, and Tancoyol is the quietest of them.

The country around is lush and humid, a contrast with the dry plateau farther south, and it is part of the Sierra Gorda Biosphere Reserve, with a wide range of habitats from cactus scrub to cloud forest. Orchards of citrus, coffee and avocado grow in the valleys, and the villages are small and quiet, with plazas where people gather in the evening. The nearest towns, Landa de Matamoros and Purísima de Arista, are small, and the larger town of Jalpan is a good half-hour's ride away.

The ride to Tancoyol is part of the attraction. The roads leave Highway 120 and wind through the hills with tight bends, steep gradients and occasional landslide damage, and some sections of road are narrow and rough, with livestock and children walking in the middle. It is slow riding, with fog and heavy rain possible in the summer, and the best time is the dry season, from November to April. Early starts help, because the light is better and the mountain roads are quieter.

There is little in the way of services in the villages, so fuel at Jalpan, about twenty-five kilometres away, is the sensible choice, and it is worth carrying water and a snack. Local people are friendly and will happily direct you, and in the evenings it is possible to find simple meals in a village kitchen, perhaps with fresh tortillas and beans. The church is still in use, so visits are best outside service times and with a quiet manner.
t.hurez sub cornet 1@47.1,23.0:
The ridge of the Meseş mountains runs like a low, wooded wall across northern Transylvania, and the Romans, after they conquered Dacia in AD 106, made it the northern frontier of their new province. They built forts in the valleys, watchtowers on the high points and a road to link them, and this area near Hurez and Cornet lies within that line. The name on our list, Sub Cornet, means below the Cornet, which suggests a hill or ridge overhead, and the pattern of sites around here is of small watchtowers positioned to see along the valleys.

Nothing here is dramatic. The watchtowers were usually small square buildings of timber on a stone base, ringed by a ditch, with a handful of soldiers, and what remains now is a mound or a faint outline in the grass or among the beech trees. The real attraction is the landscape: a gentle country of orchards, hay meadows and scattered villages, with horse carts still working the fields, storks nesting on telegraph poles, and long views over a green and rolling land. The Roman frontier here was abandoned in the third century, when Dacia was given up, and the countryside has been quietly farmed ever since.

The roads are a mixed bag. County roads between the villages are narrow, with a lot of potholes, patches and sharp changes in the surface, and dogs, geese and wandering cattle are normal hazards. Avoid riding at dusk, and expect slow going. Spring, with blossom on the plum trees, and early autumn, when the hills are gold, are the best times; summers can be hot, and winter brings snow and ice. The route toward the Meseş pass and the Roman town of Porolissum, a few valleys away, is the best of the riding, with a gradual climb through forest.

Crasna, fourteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel and shops, and Zalău, the county seat, is larger. In small villages you will find a shop and perhaps a bar, so carry water and snacks. Plum brandy, called țuică or pálinka, is the local drink, offered with generosity, and a rider should be careful with the offer.
t.buciumi gradiste@47.0,23.0:
Buciumi has a Roman fort, and a proper one. On a low hill above the village, the outline of a rectangular auxiliary fort has been excavated, with walls, gates and the foundations of the buildings inside, laid out to the standard Roman pattern with the headquarters in the middle and barracks to either side. It was one of the forts guarding the road and the passes of the Meseş mountains, a few kilometres from the larger fortress and town at Porolissum, and it held a unit of auxiliary troops, soldiers recruited from the provinces rather than citizen legionaries.

Those auxiliaries came from far afield. Inscriptions from the Porolissum frontier record units raised in places as distant as Syria and Britain, which is a vivid reminder that the Roman army moved people around the empire, and that a Syrian archer might have spent his service in the beech hills of Transylvania. The soldiers' families grew up in settlements outside the walls, and when their service ended, they were given citizenship. Grădiște, the name on our list, simply means the site of a fortification in Romanian, a sign that locals have known there was something here for centuries.

For the ride, Buciumi lies in a quiet corner of Sălaj county, in a landscape of low forested ridges, orchards and small valleys, with the Agrij river nearby. The roads are narrow and not always smooth, with patched asphalt, blind bends and the occasional herd of cows, and the pace has to be slow, but the scenery makes up for it. Mornings in late spring are lovely, with mist in the valleys and the smell of cut hay, and September is also good. Rain can turn dirt tracks to mud.

Buciumi itself is a village of under three thousand people with a shop or two, and for fuel the sensible choice is Crasna, eighteen kilometres away, or Zalău a little farther. Agrij and the neighbouring villages sell homemade cheese, plum jam and honey, which are good to try if you find a stall. The Romanian people you meet here tend to be curious, hospitable and happy to chat, even if the conversation consists mainly of gestures.
Zalău is the county town of Sălaj, a modern small city of about sixty thousand people that grew fast in the communist period, and the countryside around it is far more interesting than the blocks of flats. Brusturi, a few kilometres off, sits in the hills that lead up toward the Meseş mountains, and the name on our list points to a Roman fort called Certiae, one of the line of military posts that kept watch on the northern edge of Dacia, along with a ruin the locals link with an old legend of robbers. I cannot say what stands at exactly these coordinates, but the pattern is clear.

Trajan's conquest of Dacia in the early second century turned this part of Transylvania into a Roman province, with roads connecting the garrison towns, and Napoca, now Cluj, was one of its main cities. The Romans stayed until the 270s, when the emperor Aurelian withdrew the army and the administration south of the Danube. A good deal of Romanian national identity is wrapped up in this story, which is why the Roman remains are marked on tourist maps and signposted in the villages.

The countryside here is rolling, green and agricultural, with hay meadows, plum orchards, small vineyards and villages where Romanian and Hungarian communities live side by side. Riding is easy and relaxed, though not fast: the main roads out of Zalău are busy with lorries, and the minor ones are potholed, with some stretches of broken surface that appear around a bend. In spring the orchards are in blossom, and in autumn the harvest brings tractors onto the roads. Keep an eye out for horse-drawn carts, which are still common and may have no lights.

Zalău has everything a rider needs: several fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants serving good, hearty Romanian food, such as stuffed cabbage rolls, soups sharpened with sour cream and polenta with cheese. Smaller villages have fewer services, so fill up before you go. The Sălaj County Museum in Zalău holds finds from the Roman sites and is a good place to make sense of the scattered ruins.
t.negreni dealul hoancelor@47.3,23.5:
A ridge called Dealul Hoancelor does not make it onto many maps, and the place is better understood from the landscape around it. This is the country of the Someș river in the north of Transylvania, between the Meseș mountains in the west and the hills of the Transylvanian plain to the east, and the valleys are broad, green and thickly farmed. The nearest places on our list are tiny villages, Lozna and Letca, and the closest town, Jibou, is about twenty kilometres away. I cannot honestly say what lies at these precise coordinates, but the setting is typical of the Roman frontier country of northern Dacia.

Jibou is the more interesting place to stop. Its castle, once the seat of the Wesselényi family, a Hungarian noble house, stands in a large landscaped park that has become a botanical garden, with old trees, glasshouses and quiet paths, and it is a surprise to find in a small Romanian town. The garden dates back to the late eighteenth century, when the Wesselényis laid out a park in the fashionable English style, and the castle houses a small museum. The Someș river, which runs nearby, is wide and slow, and herons and storks hunt along its banks.

The riding is quiet and mild. Roads over the low ridges give lovely views over fields and woodland, with gentle gradients and easy bends, but the surface can be rough, with patches, potholes and loose gravel at the edges, and village streets are shared with chickens, dogs and the occasional goat. There are few cars, which makes it a pleasant ride for a slow and curious day, rather than a fast one. May and June are green and fresh, September has warm, golden light, and winter can be icy.

Fuel and food are best found at Jibou, where there are stations and shops, and the larger city of Zalău is within reach. In the villages you will find a shop and a bar that serves coffee and perhaps a plate of fried eggs and sausage. Drinking water and a rain jacket are sensible companions, since summer thunderstorms build quickly over the hills.
t.racovita praetorium ii cetate@45.4,24.3:
Here the Olt does something that rivers are not supposed to do: it cuts straight through the Carpathians. Between Sibiu and Râmnicu Vâlcea the river runs through a gorge that the Romans knew well, and Racovița lies in its southern stretch, where steep wooded slopes close in on both sides. The Romans built forts along it as part of the Limes Alutanus, and the name Praetorium on our list is one of those, a small fort that guarded the road along the water. Not far away, Caput Stenarum, near Boița, held the pass at the northern end of the gorge.

The road that follows the Olt today, the DN7, is the main route between Transylvania and the south, and it has a reputation. Lorries grind along it in both directions, the bends are tight, and passing is risky, so it is a road you take with patience, rather than speed. At the same time the scenery is excellent, with forest, rocks and the river below, and a short way along, the Cozia monastery, built in the fourteenth century by the Wallachian prince Mircea the Elder, stands on the bank, with its fine proportions and royal tombs. The mountains above are part of the Cozia National Park.

Riding the gorge is best on a weekday morning, when traffic is lighter, or in the shoulder seasons, since summer weekends bring queues. The surface is generally fine but patched, and rockfall or roadworks can slow things down. From Cârțișoara, further north, the Transfăgărășan climbs to more than two thousand metres, which most riders consider the great prize of the region, though it is closed by snow for much of the year and usually opens around the end of June.

Brezoi, about eight kilometres away, is a small town with fuel and food, and Călimănești, down the valley, is a spa town with hot springs, hotels and restaurants. The river is popular with anglers and rafters. A coffee at a lay-by cafe, with the noise of lorries behind you and the green water in front, is part of the Olt experience.
t.perisor paltinis@47.3,24.2:
The hills of northern Transylvania, in Bistrita-Nasaud county, are quieter than the better-known Saxon towns further south, a country of wooded ridges, narrow valleys and farming villages where hay is still cut by hand and stacked on wooden poles. The Perisor to Paltinis label sits in this landscape, about four kilometres from the village of Spermezeu and not far from Zagra, in the foothills below the Rodna mountains. I do not know what the hilltop at this exact point is, so I will describe the region and what it offers a rider.

The area belonged for centuries to the Habsburg border guard, which recruited Romanian peasants from the Nasaud district to defend the empire's frontier, and in return gave them schools and a degree of freedom, which made this one of the best-educated parts of the Romanian countryside. Villages are strung along the streams, with wooden gates, tall steeples and fields divided by hedges. Hill sites with the name of cetate or fortress are common in this region, and archaeologists have found fortified settlements from the Bronze Age, from the Dacians and from the medieval period on many hilltops. Without a local guide it is hard to tell which are accessible, so do not count on a signposted visit.

To the north rise the Rodna mountains, the highest range in the eastern Carpathians, with peaks above two thousand metres and a national park of alpine meadows, glacial lakes and rare flowers. The roads through the hills are often narrow and patched, with sudden potholes, horse carts, flocks of sheep and unfenced livestock, so stay alert, particularly at dusk. They can be a joy for a relaxed rider, with long views over rolling hills, haystacks and little churches. Summers are warm, and thunderstorms come quickly in the afternoon. Autumn is gentle and golden, and winters are cold with heavy snow.

Nimigea de Sus, about ten kilometres away, has about five and a half thousand people and is the nearest sizeable place for fuel, and Spermezeu and Zagra have small shops. Food in the villages is hearty, with mamaliga, cornmeal porridge, served with sour cream, cheese or smoked sausage, and stuffed cabbage rolls called sarmale. Plum brandy, tuica, is offered to guests, and refusing politely is acceptable.
t.gilau dealul cetatii@46.7,23.4:
Gilau sits where the flat plain of the Somesul Mic river meets the first hills of the Apuseni mountains, about fifteen kilometres west of Cluj-Napoca, in Transylvania, and the hill called Dealul Cetatii, which simply means Fortress Hill, rises almost on the edge of the town, about a kilometre away. The town has nearly eight thousand people, and from the road you can see the high, forested ridges of the Apuseni to the west.

Gilau has long been a strategic point, because it guards the route from the Transylvanian plateau into the mountains and on towards the plain of western Romania, along the old road to Oradea. A fortress stood here in the Middle Ages, and a castle belonging to great Transylvanian noble families stood in the town. I cannot say what remains today on the hill, and the label is more a pointer to the area than a promise of ruins, but the setting is good for a short walk with a view of the valley.

The mountains behind hold one of Europe's oldest mining regions. At Rosia Montana, a few hours away to the south-west, the Romans mined gold at a place they called Alburnus Maior after they conquered Dacia in AD 106, and they left galleries cut by hand and wax writing tablets found in the tunnels. The Rosia Montana Mining Landscape was inscribed by UNESCO in 2021. The Apuseni are also full of caves, karst plateaux, waterfalls and beech forest, and the villages of the Motzi people, with their tall wooden houses and shepherd traditions, are among the most distinctive in Romania.

The road west from Cluj, the E60 to Oradea, is busy and often congested with lorries, so it is better to take the smaller road through Gilau and along the lake of Gilau, which climbs into the hills towards Belis with a series of pleasant bends, forests and views. Surfaces vary, with patches and some potholes, and traffic is heavier at weekends when people from Cluj head for the lakes. The best months are May to October, and winters bring snow and ice in the hills.

Gilau has fuel stations, shops and cafes, and Cluj-Napoca, Transylvania's lively university city, has everything else, with a big old centre, a cathedral on the main square and excellent restaurants. Try papanasi, fried doughnuts with sour cream and jam, and a bowl of sour soup, ciorba, in a small local place.
Zalău is the county seat of Sălaj, a city of around sixty thousand people sitting in a shallow valley where the Meseș hills fold down toward the Transylvanian plain. The stop sits just north of the Măgurii stream, on the edge of the town, which means you arrive through suburbs and allotments rather than through any grand gateway. That suits the county. Sălaj is not a place of famous passes; it is a place of rolling ridges, orchards, hay meadows and small roads that wander from one village to the next without much of a plan.

The riding here is gentle and honest. Expect narrow asphalt with patches, the occasional cart or flock of geese, and gradients that never ask much of the bike. The pleasure is in the pace: beech woods closing over the road, a church tower every few kilometres, and long views across the hills when you gain a ridge. Spring brings plum blossom, early autumn brings woodsmoke and the smell of fermenting fruit, because this is plum-brandy country and nearly every yard has a tree or two.

The history is deeper than the town suggests. Zalău was Zilah to the Hungarians, who still make up a large share of the county, and to the north the Meseș Gate was the Roman frontier of Dacia. The fort and town of Porolissum, at Moigrad, guarded that pass, and its excavated walls and amphitheatre are worth a detour if you have a morning. The Roman soldiers who watched this ridge had the same view of the weather rolling in that you will.

Fuel and food are no problem, since Zalău is a proper city with several stations and plenty of places for a bowl of ciorbă or a grilled something with polenta. Fill the tank here before heading into the smaller villages around Hurez and the hills to the north, where a station may be a long way off. Neighbouring Aghireș and Treznea are small, so plan on the city for anything beyond a coffee. Go in the morning, when the valley fog is lifting and the traffic is still asleep.
t.preluci piatra prelucilor 1@47.3,23.4:
Preluci is the sort of place that does not appear in guidebooks and does not seem to mind. The name on the stop points to a stone, a crag or outcrop above the village, and the ride starts and ends here, which gives you a good excuse to look at it properly before you go. The country around is the Sălaj hill belt where it nudges toward the Someș valley, a mix of oak and beech forest, pasture, and villages strung along small streams.

Your neighbours at this end are modest: Băbeni a couple of kilometres off, Lozna and Letca not much farther. None of them is large, so do not count on a station or a restaurant in the immediate area. The nearest real town is Jibou, about fourteen kilometres away, and it is the sensible place to top up the tank and eat before you commit to the back roads. Jibou also has the Wesselényi castle with its botanical garden, one of the older ones in Romania, a pleasant hour if the weather turns.

The roads between these villages are the kind that reward a relaxed hand. Surfaces are mixed, with good stretches and a few that were patched by optimists, and in wet weather clay from the fields ends up on the asphalt. Slow down in the villages, where dogs, hens and the odd horse-drawn wagon treat the carriageway as a shared yard. In return you get long, quiet ridge sections where the only sound is your engine and the wind in the hay.

Good light comes early and late. At seven in the morning the hills have a blue haze, and the stone, whatever shape it takes, throws a proper shadow. Summer afternoons can be hot and thundery, and in these hills a storm builds fast, so keep an eye on the western sky. Autumn is the best season: the beeches turn copper, the roads are empty, and the villagers burn leaves in the evening. Come back through the same village on the way home and you will notice how different it looks with the light behind you.
t.buciumi padurea dosu@47.1,23.0:
Dosu forest lies above Buciumi, in the hills where Sălaj starts rising toward the Meseș range. It is a working woodland, not a showpiece: beech and oak, a few hornbeam, tracks cut by loggers, and a floor that smells strongly of leaf mould after rain. If you stop and kill the engine, the quiet is very complete. Wild boar and roe deer use these slopes, and the ground along the verges is often turned up by the former.

Buciumi itself is a village of under three thousand people, and the neighbours, Stârciu and Cizer, are smaller still. The nearest town of any size is Crasna, about thirteen kilometres away, which has the fuel and the shops. Treat the forest as somewhere you arrive with a full tank and a snack, because between the villages you will find little more than a standpipe, a bus shelter and occasionally a roadside crucifix hung with faded cloth.

The riding is the main reason to be here. The road climbs and drops in short pitches through the forest, with tight, shaded bends where moss and damp can linger well into the morning. Take them gently in the first hour. Once the sun gets through the canopy, the surface dries and the corners become fun, rhythmic and not at all frightening. Between the trees you catch glimpses of open pasture with haystacks built on tall poles, an old way of drying hay that you still see all across this part of Transylvania.

This is Hungarian and Romanian country mixed together, and you might hear both languages in the same village shop. Plum brandy is offered with disarming generosity, and you should decline politely if you are riding. Autumn is the season to come, when the forest turns gold and rust and the first mist sits in the valleys at dawn, though a clear spring morning, with new beech leaves the colour of lime, is almost as good. In winter these tracks ice over, so leave them alone.
t.iaz tibiscum satu batran@45.5,22.2:
Where the Bistra and Timiș rivers meet, the Romans built one of the more important towns in their province of Dacia. Tibiscum, near the village of Jupa, grew from a fort into a sizeable settlement, and the low foundations, streets and bath remains can still be walked today with a small museum alongside. Iaz and Satu Bătrân are the neighbouring places on the map, and the whole district sits in the Caransebeș basin, hemmed in by the Țarcu and Semenic mountains.

Caransebeș is about six kilometres away and has fuel, restaurants and supermarkets, so there is no worry about supplies. It is also a pleasant old Banat town with a Habsburg-era feel; locals will tell you proudly about the Battle of Karansebes, an infamous night in 1788 when Austrian troops reportedly fired on each other in the dark. Historians argue about how much of it is legend, which only adds to the fun at the café table.

For a rider this is the crossroads of some of Romania's best southwestern roads. To the south the Cerna valley opens toward Băile Herculane, with its Habsburg spa buildings and the wild limestone of the Domogled massif, and the long run down toward the Danube and Drobeta-Turnu Severin follows the old Roman lines. The road along the Timiș is smooth and fast enough to relax into, with wide bends through meadows and plum orchards. As you approach the mountain edges the corners tighten, and you start to feel the gradient in your wrists.

Come in late spring or September. In July the basin traps heat and the afternoons can feel heavy, while winters bring fog and ice in the valleys. Spend some time at the Roman site before leaving: it is a rare chance to stand where a frontier town of the empire once bustled, and the setting among the meadows is gentler than most ruins. The Roman road network here connected to the Iron Gates of Transylvania pass, and in a way you are riding the same corridor of movement that the legions used.
t.ciceu poieni fata carpenului 3@47.3,24.1:
Ciceu-Poieni is a scattered village in the hills of Bistrița-Năsăud county, with the ruins of Ciceu fortress somewhere in the story. The stronghold stood on a hilltop here, and in the fifteenth century Hungary's King Matthias Corvinus granted it, along with Cetatea de Baltă, to the Moldavian prince Stephen the Great, which tied this remote corner of Transylvania to Moldavia's fortunes for decades. Today little remains but crumbling walls and a good view, but the history gives the hills a certain weight.

Fața Carpenului, as the name suggests, is a slope with hornbeam, the carpen of Romanian. The point on the map sits among such hills near Negrilești, Breaza and Spermezeu, all small villages with under three thousand people each. The nearest town of any size is Căianu Mic, about ten kilometres away, and that is where you should plan to buy fuel and a proper meal. If you ride from the north or east, fill up before you leave the larger roads.

The ride between these settlements is secluded and lovely. Roads wind along ridges and drop into stream valleys, often between hay meadows with wooden haystacks and small clusters of houses in the folds of the land. Surfaces vary, from smooth recent asphalt to patched sections with gravel at the edges. Take your time in the villages, where children, dogs and old women with buckets cross the road without warning, and expect a friendly wave from almost everyone who passes you.

In summer the meadows are thick with flowers, and the hills smell of cut hay. Evenings are cool even in July, and thunderstorms can roll in from the Rodna mountains to the north. In autumn there is smoke from stubble and kitchen stoves, and the beech woods go amber. A visit to this area makes a good half day in itself, but it pairs well with the neighbouring routes toward Tihău and Lozna, because the landscape is so consistent: quiet, rolling, and mostly untouched by anything fast.
t.caves of aggtelek karst and slovak karst:
Under the hills on the border of Hungary and Slovakia lies one of the largest cave systems in Europe. The Baradla cave, entered from Aggtelek on the Hungarian side and from Domica on the Slovak side, runs for some twenty-five kilometres through limestone, a gallery of stalactites, stalagmites and underground rivers, and parts of it are open to visitors. It is the heart of the Aggtelek and Slovak Karst, a cross-border UNESCO site of more than seven hundred caves, listed in 1995 and extended in 2000. Concerts are held in the largest chamber, where the acoustics are excellent, and the temperature underground stays at a constant cool level, a relief in summer.

The label points to the hills around Rudabánya, to the south-west of the main caves, where the same limestone country meets older volcanic and iron ore ground. Rudabánya is a former mining town, and its quarries and pits have yielded something unexpected: the fossils of a Miocene ape, Rudapithecus, which lived here ten million years ago, when the land was a subtropical forest, and which is considered one of the possible ancestors of the great apes. A small museum in the town tells the story.

Above ground the landscape is a rolling, wooded karst of oak, hornbeam and beech, with small valleys, sinkholes and clearings of dry meadow. Wildlife includes deer, wild boar and the occasional lynx, and in spring the meadows are full of orchids and pasqueflowers. The smell is of leaf mould and wet stone, and the villages, with low whitewashed houses and church towers, feel far from the cities.

Riding here is quiet and pleasant. The roads wind through the hills with gentle curves, a few steep climbs and long views, and traffic is almost absent outside the main routes. The surface is mixed, and care is needed on rough patches. Putnok and Szendrő are the nearest towns with fuel and supermarkets, and the villages have small shops and inns. The local food is hearty, with stews, sausage and dumplings. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the cave is open all year.
t.ungvari wine cellar@48.4,21.7:
Sátoraljaújhely is a town split in two by a river and a border. The Ronyva stream divides it into a Hungarian half and a Slovak half, Slovenské Nové Mesto, and the line became a national frontier after the First World War, when streets and gardens were cut in two. Today the border is open and easy to cross, and a pleasant walk takes you from one country to the other along the bank. The town sits at the northern tip of the Tokaj wine region, where the Zemplén hills fall to the plain, and it is a good starting point for exploring that country.

The wine of Tokaj is among the oldest and most famous in Europe. Tokaji aszú, a sweet wine made from grapes shrivelled by noble rot, was called the wine of kings and the king of wines, and it was prized at courts from Versailles to St Petersburg. The vines grow on volcanic hillsides, mostly Furmint and Hárslevelű, and the cellars are dug into soft rock under the villages, forming a labyrinth of tunnels covered in a black mould that is said to help the ageing. The whole region was listed by UNESCO in 2002 as a cultural landscape.

Ungvári is one of the cellars, a reminder that wine is as much an underground craft as a sunny one. The town also has a link with literature, since Ferenc Kazinczy, the man who led the revival of the Hungarian language in the late eighteenth century, lived at nearby Széphalom, where a museum remembers him.

The riding is easy and relaxed, with roads climbing from the town through vineyards and woods in long, gentle bends, with views over the valley and the plains of the Bodrog. Traffic is light, apart from tourist buses in summer, and the surface is mostly good. Sátoraljaújhely has fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and Sárospatak, a pretty town with a castle and a college, is a short ride along the valley. If you ride on, mind the glass: a tasting in a cellar is a very good reason to hand over the keys. Autumn, at the harvest, is the best time.
t.component neighbouring silica and jasov@:
The Silica plateau is a high, flat limestone table in the Slovak Karst, a few kilometres north of the Hungarian border, and it forms part of the same cross-border UNESCO site as the Aggtelek caves. The label points to the country around Silica and Jasov, a landscape of dry meadows and beech woods broken by sinkholes, gorges and caves, with small villages tucked in the folds. Jasov, in the valley below, has a large Premonstratensian monastery, founded in the thirteenth century, with a grand Baroque church and a cave beneath the hill that is open to visitors. Nearby is the Ochtiná Aragonite Cave, one of very few caves in the world with spiky, branching aragonite crystals.

The nature is excellent. Grazing has kept the plateau open, and in late spring the grassland is rich in orchids and other flowers. The woods hold lynx, wolves, wild boar and many birds, and the sinkholes, some of them deep, are cool, damp and full of ferns. In autumn the beech woods turn copper. The smell of damp earth and limestone fills the gorges.

Rožňava, the largest town of the area, was a mining centre for iron, silver and copper in the Middle Ages, settled by Saxon miners, and it has a cathedral, a market square and a large old town. The Krásna Hôrka castle, on a hill some distance away, is one of the best-preserved in Slovakia, and its tall tower can be seen for miles.

Riding here is a quiet pleasure. The roads wind through the hills with steady curves, climb to the plateau in a few steep bends and descend into valleys with old villages. Traffic is light, and the surface is mixed, with some rough patches. Rožňava has fuel and shops, and the smaller villages have only a pub or small store. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and winter snow can close the plateau roads.
t.uholka shyrikyi luh@48.3,23.7:
The Uholka and Shyrokyi Luh massif, in the Carpathian Biosphere Reserve of western Ukraine, is the largest tract of virgin beech forest in Europe. It lies in the upper valley of the Tisza, in Zakarpattia, among steep slopes between roughly four hundred and twelve hundred metres, and it forms a key part of the UNESCO listing for the primeval beech forests of the Carpathians and other regions of Europe, inscribed in 2007. Here the trees have never been logged, so the forest has the structure that old Europe once had: giant trunks, fallen and rotting wood, moss, fungi, and gaps where a tree has died and light floods in.

Walking in it is like entering a cathedral. The beech trunks are grey, smooth and tall, and in spring the forest floor is covered with wildflowers before the leaves close the canopy. In autumn the whole slope turns copper and gold. Brown bears, lynx, wolves and wildcats live here, though you are unlikely to see them, and the woods are rich in birds, including woodpeckers and owls. The forest, with its fallen giants, is a living laboratory for scientists who want to understand what unmanaged woodland looks like.

The nearest settlements are small mountain towns such as Drahovo, Kolochava and Berezovo, which have a long tradition of farming and forestry. Kolochava has an open-air museum of old village life, with wooden houses and tools, and it is a good place to understand how people lived in these valleys. The roads here are narrow, patched and often unpaved in the villages, with livestock and horse carts as everyday traffic, so a robust bike and a relaxed pace are advisable.

Anyone planning a ride here should check the current situation carefully, since the war in Ukraine has changed travel conditions throughout the country, and rules can shift quickly. Beyond security, the practical points are simple: petrol is sold in Khust and the other bigger towns, but not in the hills, and weather in the Carpathians changes rapidly, with cold nights even in summer. Late spring and autumn are the best seasons for the forest itself. Take simple provisions, because shops are small, and the food in village houses is hearty, with bryndza cheese, mushrooms and cornmeal mamalyga.
t.brebi dealul mare 3@47.2,23.2:
Most people who know the Roman Empire think of Hadrian's Wall or the Rhine, but there was also a Roman frontier in the hills of north-western Transylvania, and this is part of it. The province of Dacia Porolissensis was guarded by a line of forts and wooden watchtowers on ridge tops, and the great fort and customs station at Porolissum, at Moigrad, was its centre. UNESCO added the Dacia Porolissensis frontier to its listing of Roman frontiers in 2024. Brebi lies close to Porolissum, and the ridge called Dealul Mare gives a sense of why the Romans chose these hills: wide views over the valleys and the approaches from the north.

The ground here is rolling country of the Meseș mountains and their foothills, with grassy ridges, beech and oak woods, plum orchards and villages with long, sloping streets. A watchtower site looks like very little today, a low mound or the outline of a ditch under grass, so it asks for some imagination. Think of a small garrison, a signal fire or a horn, and a long, lonely watch over the border with the free Dacians and the tribes beyond.

Riding here is quiet and unhurried. The county roads are mostly asphalt, sometimes worn, with villages every few kilometres, horse carts, dogs, and a lot of sheep. Bends are gentle and views are wide, especially from the ridge roads, and the traffic is very light outside the towns. In summer the haystacks along the fields look like small houses, and in autumn the plum harvest fills the air with a sweet smell that anyone who has smelled fermenting plums will recognise; this is the home of tuică and pălincă, the fruit brandies that Transylvanians offer with great generosity.

Mirșid, Creaca and Dobrin are small villages with a few shops and bars, while Zalău, the county town a short distance to the north-east, has fuel, supermarkets, restaurants and a proper hotel. Do not count on fuel in the villages. The best months are May to October, and in winter the snow can close small roads for days. Stop at Porolissum if you can, where the walls of the fort, the amphitheatre and the customs post give shape to the whole frontier.
t.iaz tibiscum damb@45.5,22.2:
Tibiscum was a Roman town at the meeting point of two rivers in the Banat, in the west of today's Romania, and the Iaz Dâmb is one of its pieces: a low rise where archaeologists have traced buildings, defences and the signs of a busy settlement. The Romans founded a fort here after the conquest of Dacia in the early second century, and a civilian town grew around it, with workshops, houses, a bath and a temple. It stood on the route that linked the Danube with the heart of the new province, and it was important enough to be given the rank of a municipium.

Caransebeș, only a few kilometres away, is the modern successor, a market town of about twenty-seven thousand people below the southern mountains. It has its own place in the stories of the region. According to a famous tale of 1788, an Austrian army camped near here was thrown into chaos at night when soldiers began shouting and shooting at one another in panic, and it is often cited as one of the most embarrassing battles in military history, though historians argue about how much of it is true. The legend has certainly stuck to the town.

The landscape around is soft and green, with hills lying to the north and the great wall of the Țarcu and Retezat mountains rising to the south and east. The Timiș and Bistra rivers join here, and the meadows by the water flood in spring. The roads are good and the traffic moderate, with the European route through the valley carrying the heaviest flow. For a quieter day, choose the side roads toward Păltiniș and Obreja, where villages sit among orchards.

Fuel is easiest in Caransebeș, and there are simple restaurants serving grilled meat, polenta and the sour soup called ciorbă. The ride continues south-west to Drobeta-Turnu Severin and the Danube at the Iron Gates, where Trajan's engineer Apollodorus of Damascus built a famous bridge over the river, a good reminder of why the Romans valued these roads. Early autumn is a pleasant time, with warm days, cool evenings and apples in the orchards.
t.synevyr darvaika@48.5,23.8:
Lake Synevyr is the largest lake in the Ukrainian Carpathians, a deep, dark mountain lake at about a thousand metres, ringed by spruce forest and fed by springs. It sits in the Synevyr National Nature Park, in Zakarpattia, and the Darvaika forest to which the label refers is a part of the park's old beech woods, that UNESCO lists among the old beech woods of the Carpathians. The lake owes its name to a legend: a count named Shenborn had a daughter, Synya, who fell in love with a shepherd called Vyr, and when the count killed him, her tears made the lake, while the island in the middle is the shepherd's grave.

Around the lake you will find a small rehabilitation centre for brown bears, which rescues animals that were kept in cruel conditions and gives them space in the forest. The wider park has lynx, deer, wolves and a good number of wild bears, though your chance of seeing one is low, and you should treat the area with the respect the animals deserve. Silence, cool air and the scent of resin hang over the forest, particularly in the early morning when mist hangs over the water.

The mountain roads here are narrow and winding, with the occasional pothole and often a log truck coming the other way. Slopes are steep, the bends tight, and sudden rain or fog is part of life in the Carpathians. Locals drive fast and cut corners, so keep to your side. Autumn brings gold and red to the beech forests, and winter brings deep snow and closed roads, so most visitors come from May to October. The lake is a popular stop for Ukrainians, and its car park fills at weekends.

Kolochava, about nine kilometres away, is a mountain town with an open-air museum, and Synevyr village is a little farther. Fuel stations are few and far between, so fill the tank at Khust or Mizhhiria before heading into the hills. As elsewhere in Ukraine, check the current security and travel advice before planning a trip, as conditions can change. In the villages, home cooking is generous: dumplings, borscht, mushroom dishes and the sour cheese bryndza, served with strong coffee or herbal tea.
t.muncel comorita@47.3,23.8:
On the hills between the valley of the Someș and the Meseș mountains, in the north-west of Transylvania, the ground rises in gentle ridges, and this is the highest point in a small stretch of country near the villages of Vad, Gâlgău and Poiana Blenchii. The label is Muncel, meaning little hill, and Comorița, which carries the sense of a small treasure, and both names tell you about the country: low, open, rounded hills, used for generations as pasture and orchard land. A lot of local folklore has treasure buried in hills like this, and many an old shepherd has a tale of a hoard or a lost mine.

This part of Romania lies along the line of the old Roman frontier in the province of Dacia Porolissensis, with watchtowers on the ridge tops, and the hills have the sort of long views that suited a lookout. The Romans came in the early second century and left in the 270s, and what remains today is mostly in the ground. What you see above it is the working landscape of Transylvania: hay meadows, strip fields, plum trees, wooden fences and farms with a horse in the yard.

The riding is a pleasure of the unhurried kind. Small county roads wind through villages and across ridges, with long open views toward the blue shapes of the mountains. The asphalt can be patchy, and there are sometimes gravel tracks, farm vehicles and herds of cows to share the road with, so a relaxed pace is the way to go. In late spring the meadows are full of flowers, in July the hay is cut and the smell is wonderful, and in autumn the woods turn gold. Winters are snowy, and minor roads can become hard going.

Vad, Poiana Blenchii and Gâlgău are small places with a couple of shops and little else, so plan your fuel in advance and treat these villages as a place to stop for water and a chat. The larger towns in the area have fuel and food, and ask locally for the cheaper restaurants, where a plate of grilled meat, sour soup and polenta will fill you up for a modest sum. The sparse traffic, the blue hills and the sense of unchanging rural life are what makes this part of Romania such a good place to ride without a plan.
t.jupa tibiscum cetate@45.5,22.2:
Jupa is a village in the Banat, just beside the site of Tibiscum, the Roman town that grew where the Timiș and the Bistra meet at the foot of the Southern Carpathians. Today it has an archaeological museum and a field of excavations, with the remains of the fort, the baths and the civilian houses that once stood here. The Romans took over the Dacian lands in the early second century, and Tibiscum, sitting on a main road to the Danube, became a busy place of soldiers, merchants, craftsmen and priests. Some of the finds from the town show how mixed it was, with Greek, Roman and local gods all being worshipped.

The land is gentle, with meadows, willow-lined streams and low hills that lead toward the mountains of Țarcu, which stand to the south on clear days. It is a place for a slow walk among the stones rather than a long visit, and the field is open and unfenced in many parts. Roman bricks and fragments still turn up in the ploughed fields around, a sign that the town stretched much farther than the area now excavated. The grass is full of butterflies in summer, and storks nest on the village poles.

On a motorbike, Jupa is a calm stop on a longer day. The roads in the valley are good, with the main route to Caransebeș busy with trucks and cars, but side roads through Păltiniș and Obreja are quiet, with gentle bends and the odd tractor. A ride along the valley toward the mountains in spring, when the orchards are in blossom and the snow still shines on the high ridges, is one of the most pleasant in the region. Autumn is just as lovely, though cooler in the mornings.

The closest large town is Caransebeș, a few kilometres away, with fuel, restaurants and shops; Păltiniș and Obreja are smaller, so do not count on a station in either. The ride heads toward Sarmizegetusa, the first capital of Roman Dacia, founded by Trajan after the conquest and named Colonia Ulpia Traiana Augusta Dacica Sarmizegetusa. It stood in the Hațeg basin, far from the Dacian mountain fortress of the same name. If you are curious about the difference between the two, ask at the museum, where the staff love to talk about it.
t.perisor varful zgaului@47.3,24.2:
Perișor lies in the hills north of Năsăud, in the county of Bistrița-Năsăud, and Vârful Zgăului is the hilltop to which the label points. Zagra and Spermezeu are the nearest villages, while the great wall of the Rodna Mountains stands to the east, the highest part of the northern Eastern Carpathians, with peaks over two thousand metres and glacial lakes among the crags. The Rodna range is a national park and a biosphere reserve, home to chamois, marmots, brown bears and a rich alpine flora. On a clear day the sharp, pale line of the ridge can be seen from many of the hills around.

The hills here are rounded and wooded, with fields cut into the slopes, haystacks stacked on poles and villages strung out along the valleys. The region has a long tradition of border guarding: in the eighteenth century the Habsburgs set up a frontier regiment here, and the Năsăud district carried a special identity, with its own schools, a famous grammar school and a local culture that valued education. The hilltop itself is not a monument, only a viewpoint, and it is worth treating it as a place to look at the land and the mountains rather than a sight.

The riding in this part of Transylvania is among the most enjoyable in Romania. The roads climb and fall through forests and meadows, with bends that are neither tight nor boring, and the traffic is light outside the towns. The famous route over the Prislop Pass, at around 1,400 metres, crosses the mountains to Maramureș, and in summer it is one of the favourite routes for riders. Fog, sudden showers and cold mornings can come at any time, and in winter the snow closes the higher roads. Late May to early October is the best time.

Nimigea de Sus, the largest nearby place, has some shops and fuel, but for more choice try Năsăud or Bistrița, where there are fuel stations, restaurants and hotels. In the villages, stop for a bowl of sour soup, a plate of stuffed cabbage rolls and a glass of homemade juice. The people here are proud of their landscape and happy to talk to visitors, even with only a few shared words.
t.poieni cornu sonului@46.9,22.9:
Poieni, which means clearings or glades in Romanian, is a small village in the hills of Cluj county, on the edge of the Apuseni mountains, and the point called Cornu Sonului lies a few kilometres from it. The landscape is that of western Transylvania as it begins to climb: rolling green hills, patches of beech and oak forest, meadows and farms with steep tiled roofs. To the east and south the land rises toward the great limestone country of the Apuseni, with its caves, gorges and high pastures, while to the west the road drops toward Oradea and the Hungarian border.

Ciucea, a few kilometres away, was the home of the poet and politician Octavian Goga, one of the most important Romanian writers of the early twentieth century, who died there in 1938. His castle, now a museum, stands in the town and is a fine place to see how a cultured Transylvanian lived between the wars. Ciucea also sits on the main route between Cluj and Oradea, so it has always been a place where traffic pauses, and it has a railway station with services in both directions.

The landscape also holds traces of the Roman frontier of Dacia Porolissensis, whose watchtowers ran along the ridges of the northern hills, and the Cornu Sonului name seems to point to a high, exposed place with a view. Whatever the local story is, the hill gives the right feeling: air, wide skies and distance. It is also a place where old life persists, with horse carts on the road and wood smoke rising from chimneys.

The road through Ciucea is a busy one, with trucks and cars hurrying between two cities, so use the quieter lanes through Poieni and Negreni where you can. The bends are open, the asphalt is usually decent, and the countryside is calm. Spring blossom, summer meadows and autumn leaves are all lovely, and winter brings snow and ice to the higher lanes. Ciucea has fuel, a few cafes and shops; Negreni and Poieni are smaller, so check your fuel level at Ciucea before heading into the hills. For a proper meal, look for a roadside restaurant with grilled meat and homemade sour cherry juice, and ask about the local cheese.
t.comarnicel i@45.6,23.4:
The coordinates put you on the northern slopes above the Jiu valley, in the rounded, forested Șureanu mountains of south-west Transylvania, a few ridges from the heart of the old Dacian kingdom. Comărnicel is the name on the map, and the Dacian fortresses of the Orăștie mountains, listed by UNESCO in 1999, are the reason this country matters. Here, in the first century BC and the first century AD, the Dacian kings built stone citadels on mountain tops, with terraces, walls and sacred precincts, the grandest of them Sarmizegetusa Regia, not far to the north-west.

The Dacians were a formidable people who gave Rome a lot of trouble. Their last king, Decebalus, fought Trajan's legions in two wars, in 101 to 102 and again in 105 to 106, and after the second the kingdom was conquered and turned into a Roman province. Trajan's Column in Rome shows these campaigns in a spiral of carved scenes. Roman gold from the mines of Dacia helped to fund the empire for a generation, and the memory of the Dacians has become a central strand of Romanian national identity.

The landscape does the rest. The Șureanu range is a broad, grassy massif cut by forested valleys, with high pastures where shepherds still graze flocks in summer, and the scent of crushed thyme on the air. To the south, beyond Petrila and Petroșani, the Jiu valley is a coal-mining region, with industrial towns tucked among the hills, and farther south rise the high ranges of Retezat and Parâng. The famous Transalpina road, the highest in Romania at over two thousand metres, crosses the Parâng range not far to the east, but it is closed by snow for much of the year, usually opening in early summer, so check before you plan a day around it.

Roads in the area are a mixed lot, some excellent and some patched, with heavy trucks in the Jiu valley and very little traffic on the mountain lanes. Fog and sudden storms are common in the high country, and nights are cold even in July. Fuel is easy to find in Petroșani and Petrila, both towns of tens of thousands, but not in the villages on the slopes. The ride goes on toward Cigmău and the old Roman thermal baths of Germisara, where the Romans dedicated altars to the nymphs of the hot springs, a pleasing contrast to the grim stone of the mountain forts.
t.huta salhiger@47.0,22.9:
Huta is a Romanian word for a glassworks or ironworks, and the name usually points to an old forest industry: a place where charcoal burners and glassblowers once worked in clearings in the beech woods. The village of this name lies in the hills between Ciucea, in Cluj county, and the villages of Cizer and Stârciu in the neighbouring county of Sălaj, in the broken country where the Meseș and Plopiș mountains meet. I could not place the name Salhiger with any confidence, so I will not pretend to a specific story; what I can describe honestly is the land and its history.

The hills are green, wooded and steeply folded, with farms in the clearings, hay meadows scattered up the slopes and orchards of plum and apple near the houses. The area lay close to the Roman frontier, with watchtowers scattered along the high ground, and in later centuries it belonged to the Hungarian kingdom and then to the principality of Transylvania, with Hungarian and Romanian villages sitting side by side. You see both cultures in the church towers, the village names and the food.

For a rider, this is quiet, winding country. The lanes are narrow and the asphalt varies, with some good stretches and some broken edges where the tarmac meets the verge. Cows, horse carts and walkers use the road, so approach each bend with care. There are fine views from the ridges in clear weather, with layer after layer of hills fading into blue, and in early morning mist fills the valleys. In spring the meadows are full of wild flowers, in late summer the air smells of hay and ripe plums, and in autumn the beech woods turn a deep copper. Winters bring snow and ice to the minor roads.

Ciucea, on the main road between Cluj and Oradea, is the place for fuel and a proper meal, and Cizer and Stârciu have little more than a shop and a bar. The closest real town to the north is Zalău, in Sălaj county. Carry some cash for village shops, and be ready for a friendly interrogation about where you are from and how much the bike cost. A glass of homemade plum brandy, tuică, is the polite thing to refuse with a smile when you are riding, and to accept with a nod if you are staying the night.
t.tornea alatornion kirkko@65.8,24.2:
Two countries share this river valley, and two currencies, and, curiously, two clocks, since Finland is an hour ahead of Sweden. Tornio on the Finnish side and Haparanda on the Swedish are twin towns divided by the Torne river, and the line between them is a short bridge. The big grey church of Alatornio stands on the Finnish bank a few kilometres upstream, a stone building from the late eighteenth century, in a region where wooden churches are far more common. The Torne itself flows free of dams, one of the great wild rivers of Europe, and every spring its ice breaks up in a spectacular rush.

The country around here is flat and watery, with pine and birch forest, marshes and long straight roads. Riding is easy, with smooth asphalt, modest traffic and strictly enforced speed limits on both sides of the border. Elk and reindeer can wander onto the road, so be careful at dusk, and in midsummer the sun barely sets, so you can ride in a pale, golden light at midnight. Winter is brutal, with ice and darkness, and the riding season is short, roughly from May to September. Mosquitoes in early summer are fierce, so bring repellent.

Haparanda has nearly seven thousand people and Tornio over twenty-one thousand, so fuel, food and shops are plentiful, and the border is open, with no formal checks on most days. Haparanda is known, perhaps unexpectedly, for a large IKEA store that opened in the 2000s as a deliberate boost to the town, and the two towns share a town square straddling the border. A few kilometres up the river, the rapids at Kukkolaforsen are famous for whitefish, caught with long-handled nets in the old way and served grilled at the local restaurant.

Both languages are spoken here, along with Meänkieli, a Finnic tongue native to the Swedish side. People switch easily between Swedish, Finnish and English, and will often pay in euros or kronor without fuss. After a day on the road, order grilled whitefish with boiled potatoes and dill, a northern classic, and let the sunlight linger.
t.ancient and primeval beech forests of th:
Snina is a small town at the foot of the Bukovské Hills, in the far north-east corner of Slovakia, a place where the road seems to run out of country. Beyond lies the Ukrainian border and the forests of the Eastern Carpathians, and the ancient beech woods around Rožok are part of a transnational UNESCO site, listed in 2007 and since enlarged, that protects some of the last primeval beech forests in Europe. Here the trees grow in the old way, with fallen trunks left to rot, mosses carpeting the forest floor and giant beeches reaching skyward. The silence is deep and green.

The ride to this corner of the country is a long one, and that is part of its attraction. Roads cross wide valleys and rolling hills, with small villages and wooden churches of the Carpathian Rusyn tradition, built without nails and capped with onion domes. Several of these churches in Slovakia are listed by UNESCO as well, and some stand near the route. The surface can be uneven, with frost damage in places, and traffic is light. Mist forms in the valleys, and the temperature drops quickly in the evening, so layers are essential. Late spring and early autumn are lovely, with the beech leaves fresh or golden.

Snina has over twenty-two thousand people, ten kilometres away, and it is the place for fuel, food and a bed, with the cheerful practicality of a border town. Sobrance, farther south-west, is smaller, with about six thousand inhabitants. The villages in between have shops and an inn or two, but late hours are a rarity. The Poloniny National Park, which adjoins the beech forests, is home to brown bears, wolves and lynx, and the chances of seeing any of them from the road are slim but not zero, so keep a watch at dusk.

The reserve itself is for walkers, and entry to the strictest zones is limited, so check before you go. The paths are well signed, and the beech woods are a rare chance to walk in a forest that has never been managed. Take your time, listen for woodpeckers, and give the trees a minute of your attention. Some are over three hundred years old.
t.tolcsva wine museum cellars@48.3,21.5:
Under the village of Tolcsva, in the foothills of the Zemplén mountains, there are wine cellars cut into volcanic rock. The Tokaj region in the north-east corner of Hungary is one of the oldest wine landscapes in Europe, and UNESCO listed it in 2002 as the Tokaj Wine Region Historic Cultural Landscape. The soil is volcanic, the hills are covered in vines, and the villages are full of cellars that run deep into the soft tuff. The temperature underground stays cool and constant, which is exactly what sweet wine needs.

A wine museum in Tolcsva, with cellars that may be visited, brings the story down to ground level. Tokaji is the wine of kings, or so it was said, and Louis XIV of France is supposed to have called it the wine of kings and the king of wines. The sweetest versions, called aszú, are made from grapes shrivelled by a fungus known as noble rot, picked berry by berry and added to base wine in measured baskets, called puttonyos. The cellar walls are covered in a velvety black mould that feeds on the alcohol fumes, a sign of a healthy cellar.

The landscape is gentle, with hills the colour of straw and green, villages of low whitewashed houses and church spires, and the broad Bodrog river running through the plain. Sárospatak, eleven kilometres away, has a lovely Renaissance castle and a famous Reformed college, and the town of Tokaj, to the south, stands at the meeting of the Bodrog and Tisza rivers. The area has been a crossroads for centuries, and the mix of Hungarian, Slovak and Jewish culture is still visible in the architecture.

Riding here is relaxed. Roads between the villages are quiet, with gentle bends and open views of vineyards, and the surfaces are generally decent, though patched. Autumn is the best time, with the harvest in full swing and the vines turning gold and red, and summer is warm and pleasant. Winter can be foggy and cold.

Fuel is available in Sárospatak, which has fourteen thousand people, and Tolcsva has a few shops. If you plan to taste wine, remember that Hungary has a zero alcohol limit for drivers.
t.village of biertan@46.1,24.8:
Biertan is a small village in the hills of southern Transylvania, and its church looks like a castle that happens to have a nave. In the sixteenth century the Saxon community, German-speaking settlers who had been invited into the region by the Hungarian kings in the twelfth century to farm and defend the frontier, enclosed the church on its hilltop with three rings of walls, towers, covered stairways and storerooms, so that the villagers could withstand a Turkish raid. Inside the walls each family kept a room for its food and valuables, and the bacon hung in the towers. The ensemble, listed by UNESCO in 1993, is one of the best examples of the fortified churches that dot the Saxon lands, and it has the feel of a place built by people with much to protect.

The church itself is late Gothic, with a vaulted hall and a wing altar from the late fifteenth century, with painted panels in the German style. From 1572 until 1867, Biertan was the seat of the Lutheran bishops of the Saxons, which explains the grandeur of a church in so small a place. A story the guides tell concerns a small room in the walls where quarrelling couples were locked up together for two weeks with one bed, one plate and one spoon, and it is said that in three hundred years only one couple went through with divorce. I cannot vouch for the figures, but it is a good story and the room is there.

Most of the Saxons left for Germany after 1990, and the villages are now quiet, with colourful houses in a row and storks nesting on the chimneys. The country around Biertan is a landscape of gentle hills, vineyards and orchards, known for its white wines of the Târnave region, and the lanes between the villages are some of the sweetest riding in Romania. Roads are narrow, and the surface can be rough, with potholes, horse carts and herds of sheep to watch for. Spring brings green hills and blossom, and September is the harvest.

Fuel is not in the village itself. Șaeș and Apold are small, so the dependable places are Sighișoara, the walled medieval town to the north-east, and Mediaș, to the west, both a short ride away. For a meal, look for ciorbă, a sour soup, and mămăligă with cheese.

Climb the covered stairway to the walls and look out over the red roofs. It is a view that has not changed much in five hundred years.
t.cormenis rapa malului 2@47.3,23.5:
Place names on a map can be more honest than any guide. Râpa Malului means the bluff or the scarp of the bank, and Cormeniș, the village the label names, lies as far as the coordinates say in the hills of Sălaj county in north-western Romania, in the region called Țara Silvaniei, the Silvanian Land, named from the Latin for forest. The label comes from an archaeological register, and I cannot tell you what turned up at this particular spot, only that someone found enough here to write down its name. That is how much of the prehistory of Transylvania is known: through scatters of pottery and flint on a hillside above a stream, recorded by local museums, with little left to see on the surface.

What the surface does offer is a pleasant slice of rural Romania.
