The hills here are low and rolling, planted with plum orchards, maize, and hay meadows, with small villages strung along the valleys, each with a church and a cluster of whitewashed houses. The Someș river runs to the south-east, and the Meseș range rises to the west. Plums are the great local crop, and the autumn smell of fermenting fruit and the sight of cauldrons steaming outside farms, where the plum brandy called țuică is distilled, mark the season.

Riding here is gentle and slow. Roads are often narrow and lightly surfaced, with potholes after winter, and the biggest hazards are horse-drawn carts, geese, and the occasional stray dog. On the main roads, lorries and local drivers overtake with enthusiasm, so stay alert on blind bends. Late spring, when the orchards are in blossom and the grass is long, is lovely, and early autumn brings golden light and the harvest. Winter can be snowy, with the minor roads icy for weeks.

Lozna and Letca are small villages, and I would not count on finding a pump in either, so plan on filling the tank at Jibou, a small town a short distance south, or at Zalău, the county seat, to the west. Cafes in the villages are simple, but a roadside stall may sell honey, plum jam or cheese.

Ask in the village if you want to see the hillside. People are often happy to point, and a little Romanian goes a long way.
t.ciceu corabia ponita@47.3,23.9:
Ciceu is a name that carries more history than its size suggests. The ruins of Ciceu Castle stand on a high hill in the north of Transylvania, in the border country of Bistrița-Năsăud and Cluj counties, in the hill country between Dej and Bistrița. In the fifteenth century the fortress and its estate were granted by the Hungarian crown to Stephen the Great, the ruler of Moldavia, along with the castle of Cetatea de Baltă, a rare case of a prince from beyond the Carpathians holding lands inside Transylvania. Little remains of the castle today, though the walls on the hilltop still give an idea of its position.

The ride titles point to Corabia-Ponița and Bologa-Grădiște, which are archaeological sites in the hills nearby. Corabia means ship in Romanian, but I do not know what the name refers to on the ground, and I cannot say what was found there. Bologa is a village with a ruined fortress, on the road between Cluj and Oradea, in a different valley. The word grădiște, which turns up on the map all over Romania, usually marks an old hillfort, and the landscape is full of them, from the Iron Age Dacians to the medieval period.

The countryside is the best of the matter. It is a country of beech and oak woods, steep pastures, hay barns and small farmsteads. Roads are narrow and winding, with sharp bends and some rough patches, and a rider can go for an hour without meeting another vehicle, apart from a horse cart or a flock of sheep. The weather is changeable, and summer thunderstorms are fierce, with the temperature dropping after rain. Late spring and early autumn are the best times, with September particularly beautiful when the beech woods begin to turn.

Chiuiești and Rugășești are small places, and I would not rely on fuel there. The reliable stops are Dej, a small industrial town on the Someș, and Cluj-Napoca, the great city of the region, which is some distance south. Carry water and a snack, and a phone with a map downloaded in advance, as the signal in the valleys is patchy.

Stand on the hill and look over the hills for a while. The old lords knew what they were doing when they picked it.
t.valea lesului piciorul andreichii 1@47.3:
A valley is the simplest of landscapes, and the one that goes by the name of Valea Leșului lies in the hills of Sălaj, in the north-west of Romania, a few kilometres from the village of Lozna. The second part of the ride title, Piciorul Andreichii, uses the word for foot in the sense of a spur of land running down a hillside, so the label describes a ridge beside a stream, and again it comes from an archaeological register. I can say what the place is, but not what was found, and I would rather leave it there.

Hay is the thing that defines this country in early summer. The meadows are not sprayed or ploughed, and in June they are full of wild flowers, with clover, sage, orchids and knapweed, a mix that has almost vanished from western Europe. Farmers cut the grass by scythe or small mower and stack it into haystacks on tall poles, which stand in the fields all winter, and the sight of them under frost is a classic of the Romanian countryside. Storks nest on telegraph poles in the villages, and the evenings are loud with frogs.

The riding follows the valleys. A rider here travels a narrow ribbon of tarmac along a stream, past wooden gates, fruit trees and a church with a tin roof, and every few kilometres there is a bend that opens a view of a ridge covered in oak and hornbeam. The surface often changes without warning, from smooth to broken, and some side roads end in gravel. Livestock, children and old bicycles share the road, and local drivers expect you to give way. The dry season is from May to September, with thunderstorms in July, and October brings fog in the valleys, which burns off by midday.

Lozna, with around a thousand people, and Letca, with two thousand, are the nearest settlements, and I would not count on finding fuel in either. Jibou, to the south, and Zalău, to the west, are towns with stations and shops. A village shop can sell bread, salami, sheep cheese and sweet biscuits.

If you stop for a moment on a ridge, you can smell the hay on the wind, which for a rider is as good as any monument.
t.poieni dosu marcului@46.9,22.9:
Poieni is a village in the foothills of the Apuseni Mountains, a few kilometres from Ciucea, in the west of Cluj county, and the hill the label calls Dosu Marcului is part of the rolling ground at the edge of the Vlădeasa massif. The massif is the high point of the area, a broad, forested range with a summit of 1,836 metres, and its slopes hold beech and spruce forest, mountain meadows, and a few remote chalets used by shepherds and hikers. In winter the peaks are white, and the snow lies from November to April.

The Apuseni are the western range of Transylvania, a mountain country apart from the main Carpathian chain, known for karst caves, gorges, and a distinct community of mountain farmers called the Moți. The land is cut by the Crișul Repede river, which flows west to Hungary through a deep valley, and the main road and railway between Cluj and Oradea squeeze through the gorge at Ciucea and Bratca. It is a historic crossing between Transylvania and the Hungarian plain, and traders, armies and pilgrims have used it for centuries.

I cannot tell you what lies on the hill that bears the name, as the ride titles use it as a label from an archaeological register, and I do not want to guess. What I can say is that the hillsides in this region have a long record of settlement, from Iron Age communities to the medieval period.

Riding here is excellent, though it requires attention. The E60, the main road between Cluj and Oradea, is busy, with heavy trucks, and overtaking is a game of nerve on the bends. For a calmer experience, turn off onto the side roads that climb into the villages, where the tarmac narrows and the traffic disappears. Spring brings fresh green, summer is warm with sudden thunderstorms, and autumn turns the beech forests to copper. Fog often hangs in the valleys on October mornings.

Ciucea, with a population of about four thousand, has fuel, shops and cafes, and Huedin, a larger town to the east, has more. Poieni itself is small, so fill up first. A bowl of sour soup and a plate of grilled meat in a roadside restaurant will keep you going. Keep an eye out for horse carts at dusk, and if the weather turns, find shelter early, because the mountain storms arrive fast.
Some summits have a name that is hardly more than a shrug, and Vârful Ciungii is one of them. Vârf means summit or peak, and ciung is the Romanian word for a stunted or crooked thing, a word used for gnarled trees and bent hills. It stands above the village of Mesesenii de Sus, on the ridge of the Meseș Mountains, a low, long range of wooded hills in north-western Transylvania that forms a barrier between the Transylvanian plateau and the plains of the Pannonian basin to the west. It is not a spectacular range, with its highest points just under a thousand metres, but it has an importance out of proportion to its height.

The reason is the gap. Through the Meseș ridge runs a pass, the Meseș Gate, which has served for two thousand years as the main route between Transylvania and the west, and the Romans guarded it with a fort and a town, Porolissum, just along the ridge. Medieval frontier guards later used the same gap. A hillfort or settlement on a summit like this one would have commanded the traffic along the pass.

The ride is quiet and rural. The country is made of rolling forested ridges, with beech and hornbeam, and small valleys with orchards and hay meadows. The roads are narrow and winding, and the surface ranges from fresh to broken, with livestock and carts common. In spring and autumn the road gets muddy after rain, and fog can drop into the valleys. A clear June day, with the orchards over and the hay cut, is a joy.

Aghireș, Mesesenii de Jos and Zalău are the nearest places. Zalău, a county town of about sixty thousand, is where you can find fuel, supermarkets and a good lunch. The villages have small shops and the occasional stand selling cheese and fruit. Carry water on the ridge, since there are few facilities.

At the top, wind and a view over a sea of hills. In summer, the crickets sing in the grass.
t.preluci piatra prelucilor 2@47.3,23.4:
Piatra Prelucilor is the rock of the Preluci people, or the rock of the place called Preluci, and the Romanian word piatra tells you to expect an outcrop, a crag, or a stony brow above the village. The hills of Sălaj here are made of soft sedimentary rock, sandstones and clays, laid down in an old sea and then pushed up, and where a harder band shows through, it forms a ledge that locals have named. Preluci lies in the hills near Băbeni, in the country that drains towards the Someș and the small town of Jibou, and the label comes from an archaeological register rather than a monument.

Jibou is worth a stop on the way. It has a castle built by the Wesselényi family, a Hungarian noble house who held huge estates in the region, and its grounds contain a large botanical garden, laid out in the twentieth century on the old park, with greenhouses, rare trees and quiet paths. In a part of Romania where large attractions are few, the garden is a pleasant place for an hour in the afternoon.

The riding is gentle and enjoyable. The roads between Jibou, Băbeni and the villages run along ridges with views of orchards and meadows, then drop into valleys, with some tight bends and short climbs. Traffic is light, but the surface changes a lot, and in wet weather clay on the tarmac can be slippery. Summer evenings are warm, with the smell of cut hay, and the best time for riding is from May to October. In winter the lanes can be icy.

Fuel is available in Jibou, which is the sensible bet, since Băbeni and Lozna are small places. The town has supermarkets and a few restaurants, and local honey and plum products are sold in the market.

The pleasure of this sort of landscape is that nothing is in a hurry. A stop beside a field, a flask of coffee and a few minutes of watching the clouds make a good break.
t.mirsid poguior@47.2,23.1:
Mirșid sits on the southern flank of the Meseș Mountains, in the county of Sălaj, a few kilometres from Zalău, and it is almost within sight of one of the best Roman sites in Romania. Porolissum, on the ridge above the village of Moigrad, was the capital of the Roman province of Dacia Porolissensis and a great frontier post on the northern edge of the empire, with large military forts, an amphitheatre, a customs post and a town with temples and baths, built after Trajan's conquest of Dacia in the early second century AD. The site is now an archaeological park, with the outline of the fort on a spur and, below, an amphitheatre cut into the hillside, and from the walls you can look over the Meseș Gate, the pass the Romans were guarding.

Poguior, the name on the ride list, is a hill or a place name nearby, and I cannot say what it holds. The region is full of hilltop sites from before and after the Romans, and in this country, a spot with a name on an archaeological list is a sign of occupation by Iron Age or medieval people.

The landscape is a pleasure to ride. From Zalău, the road climbs on a gentle gradient to the villages along the ridge, with orchards, meadows and beech forest, and views over the county to the east. The roads are narrow, with a mixed surface, and the traffic is light. The best time to visit is late spring, when the flowers are out, or autumn, when the leaves are turning and the air is clear. In summer, afternoon thunderstorms are common.

Zalău is a county capital with sixty thousand inhabitants, so fuel is easy, as are shops and restaurants. Mirșid itself is a village of a couple of thousand, with small shops. For a meal, look for a plate of sarmale, cabbage rolls with sour cream, and a glass of local plum brandy for the evening.

Walk on the ridge at Porolissum in the late afternoon, when the stones glow in the low sun. From the walls the frontier makes sense.
t.poieni dealul bonciului@46.9,22.9:
Anyone riding west out of Cluj on the E60 meets the same sequence: a long climb to Huedin, a market town on a wide valley floor, then a long run down towards Ciucea and the gorge of the Crișul Repede, with the Apuseni Mountains closing in on the south. Dealul Bonciului, the Hill of Bonciu, belongs to the country just off that road, near the village of Poieni, and the ride title uses the label of an archaeological register, so I cannot tell you what sits on top. What I can describe is the way the road behaves.

The E60 is the main artery between Transylvania and the Hungarian border at Borș, and it carries a heavy load of trucks, buses and impatient cars. The surface is generally decent, but the road is narrow for its traffic, with long uphill sections where lorries crawl and drivers pass on short gaps. The sensible approach is to be patient, take the passes in your stride, and let the faster ones go. Better, take a side road. Within a few minutes of leaving the highway the traffic vanishes, the tarmac narrows, and you are among haystacks and wooden gates, with a small church on the ridge and the Vlădeasa range in the background.

The weather in the Apuseni is changeable. Fog fills the valleys in autumn, and snow can arrive as early as October on the higher roads, while in July the afternoon thunderstorms roll across the ridges with sharp gusts. Spring is often wet. The best months are probably June and September, when the meadows are lush and the air is clear.

Huedin is the place for fuel and a proper meal, with several stations, supermarkets and cafes, and Ciucea, a smaller town, has stations too. Poieni is a village of a thousand people, and the shop sells the basics. The local specialities are cheese, smoked sausage and a strong plum brandy, and many households sell honey from roadside tables.

Keep an eye on the weather over the mountains and, if clouds build, find a cafe and wait. The storms pass quickly, and the light afterwards is superb.
t.poieni cetatea@46.9,22.9:
Cetățea is a diminutive, a little citadel, and the word appears again and again on the map of Transylvania, wherever a hill carries the trace of an old enclosure. The one at Poieni, in the foothills of the Apuseni west of Cluj, is a label from an archaeological register, and I do not know what has been found there. I can say what kind of site the name suggests: a hilltop settlement ringed with ditches and banks, of the sort the Dacians built in great numbers in the centuries before the Roman conquest.

The Dacians were the people of what is now Romania, closely related to the Thracians, and by the first century BC they had formed a powerful kingdom under Burebista and later Decebalus. Their most famous strongholds, the fortresses of the Orăștie Mountains in the south, with their stone walls, terraces and sanctuaries, are a UNESCO site, but the whole of Transylvania is dotted with smaller hillforts that served as refuges, farms and workshops. Gold and iron were the wealth of the country, and the Romans, who conquered it after two hard wars early in the second century AD, carried off a vast treasure.

In the Apuseni, these hills are covered in a patchwork of meadow and forest, and a rider can enjoy the landscape without worrying about what is under the turf. The roads off the E60 are narrow, winding and generally quiet, and a few are gravel. A good option is to follow a stream up from Ciucea, past farms and sawmills, to a village where the road ends and the forest begins. Autumn is the best season, with a haze in the valleys and a smell of woodsmoke, and late spring brings a green so bright it seems almost artificial.

The towns of Ciucea and Huedin have fuel and supplies, and Ciucea has a small castle on a hill with a view over the valley. Poieni itself is a small village, and I would not count on a pump there.

If a local points to a hill and says cetate, take it as an invitation. There is often a path, a view, and a story nobody has written down.
t.zagra dealul ciorilor@47.3,24.3:
Zagra lies on the southern skirts of the Rodna Mountains, in the north-east of Transylvania, and the first thing you notice is the size of the range behind it. The Rodna massif is the highest part of the Eastern Carpathians, a long ridge of crystalline rock with many peaks above two thousand metres, the highest of them, Pietrosu Rodnei, reaching 2,303. A national park protects its glacial lakes, alpine meadows and a rich flora that includes edelweiss and several species that grow nowhere else. The villages at its foot are quiet, with wooden fences and haystacks.

The names on the ride list, Dealul Ciorilor and Coama Pietrar, are hills near the villages of Zagra and Dăbâceni, and they come from an archaeological register, so I do not know what has been found. Dealul Ciorilor means the Hill of the Crows, which is a good name for a place with a view over a wide valley, and the word coama, mane, is used for a long ridge. Both describe the kind of landscape in which people have long chosen to live: a defensible spur above a stream, with fields below and forest above.

The riding here is a mix of mountain and valley. The roads along the valleys under the Rodna ridge are quiet and scenic, with views of the peaks, and the side roads, lined with orchards and barns, are narrow and sometimes rough. The weather in the mountains can be sharp. Snow lies on the high ground into May, thunderstorms are strong in July, and the first frosts arrive in October. The best months for riding are June to September, with the road clear and the meadows in flower.

Zagra is a place of nearly four thousand people, with shops and a few cafes, and I would check the pump situation locally before relying on it. The larger towns of Năsăud and Bistrița, to the west, have more stations and shops. Local honey, cheese and plum jam are sold at village stands.

Look up at the ridge in the evening, when the sun lights the rocks and the valley is already in shadow. It is a good place to be.
t.costesti gradiste@45.7,23.2:
The kings of Dacia put their holy places and their fortresses on the tops of mountains, and the best of them lie in the Orăștie Mountains of Hunedoara county, where six fortresses were built in the first century BC and first century AD to defend the heart of the kingdom. Costești is the entry point. The fortress of Costești-Cetățuie, on a steep hill above the valley of the Orăștioara, and its neighbour Blidaru, stood on limestone ridges with thick walls of carefully dressed stone, murus dacicus, a technique that combined stone facing with timber lacing. The Dacians fought Rome in two wars, in AD 101-102 and 105-106, under their king Decebalus, and the Romans eventually took and destroyed the fortresses, stripping the hills of their defences. UNESCO listed the group in 1999.

Beyond them, high on a mountain terrace at around 1,200 metres, lies Sarmizegetusa Regia, the Dacian capital, with its circular sanctuary of stone columns and a large stone altar. Seen from the approach road, the forest, the open clearing and the stone discs of the sanctuary make an uncanny sight, almost like a cousin of Stonehenge. The Romans built a new town for veterans, Colonia Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, far to the south-west, and it later became the Roman capital of the province.

The ride is a good one. From Orăștie, a small town below the mountains, the road climbs south through the valley, passing the village of Costești and its fortress, and continues into the mountains to the capital. The surface is generally paved but can be narrow and patchy, with potholes, and the last part is steep and winding through beech and spruce forest. In wet weather or in winter it can be slippery, and fog in the mountains makes it hard to see. The best months are May to October. Expect cattle, sheep and woodcutters' trucks on the road.

Fuel is in Orăștie and the towns along the main road, but not in the mountains, so fill up before you go. The villages of Boșorod and Orăștioara de Sus have shops, and some local houses offer rooms and home cooking, including polenta with cheese and sour cream, and smoked meats. The ride list also mentions Germisara, the Roman spa at Geoagiu-Băi, where thermal springs still bubble out of the hillside.

Walk up to the fortress early, before the day trippers arrive, and listen to the wind in the stones.
t.hurez arsura 1 2@47.0,22.9:
Arsura is Romanian for a burn, a scorch, or a heat rash, and it turns up on rural maps wherever a hillside was cleared by fire. The sites called Arsura 1 and 2, near the village of Hurez in the hills of Sălaj, belong to the same family of archaeological labels as the other points in this area, and I cannot tell you what was found on them. The name, though, tells a small story of its own, since a clearing burned for pasture or for planting is exactly the sort of place where people leave pottery, charcoal and traces of a settlement.

The ride title pairs the place with the Church of the Holy Archangels, and Romania has many churches with that dedication, including a number of timber ones in Maramureș, which lies a day's ride to the north and has a group of wooden churches listed by UNESCO in 1999. They are tall, narrow buildings, with steep shingled roofs and slender towers that look like pencils pointing at the sky. Even in Sălaj, the villages kept a tradition of wooden churches, though many have been replaced by concrete ones over the last century. If you spot a dark, shingled steeple among the trees, it is worth a detour.

The landscape around Hurez and Cizer is of low, forested ridges and shallow valleys, with fields of maize and hay and orchards of plum and apple. The roads are narrow and winding, with a mixed surface, and tractors, carts and flocks of sheep are common. In early summer, the air smells of cut grass and elderflower. In October, the beech woods turn yellow and gold and the roads are covered with leaves. Winter is cold, with snow, and the minor roads are rarely ploughed early.

Hurez is small. Cizer, with a population of about two and a half thousand, and Stârciu are villages with shops, but I would fill the tank in Zalău or Jibou before heading out. Take a little cash for farm stalls, where you can buy cheese, bread and honey.

On a still evening, the sound of church bells carries a long way in this country, and the smoke from the chimneys hangs low over the valley.
t.poieni dambul varadestilor@46.9,22.9:
Octavian Goga is the reason many Romanians have heard of Ciucea. He was a poet, a nationalist politician and, briefly, prime minister in 1937 and 1938, and he died in his castle in the village in 1938. The building, a handsome mansion on a hill with a view over the valley of the Crișul Repede, is now a museum, and the poet's grave lies nearby. Poieni, a few kilometres away, is a quieter place on the hills nearby, and the ride title gives it the name Dâmbul Vărădeștilor, the hill of the people of Vărădești, from an archaeological register, and I do not know what was found there.

What I do know is that the region has a long history of crossing. For centuries, the valley of the Crișul Repede has been the highway between Transylvania and the Hungarian plain, used by Roman soldiers, Hungarian armies, Ottoman raiders and now the railway and the E60. Villages in the side valleys kept to themselves, and their traditions of costume, carving and song survived into the twentieth century. The nearby Apuseni Mountains, home to the Moți, are known for their wooden houses and for the distinct way people there herd sheep and gather in fairs on the mountain tops.

For a rider, the pleasure is in turning off the main road. The E60 is crowded with lorries, but a few kilometres to the side, the lanes are empty and green, with orchards, haystacks and wooden barns. The surface is a bit rough, and corners can be sharp. In summer, the heat is moderate, and thunderstorms in the afternoon bring fresh air. Spring, with blossoms and a high river, and autumn, with the red and gold of the beech, are the best times. Early morning mist often fills the valleys until nine or ten.

Ciucea has fuel, a few shops and cafes, and a train station on the Cluj to Oradea line, and Huedin, to the east, has a larger selection. Roadside tables sell honey, jam and plum brandy, and in the village restaurant you can find stuffed cabbage with polenta.

Stop at the castle if you have time. The view alone is worth the climb.
t.san miguel conca@21.4,-99.6:
The five Franciscan missions of the Sierra Gorda are a very odd thing to find in the Mexican mountains: grand baroque churches, painted in pinks and yellows and covered in stone carvings, set in villages that are otherwise made of low houses and cornfields. San Miguel Conca is one of them. Father Junipero Serra, who would later found the missions of California, led the work here in the 1750s with the help of the local Pame people, and the facade of the church shows the mix of cultures that built it, with saints and angels carved beside local plants, mermaids and faces that look more indigenous than European. All five missions were listed as a World Heritage site in 2003.

The Sierra Gorda is a rugged wall of green folds running north from Queretaro towards San Luis Potosi, a place of cloud forest, deep canyons and caves, where the tropical lowlands of the Gulf meet the dry plateau of the centre, and the diversity of plants and birds is high. In the early morning, mist hangs in the valleys, and by noon the sun is hot. The village of Conca has a quiet plaza, a few shops and a smell of woodsmoke, and the church bells ring across the valley.

Riding here is a pleasure, and also a test. The roads are narrow, twisting and often steep, with sharp hairpins on the climbs, surface patches that vary from smooth to broken, and sometimes stray animals or fallen rock after rain. The highway from Jalpan toward Xilitla is a classic of its kind, with a rhythm of tight bends and long views. Stay away from the roads at night, when livestock and unlit trucks are a hazard, and go slowly where the road is wet. The best seasons are autumn and winter, when the air is clear and the heat is mild, while summer brings rain and landslides.

Fuel is a point to plan for. The nearest big town according to the map is San Ciro de Acosta, about thirty kilometres away, and Jalpan, the small town that serves as the mission region's centre, has stations and basic lodging. In the villages, services are simple but friendly, with tamales, tortillas and strong coffee on offer, and local people are happy to point the way. It is wise to carry some cash, since cards are not always accepted, and to fill up whenever you pass a station.
t.stretch of the camino real between the b:
Aculco is a small town in the highlands of the State of Mexico, a place of cobbled streets, white walls with red trim and a church that stands over everything, and it has been a stop on the road north for as long as there has been a road. The Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the old silver highway that connected Mexico City with the mines of Zacatecas and the far north, passed through this area, and a stretch of it near Aculco, with old paving and stonework, survives as part of the World Heritage listing. The Franciscans founded a convent in Aculco in the sixteenth century, and the town retains its colonial look, with arcades around the plaza and a quiet that comes from being a few hours from the capital and a world away.

The countryside here is rolling, high farmland at about two and a half thousand metres, with pine and oak woods, fields of maize and oats, sheep and dairy cattle, and a number of small reservoirs. The local people are mainly Otomi, and the region is known for its cheese, its pulque, the fermented sap of the maguey plant, and its weaving. The air is cool, even in summer, and clouds roll in from the afternoon to bring rain between June and September.

The ride from here is a cross-country run toward Teotihuacan, the great pre-Hispanic city north-east of Mexico City, and it crosses a landscape of plateau and low ridges. The roads are mostly paved, but many are narrow, with potholes and topes, the speed bumps that appear without warning in every village, and the mountain bends can be damp and slippery in the rain season. Watch for farm animals, and avoid riding after dark. In dry season, from November to April, the air is clear, the days are sunny and the nights are cold, and the best light is early.

San Miguel Vindho, the village nearby, is small, and the closest town of any size is Aculco itself, where you will find a fuel station, basic hotels and restaurants. Local fare includes barbacoa, slow-cooked lamb, and quesadillas with squash blossom, while fresh bread and coffee are standard. As elsewhere in the central highlands, it makes sense to fill the tank before heading into the back roads, and to check the weather in the afternoon, when storms can build quickly.
t.baljatz vaara baelljasvarri@69.0,23.3:
The Finnmark plateau is one of the emptiest places in Europe, and a surveyor in 1850 would have thought the same. Baelljasvarri, a modest hill in the Sami heartland of northern Norway, is one of the points that Friedrich Struve's expedition used for the great meridian arc, which ran from this Arctic country down to the Black Sea, and it is part of the World Heritage listing. The surveyors worked here in the 1840s, hauling instruments up bare hills and building cairns to sight from one to the next, in a climate that allows only a short working season. Summer was when they came, and with the midnight sun they could work all night.

The land is the Finnmarksvidda, a rolling upland of tundra, dwarf birch, bogs and thousands of small lakes, at about three hundred metres above the sea, and the home of the Sami reindeer herders. The roads are long and nearly empty, so you can ride for an hour without meeting a car, and the largest hazard is a reindeer wandering across the tarmac. Herds move over the plateau with the seasons, and in autumn and winter they are everywhere, often at dusk, so slow down. The surface is generally good, and the bends are gentle, but frost heaves can crack the asphalt, and strong winds are common.

Kautokeino, the town nearby, is the centre of Sami culture, with a Sami theatre, a school for reindeer herding and in March the Easter festival, with reindeer races and music. The language of the area is North Sami, and the signs are written in two languages. Sami silverwork, knives, and the bright wool clothing called gakti are sold at small shops. Reindeer meat, dried or stewed, is the local food, with cloudberries picked on the bogs in August. The aurora shows from late September through March, and the sky is dark and clear.

Fuel is the most important practical point. Stations are far apart, and often small, so fill the tank in Kautokeino or Alta, and carry some extra if you can. The best months to ride are June to September, when the days are long, and mosquitoes, which can be fierce in July, are a nuisance, so bring repellent and a head net. In winter the temperature drops to minus thirty or below, and the roads are covered in ice, making it a place for specialists only.
t.lohdizhjokki luvdiidcohkka@69.7,23.6:
Alta calls itself the northern lights town, and it has some right to the claim. The little town on the Alta fjord, about a degree and a half south of the North Cape, has some of the clearest, most dependable aurora in Norway, and visitors travel from across the world in winter to stand in the cold and wait. In summer, the same sky never gets dark, and the midnight sun lights the fjord and the hills for weeks. The nearest large settlement to this stop on the plateau, Alta has about twelve thousand people, and it is thirty-six kilometres away.

Luvdiidcohkka, or Lohdizhjokki in the old spelling, is another of the stations of the Struve Geodetic Arc, the chain of survey points that crossed ten countries. This one stands on high ground in the hills inland from Alta, where birch scrub gives way to open tundra. From here the surveyors could see their next marker across the bare hills, and the clear air of the north helped them. A few of the points are marked by a drilled hole in the rock, others by a cairn, and the whole group was recognised by UNESCO for its scientific history.

Alta has a heritage older than any survey. The rock carvings at Hjemmeluft, a World Heritage site since 1985, contain thousands of figures of reindeer, boats, people and bears, chiselled into the rock between about six and a half thousand and two thousand years ago, and a museum explains them. West of the town the Sautso canyon, one of the biggest in Europe, cuts the plateau with the Alta river, a famous salmon stream that was the centre of a bitter dispute in the 1970s over a dam, a conflict that did much to awaken Sami political life.

The riding is open and wide. The E6, the main north road, runs through Alta, and inland the roads cross rolling tundra with long views, so a bike can cover a lot of ground. Watch for reindeer, and for the wind, which comes off the fjord and plateau without warning. In summer the weather is mostly mild, though a cold front can bring rain and a drop to a few degrees, and in autumn the birches and bogs turn to red and gold.

Alta has all the services you need, with fuel, supermarkets and cafes, and the last chance for a bed and a meal before the empty country. Local dishes include fresh salmon, reindeer, and cloudberry cream. Fill the tank before you leave town.
t.rohatyn tserkva of the descent of the ho:
Local tradition says that Roksolana, the girl who became the wife of the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, was born in Rohatyn. Whether or not that is true, the town in the Galician foothills of western Ukraine has been telling the story for centuries, and a statue and a museum keep it alive. Rohatyn sits on the small river Hnyla Lypa, east of the Carpathians, in a country of low hills, orchards and wheat fields, and its pride is a small wooden church dedicated to the Descent of the Holy Spirit, built in the late sixteenth century and still standing near the old market square.

The church is one of the wooden churches of the Carpathian region that were added to the World Heritage list in 2013, a group of Ukrainian and Polish buildings that show a tradition of timber construction going back many centuries. The Rohatyn church has a modest tripartite form, with three connected sections under tall shingled roofs and a bell tower beside it, and inside, painted icons and an ornate iconostasis fill the interior with colour. Some of the painted decoration is later than the structure, but the feeling of age is real, and the smell of old wood, wax and incense is hard to forget.

On a motorbike, western Ukraine rewards patience. The main roads between towns are busy with lorries and minibuses, and the surface may be broken and patched, so potholes are the chief hazard, and you learn to read the asphalt. The side roads are quieter, with villages of whitewashed houses and wells, storks nesting on poles, and haystacks in the fields, and they lead to places like Potelych, where another wooden church stands, the ride's next stop. Check the current security situation and official travel advice before you plan any journey in the country, since conditions have changed greatly and may vary by region.

Rohatyn has about eight thousand people, with a few shops, cafes and fuel stations, and bigger options at Burshtyn, seventeen kilometres to the south, and Ivano-Frankivsk beyond. The local food is hearty and generous: borscht, dumplings with potato or cheese called varenyky, pancakes with sour cream, and strong sweet tea or coffee. The best months are May to October, with green fields in early summer and golden light in September. Winters are cold and snowy, and the spring thaw turns the lanes to mud.
t.ensemble of st yuri the dragonfighter ch:
High on a hill above the old town of Lviv sits a cathedral that looks as if the baroque had a sense of humour. St George's, the main church of the Ukrainian Greek Catholic community, was built in the middle of the eighteenth century, in a style that mixes baroque and the lighter rococo, with a pale stone facade full of sculpted saints, columns, and a swirl of decoration across the pediment. The figures were carved by Johann Georg Pinsel, a sculptor whose twisting, ecstatic figures are among the most original in central Europe. The ensemble includes a bell tower, a chapter house and a palace for the metropolitan, all set around a courtyard with a long view down to the city.

Lviv is a place where empires have layered themselves. Founded in the thirteenth century by a Galician king and named for his son Lev, it belonged at various times to Poland, Austria, where it was called Lemberg, and the Soviet Union, and the historic centre is a mix of Gothic, Renaissance and baroque, with streets of tall merchant houses, Armenian, Latin and Orthodox churches, and a market square. The centre is a World Heritage site. Lviv is also known for its cafes, where coffee is a serious matter, and its chocolate and its honey cakes, and the courtyards hide small bars and bookshops.

Riding in Lviv is a lesson in surfaces. The old city is paved in cobbles, which are slick in rain, and the tram lines cross the road at awkward angles, so a wheel can catch a rail. Traffic is thick on the main avenues, and parking in the centre is a puzzle, so it makes sense to leave the bike at a hotel and explore on foot. The hill on which St George's stands is a short walk above the centre, and the street up to it is steep and narrow. Early morning is the best time, when the light falls across the facade and the courtyards are quiet.

The ride continues west toward the wooden church at Chotyniec, across the Polish border, along roads that cross rolling farmland. Lviv has fuel stations on all the main roads and plenty of cafes and restaurants, so there is no difficulty in preparing for the day. Before you travel, check the current official advice, since the security situation in Ukraine has changed greatly, and air-raid alerts and curfews can affect plans. The city has remained a refuge and a cultural centre throughout, and visitors who go carefully are welcomed.
t.brunary wyzne tserkva of saint michael t:
Three small wooden churches in the Beskid Niski could tell you more about the Lemko people than a library. Brunary Wyzne is a village in the Low Beskids of southern Poland, not far from the Slovak border, and its church of St Michael the Archangel, built at the end of the eighteenth century, stands at the edge of the settlement with a shingled tower and the typical three-part structure of the Lemko tradition. Inside, the painted iconostasis separates the nave from the sanctuary, as in all Eastern Christian churches, and the walls are dark with age. The church is part of the group of wooden churches of the Carpathian region on the World Heritage list, inscribed in 2013.

The Lemkos are a Carpathian people with their own dialect and customs, who lived in these mountains for centuries. After the Second World War, many were forced out of their villages, some to the Soviet Union and the rest, in Operation Vistula in 1947, to the north and west of Poland, and many villages vanished from the map. Some people have since returned, and the little churches that survive are the most visible link to the time before. The surrounding hills hold many such sites, and a ride through the area passes abandoned orchards, stone crosses and graveyards in the middle of fields.

Beyond the churches, the Low Beskids are a pleasure to ride. The hills are rounded and forested, rather than harsh, and the roads wind through valleys, climb over low passes and run along streams, with a gentle pace and few other vehicles. Gorlice, the larger town to the north, was the site of a major battle in 1915, and the area is dotted with First World War cemeteries designed by the Slovak architect Dusan Jurkovic, which have a haunting, carved-wood look. In the same district, the early oil industry of Europe took shape, with some of the earliest oil wells in the world nearby, and the museum at Bobrka tells the story.

Grybow, twelve kilometres away, is the nearest town with fuel, shops and a few cafes, and Gorlice has more. Smaller villages offer a simple meal at best, so plan accordingly. Autumn is lovely, with beech woods turning orange and red, and the roads dry, while spring brings blossom and mud. Winter snow is common, and it can linger on shaded bends. Local specialties include pierogi, sour rye soup and strong plum brandy.
t.drohobych tserkva of saint george t@49.3:
Bruno Schulz was born in Drohobych in 1892, spent most of his life here and was shot in its streets by a German officer in 1942. The writer and painter, whose strange, dreamlike stories turned this small Galician town into a place of myth, drew on the old market square, the narrow lanes and the attic rooms of a Jewish merchant family, and the town today is part of his legacy. Drohobych, with a population of nearly eighty thousand, grew rich on salt and oil, and the oil wells of nearby Boryslav gave the region the nickname of Galicia's Texas in the late nineteenth century. Ivan Franko, the great Ukrainian writer, went to school here.

In the middle of the old town, the wooden church of St George stands behind a low wall. A few centuries old, it is a tiered structure with a shingled roof that rises like a pagoda over the nave, a typical Galician form, and it is one of the wooden churches of the Carpathian region on the World Heritage list. The interior is painted with scenes and saints, and the wood has darkened with time, with a smell of wax and old timber. Beside it stands a bell tower, also wooden, and an old cemetery of crosses.

The ride from here goes west into the Carpathians, toward the Polish and Slovak borders, to Polonina Wetlinska and Smerek in the Bieszczady and the Bukovske Vrchy on the Slovak side. These are the wild, grass-covered ridges of the eastern Carpathians, famous for their bison, bears and lynx, and for a sense of emptiness that is rare in Europe. The mountain roads are narrow, often unpaved in places, and the borders have official crossings where queues can build up, so check the opening hours and rules. The landscape is gentle and open, with beech forest, and in autumn the forest glows orange.

Please check the current travel advice before planning any ride in Ukraine, because conditions can change quickly and vary by region. Drohobych has fuel stations, supermarkets and cafes, and Stebnyk, a town just to the east, has a known history of salt mining. The local cuisine includes borscht, varenyky, and honey cake, and Truskavets, a spa town nearby, is famous for its mineral water. In summer, the town is warm and leafy, and in winter snow lies thick on the roofs of the old church.
t.hurez dealul boului sumanda@47.0,22.9:
The ridge that runs across Salaj County, in north-western Romania, is the Meses range, and in the Roman age it was the edge of an empire. When the emperor Trajan conquered Dacia in two hard wars, finished in 106, the new province needed protection on its northern side, and the Romans built a line of forts, watchtowers and earthworks along the crest of the Meses hills, controlling the pass through the mountains, now called the Meses Gate. The best known of the settlements is Porolissum, a garrison town and customs post at the gate. In 2024, the frontier of Roman Dacia was added to the World Heritage list, and the many small sites along it, among them Hurez, are part of the story.

Dealul Boului, Ox Hill, and Sumanda are names for the grassy hills that carry the line. I cannot tell you exactly what remains at this point, but such sites are generally low banks and ditches under grass and scrub, the footprint of a tower or small fort, with the ground lifting gently to a view along the ridge. The point of such a spot was always the view: from here, soldiers could see the next tower along the ridge, and the valley below, and warn of any movement on the northern side.

The countryside is the real reward. Salaj is a green, rolling land of small hills, orchards and meadows, dotted with villages where the houses have tall wooden gates and the churches have tall, slender spires. The roads are modest, many of them narrow, with patches and potholes, and horse-drawn carts are a normal sight. Tractors, dogs and herds of sheep are part of the traffic, and mud is common after rain. Summer is warm and golden, autumn brings misty mornings and plum harvest, and winter is cold, with snow on the ridge. Take your time, and look for the small stone and wooden churches that stand on the hilltops.

Crasna, the nearest town, is some seventeen kilometres away and has fuel and basic shops, and Zalau, the county capital, offers a wider choice. Between these places, services are scarce, so keep the tank topped up. Locals are friendly, and a stop at a village shop for a coffee, a bottle of water or a slice of fresh bread often turns into a conversation. If you like a drink, the plum brandy known as tuica is the local pride, and it is best enjoyed in small glasses.
t.zalau dealul dojii 1@47.2,23.1:
Zalau is the sort of city that many riders cross without noticing, and that is a pity, because the capital of Salaj County is a lively, youthful place with a long past. Its population of over sixty thousand makes it the largest town in this part of north-western Romania, set in the valley of the Zalau river at the foot of the Meses hills, and it has a mixed Romanian and Hungarian heritage that shows in street names, churches and food. The Hungarians called it Zilah, and the poet Endre Ady, one of the great voices of Hungarian literature, went to school here in the 1880s.

The hill known as Dealul Dojii rises above the city, and the ridges around it belong to the Roman frontier that guarded the province of Dacia. Not far to the north, at Moigrad, are the ruins of Porolissum, a Roman town and military base with a reconstructed amphitheatre, forum and customs post, one of the best-preserved Roman sites in Romania. The frontier system, a chain of forts and towers along the ridge, is now a World Heritage property. In Zalau itself, the county museum holds finds from the area, including Roman inscriptions and tools.

For riding, the city is a gateway to one of the quieter parts of Transylvania. North and east, the roads climb into the Meses hills, with smooth bends through beech and oak woods, villages with long fences and the odd shepherd's hut. Traffic on the main roads is mixed, with lorries, minibuses and impatient overtakers, so it is better to take the back lanes, where cows, geese and horse carts set the pace. Be aware that dogs often run out at bikes, and potholes can appear after winter. A few surviving stretches of old cobbled road are slippery in rain.

Zalau has everything you need, with several fuel stations, supermarkets, repair shops and hotels, and its centre has a pedestrian street with cafes and bakeries. The local cuisine is Romanian with a Hungarian accent: stuffed cabbage, soup with sour cream, and sweet pastries, including kurtoskalacs, the chimney cake baked over coals. It makes sense to stock up here before going on to Muncel and the smaller villages, where services are fewer. Spring and early autumn are the best times, with comfortable temperatures and a landscape that is green or golden.
t.hurez dealul prislop 7@47.0,22.9:
To understand the little hills around Hurez, you have to go back to the winter of 101. The emperor Trajan marched into Dacia with legions, and the king, Decebalus, resisted fiercely from his mountain strongholds in the south, until the Romans broke through in 102 and again in 105 and 106. Trajan's column in Rome shows the soldiers building roads, bridges and forts. The new province brought gold and salt to the empire, and in the north, a line of watch posts and forts along the Meses hills defended its edge against the free Dacians and others beyond.

Dealul Prislop, one of the hills in the Hurez area, is one of the points that stood in that line. I cannot say what you will see on the ground, for most such towers have long since decayed into low earthen platforms among grass and trees, but the site belongs to the World Heritage property of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire in Dacia, added in 2024. The number 7 in the name looks like a survey label for one of a series of similar spots, which gives a sense of the density of the system, a tower every few kilometres, each in sight of the next.

The ride pairs the hill with a church dedicated to the Holy Archangels, one of the wooden churches typical of this region. Salaj has many of them, with tall slender spires and shingled walls, built by village carpenters in the eighteenth century and after, and some hold painted interiors. The roads between are small and often rough, and it is easy to find yourself on a farm track with a view across the hills and not a person in sight. Be ready for mud, loose gravel, free-ranging dogs and the occasional cow standing in the road. Spring and autumn mornings bring mist, and summer afternoons bring brief, violent thunderstorms.

Crasna, about fifteen kilometres away, is the nearest town with a fuel station and a shop, and Zalau, farther east, has the full range of services. In between, you may find a village shop that sells bread, cheese and cold drinks. Take water, because the hills are hot in July, and a rain layer is always sensible. The farmers here make hay in June and plum brandy in autumn, and if you come at the right time, the smell of cut grass or boiling plums will tell you where you are.
t.tihau pe gradiste@47.2,23.3:
Jibou is a small town on the Somes river, and it holds a surprise that has nothing to do with Romans. The Wesselenyi family, Hungarian nobles who owned much of this part of Transylvania, built a castle here in the eighteenth century, and its grounds became the town's botanical garden, which is still a garden today, with glasshouses, old trees and flower beds that bring visitors from far afield. It is a quiet, slightly faded estate, and it makes a pleasant hour. Tihau lies six kilometres away, on the same river plain, among low hills that rise toward the Meses range.

The name of this stop, Pe Gradiste, means on the stronghold or on the fort mound, and it is a type of name that turns up all over Romania for any hill with traces of ancient fortification. It is on a ride that links it with Budacu de Jos and the hill known as Dealul Cetatii, hill of the fortress, which suggests that the theme is hilltop forts, perhaps Dacian or Roman, perhaps medieval. I am not able to say what is visible at this exact spot. Treat it as a viewpoint over the valley of the Somes and a reminder that this ground has been fought over and fortified for two thousand years.

The Somes valley is good riding in a gentle way. The river meanders through meadows and willow, and the road follows it, sometimes straight and fast, sometimes looping through a village. The surface is mixed, with new tarmac in some places and rough patches in others, and lorries are frequent on the main road between Zalau and Cluj. On the back roads, you share the way with horse carts, flocks of geese and old men on bicycles. Summers are warm, autumn is wet and golden, and winter fog lies thick in the valley floor.

Jibou has about eleven thousand people, so you can fill the tank, buy supplies and find a meal. The town also has a good reputation for its pastries, and the local plum brandy is strong. The Hungarian presence in the region shows in the signs and in the food, with goulash and sweet cakes on the menu alongside Romanian dishes. If your timing is right, finish the day at the garden, where the evening light on the old trees is lovely, and the quiet of a country estate settles over everything.
t.spermezeu sunatoare@47.3,24.2:
Sunatoare is the Romanian name for St John's wort, the yellow-flowered herb that people have gathered for centuries to make tea and oil, and the hill that bears the name above the village of Spermezeu must have been covered in it once. Spermezeu lies in the north of the Transylvanian plateau, in the hills that separate the valley of the Somes from the counties of Salaj and Bistrita-Nasaud, a landscape of rounded ridges, small streams, hayfields and woodland. Midsummer is the time when the yellow flowers open, and in the old custom of the region, people picked them around the feast of St John, on the twenty-fourth of June.

I do not know what lies on this particular hill, and I would rather say so than invent it. The ride that includes it pairs it with Surduc and the heights above the Hraii valley, which suggests that the theme is high places along an old frontier or settlement line, the kind of place that gives a view over the valley. Whatever you find, it will be an open ridge with long views over hay meadows and woods, a good place to stop the bike and listen to skylarks and the wind in the grass.

The roads here are the sort that make you slow down. Narrow ribbons of asphalt climb from the villages to the ridgetops, with patches, potholes and gravel on the edges, and the hills keep the traffic light. In June, hay is cut by hand and with small machines, and the smell of drying grass fills the valleys, with farmers piling hay into stacks around wooden poles. Dogs guard the sheepfolds and they take their job seriously, so slow down near flocks. Rain can arrive suddenly, and the clay roads on farm tracks turn slippery in minutes.

Spermezeu is a small place, and for fuel and groceries the nearest town of any size is Caianu Mic, about seven kilometres away, with Beclean and Dej a little farther on. Take water and snacks, since village shops close early and may not have much. Autumn is a fine time for the ride, with woods turning gold and the first mist in the valleys, and the plum harvest bringing the village stills to life. People are generally hospitable to travellers who stop to ask the way, and a few words of Romanian help.
t.razboieni sat razboieni cetate sat@46.4,:
There are two Razboienis in Romania, and the one on the Mures river has nothing to do with the famous battle in Moldavia. This village lies in Alba County, in the broad valley of the Mures where the river runs between the Transylvanian plateau and the western ridge of the Apuseni Mountains, close to the town of Ocna Mures. Ocna means salt mine, and the name is no accident: the ground here sits on enormous salt deposits, and salt has been taken from it since Roman times, with a number of flooded old workings now serving as lakes where people swim in the briny water.

Cetate, in the name, means fortress or citadel, which marks a hill or a ruin of some age, and the label suggests there is a fort or old fortification near the village. I do not have details of what is preserved on the ground, and would rather point to the setting. The Mures valley was the main corridor of Roman Dacia, linking the old capital at Sarmizegetusa with the military and civil centres of Apulum, near present-day Alba Iulia, and Potaissa at Turda, and it remained the main route through Transylvania long after.

The road along the river is busy and fast, a main artery for lorries and cars, with a mix of straight sections, long curves and village speed limits enforced with cameras and police. The hills on either side are covered in vineyards and orchards, and Aiud, a short way north, is known for its wine. The better riding lies off the main road, on the lanes that climb into the hills, with views across the valley. The Turda Gorge, near Cluj, is a short ride away to the north, a deep limestone canyon that makes a fine detour.

Ocna Mures, two kilometres away, has about fifteen thousand people, fuel stations, shops and basic places to eat, with more in Alba Iulia, the old fortress town to the south, where a huge star-shaped Vauban-style citadel of the eighteenth century is worth seeing. The Mures is also a river for anglers and kayakers, and in summer the banks are busy at weekends. Spring and early autumn are good times for a ride, with comfortable temperatures and long evenings, and you will find that the riverside restaurants serve grilled fish and local wine.
t.hurez dealul prislop 2@47.0,22.9:
Before telegraphs, there were bonfires. A Roman frontier needed a way to send a message along a ridge faster than a rider could gallop, and the answer was a chain of watchtowers, each within sight of the next, where a guard could light a fire at night or raise smoke by day to warn of an attack. Trajan's Column shows such towers, with a torch at the top and a ladder. On the Meses hills, in what is now north-western Romania, the line was dense, and each hilltop had to be chosen with a careful eye for what could be seen from where.

Dealul Prislop, one of the grassy hills near Hurez, belongs to this system, and the number 2 in its name suggests that this is the second of several marked places on the same hill or ridge. I do not know what has been found here, and the ground is probably a low rise under grass and bushes, but the logic of the place is still visible: stand on the crest and you will see ridges to either side, the valley below and, on a clear day, the next high point along the line. It is a lesson in how an empire used geography. The sites are part of the World Heritage listing of the Dacian frontier of the Roman Empire.

The ride goes on to Mirsid and La Stramtura, in the Meses range, and the pass called the Meses Gate, where the road squeezes through a gap in the hills and where the Romans built their customs post. The country is pastoral, with meadows, scattered oaks and clumps of hazel, and the roads are narrow, with sudden turns, gravel at the edges and the occasional herd of cattle. Weather can change fast, with fog in the morning and thunderstorms in the afternoon in summer. A rain layer, gloves and patience are the best equipment.

Crasna, the nearest place with a fuel station and a shop, is seventeen kilometres away, and Zalau has larger stores and a repair shop or two. Along the way, the villages have small shops with bread and cold drinks, and the people are curious about visitors. Be careful at dusk, when deer and wild boar cross the roads, and dogs are always active. The hills are at their best in late May, when the meadows are full of flowers, and in early October, when the beech woods turn the slopes bronze.
t.huta@47.0,22.9:
Huedin is the gateway to the Apuseni Mountains, and most travellers go straight through it on the road from Cluj to Oradea without looking up. The town, of about nine thousand, sits on a plain between the Calata hills and the Vladeasa massif, which rises to nearly eighteen hundred metres to the south, and it has a mixed Romanian and Hungarian population, with the Hungarian name Banffyhunyad still seen on old maps. The countryside around, known as the Calata area, is famous for its folk costume and embroidery, and on feast days the women still wear elaborate dress.

Huta is a small hill hamlet some sixteen kilometres from Huedin, near the border between Cluj and Salaj counties, in the northern foothills of the Apuseni. It is the kind of place that appears on rides because of what lies near it, and in this case the ride joins it with Romanasi, where the Roman site of Largiana and a hilltop fort lie a short distance away. Romanasi is on the line of Roman watchtowers and forts on the Meses ridge, the frontier of Dacia, a World Heritage property since 2024. I cannot tell you what you will find at the hamlet itself, and I would not pretend, but the hills here are the very ones the Roman soldiers watched.

For riding, the Huedin area is a good one. The main road to Oradea climbs from the plain into the mountains, with long bends through forest and a high pass, and it carries heavy traffic, so be patient on weekends. The back roads that wander into the Calata hills are quieter, with tight bends, short climbs, hay meadows and views toward the snowy peaks in early spring. Fog is common in the valleys on autumn mornings, and winters bring deep snow, so the roads may be closed or icy.

Huedin has fuel stations, supermarkets, bakeries and a few small hotels. Try the local sweet bread and the strong cheese that shepherds make in the mountains. In the hills, services are limited, and the roads are often rough, so keep your speed under control. Spring, when the apple trees blossom and the streams run full, and early autumn, with golden beech woods, are the best times. In summer, afternoon storms build quickly over the mountains and sweep across the hills with hail.
t.iaz tibiscum traianu@45.5,22.2:
The Romans called it Tibiscum, and it stood where two rivers meet, at the entrance to a pass. Near the village of Iaz, close to the town of Caransebes in the Banat region of south-western Romania, are the remains of what was once one of the more important Roman towns of Dacia, with a military fort and a civil settlement that grew beside it. The site lies at the junction of the Timis and Bistra rivers, on the road that led through the narrow pass known as the Iron Gate of Transylvania, and its position explains its importance: whoever held it controlled the route from the Danube plain into the Transylvanian heartland. Soldiers and traders left behind bath buildings, workshops, inscriptions and the outline of a fort, and a small museum nearby displays what has been found.

Tibiscum is part of the World Heritage listing of the Dacian frontier of the Roman Empire, and the ride connects it with Sarmizegetusa, the colonial capital of the province, in the Hateg basin on the other side of the pass. To go from one to the other is to follow the old Roman route, through a landscape of forested hills and open meadows. The road crosses the Iron Gate pass between the Retezat massif to the south, with its glacial lakes and peaks above two and a half thousand metres, and the Tarcu mountains, and it is a good, smooth road with gentle gradients and long, flowing bends.

Caransebes, with about twenty-seven thousand people, is a lively market town with fuel, supermarkets and hotels, the place to stock up before the mountains. The area is multi-ethnic, with Romanians, Serbs, Hungarians and Germans mixed together over centuries, and the food reflects this, with grilled meats, stuffed peppers and sweet pastries on the menu. The nearby hills produce plums and apples, and the local brandy is strong. In the lowlands, summer can be very hot, while in the mountains, it is cooler and often foggy in the mornings.

Be careful on the main road, because lorries are numerous and the overtaking can be bold. Quiet side roads lead to villages and sheepfolds, where shepherds keep large guard dogs that deserve respect. The best months are May to October, and September has the clearest air and the warmest light. In winter, the pass can be snowy and icy, and the temperature drops well below freezing, so check conditions before you set out. A walk around the Roman remains takes less than an hour and is easy to combine with lunch.
t.muncel dambul lui golas@47.3,23.8:
Muncel is a village in the hills north-east of Dej, and the thing to know about Dej is salt. The town, with about thirty-eight thousand people, stands at the confluence of the Somesul Mare and the Somesul Mic, the two rivers that together form the Somes, and for centuries it was one of the centres of salt production in Transylvania, with a mine at Ocna Dej whose old galleries and ponds are now used for swimming and health cures. Salt was the white gold of the Middle Ages, and the Hungarian kings, and the Romans before them, took good care to control it.

Dambul lui Golas, the Hill of Golas, is a rounded hill above the village, and the ride that includes it also goes to Brancovenesti, a village on the Mures with a sixteenth-century castle, home to a Hungarian noble family. I cannot tell you what has been found on the hill, and the area belongs to the same ridge of low hills that make up this part of the Transylvanian plateau. What I can say is that from such a vantage you look across a land of sheep, orchards, beech woods and small valleys, with the blue outline of the Meses range in the distance.

The riding is easy and unhurried. Dej is on the main road between Cluj and Baia Mare, heavy with lorries, but turn off onto the side roads and the traffic disappears. The valleys are wide and the climbs are gentle, with sweeping views, though the surface may be broken, with sudden drops of tarmac on the bends. Fog fills the lowlands on autumn and winter mornings, and in spring, melting snow brings mud to the farm tracks. Summer is hot and dry, with thunderstorms in the late afternoon.

Dej has all the services you need, including several fuel stations, a market, and an old centre with a Gothic Reformed church, whose tall tower dominates the skyline. The restaurants serve grilled meat, polenta with cheese and sour cream, and cabbage dishes, with local wine from the hills. Sixteen kilometres separate the town from the village, and the villages in between have little in the way of shops, so fill up and buy your food beforehand. Villagers still make hay with scythes and rakes, and wooden gates and well sweeps mark the farmsteads.
t.valea lesului piciorul andreichii 2@47.3:
Winter closes this country more completely than visitors expect. In the hills of Salaj, north of the Somes, the valleys fill with fog in November, the clay roads freeze and thaw, and by January the snow can block lanes for days. Valea Lesului, the Valley of Lesu, is a village at the end of one such valley, with the hill known as Piciorul Andreichii, Andreica's foot or spur, rising above it. The ride that uses it connects to Popeni, a village known as Dumbrava, a word that means an oak grove, and the name tells you about the woods of oak that cover many ridges in this area.

The spur is probably one of the points on the frontier of Roman Dacia, since the number 2 in its name follows the pattern of the other sites along the Meses ridge, and it would have given a view over the valley of the Somes, the main river of the north-west. I do not know exactly what remains, so I will not claim more. What I can describe is the quality of this landscape in the changing seasons: spring comes late and green, with cherry and plum blossom in the villages in April, followed by hay in June, ripening plums in September, and a long, mellow autumn.

Riding here depends heavily on weather. After heavy rain, the clay roads turn to grease, and even gravel surfaces become treacherous, so be prepared to turn back. In dry weather, they are firm and pleasant, with rolling curves and open views, and the villages are strung along the valleys with wooden churches and well-kept gardens. Horse carts are still common, loaded with hay or firewood, and they move at a walking pace, so patience is needed. The Somes river lies to the south, and there are quiet roads along its banks.

Jibou, twenty kilometres away, is the nearest town of size, with fuel stations, a supermarket and a few places to eat, and a good place to turn back if the weather changes. Smaller villages have shops with basic supplies, and many have a local bar where men gather in the evening for a glass of plum brandy. Autumn is the most reliable season, with stable weather, dry tracks and a warm, low light on the oak woods, and the harvest of walnuts, apples and maize gives the countryside a busy, cheerful look.
t.hurez dealul boului la frapsin@47.0,22.9:
Plum trees are the quiet monarchs of Salaj. From the foot of the Meses hills down to the Somes valley, farmers keep orchards of plums, and every autumn they harvest the fruit, boil it in copper stills and make tuica, the strong clear brandy that is offered to guests, used for celebrations and funerals, and blamed for the occasional sore head. A village near Dealul Boului, the Ox Hill, is the kind of place where you might see a still smoking in a yard in October, with neighbours gathered around and a tray of cheese and bread on the table.

La Frapsin, the name of the spot, is the local name for a patch of hillside, and I have no information about what lies there, though it belongs to a series of sites along the frontier hills of Roman Dacia, which now have World Heritage recognition. For a rider, the more interesting aspect is the way of life that surrounds them. Hay is cut and dried in summer, and stacked around poles, houses have carved wooden gates, and old women in headscarves sell eggs or cheese at the roadside, while men with scythes work the steep fields where no machine can go.

Roads in this area are small and rough in places, with narrow strips of asphalt that vanish into gravel as they climb, and the speed is naturally low. Horse carts, cows being driven home at dusk, and dogs that lie in the road are all part of the experience, and you will find that waving to people and slowing down earns friendly nods. Keep an eye on the weather, for storms in summer can turn the road to a stream. The light in the late afternoon is the best for photography, with warm tones on the hay and the hills.

Crasna, the nearest town, is fifteen kilometres away and has a fuel station and a few shops, while Zalau, a larger town, offers the full range. If you plan to stay overnight, ask about guesthouses in the villages, where hosts often serve a dinner of soup, stuffed cabbage and polenta, with homemade cheese, pickles and a small glass of tuica. Take cash, since cards are not always accepted, and a few words of Romanian are appreciated. Spring and autumn are the best times for the ride, with fresh air and soft colours.
On the hill above Hurez, the best company is a buzzard. The oak and hornbeam woods of the Meses hills, with their patches of meadow and scrub, support plenty of birds of prey, and on a warm day you can watch them circle on thermals, calling thinly. Roe deer step out at dawn and dusk, wild boar leave rooted ground in the woods, and foxes cross the lanes, while in spring the meadows fill with orchids, cowslips and wild garlic. The hills are rich in life partly because the old farming methods, with hand-mown hay and grazing, have kept the meadows open and varied.

La Frapsin, at Dealul Boului, is one of a series of spots on the frontier ridge of Roman Dacia, the line of towers and forts that now make up a World Heritage property, and the word coast in the label suggests the slope on the side of the hill. I cannot say what the ground shows here, but the place offers a view over the valleys and the hills beyond, and it makes a good point for a pause, to listen to the sounds of the meadow: crickets in summer, skylarks in spring, and the wind in the oaks.

The way in is by country lanes that thread among the hills, and the riding is slow and pleasant rather than fast. The roads have patches and pot holes, and gravel in places, and a medium-sized bike with some ground clearance is the right tool. Mist often lies in the valleys in the early morning, and burns off by ten, leaving a clear, soft light, while in summer thunderstorms build in the afternoon and break over the ridge. Be careful of ticks in the long grass if you walk, and wear boots rather than trainers.

Crasna, fifteen kilometres to the east, is the nearest place with fuel and food, and Zalau is the next choice for anything bigger. Carry water and something to eat, as the villages are small and the shops are few. At the end of the day, a cold beer on a village bench, with the sun going down over the hay, is hard to beat. The best seasons are late spring, when the meadows bloom, and early autumn, when the woods turn copper and the air is clear.
t.knysna@-34.0,23.0:
Knysna lies around a tidal lagoon on the Garden Route, with a pair of sandstone cliffs known as the Heads guarding the narrow channel to the sea. Forest runs down to the water, and the whole town has a green, relaxed look, with a population around sixty-nine thousand and a waterfront full of small shops and restaurants. The lagoon is an estuary, home to rare seahorses and a rich oyster industry, and every year there is an oyster festival in the winter that fills the town.

The forest behind the town is the largest area of indigenous forest in South Africa, and it is full of yellowwood trees, ferns and birds. Knysna loeries, bright green birds with red wing flashes, live in the canopy, and a small, very elusive population of forest elephants survives deep in the trees, though you will not see them on a casual visit. Timber from the forest was once the main business here, and furniture-making is still a local craft. In June 2017, a terrible fire swept the area and destroyed many homes, and recovery has been steady.

For riders, Knysna is the end of a good day on the Garden Route. The N2 highway runs through, with the ocean on one side and mountains on the other, and the older roads inland, like the passes over the Outeniqua Mountains toward Oudtshoorn, offer more twists. Traffic in the holiday season, around December and January, can be heavy, and rain comes off the sea without much warning. Take care at night, as animals and pedestrians can appear on the road.

Fuel is plentiful. The town has several stations, along with supermarkets, repair shops and plenty of places to stay. Seafood is a good choice for dinner, and you can walk along the waterfront in the evening. The Heads, on the eastern side, have a viewpoint with a good look at the channel and the surf, and are worth the short detour at sunset.
t.montagu@-33.8,20.1:
Montagu sits where the Little Karoo begins, in a fold of the Langeberg mountains, and the way you reach it is part of the charm. From the west, the road runs through Cogmanskloof, a narrow gorge with a short tunnel, and then the valley opens into a landscape of orchards, vineyards and red rock. The little town, with about fifteen thousand people, lines up along Long Street with Cape Dutch and Victorian houses, many carefully restored, and it has been a favourite weekend stop for people from Cape Town for decades.

The gorge was opened to traffic in the 1870s, designed by the road engineer Andrew Geddes Bain, a name that appears all over the passes of the Cape. The town itself grew around a spring, and the hot springs just outside still draw visitors, though the pools are busy at weekends. The area is known for its dried fruit, apricots and peaches laid out to dry in the sun, and for sweet muscadel wine, made from a grape that thrives in the heat.

Route 62 is the long alternative to the N2 highway between Cape Town and the Garden Route, and Montagu is one of its best-known stops. The riding is relaxed. Roads through the valleys are mostly well surfaced, with long straight stretches and the occasional pass, and the scenery changes from green fruit farms to dry, rocky hills in the space of a few kilometres. Summer afternoons can be intensely hot, over thirty-five degrees, and winter nights are cold, so layering is useful. Early morning light on the cliffs is the best of the day.

Fuel is in town, along with cafes, a bakery and various places selling dried fruit and preserves. If you have time, the short walk into the Cogmanskloof gorge or a drive up to the mountain viewpoints is worthwhile. Book a bed in advance on weekends and public holidays, because the town fills up, and expect a slow pace at lunch.
t.barrydale@-33.9,20.7:
The R62 through Barrydale is a road of long distances and small surprises. The town is a modest place, sitting in the Little Karoo between the Langeberg and the Swartberg ranges, a few tidy streets, a main road, and a population of a few thousand. It was founded as a farming settlement, and its economy still depends on fruit, olives, sheep and now, increasingly, on travellers on Route 62 who stop for a meal and some air.

West of the town, the road runs back towards Swellendam, and east of it the Tradouw Pass cuts through the Langeberg, built in the 1870s by Thomas Bain, the son of the same Andrew Geddes Bain who engineered Montagu's gorge. The Tradouw is short and enjoyable, a smooth, curving climb through rock walls with proteas and fynbos on the slopes, and the road is a real pleasure on a bike. Farther east, you reach a famous roadside bar, Ronnie's Sex Shop, whose name began as a joke after a prank sign and became a landmark, covered inside in scrawls and bras. It is exactly as odd as it sounds, and a good stop for a cold drink.

Weather matters. The Little Karoo is dry, with hot summers and cold winter nights, and storms can flood the dry riverbeds quickly. Watch for livestock, baboons on the pass, and trucks in the narrow sections. The wide open landscape gives long views, but the light can be harsh at midday, and early morning and late afternoon are best.

There is fuel in town, and a handful of cafes, craft shops and guesthouses. It is a gentle place to pause, with the feeling of the old Karoo, where the main event of the afternoon is a long lunch on a shaded stoep. Leave time to wander and talk, because people here are usually keen to chat about the road and the weather.
t.koporosi cellars@48.3,21.6:
Tokaj wine country is a hilly corner of north-east Hungary where the Zemplén mountains drop toward the plains and the Bodrog river runs south to meet the Tisza. The volcanic soil, the long autumn mists and the noble rot, a fungus that shrivels the grapes and concentrates their sugars, are the ingredients of Tokaji Aszú, the sweet wine that Louis XIV of France is said to have called the wine of kings and the king of wines. The region was one of the first in the world to classify its vineyards, in the eighteenth century, and UNESCO now lists it as a cultural landscape.

This cellar sits near Sárospatak, a small historic town on the Bodrog with a Renaissance castle that belonged to the Rákóczi family, leaders of Hungary's uprisings against the Habsburgs, and a famous Reformed college where Comenius, the Czech educator, once taught.
