The town, with about fourteen thousand inhabitants, has petrol, supermarkets, a thermal bath and plenty of cafés, so everything practical is easy. Sátoraljaújhely, about ten kilometres away on the Slovak border, is a larger town with the same facilities.

What is special about the cellars of the area is that many are dug into soft volcanic tuff, a rock that is easy to carve, forming long cool tunnels that stay at a steady temperature all year. They are often coated with a dark, velvety mould that feeds on the alcohol fumes from the wine and which locals treat as a sign of good health. A rider should be aware that tastings are plentiful but that Hungary has a strict zero alcohol limit for drivers, so a spit bucket or a bottle for later is the only safe approach.

The roads between the villages are quiet, with gentle climbs between the vineyards, smooth enough for any machine and good for slow enjoyment, with views of terraced slopes and the Zemplén hills. Expect some patched tarmac, agricultural traffic at harvest time and the occasional herd of geese. The best months are late September and October, when the harvest is in and the hills turn yellow and red.

Food here is hearty: goulash, stuffed cabbage, fish soup from the river, and sweet cakes. A coffee at a village shop and a stroll between the vines will fill an hour pleasantly.
t.gomboshegyi cellars@48.3,21.6:
Between the Bodrog and the first folds of the Zemplén hills, Sárospatak is a town you ride into slowly, because the streets are cobbled, narrow and full of people who are in no hurry. The Gomboshegy cellars lie barely a kilometre from the centre, on the slope where the vineyards begin, and that closeness is what I like about them: the wine is not a trip out into some remote estate, it is a few minutes from the bakery. Furmint and Hárslevelű are the grapes you will hear named, the two workhorses of the Tokaj region, and they make everything from dry whites with a flinty edge to the legendary sweet Aszú.

The history of the town runs through the Rákóczi family, the Hungarian princes who made Sárospatak their seat. Their castle, a mixture of a medieval bastion and a Renaissance palace, stands by the river and has a famous Red Tower. Zrínyi Ilona, the wife of Ferenc Rákóczi I, lived here before she defended Munkács castle against the imperial army, and her son Ferenc II became the leader of the great uprising of the early eighteenth century. Alongside the castle, the Reformed College has trained generations of teachers and ministers and houses a library that has survived wars, fires and regimes, which says something about the stubbornness of the place.

Practically, Sárospatak is a town of fourteen thousand, so fuel, a supermarket, a bank machine and a thermal bath are all on the doorstep. Tolcsva, nine or ten kilometres south, is a small wine village with a couple of cafés but little else, so use Sárospatak as your base. Hungarian wine cellars often belong to families who keep irregular hours, and many of the small ones in the hills are open by arrangement only, so do not expect a door to be open just because it is lunchtime.

The riding is easy and unhurried. Roads run along the Bodrog's flat valley, and then rise gently through cherry orchards and vines to wooded ridges, with views of the Slovak border hills to the north. Traffic is light, tractors are common at harvest, and the tarmac is patched but sound. Autumn mist often sits in the river valley in the morning, then burns off to leave clean light on yellow leaves.

A bowl of fish soup, a plate of sausage and a slow afternoon seem the right way to treat the place, and if you decide to stay the night, the town has guesthouses at moderate prices.
t.wilderness@-34.0,22.6:
Wilderness is a quiet beach village on the Garden Route that has quietly kept out of the way of the bigger towns on either side. It sits where the Touw River and a string of freshwater lakes meet the Indian Ocean, about twelve kilometres east of George, at the foot of the forested Outeniqua mountains. The coastline here is a mixture of long sandy beach, tidal lagoon, lake and indigenous forest, and it forms part of the Garden Route National Park, so the development is limited and the birdlife is rich. Kingfishers, fish eagles and herons are common around the lakes, and the Knysna loerie, a bright green forest bird with a crimson flash in its wings, can be spotted in the trees.

In the early twentieth century a railway line, the Outeniqua Choo-Tjoe, ran along the coast and across the dramatic Kaaimans River bridge, and the old rail line is still a feature of the landscape. The Map of Africa viewpoint, on the hill above the village, takes its name from the shape of the Touw River as it winds through the lowlands, and gives a sweeping view over the lakes. Paragliders launch from the ridge in good conditions and drift over the beach, a spectacular sight.

The ride along the N2 here is not twisty, but it is superb in its way. Between George and Knysna the road runs along the coast, then climbs through forest and cuts across the deep, wooded gorges of the Kaaimans and Touw rivers. The surface is good, the curves long and easy, and the views are consistently lovely. Traffic can be heavy, with trucks and holiday cars, and speed enforcement is active. A more adventurous option is the Seven Passes road, the old route from George to Knysna, which winds through forest and across old stone bridges, with several gravel patches.

George, twelve kilometres west, has full services, including fuel and a good selection of shops, and Wilderness has a handful of fuel and food options too. The weather can be changeable, with sea mist in the morning and sudden showers, and a warm, humid wind off the Indian Ocean. Between July and November, southern right whales come into the bays to calve, and you can watch them from the cliffs.
t.vidraru dam@45.4,24.6:
The Vidraru Dam closes off the Argeș river in a deep, narrow gorge in the Făgăraș mountains, and it is one of the most imposing pieces of engineering in Romania. An arch dam about 166 metres high, completed in the mid-1960s, it holds back a long, dark lake, whose surface reflects the steep, forested slopes around it, and the view from the top of the wall is dizzying. A statue of Prometheus stands on the edge of the dam, with the lake behind him, and a bungee platform has made the dam a place of some notoriety.

Above the lake, the Transfăgărășan road climbs towards the high ridge of the mountains. Ordered by Nicolae Ceaușescu after the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, as a military route that would allow troops to cross the Carpathians quickly, it was built between 1970 and 1974, largely by army conscripts, with dynamite and enormous effort. Many men died in the construction. The road reaches about 2,040 metres at the Bâlea tunnel, near the glacial Lake Bâlea, and is closed by snow for much of the year, usually from late October to late June. Jeremy Clarkson called it the best road in the world, and the crowds followed.

Not far from the dam, near the village of Arefu, stands Poienari Castle, the real fortress of Vlad the Impaler, the fifteenth-century prince who inspired the legend of Dracula. It perches on a crag above the valley, reached by a climb of about 1,480 steps, and the view from the ruined tower is spectacular. The forests around the lake are home to bears, wolves and lynx, and bears are often seen near the road, so do not feed them and do not stop too close.

The riding is magnificent but demanding. The southern side climbs through forest with long, wide curves, then a series of tight hairpins and tunnels, and the surface is mostly good, though patched in places by rockfall and frost. In summer the road is crowded with cars, buses and bikes, and speeds are low. Go early, and take care on wet days, when fog and rain turn the road slick.

For fuel and food, Corbeni, seven kilometres away, has stations and shops, and Curtea de Argeș, to the south, has more. Around the lake, stalls sell grilled sausages, cheese, honey and jam, and small restaurants serve ciorbă soup and polenta with sour cream. Fill the tank before climbing.
t.george@-34.0,22.5:
George lies at the foot of the Outeniqua Mountains, a long blue ridge that shuts off the sea breezes to the south and gives the town a warm, sheltered feel. It is the largest town on the Garden Route, and it sits in a strip of green country between the mountains and the Indian Ocean, with forest, farmland and rivers close by. The Dutch founded the settlement in 1811 and named it for King George III, and the old oak tree planted in the early days still stands in the centre of town, protected as a national monument.

Timber built George, and the Outeniqua forests were a source of the yellowwood and stinkwood used in the furniture of the Cape. The mountain passes that cross the range, many of them engineered in the nineteenth century by Thomas Bain, opened up the interior, and several of them still carry the main roads. The Outeniqua Pass leads north to Oudtshoorn and the Karoo, while the Seven Passes Road heads east toward Knysna, winding through forested gorges and across several rivers on old stone bridges. This is the old coast road, quieter than the highway, and a lovely way to see the Garden Route.

As the start of the ride, George is a convenient base, with fuel at several stations and everything a rider might need, including supermarkets, bakeries and repair shops. The town has a lively centre and a good range of cafés. It is worth fuelling the bike and the rider here, as the Seven Passes Road has few services.

The weather on the Garden Route is mild but changeable, with rain possible in any month and mist in the mountains. Summer is warm and busy, and winter days are cool and often clear. The surface on the main roads is generally good, but expect wet leaves and the odd rockfall on the passes, plus slow trucks and tourists. Leave early, bring a rain jacket and enjoy the green hills.
t.avontuur@-33.7,23.2:
Prince Alfred's Pass runs north from the forests of Knysna over the Outeniqua range to the dry valley called the Langkloof, and Avontuur sits at its far end, a small farming outpost where the green of the coast gives way to orchards and rock. The name means adventure in Afrikaans, and the pass, opened in 1867 and designed by the road engineer Thomas Bain, is among the finest of his works, climbing in great bends through indigenous forest, across a high stretch of mountain fynbos, and down the northern slope.

The pass is largely gravel. It runs for around seventy kilometres, with a surface that is usually passable for a bike but can be loose, rutted or slick after rain. Corners are wide, the gradients are gentle, and the dense forest of yellowwood and stinkwood gives way to open views of mountains. Weather in the high part can turn cold and misty. It is a road for an adventure bike, or a careful touring rider with the right tyres, and anyone in doubt should ask locally about conditions.

The Langkloof is a long, narrow valley between two mountain ranges, famous for apples and other fruit. Orchards of apple and pear stretch along the valley floor, and in spring the blossom is spectacular. A narrow-gauge railway, known as the Apple Express, once carried fruit from here to Port Elizabeth, and the line was among the longest narrow-gauge lines in the world. The valley is dry, quiet and wide, with a feeling of space after the dense forest.

Practicalities matter here. Fuel is scarce along the pass and in the valley, so fill up in Knysna before you set out, and carry spare water and a puncture kit. Services in Avontuur are minimal, and cell reception is patchy. Allow plenty of daylight, since the pass takes longer than the distance suggests, and avoid it in heavy rain, when the surface can be dangerous.
t.balea lake tunnel@45.6,24.6:
The Bâlea Lake tunnel marks the roof of the Transfăgărășan, the highway that crosses the Făgăraș Mountains in Romania, and at 2,042 metres the air is thin and cold, even in summer. The road was ordered by Nicolae Ceaușescu after the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, as a military route in case of an invasion from the east, and was built between 1970 and 1974 largely by army conscripts using dynamite and hand tools. It was an extraordinary and costly effort, and many workers lost their lives. Today it is known as one of the best driving and riding roads in the world.

The tunnel, about 880 metres long, passes under the main ridge, and just beyond its northern portal sits Bâlea Lake, a glacial tarn in a high cirque surrounded by sharp, grey peaks. A cluster of cabins and a small hotel sit on the shore, and in summer visitors arrive in large numbers by car, motorcycle and cable car, which climbs from the northern side. In midwinter an ice hotel is built on the lake. Chamois and marmots live among the rocks, and bears roam the forests on the lower slopes, so keep food out of sight and do not feed them.

The riding is superb: tight hairpins, long ramps and fast sweepers along a narrow, well-surfaced road, with sheer drops and endless views. On the south side the road passes Vidraru Dam, a huge arch dam from 1966, and the ruins of Poenari Castle, associated with Vlad the Impaler, are a short distance away. Conditions are fickle. Fog, rain and wind can arrive at any moment, and ice is possible at the top even in July. The road is closed to traffic in winter, normally from late autumn until around late June or July, and the dates vary, so check them.

Fuel is not available near the summit, so fill up in Curtea de Argeș to the south or at Cârțișoara on the north side, near Victoria. Mountain restaurants sell soup, grilled sausage and polenta. Weekends are busy, so go on a weekday and leave early.
t.ustrzyki gorne@49.1,22.6:
Ustrzyki Górne is where Poland starts to run out, and that is the whole charm. The village sits in the Bieszczady, the far south-eastern corner of the country, in a landscape of open grassy ridges called połoniny, with the Ukrainian border only a short distance away. The road comes up from Lutowiska through beech forest and valley meadows, and the last villages feel more like the edge of a frontier than a tourist area. You arrive at a small settlement with a handful of guesthouses, trailheads for the hills, and the sensation of having left the busy Poland behind.

The reason the countryside looks so empty is history. Before the Second World War this was a mixed region of Boyko and Lemko villages with wooden churches, orchards and small farms. After the war, forced resettlement in the late 1940s and border changes emptied whole valleys, and forest grew over the old village sites. Walk even a short way off the road and you may find an old orchard, a cemetery gone to moss, or the stone foundations of a church. It gives the place a quiet, thoughtful atmosphere that sits well with the wide ridges.

Nature has taken the space back. The Bieszczady National Park around here is one of the wildest areas in Poland, home to brown bears, wolves, lynx and a herd of European bison, and in the evening it is not unusual to see deer along the roadside. Riders should keep speeds moderate at dusk, because animals appear without warning, and the narrow roads have blind bends and occasional gravel. The beech forests turn gold in October, which is perhaps the best time to come, though early summer with wildflowers on the ridges is a close second.

Services are thin. There are small shops and simple restaurants serving pierogi, żurek and trout, but fuel should be organised beforehand: Lesko and Ustrzyki Dolne to the north are the sensible places to fill the tank, and Lutowiska behind you has only a little. Weather turns quickly in the hills, so pack a rain layer, and be aware that the border zone means you should carry your documents.

Most people come to ride the Bieszczady loop and then walk up one of the big meadows for the view. Do both if you can, and leave time for a slow lunch.
t.bukowina@49.3,20.1:
Bukowina is what happens when a mountain village decides to become a ski and spa resort and only partly forgets its roots. It lies on the Podhale plateau, the high rolling country at the foot of the Tatras, and the view from the open ridges around it is the thing you ride for: the whole Tatra wall standing across the southern horizon like a stage set, with Slovakia just behind. On a clear morning the sharp summits look almost close enough to touch.

The road along the foothills here is a gentle one, with rolling hills, wooden farmhouses, hay meadows and little chapels at every second bend, and it makes an excellent counterweight to the high mountain roads further south. Traffic is heavy at weekends and in peak holiday season, when day-trippers from Kraków and Zakopane clog the main road, so early mornings and weekdays reward you with an emptier tarmac. The surface is generally good, with occasional frost damage on the side lanes. Autumn is lovely, with a clear light and the first snow dusting the high peaks while the meadows below are still green.

The people of Podhale, the górale or highlanders, have a distinct culture with their own dialect, music, carved wooden architecture and food. You will see houses in the traditional style with steep roofs and decorated gables, and stalls selling oscypek, the smoked sheep's cheese pressed in wooden moulds, usually served grilled with cranberry jam. It is salty, smoky and surprisingly addictive. Warm soups and kwaśnica, a sauerkraut stew, are the right order of the day if it is cold. Bukowina also has thermal pools, drawn from hot water deep below the plateau, which are a good reward after a rainy ride.

Fuel is not an issue in the wider area, but the village is small, so use Zakopane, about twelve kilometres away, for a proper selection, or the nearer larger villages along the main road. Parking is easy and the many guesthouses are used to motorcyclists with muddy boots. Come early, take a slow lunch, and let the plateau do its work.
t.ranca@45.3,23.7:
Rânca is a ski village at the foot of the Parâng mountains, built on an alpine meadow that was grazing country for shepherds long before anyone put in a chairlift. It sits at around sixteen hundred metres on the southern side of the Transalpina, the high road that crosses the Southern Carpathians, and from here the road to the pass above takes off in earnest. The village is a scatter of chalets, guesthouses and cafés in the middle of grassy slopes and spruce woods, and in summer the main sounds are cowbells and the odd chainsaw.

Transalpina is a road with a history. It follows an old shepherds' track that was improved as a military route in the twentieth century, and for decades it was known only to locals. Modern asphalt turned it into one of Romania's best-known mountain roads, running from the foothills near Novaci up through meadows and forests to open alpine ridges. The surface is generally smooth, though frost heaves and potholes show up in places, and the bends are long and rhythmic. Sheep and cows on the road are not unusual, and a shepherd's dog will sometimes bark at passing bikes.

Weather changes the whole experience. On a clear summer morning, the mountains glow and you can see ridgelines for miles, while on a wet afternoon the cloud sits down over the meadows and the air turns cold. Snow closes the higher sections for much of the year, and the road typically opens only in summer; check before you go. Bring warm layers even in July, since temperatures drop quickly with altitude.

Novaci, about thirteen kilometres down the valley, is the nearest proper town, and it has fuel, shops and restaurants, so fill the tank there before you climb. In Rânca itself there are pensions and restaurants serving grilled meat, polenta, soups and a dish called tochitură, a rich pork stew; there is also usually cheese from local shepherds, salty and smoky and good with bread. Prices are reasonable and the portions generous.

Spend a little time walking on the meadow above the village. The air is clear, flowers are thick in June, and you can look up at the high ridge you are about to ride and decide whether the weather will let you.
t.urdele pass@45.4,23.7:
At 2,145 metres, Urdele is the highest paved road pass in Romania, and the Transalpina makes sure you earn it. The final stretch from Rânca runs along the bare crest of the Parâng range, above the tree line, where the landscape is grass, rock and sky. Wind is the main sound, and the clouds seem close enough to touch. There are no trees at all, only mountain pasture dotted with sheepfolds, and on the right day you can see almost the full length of the Carpathian chain.

The road has an old story. The route is said to follow a line used since Roman times, but what is certain is that shepherds drove their flocks across it for centuries, taking sheep to high summer pastures and bringing them down for the winter. In the twentieth century the track was widened for military use, and only in recent decades has it been fully paved. Today you share it with motorcyclists, cyclists and the odd tractor, along with flocks and guard dogs. Cattle grids are rare, so expect animals on the tarmac and give them room.

The riding is exhilarating but exposed. The road climbs in long, easy bends with generous views, and on the crest it drops steeply on one side with little in the way of barriers. Fog and cold rain can arrive in minutes even in summer, and a sunny morning can turn into sleet by afternoon. The pass is normally open only from early summer to autumn and can close at any time if snow falls, so check locally before you set out. Start early to enjoy the clearest light, and take extra care on damp surfaces.

Nobody sells petrol at this height. The nearest places to fill the tank are Novaci on the south side and Petroșani or Petrila on the north, around twenty kilometres away, so plan your range carefully. A few seasonal stalls sometimes sell cheese, honey and warm drinks near the summit, but do not count on them.

Take a few minutes at the top to enjoy the quiet. The air is thin, the horizon enormous, and the sense that you have climbed above everything is hard to forget.
t.obarsia lotrului@45.4,23.6:
Obârșia Lotrului means the source of the Lotru, and the name explains the place. The Lotru River rises in these mountains and flows down through a long wooded valley to the Olt, and here at its head the landscape opens into forest, meadow and the glint of lakes. It is a quiet mountain hamlet on the northern side of the Transalpina, with a handful of cabins, guesthouses and a ski area that is lively in winter and gentle in summer, and it makes a good pause after the bare heights of the pass.

The countryside feels remote. Dense spruce forest covers the lower slopes, and above it the meadows climb toward the ridge of the Parâng range. This is a region of bears, wolves and lynx, and signs of them are more common than sightings, though you might see deer or hear the crack of a branch at dusk. The water is cold and clear, and large dams along the Lotru valley have created reservoirs, including Vidra, whose long blue shape you may glimpse from the road, used for hydroelectric power.

The road from Urdele descends here in gentle curves through forest and clearing, with good tarmac in most places, though frost and rockfall can leave rough patches. It is a wonderful stretch of riding, less dramatic than the ridge but more intimate, with shafts of light through the trees, fresh air and almost no traffic on weekdays. In early autumn the leaves turn and the air has a faint smoky smell from the stoves in the village. Watch for logging trucks and for animals crossing at dusk, and slow down in the shade, where damp patches linger late into the morning.

Services are limited. There are small pensions and cafés serving grilled meat, soup and polenta, and a shop or two for the basics, but do not rely on fuel being available. Petrila and Petroșani, to the north, are the nearest larger towns with proper stations, and you should arrive here with a good reserve in the tank.

If you have an hour, walk to the water or a nearby meadow and listen. The valley is quiet in a way that big roads rarely allow.
t.surdesti@47.6,23.8:
Some churches are tall for the sake of it, and Șurdești's is one of them. The wooden church of the Holy Paraskeva, in the village of Șurdești in Maramureș, has a bell tower that stabs about fifty metres into the sky, which is often claimed to be the tallest wooden church in Europe. It was built in the eighteenth century by local carpenters using oak and spruce, with a steep, slender spire that rises from a modest nave like a pencil from a pocket. Along with several others in the region, it is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Maramureș villages sit in hills and valleys in northern Romania, and they preserve a way of life that has vanished from most of Europe. Hay is stacked in conical ricks around wooden houses, carved gateways stand in front of farmyards, women in headscarves walk beside horse carts, and the churches are tucked among orchards and fields. The building tradition is more than decoration: after the Tatar raids of the Middle Ages, and later under foreign rule when Romanian Orthodox and Greek Catholic communities were limited in how high or grand their stone buildings could be, the villagers built in wood instead and turned the material into art.

The riding here is slow and rewarding. The roads between villages are narrow and winding, mostly asphalt but patchy in places, with horse-drawn carts, cyclists and grazing animals sharing them. Do not push the pace. The best moments come when you stop beside a hayfield, switch off the engine and listen to the bells. Early autumn is lovely, with plum brandy being distilled in the yards and the hills turning orange, while spring brings meadows full of wildflowers. In rain the track to the church can be muddy, so keep to the paving.

You can usually find someone to open the church if you ask politely, and a small donation is appropriate. Dress modestly: covered shoulders and knees are respectful inside. Fuel is not a given in Șurdești, so use Baia Sprie or Baia Mare nearby, where there are proper stations, and fill up before you wander the side roads.

The local food is hearty, with cabbage rolls, polenta, smoked meats and sweet cheese pastries, often served with a glass of țuică, the plum spirit, which you should take in moderation if you are riding.
t.strbske pleso@49.1,20.1:
Štrbské Pleso is a lake at the foot of the High Tatras, around thirteen hundred metres up, and it was made by ice. A glacier dropped a pile of rock and gravel here, a moraine, and meltwater pooled behind it, giving a clear, cold lake set among spruce woods with the dark wall of the mountains behind. On a still day the peaks mirror in the water, and the sharp ridge of Mount Krivan, a national symbol of Slovakia, rises in the distance.

The resort around it has a long history as a mountain retreat, and it has hosted major winter sports events, including the Nordic World Ski Championships in 1970. A tall ski-jumping hill still stands near the lake. A rack railway climbs here from Štrba, down in the valley, and there are cable cars and chairlifts up into the high country. The architecture is a mixture of old wooden villas and big concrete hotels from the communist period, which gives the place a slightly odd, faded character, but the setting is unbeatable.

The Slovak High Tatras are small but dramatic. They are the highest part of the Carpathians, a compact range of granite peaks with sharp crests, glacial lakes and steep valleys, and they pack Alpine scenery into a remarkably small area. The Freedom Road, the Cesta Slobody, runs along the foot of the range from end to end, linking the resorts through forests of spruce and dwarf pine. It is a fine road, with smooth surfaces and gentle bends, rather than a wild one, and its pleasure is in the constant views of the mountains. Speed limits are strict and enforced, and wildlife, including bears, can appear near the forest edges.

In 2004 a violent windstorm flattened huge areas of forest across the Tatras, and the regrowing slopes still show the scars. Weather here can change quickly, with cold rain even in summer, and snow possible from autumn to spring. Mornings usually give the clearest views.

Fuel is not available at the lake itself, so use Štrba or Svit nearby, or Poprad a little farther, and fill up before you come. There are cafés, hotels and restaurants around the lake, serving Slovak classics like bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep cheese, which is hearty and delicious after a cold ride. A walk around the lake takes about half an hour.
t.stary smokovec@49.1,20.2:
Starý Smokovec is the grandfather of the High Tatras resorts. It was founded in the late eighteenth century and developed as a spa and mountain retreat over the next century, when the first hotels and villas went up among the spruce trees, and it still has a faded, Central European elegance that the newer resorts lack. Wooden houses with carved balconies and pointed roofs stand on the slopes, grand old hotels face the mountain, and a rack of walking trails leaves from the village into the high valleys.

It is also the hub of the little electric railway that links the resorts along the foot of the range, and the trams that run from Poprad to Starý Smokovec and onward are part of the local scene. A funicular climbs from the village to Hrebienok, a viewpoint and trail junction at around thirteen hundred metres, from which paths lead to waterfalls, huts and glacial valleys. From the top, the wall of the Tatras seems to rise just in front of you, a broad panorama of grey granite and dark forest.

The surrounding landscape was heavily marked by the great windstorm of 2004, which flattened large areas of forest, and you can still see the younger trees growing back across the slopes. Brown bears live in these mountains, and so do chamois and marmots, and residents will tell you that it is wise to keep your food stored and to stay on marked paths. In the village itself, the smell of woodsmoke and baking drifts from the cafés in the cool air.

The Freedom Road passes through here as it traces the Tatra foothills, a smooth, well-kept route with gentle bends and constant views of the peaks. Traffic can be heavy in summer and in the ski season, and speed limits through the resort villages are low. Parking can be tight at the funicular station, so arrive early or take the train. Autumn is a particularly lovely time, with clear air and golden larches, though first snow can fall in October.

Starý Smokovec is a real centre, with shops, pharmacies, cafés and restaurants, and it is an easy place for coffee and cake or a hearty plate of dumplings. For fuel, Svit and Poprad are the nearest towns with larger stations, so it is sensible to fill up before coming to the resort belt.

Take time for a slow walk along the village promenade.
t.tatranska lomnica@49.2,20.3:
Tatranská Lomnica is the eastern anchor of the High Tatras resorts, and it sits beneath one of the most striking peaks in the range, Lomnický štít, at 2,634 metres. A cable car runs up from the village to the summit in stages, carrying visitors to a stony top with an observatory and, on a clear day, a view over Slovakia and into Poland. The old cable car has been a Tatra institution for generations, and queues form on sunny days in summer.

The village has the feel of a place built for health and leisure. Villas and guesthouses in wooden or stone styles line the streets, with a main square, a small park and a railway station where the little electric trains arrive from Poprad. There is an astronomical research station on the nearby peak, and a small museum in the village tells the story of the Tatras and the people who explored them. Autumn is a favourite season, with crisp air and snow on the peaks, but summer brings the biggest crowds.

The Freedom Road reaches its eastern end here, after running along the foot of the range from the western resorts. Riding it is a relaxed pleasure, with views of the mountains opening between the trees, smooth tarmac and gentle bends, though speed limits are strictly enforced and there are many pedestrian crossings in the resort villages. In the evening, deer sometimes come to the verges, so keep an eye out near forests. Weather in the Tatras can turn quickly, and fog or rain can hide the peaks within minutes, so it is best to catch the views early.

To the east lies Kežmarok, a historic town with a castle and a wooden Lutheran church that is on the UNESCO list, and it makes a good side trip if you have time. Kežmarok, about twelve kilometres away, is also the sensible place for fuel and supplies, since the resort itself has fewer options. In the village you will find cafés and restaurants serving Slovak dishes such as potato pancakes, bryndzové halušky and venison, and cakes to go with strong coffee.

Spend a quiet half hour by the station, where the old trams still rattle in, and listen to the mountain wind.
t.debrecen@47.5,21.6:
Debrecen is the capital of the Great Hungarian Plain, a city of two hundred thousand people where the horizon is perfectly flat and the sky does most of the work. For centuries it was the stronghold of Hungarian Calvinism, so much so that it was nicknamed the Calvinist Rome, and its yellow Great Church, the largest Protestant church in the country, dominates the main square. It was here, in 1849, that Lajos Kossuth declared Hungary's independence from the Habsburgs, and for a short time Debrecen served as the capital of the revolution.

The city's food is simple and generous. The Debreceni sausage, paprika-red and smoky, is known across Hungary, and a plate of it with mustard and bread is a fair lunch. Pastry shops sell túrós csusza, noodles with cheese and bacon, and in August the flower carnival on the twentieth fills the avenues with floats made entirely of blossoms.

For a rider, the plain is both gift and challenge. Roads run dead straight for kilometres, with poplar and acacia windbreaks and fields of sunflower, maize and wheat, and the pace is relaxed. The Hortobágy, to the west, is a protected steppe where grey cattle and racka sheep graze under tall sky, and traditional horse herders still show their skills. Wind can be a nuisance, and the summer sun is fierce, but the evening light across the puszta is spectacular. Watch for agricultural vehicles, and for wildlife crossing at dawn and dusk.

The long day ride heads north toward the Tokaj wine country and the cellars of Tolcsva, where the plain gives way to wooded volcanic hills covered with vines. Tokaj's sweet aszú wine was famed in the courts of Europe, and the volcanic cellars cut into the hillsides keep a cool, damp air all year. Fuel is plentiful in Debrecen, which has big stations on every ring road, and in the larger towns on the way. Keep the tank full in the countryside, where villages are small. Eat early, since kitchens in small places close early, and carry some forints for cash-only places.
t.pajtas vaara tynnyrilaki@68.3,23.0:
Pajtas-vaara is a fell, a rounded, treeless hill in the far north of Finnish Lapland, in the municipality of Enontekio, where the country narrows between Sweden and Norway. The name is Sami, and the land belongs to the Sami homeland, where herders have followed reindeer across the fells for a very long time. I cannot tell you about a particular site on the hill, and it would be dishonest to pretend, but the surrounding country is worth talking about. It is open, quiet and big, and on a clear day you can see for fifty kilometres.

The fells here are low, worn mountains, rising above the birch woods and carpeted with crowberry, lichen and dwarf birch. Above the tree line the ground is bare and stony. Lakes lie in every hollow, and rivers run slowly through the bogs. In the short summer the light never fully fades, and the midnight sun lasts from late May to mid July. In September the colours of ruska, the autumn leaf season, turn the slopes red, orange and gold, and the air is crisp and clear. Winter is long and dark, but the northern lights are often visible on clear nights.

The roads in this region are long, quiet and smooth. Highway 21 runs up the western border toward Kilpisjarvi, through Muonio, with the road to Hetta branching off to the northeast, and the stretches between villages can be fifty kilometres or more. The surface is good, and the main hazard is reindeer, which wander across the road in herds and stand on the tarmac as if it were theirs, which in a sense it is. Slow down when you see them, and wait. Speed limits are low in summer and lower in winter, and Finnish police are strict about them.

Fuel is the thing to plan. Enontekio, about thirty kilometres away, is the nearest village with services, and beyond it stations are few, and some close early or on Sundays. Fill the tank at every chance. Mosquitoes are fierce in July, so carry repellent. Food is simple, with reindeer stew, salmon soup and cloudberry desserts. Enontekio has small shops and a cafe or two, and in Hetta the hiking centre has more.

The best time to ride is from June to early September. Take your time, and watch the horizon.
t.ortelec dealul magurice 2@47.2,23.1:
Ortelec is a small village on the outskirts of Zalau, in the county of Salaj, in northwestern Romania, and the hill that rises behind it is one of the first ridges of the Meses Mountains. The Meses range is low, wooded and long, running southwest to northeast as a green wall between the Transylvanian plateau and the plains toward Hungary. I cannot point to a specific monument at the spot where this stop lies, but the landscape around it is worth knowing. The hill is a rounded, grassy summit with beech and oak forest on its slopes, and its crest gives wide views over the valley to the town below.

Zalau, about four kilometres away, is a town of sixty thousand people and the county seat. It has fuel stations, supermarkets, restaurants and hotels, so it is a convenient base. The town has a long history, mentioned in documents in the early thirteenth century, and its Hungarian name is Zilah. For centuries this region was part of the Kingdom of Hungary, and before that the Romans held the frontier here, at Porolissum, on the pass just to the north.

The riding in Salaj is good and mostly unspoiled. Roads climb over wooded ridges and follow quiet valleys between hay meadows, orchards and villages of long, low houses with sheds and wells. Surfaces vary. Main roads are generally sound, while village lanes may have potholes, gravel or livestock, and horse carts are still part of daily traffic. Distances are short, and you can cover a lot of countryside in a day. Spring has blossom in the orchards, and autumn is soft and golden.

Food is hearty and cheap. Expect sarmale, cabbage rolls stuffed with pork and rice, mamaliga, the cornmeal porridge served with sour cream and cheese, and grilled sausages. Plum brandy, called tuica here, is the local spirit, and the plum orchards of Salaj are well known. Hosts may offer a glass, and it is polite to accept a small one, though a rider should be careful.

In summer, the hills can be hot and storms build in the afternoon. Wild boar, deer and foxes live in the forests, and bears and wolves exist in the wider region, though you are unlikely to see them. Try to be off the forest tracks by dusk.
t.ortelec dealul clocotal@47.2,23.1:
Clocotal is one of the low hills that crowd around Zalau, in northwestern Romania, and its name, Dealul Clocotal, simply means Clocotal Hill. Nothing marks it as a famous monument, and honesty is the best approach here: this is a stop in the country, and the interest is in the land itself. The hill is part of the rolling Salaj landscape, a region of wooded ridges, small valleys and farmland on the western flank of the Transylvanian basin, where the foothills of the Meses Mountains slope toward the Somes plain.

The forest is mostly beech and oak, with hornbeam and wild cherry, and in spring the woodland floor is covered with wild garlic and anemones. Autumn brings rich colour, with golden beech leaves lying thick on the ground and the smell of damp earth and mushrooms. Locals pick mushrooms and forest berries, and shepherds still graze flocks on the open ridgelines. Birdlife is varied, with buzzards circling above the clearings and woodpeckers drumming in the trees. At night, you can sometimes hear owls.

The tracks that climb the hills are a mix of paved village roads, gravel and dirt, and some are steep and rutted after rain. A touring bike will manage the paved roads easily, but light trail machines are happier on the tracks. Always check the surface when the weather has been wet, because the clay is slick. Trucks hauling timber can appear on narrow roads. Mobile signal is generally good near the town, but weaker in the valleys.

Zalau, four kilometres away, provides everything: fuel, food, repairs and places to sleep. A little further, the village of Mirsid, with just over two thousand people, has shops and a few cafes. The area is rural, and the pace of life is slow. In the countryside, you may see people making hay by hand in July, with wooden rakes and haystacks built around a central pole, a sight that has vanished in much of Europe.

A day here is best taken slowly, with time to stop at a village well or to talk to a shepherd, if you have a few words of Romanian. A small gift of goodwill goes a long way.
t.zalau padurea orasului 2@47.2,23.1:
Zalau's city forest, the Padurea Orasului, is the green lung on the edge of town, and it is the sort of place that people in the town use without thinking about it: for Sunday walks, mushrooming, running, and picnics under the oaks. The label puts this stop in the second of two spots in the forest, and I will not pretend there is a particular monument to see. It is a stretch of managed woodland on the slopes above the town, with paths, a few clearings and views down over the roofs.

The forest tells you something about the geology. Salaj sits on soft sedimentary hills, sandstone and marl, which erode into rounded ridges and sticky clay soils, and it is cut by streams that flow west to the Crasna and the Somes. In the shade of the beeches the ground is spongy with leaves, while the oaks on the drier slopes let in more light. Hazel, hornbeam and wild pear grow along the edges. Squirrels, jays and deer live here, and the dawn chorus in May is loud.

Zalau itself is a town you may be glad of. It grew in the twentieth century as an administrative and industrial centre, and its centre has some interwar and Habsburg-era buildings, a large Reformed church and a modern civic core. It has a good reputation for handball. The Hungarian poet Endre Ady went to school here, and the Reformed college where he studied still stands. The town has a mixed population of Romanians and Hungarians, and you will hear both languages on the street.

For riders, the town is the place to refuel and to eat. Restaurants serve ciorba, a sour soup, and grilled meats, and cafes along the main street are pleasant for a rest. Roads out of town lead west into the Crasna valley, east to the Meses range, and north toward Porolissum, with gentle gradients and light traffic. Cobbles are rare, but potholes in side streets can be sharp.

The forest is at its best in late April and October, when the leaves are fresh or gold.
t.sarmizegetusa@45.6,23.3:
Sarmizegetusa Regia was the capital of Dacia, a kingdom that once stood between the Carpathians and the Danube, and the ruins lie high in the Orastie Mountains, in the county of Hunedoara. The Dacians were a sophisticated people, with fortified hilltop towns, gold and iron work, and a priesthood. Under their king Decebalus they fought the Roman Empire in two wars, and the emperor Trajan finally conquered the kingdom in 106 AD. The Romans destroyed the capital, but the site survived as a series of terraces cut into a steep mountainside, and it is part of the UNESCO group of Dacian Fortresses of the Orastie Mountains, listed in 1999.

What stays in the mind is the sanctuary, a place of circular and rectangular platforms with rows of stone bases that once held wooden pillars. The largest circle is often called the Great Round Sanctuary, and next to it stands a disc of andesite known as the Andesite Sun. Experts disagree about their meaning, and some think they were used to measure time or track the calendar. The stone blocks of the fortress walls were fitted without mortar in a style called murus dacicus, with timber binding, and parts of the walls survive.

The road to the ruins is one of the most beautiful in Romania. From Orastie, in the valley, a narrow, winding forest road climbs for a long way through beech and spruce, with steep slopes, tight bends and little traffic. The surface is patchy in places, with potholes, loose gravel and washouts after heavy rain. Speed limits are low, and the pace is slow, which suits the setting. Wild boar, deer and, in the deeper forests, bears are present.

Fill the tank in Orastie, the main town of the area, and bring food and water, since services at the site are limited. The village of Orastioara de Sus, the nearest settlement, has a few shops and guesthouses. Temperatures at the site can be cool even in summer, and mist is common. The best time to visit is from late May to early October, since snow can block the road in winter.

Walk the site slowly, and look out across the forested hills to feel why Decebalus chose the place. The silence is remarkable.
t.popeni dealul manastirii@47.2,23.2:
Popeni is a village among the hills of Salaj, in the north-west of Romania, and its Dealul Manastirii means Monastery Hill, a name that suggests there was once a religious house on the slope, though nothing prominent remains to point out. Names like this are everywhere in Romania, and they hint at a landscape in which monks, farmers and shepherds had a long hold. In Transylvania, many monasteries were destroyed in the eighteenth century, when the Habsburg authorities, worried about Orthodox influence, ordered them closed, and the names sometimes outlived the buildings.

The countryside around is gentle and agricultural. Fields of wheat, maize and sunflowers fill the valleys, and the ridges between are covered with oak and beech. Villages are strung out along a single street, with houses facing the road behind painted fences and a church with a slim, tall steeple at the centre. Many households keep geese, hens and a cow, and in the evening the cows are driven home along the road. This is a rural scene that is vanishing, and it is a pleasure to see it still alive.

On a motorcycle, the road here is typical of the Romanian interior: reasonably good tarmac on the main routes, with potholes and patches on smaller ones. Corners are moderate and visibility is generally good, but farm vehicles, horse carts and animals are a hazard, particularly at dusk. Dogs may chase a bike in the villages, and it is best to slow down and not to react. Speed limits are low in villages and heavily enforced by police with radar guns.

Creaca, about four kilometres away, is a village with basic shops, and Zalau, the county town, is within easy reach for fuel and food. Local specialities include smoked sausage, cheese and homemade bread, and in autumn you can find fresh walnuts and plums. Wine is made in many households, and it is generally honest and strong.

A good time to come is in late spring, when the hills are green and the fruit trees bloom, or in September, when the harvest is on and the evenings are warm. Summer days can be hot. The light is lovely in the early evening, when the hills turn blue and the church bells ring.
t.mirsid dealul mare 2@47.2,23.2:
Mirsid lies on the edge of the Meses Mountains, and what makes it special is a Roman frontier post just up the road. At Porolissum, in the village of Moigrad, the Romans built a fort, a town and a customs station on the high ground above the pass, and from here they controlled the northern gate of their province of Dacia. Trade and troops passed through the Meses Gate, a narrow notch in the mountains, and the ruins, including the walls of the fort, the remains of an amphitheatre and a customs post, can still be seen on the hill. Porolissum is one of the best-preserved Roman fort complexes in Romania.

Dealul Mare, the Big Hill, is one of the ridges nearby, and the label has no feature to offer beyond the view: a wooded height in the Meses range, with grassy clearings and the typical pattern of oak on the sunny slopes and beech on the shady ones. From the crest, on a clear day, you can look over the hills of Salaj and across to the Somes valley.

The roads in the area are enjoyable for a leisurely ride. Between Zalau and the pass, the road climbs gradually through forested hills and villages, with a pleasant series of curves, though lorries and local traffic mean you should not hurry. Surfaces are generally acceptable, with occasional potholes. In winter, the pass can be icy, and snow may fall as early as November.

Mirsid, with a bit over two thousand people, has shops and a few places to eat, and Dobrin, to the south, is smaller. Zalau, a short ride away, is the place for fuel and larger supplies. The countryside around produces plums, apples and walnuts, and a roadside stall may offer jars of honey or plum jam in season.

The dry months of June to September are the best time for the ruins, but autumn is attractive, with the forest colours. At the site, take water and a hat, since there is little shade, and watch your step on uneven stones.
t.ciceu poieni strunga gavojdenilor@47.3,2:
The hills east of Bistrita are the northern edge of the Transylvanian plateau, and Ciceu-Poieni lies in their folds. The label, Strunga Gavojdenilor, points to a saddle or gap on the ridge, and the word strunga means a narrow passage where sheep were once driven between pastures. I do not know of a particular monument at this point, and it is better to say so than to invent one, but the region has a long and rich history that is worth describing. Bistrita, the nearest large town, was a Saxon city, founded by German settlers invited by the Hungarian kings in the Middle Ages, and its medieval centre still shows the trace of that past.

The land is a patchwork of meadows, orchards and small woods, with long ridges and shallow valleys. The villages here are strung along streams, with wooden gates and tall haystacks and church steeples at the centre. Ciceu has an old fortress above the Somes valley, which once belonged to Moldavian princes and is now a ruin. The Moldavian ruler Stephen the Great held it in the fifteenth century, an odd reach into Transylvania.

Riding in this part of Romania is a gentle pleasure. The roads are not fast, and the scenery changes constantly, with hay meadows in June, fields of ripe grain in July and a rich haze in September. Tarmac is variable, and you may meet slow tractors, shepherds with flocks and the occasional stray dog. Mobile reception is patchy in the valleys. Take a paper map or an offline one, and allow time.

Negrilesti, a village of about fifteen hundred people, is the closest settlement, and Breaza is similar. Both have small shops, but not necessarily fuel. For petrol, head for Bistrita or Beclean, where stations are on the main roads. Food in the villages is simple and filling: bean soup, polenta with cheese and sour cream, grilled sausages and doughnut-like pastries called papanasi, served with jam.

Late September and early October are lovely, with warm days, cool nights and the smell of woodsmoke. Fog fills the valleys in the early morning and lifts by ten. Summer thunderstorms can be fierce and fast.
t.zalau magura stanii 2@47.2,23.1:
Magura Stanii means the Hill of the Sheepfold, and the name tells you how this high ground has been used for centuries. Shepherds drove their flocks up to the open pastures in late spring and stayed until autumn, living in simple huts, milking the ewes and making cheese. The practice continues in parts of Salaj, though in diminished form, and a sheepfold is still a sight you may come across on the hills. The label places this stop on the second of two points on the hill, and it has no monument, but the landscape and the history of the border region make it worth thinking about.

Salaj is a border region in the sense that it has often been on the edge. The Meses Mountains were the northern limit of Roman Dacia, and in the Middle Ages the area belonged to the Kingdom of Hungary. In 1940, under the Second Vienna Award, northern Transylvania was transferred from Romania to Hungary, and the new frontier ran right through this part of Salaj, close to the villages of Treznea and Aghires. The area returned to Romania after the war. Memories of those years still run deep in local families.

The hills themselves are rounded and wooded, covered with a mix of beech, oak and hornbeam, and cut by small streams. Clearings give wide views over the surrounding country, with a faint blue line of mountains in the far distance on clear days. In spring the meadows are covered with wild flowers, including orchids, and the air is full of the sound of cuckoos.

The riding is best on the quieter lanes, where tarmac gives way to gravel as the road climbs. A touring bike will cope with most of it, though care is needed after rain, when the clay turns slippery. Treznea, a village of a thousand people, and Aghires, a little larger, have small shops. Zalau is the nearest place for proper fuel and supplies, so fill up before heading into the hills.

Sheep's cheese is the local product, sold fresh or smoked, and a slice with bread and raw onion makes a fine lunch. Evenings in the hills are cool, even in summer.
t.romanasi dealul hentesu@47.1,23.2:
Hentesu is the name of a hill near the village of Romanasi, in the Salaj hills of north-western Romania, and Dealul Hentesu is simply Hentesu Hill. It is a modest rise, but in this country of broad rounded ridges it commands good views. I have no specific landmark to offer for the spot, and the best way to describe it is as a point of access to the country around, a place to stop, look, and think about how the land is used.

Romanasi is a village in the Meses foothills, and it lies close to the Roman frontier. Archaeologists have traced a line of Roman watchtowers and small forts running along the ridges of the Meses range, the so-called limes of Dacia, and some are in good condition. A turf and timber rampart, with a ditch, once ran in front of them. Traces of the road that supplied the garrisons survive in the fields.

The hill's slopes are covered with a mixture of meadow and woodland, and farmers still cut hay with scythes in the clearings. Cherry and plum trees grow wild by the paths, and in late summer you may find blackberries and wild raspberries. Birds of prey, such as buzzards and kestrels, hover over the open ground, and hares leap through the grass. The soil is a rich brown, and after rain the smell of damp earth is strong.

For motorcyclists, the roads here suit an unhurried day. The ridge routes are narrow and not always well surfaced, but the traffic is minimal, and the sense of space is wonderful. Take care at crossings with farm tracks, where gravel can wash onto the tarmac. Treznea and Agrij, small villages within a few kilometres, have limited shops, and Zalau is the place to fill the tank and have a proper meal. Take cash, since small village shops often do not accept cards.

Late spring and early autumn are the best times. In the heat of high summer, midday is quiet, and the hay smells sweet.
t.zalau sub magura stanii@47.2,23.1:
Sub Magura Stanii means below the sheepfold hill, and the stop sits on the lower slopes, where the hill gives way to farmland and the first houses. This is the part of the landscape where people live and work: small plots of potatoes and maize, plum orchards, vegetable patches behind the houses, and a few cows grazing on the verge. The label offers no monument, so the best description is a day in the country, in a place where life goes on at the speed it always has.

The plums are the thing. Salaj is one of the main plum-growing regions of Romania, and the orchards here are old, with gnarled trees that bloom white in April and drop their fruit in September. Much of the crop is turned into tuica, a clear brandy distilled once or twice in small copper stills, often in the yard of a farmhouse. The smell of fermenting plums in autumn hangs over the villages. Locals use it as a greeting, a medicine and a mark of hospitality, and it is rude to refuse the first offer. A sip is enough.

Houses here are long and low, with whitewashed walls and tiled roofs, and many have a small porch with carved wooden posts. Hungarian and Romanian families live side by side, and in some villages you can hear both languages. Church towers mark the villages, and you will see both Orthodox and Reformed churches. The Reformed churches, plain and white, often have a painted wooden ceiling inside.

Riding on the lanes below the hill is easy and relaxed. Roads are narrow, and may be patched, with a speed limit of fifty in villages. Take care at dusk, when animals are on the road, and slow down for any horse cart. Zalau, about a quarter of an hour away, offers full services, and it is wise to fill up there.

Autumn is the time to come, when the orchards are heavy with fruit, the air is warm in the daytime and cool at night, and the smoke from distilleries drifts across the hills.
t.zalau padurea orasului 1@47.2,23.1:
Zalau's forest park is a green escape from the town, and the first of its two stops in the Padurea Orasului gives you a sense of how the people of Zalau live with their landscape. The label points to a stretch of woodland on the northern edge of town, with walking paths, a few picnic spots and a view of the roofs. There is no monument here, and nothing needs to be invented. It is a good place to take a break, and the town is a decent place to be.

Zalau has the character of a place that grew fast in the twentieth century and is still working out what it wants to be. Its old core is small, with a Reformed church and a few Austro-Hungarian buildings, and around it spread blocks of flats, a modern shopping area and a new civic centre. The county of Salaj is among the least populous in Romania, and the town's sixty thousand people give it an unhurried feel. The Romanian politician Iuliu Maniu, who was prime minister in the interwar years and a leading figure of Transylvanian politics, was born in a village nearby. Maniu died in a communist prison in 1953.

For riders, the town is a good base, with fuel stations at the main roads, supermarkets and cafes where you can sit and watch the street. The roads into the hills begin almost at the edge of town, and within ten minutes you can be on quiet country lanes. From here, a ride north climbs to the Meses Gate and Porolissum, the Roman frontier site, and is a pleasant afternoon. The roads to the east and west pass through orchards and hill villages, with gentle gradients and moderate bends.

Local food is hearty. Look for tochitura, a stew of pork with polenta and a fried egg, and for cozonac, a sweet bread with walnuts and poppy seeds, which is baked for holidays. Tea and coffee are everywhere. In summer, evenings are warm and cafe terraces are busy until late.

The forest is lovely at any time but is at its best in October, when the oaks turn bronze and the paths are covered with leaves.
t.mossel bay@-34.2,22.1:
The Garden Route is usually said to begin at Mossel Bay, and this is where the story of European contact with this coast begins too. In 1488 the Portuguese navigator Bartolomeu Dias anchored here after rounding the Cape, making the first known European landing on this part of Africa, and the town's museum complex keeps a full-size replica of his caravel. A famous old milkwood tree in the town, known as the Post Office Tree, recalls the tradition that sailors left letters in a shoe hung from its branches.

Today the place is a lively seaside town of about sixty thousand, with a working harbour, long beaches, restaurants and a lighthouse on Cape St Blaize, from which a cliff path runs round the headland. Below the point, caves such as those at Pinnacle Point yielded some of the earliest evidence of modern human behaviour, including shellfish gathering and the use of pigments, perhaps a hundred and sixty thousand years ago. Oysters and fresh line fish are what to order, usually with a cold glass of local white wine.

The ride along the coast from here is easy and cheerful. The N2 runs east to George and beyond, but the older roads are better for a motorcycle: from George you can head inland over the Outeniqua mountains by the Montagu Pass, a historic gravel pass built in the 1840s, or take the tarred Outeniqua Pass to Oudtshoorn, in the dry Little Karoo, where ostrich farms and the Cango Caves wait. Weather is mild year-round, with the Indian Ocean warm and the sun reliable, though sea fog and the odd southerly gale can arrive. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons, while the Christmas holiday period brings heavy traffic and booked-out beds.

Practical matters are simple. Mossel Bay has plenty of fuel stations, and in South Africa an attendant will fill your tank for you, so it is customary to tip a few rand. Larger George, a little under forty kilometres east, offers more shops and repair services. Take a rain jacket, because showers can sweep in off the sea, and remember that the best evening light falls on the lighthouse and the rocks at the point, a good place to watch the sun go down.
t.sighisoara@46.2,24.8:
Sighișoara is one of those Transylvanian towns where the Middle Ages seem to have paused and never quite restarted. The citadel sits on a steep hill above the Târnava Mare river, with its walls, nine surviving towers and a covered wooden stairway of 175 steps climbing to the church on the hill. It was settled by Transylvanian Saxons, German-speaking merchants and craftsmen invited by the Hungarian kings in the twelfth century, and the guilds each looked after one of the towers. The clock tower, with its painted figures, is the symbol of the town.

The old citadel is also associated with Vlad Dracul, the father of Vlad the Impaler, who lived here for some years, and the yellow house where he is said to have lived is now a restaurant. The connection to the Dracula story is slender, since the novel was written by an Irishman who never visited, but locals have learned to enjoy it. The citadel is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and the pastel houses along the cobbled lanes are a fine sight in evening light.

The countryside around is the real prize for riders. Rolling hills, wooded ridges and long valleys surround the town, with villages where horse carts are still common, haystacks dot the meadows and storks nest on the roofs. Roads outside the main routes can be rough, with patches, gravel and potholes, and you should expect animals and slow vehicles, particularly in summer. Saxon villages nearby, such as Biertan with its fortified church, are protected too, and the fortified churches of the region are a fascinating part of the story.

Sighișoara is a town of about thirty-five thousand, with fuel stations, supermarkets and plenty of places to eat. The food is hearty, with stews, sausages, polenta and sour soups, plus a local plum brandy, țuică, which is strong and generously offered. Smaller villages have little in the way of services, so fill the tank when you can.

Late spring and early autumn are the best seasons. Summers are warm, with afternoon thunderstorms, and winters are cold and snowy. Stay inside the walls if you can, for the quiet streets after the day-trippers leave.
t.poprad@49.1,20.3:
Poprad sits at the foot of the High Tatras, the smallest alpine mountain range in the world, and it is the largest town in the region, with some fifty-seven thousand people. It is a gateway more than a destination, with a long past as a Zipser Saxon trading town, and a historic quarter at Spišská Sobota, a pretty square of burgher houses and a church with a tall wooden altar. The big peaks stand behind the town, jagged and grey, with Gerlachovský štít the highest at about 2,650 metres.

The ride this stop belongs to follows the Freedom Road, the Cesta slobody, which runs along the foot of the mountains and links the resorts of Starý Smokovec, Štrbské Pleso and Tatranská Lomnica. It is a good road, smooth and with long views to the ridge, crossing forest, meadows and small streams, though traffic can be heavy in summer and winter holiday periods. In 2004, a violent windstorm flattened large areas of forest on the southern slopes, and the bare hillsides and young trees are still a visible reminder of it.

Nearby lies the castle of Spiš, Spišský hrad, one of the largest castle complexes in Central Europe, whose ruined walls sit on a hill of travertine above the plain and can be seen from many kilometres away. It is a UNESCO World Heritage site together with the nearby town of Levoča and the church of Žehra. The castle is a fine place to see the countryside from above, and the stone ramparts are a good setting for photographs at sunset.

Poprad has everything a rider needs. There are filling stations along the main road and on the edge of town, supermarkets, a few pleasant cafes in the old quarter, and plenty of guesthouses. Svit and Nová Lesná, nearby, are smaller but also have basic services. Slovak food is filling, with bryndzové halušky, small potato dumplings with sheep cheese and bacon, as the national dish, and a beer afterwards is natural.

Weather in the mountains is changeable, with cold fronts, summer storms and early snow, and mist can hide the peaks for days. Spring and early autumn are good, with fewer people and clearer air. Remember that Slovakia requires an electronic vignette for motorways, but the old roads around the Tatras are free.
t.curtea de arges@45.1,24.7:
Curtea de Argeș was one of the first capitals of Wallachia, in the fourteenth century, and its great monument is a monastery that everyone in Romania knows. The cathedral, built in the early sixteenth century by Prince Neagoe Basarab, is a white stone building covered in carved lace, with slim towers and delicate patterns that look more like ironwork than masonry. A legend tells that the master builder, Manole, was made by the prince to wall his own wife into the structure so that it would stand, and that he fell to his death trying to escape the roof. The tale is told in ballads, and every Romanian child knows it. The church also holds the tombs of the country's kings, including Carol I and Ferdinand.

The town sits where the Argeș river leaves the Carpathians and spreads into the plain, at the foot of forested hills, and it is the usual southern gateway to the Transfăgărășan. This is the road Ceaușescu ordered after the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, a military route over the mountains in case of a similar threat, built through the early 1970s with explosives and the labour of conscripts. It climbs from the south through beech and spruce, passes the huge Vidraru dam above its blue reservoir, and then heads upward in a cascade of bends toward the high bare ridge.

Just above the dam, the Poenari fortress on a rocky crag was one of the strongholds of Vlad the Impaler, and reaching it means climbing around fourteen hundred steps. The road then runs on to Bâlea Lake at just over two thousand metres, where a tunnel just under a kilometre long pierces the crest. The highway is usually open only in summer and early autumn, normally from around late June or July until about October, depending on snow, so check the status before you go. Weather on the ridge changes fast, with fog, cold wind and sudden storms, and the surface can be damaged by frost.

Curtea de Argeș has about thirty-two thousand people, and all the fuel, food and shops you need, so fill up completely here, as there is nothing on the climb. Cafes near the monastery are good places for a coffee and a plate of grilled meat before you start the climb.
t.cartisoara@45.7,24.6:
Cârțișoara is the village at the northern foot of the Transfăgărășan, at roughly six hundred metres above the sea, where the road from the Făgăraș mountains reaches the Olt valley. Behind it rises the highest range in Romania, a wall of ridges and glacial cirques topped by Moldoveanu, around 2,544 metres, and in front lies the gentle farmland of southern Transylvania. The contrast is sudden: a few kilometres of fields and orchards, and then a wall of forest and rock that climbs out of sight.

The place has a long agricultural history, with Saxon and Romanian villages scattered along the valley, many of them with fortified churches and old farmsteads. Nearby Cârța holds the ruins of a twelfth-century Cistercian abbey, one of the easternmost houses of that order, and its Gothic church, partly roofless, stands in a village field. The Orthodox monastery at Sâmbăta de Sus, a short distance away, was founded in the late seventeenth century by Constantin Brâncoveanu and is a calm place of white walls and carved wooden porches. The area is also bear country, and the forests above the villages hold lynx, wolves and chamois.

Starting from here means climbing the Transfăgărășan from the north, and the first part is gentle, following the Bâlea river through spruce woods and past a long waterfall. Then the road lifts in tight bends and long switchbacks to the high lake of Bâlea at about 2,034 metres, which has a mountain chalet and, in winter, a hotel built from ice. At the top a tunnel just under a kilometre long takes the road through the ridge, and on the far side the descent drops toward the Vidraru lake and Curtea de Argeș. The road is open in summer only, usually from around July until October, and can still be closed by snow or rockfall in bad weather, so check before setting out.

Cârțișoara is a small village, and the nearest larger town is Victoria, about ten kilometres away, with Făgăraș beyond. Roadside stalls in summer sell cheese, smoked meat and honey, and the cheese in a bread roll is a good lunch at the top.
t.timisoara@45.8,21.2:
Timișoara is a flat, orderly city in the western plain of Romania, the capital of the Banat, a region that has been Ottoman, Habsburg, Hungarian, Romanian and has a mixed memory to show for it. Romanians, Hungarians, Germans and Serbs have lived side by side here for centuries, and the city has the look of a small Vienna, with baroque squares, Secession façades, a big Orthodox cathedral and a handsome opera house with a flight of steps where people gather. It was the first city in continental Europe to light its streets with electricity, in the 1880s, and it also had one of the first horse-drawn trams.

The city is best known to Romanians for December 1989. A protest in support of a Hungarian pastor who was about to be evicted grew into a demonstration against the regime, and the army fired on the crowd in the streets. Within days the uprising had spread, and the dictator fled Bucharest and was dead by Christmas. The Revolution began here, and in the squares you can find memorials and photos. In recent years the city has restored its façades and parks, and it was a European Capital of Culture, with a lively student life and a good coffee scene on the main squares.

The riding starts flat and ends in a different world. East of the city the Banat plain gives way to low hills, and the roads toward Vărădia and the southern Banat run through farmland, sunflower fields and villages of Swabian houses, with the occasional Roman remnant, since the Romans held this country and built forts here. Further south, the land rises into the Banat mountains and the gorges of the Danube. On the plain, wind and long straight roads can be monotonous, and the surface can be patchy in the villages, so watch for potholes and for horse carts, which still use the lanes. Summers are hot and winters can be bitterly cold.

Fuel is easy around Timișoara, with stations on the ring road and every main road. Try the local sour cream-and-pork dishes, and the pastries influenced by Vienna. The Bega canal, with its walkway and its swans, is a good place for a quiet walk before or after a ride.
t.cluj napoca@46.8,23.6:
Cluj-Napoca is the unofficial capital of Transylvania, a university city of more than three hundred thousand on the Someș river, and it wears its mixed history lightly. The Romans founded Napoca here, the Hungarian kings made it a rich town, and for centuries Saxon, Hungarian and Romanian communities lived together within its walls. The great Gothic church of Saint Michael dominates the main square, with a spire visible across the roofs, and a statue of King Matthias Corvinus, who was born in the city in 1443, stands in front of it. On the hill above stands the Cetățuia fortress, which gives a view over the old town and the hills beyond.

Students are the pulse of the place. The Babeș-Bolyai University teaches in Romanian, Hungarian and German, and the cafes, bookshops and festivals reflect it. The botanical garden has a Japanese corner and glasshouses, and on a clear evening the main square is crowded with people taking an ice cream or a beer. Cluj is also an unexpectedly good food city, with bakeries selling cozonac and restaurants serving stuffed cabbage, in the Transylvanian style.

The countryside around is gentle and green, with rolling hills, sheep pasture and villages with old fortified churches. West of the city, the Apuseni Mountains rise into forest and limestone country, with caves, gorges and the lake of Beliș-Fântânele, and the roads there are twisty, narrow and quiet. East and south lie the hills of the Transylvanian Plain, with more modest roads and beautiful light in the late afternoon. About thirty kilometres south-east lies the salt mine at Turda, which has been turned into an underground attraction, and the nearby Turda gorge is a popular walk.

Traffic in and around Cluj is heavy, particularly on the main road toward Oradea and Turda, and trucks make overtaking difficult, so choose smaller roads where you can. Road quality varies, and potholes are common on side roads, especially after winter. Fuel is easy in the city, with big stations on every approach, but mountain roads have fewer, so fill up before leaving. In winter, snow and ice can close the higher roads, and spring is the time of mud and fog.
t.uniondale@-33.7,23.1:
Uniondale is a small Karoo town on the northern side of the Outeniqua mountains, a place of whitewashed houses, tin roofs and a long, wide main street that has seen little change in decades. It lies in a dry valley at the foot of the pass, on the road between the coast and the Little Karoo, and it serves as the gateway to Prince Alfred's Pass, one of the most beautiful gravel roads in South Africa. The surrounding country is open and rolling, with sheep and goats grazing among rocky hills.

The pass is the heart of the story. It was built in the 1860s by the road engineer Thomas Bain, the son of the famous Andrew Geddes Bain, and it runs from Avontuur, near Uniondale, south through the mountains to Knysna. Its builders used convict labor and hand tools to carve a road over the Outeniqua range, with dry-stone retaining walls that still stand today. The distance is about seventy kilometers, much of it gravel, and it takes several hours at a gentle pace. The route winds through fynbos and then indigenous forest as it drops toward the coast, with river crossings, deep valleys and old farms along the way.

For riders, this is a proper adventure ride, and conditions matter. The surface can be corrugated or muddy after rain, and in winter fog and cold can settle on the heights. Tyres should be suitable for gravel, and a reserve of fuel is wise. The road is narrow with drops on one side, and passing vehicles require care. Summer brings heat and dust, while spring brings wildflowers.

Uniondale is also known in local legend. A story of a ghostly hitchhiker on the road outside town, the Phantom Hitchhiker of Uniondale, has circulated since the 1960s and is told with relish in the pub. The town's historic railway at Avontuur once marked the end of the narrow-gauge line, a reminder of how remote the region is.

Services are modest but reliable for a small town. There is a fuel station, a few small shops and guesthouses, and places to eat a simple meal, but supplies are limited, so fill the tank and carry water before heading into the mountains. The nearest bigger towns, such as George and Knysna, lie on the other side of the range.
t.tsitsikamma forest@-34.0,23.9:
The Tsitsikamma coast is one of the few places in South Africa where the forest comes down to the sea. The name is thought to come from the Khoi for a place of much water, and the description fits, with rivers cutting deep gorges through the mountains and dropping into the Indian Ocean through rocky mouths. Between the sea and the Tsitsikamma mountains grows an old, damp forest of yellowwood, stinkwood and ironwood, draped in lichen and ferns, which forms part of the Garden Route National Park. Some of the trees here are hundreds of years old, and the biggest yellowwoods are said to be well over six hundred years.

The forest is full of life, though much of it hides. Knysna turacos, with their crimson wings, call from the canopy, and bushbuck move through the undergrowth. Samango monkeys live in the trees, and the rivers are stained the color of tea by tannins from the vegetation. At Storms River Mouth, a suspension bridge crosses the gorge just above the sea, and the Otter Trail, a famous five-day walk, begins nearby. The smell of damp earth and salt is strong, and the sound of surf mixes with birdsong.

The N2 crosses this landscape on high bridges, including the Bloukrans Bridge, where bungee jumpers throw themselves off the highest commercial bridge bungee in the world, about two hundred and sixteen meters above the river. The old road, the R102, winds through the forest at lower speed and gives a much more intimate feel, with tight bends, tunnels of trees and the chance to stop at small craft stalls and tea gardens. It is a good motorcycle road for a relaxed day, with moderate traffic and fine scenery.

Weather matters. Rain can come in at any time of year, and the forest road is slippery when wet, with leaf litter and moss on the surface. Mist drifts in from the sea, and in winter the temperature can drop quickly. The best season is from late spring to autumn, though holiday periods bring crowds.

Fuel is sparse inside the forest. Stations are available in Storms River village and in Plettenberg Bay and Humansdorp, but they are not frequent, so keep the tank topped up. There are good places for coffee, cake and breakfast along the route, and the old forest, with its green light, is a calming place to stop.
t.prince albert@-33.2,22.0:
Prince Albert sits at the foot of the Swartberg mountains on the edge of the Great Karoo, a small, whitewashed town with Cape Dutch gables, irrigation furrows running down the main street, and an air of having been forgotten on purpose. Water from the mountains is the secret. It runs through the town in channels, feeds orchards and olive groves, and turns a patch of desert into a place that grows apricots, figs, grapes and olives on a surprising scale.
