Nobody comes here for speed, and the town is very good at that.

For riders it is the best base for two of the great passes in South Africa. To the south, the Swartberg Pass climbs to about 1,585 metres in a series of dizzying switchbacks, cut by the engineer Thomas Bain in the 1880s with convict labour, and it is gravel, steep and exposed, with stone retaining walls that have lasted for well over a century. To the south-west, the tarmac road through Meiringspoort follows a river through a gorge of folded red and grey rock, with high walls and a waterfall at one stop. The Swartberg demands care, with loose surface, sharp bends and sheer drops, and should be avoided in rain or snow. Spring and autumn are the best times. Midsummer in the Karoo is fierce.

The town itself was laid out in the 1760s around a farm and later named after Queen Victoria's consort, and its streets of low houses, shops and cafes feel timeless. The local speciality is dried fruit and olives, and you can buy apricots, dried peaches, preserves and olive oil at roadside shops and the weekend market. A small museum covers the town's history, and the shop owners are happy to talk. Deep in the mountains, the isolated valley of Gamkaskloof, known as the Hell, was home to a community cut off for generations until a road was cut in the 1960s.

The landscape is a mix of arid and wild. Karoo scrub, aloes and succulents cover the plains, and in spring the veld blooms briefly. The Swartberg range is a World Heritage area, with rock formations twisted by ancient tectonic forces, and leopards, klipspringers and eagles live in the high country. At night the stars are brilliant, and the air smells of dry earth and sage.

You can buy fuel in town, and you should, since the mountain roads have none. Bring water, a warm layer for the pass and a cheerful attitude to dust.
t.george sa@-34.0,22.5:
George is the capital of the Garden Route, a town of oak-lined streets and sleepy suburbs on a coastal shelf under the Outeniqua Mountains, and it feels more like a market town in the English countryside than something in Africa. It was founded in 1811 and named after King George III, which also explains the unusual number of old English oaks planted along its avenues. The sea is only ten minutes away, but the mountains are what define the place: a long, green, cloud-catching wall rising behind the town.

As a rider you come to George for two reasons: to refuel and to ride the passes. The town has plenty of fuel, food and workshops, and it is the natural place to regroup. From here, the road north climbs the Outeniqua Pass to Oudtshoorn, a modern pass with good tarmac and sweeping views, while the old Montagu Pass, built in the 1840s and still gravel, winds through fynbos and forest in a narrow, quiet ribbon. To the east, the Seven Passes Road follows an old wagon route toward Knysna, crossing a series of gorges and rivers on a narrow, twisty road through indigenous forest, with a surface that varies and a limit of patience. Rain is frequent on this coast, and mist can settle on the heights.

The area's history is tied to timber and trade. The forests around George once supplied yellowwood and stinkwood for wagons, houses and furniture, and the forests were heavily logged in the nineteenth century before conservation measures took hold. The Montagu Pass was named after a colonial secretary and built to link the coast with the interior, and its stone culverts and bridges are impressive. A small museum in town tells the story of the old wagon trade, and a collection of steam locomotives recalls a time when trains hauled timber down from the mountains.

Nature is generous. The coast is lined with lagoons and long beaches, the forests shelter rare birds such as the Knysna turaco, and the fynbos on the slopes is full of proteas and ericas, flowering year-round. Elephants survive in the Knysna forests, though only a handful, and you are far more likely to see baboons on the road. The air is mild and damp, smelling of wet leaves and sea.

Fill up here before the mountains, bring a rain jacket even in summer, and take the old passes slowly.
t.balea cascada@45.6,24.6:
Bâlea Cascadă is the waterfall that gives its name to the stop, a thin silver plume that drops down a steep glacial step in the Fagaras Mountains, just below the Transfagarasan summit road. It sits at 1,234 metres, and the hairpins above it climb to a high lake and a tunnel at around two thousand metres. Victoria, a small town of about ten thousand people, is the nearest place of any size, some fifteen kilometres away as the crow flies, and fuel and food are down there or in the villages on the northern approach.

The Transfagarasan is one of the great roads of the world, and the northern side is its most dramatic. The road climbs from the foothills through beech and spruce forest, then across a high, bare alpine meadow before squeezing between rock walls and climbing the headwall in a long series of tight hairpins. The surface is generally good tarmac, though frost heaves, potholes and loose gravel appear in places, and it is common for cars, buses and bikes to share a narrow lane. Weather changes fast: sun, fog, rain and even snow can arrive in a single afternoon, even in July. The road is normally open only in summer and early autumn, closing under snow for much of the year, so check the status before heading up.

The road was built in the early 1970s on the orders of Nicolae Ceausescu, after the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968 made the Romanian leadership anxious about a quick military route across the Carpathians. Thousands of soldiers worked with explosives and hand tools, and the project cost lives, which locals still mention quietly. The result is a road that is more spectacular than practical, which riders appreciate and military planners may not. The high point has a small lake, a hotel and a cable car station, and summer weekends bring crowds of day trippers.

Nature at this height is rugged. The Fagaras range holds Moldoveanu, the highest peak in Romania at about 2,544 metres, and the slopes shelter chamois, marmots and, in the forests, brown bears, which sometimes appear near the road, so never feed them. In summer the meadows are bright with alpine flowers, and the air smells of pine and cold water. At the waterfall, stalls sell cheese, sausages and honey, and a bowl of hot bean soup tastes better here than it has any right to.

Bring warm clothing and a waterproof layer, since it can be cold even in midsummer, and fill the tank before starting the climb.
t.czorsztyn@49.4,20.3:
Czorsztyn is a small village on the shore of Lake Czorsztyn, a reservoir in the Pieniny and the Spisz region of southern Poland, and it is dominated by the ruins of a castle on a rocky hill. The castle, first built in the fourteenth century, guarded the border between Poland and Hungary, and its twin, Niedzica Castle, stands on the opposite shore, in what was once Hungary. The two fortresses face each other across the water, which was created in the 1990s by damming the Dunajec river, and the lake covers parts of old villages. Niedzica, Kluszkowce and Krośnica are the nearest settlements, each a few kilometres away.

The legend of Niedzica involves an Inca treasure, supposedly hidden here by a descendant of the Inca after the Spanish conquest, and a quipu, a knotted-string record, was reportedly found in the castle in the 1940s. Historians are doubtful, but the story persists. The ruins of Czorsztyn Castle can be climbed, and the view from the tower takes in the lake, the Pieniny hills and, on a clear day, the High Tatras to the south, with their sharp, grey peaks.

The Tatra foothills road is a pleasure for riders: gentle curves, small hills, villages with wooden houses and haystacks, and views of the mountains. The surface is generally good, with a few patchy stretches, and traffic is moderate, except at weekends in summer, when families head for the lake and the Tatras. The road passes through the Podhale region, home to the Górale, the highlanders, who keep their own customs, music, dress and dialect. Wooden churches with shingled roofs and painted barns appear along the way.

Nearby, the Dunajec Gorge in the Pieniny National Park is famous for its rafting trips, in which local men in traditional costume steer wooden rafts through the limestone canyon. The cheese oscypek, a smoked sheep's cheese, is sold at roadside stalls and is a speciality of the highlands, usually grilled and served with cranberry jam. Fuel and food can be found in Nowy Targ and Zakopane, and small cafes by the lake serve coffee and cake. Early morning, with mist over the water and the castle emerging, is the best moment.
t.lysa polana@49.3,20.1:
The tarmac ends at a border that no longer behaves like one. Łysa Polana sits on the Polish-Slovak line in the High Tatras, a clearing in spruce forest where the Białka stream comes down from the granite and the two countries simply hand the road to each other. Since both states joined Schengen there is no barrier and no queue, just a sign, a few stalls, and a lot of walkers in boots heading for the trails.

The ride here from Zakopane is the real content. You leave the town's tourist crush behind, roll through Poronin and the high farmland around Bukowina Tatrzańska, and the Tatra wall slowly builds on your right, long and jagged and much steeper than its modest height suggests. The road is mostly smooth and mostly straight, with gentle swings through meadows, and it carries heavy weekend traffic: coaches, cyclists, families, horse carts in season. Go early on a weekday, or accept that you will be following a minibus. Summer afternoons bring thunderstorms off the ridge fast, and the air turns cold the moment the sun goes.

This is górale country, the highlanders of Podhale, with their own dialect, their own wool waistcoats and a strong sense that the mountains belong to them. The food is the point of the stalls along the way: oscypek, the smoked sheep cheese pressed in wooden moulds, often grilled and served with cranberry jam, and hot tea with something in it if the day is damp. The Polish side is part of Tatra National Park, so the woods are protected, and brown bears, chamois and marmots live up in the high valleys, though you will hear more tourists than wildlife from the tarmac.

The road continues a short way to the car parks where hikers start the long walk to the lake of Morskie Oko, which is closed to private vehicles, so a motorbike will not get you any closer. Do not plan fuel here. Zakopane, about thirteen kilometres back, is the sensible place to fill the tank, with plenty of stations and every kind of food. Bukowina Tatrzańska has smaller options, and across the line in Slovakia the village of Ždiar is close. Park where the signs allow, because the national park rangers and the local police do check, and bring a warm layer even in July.
t.sapanta@48.0,23.7:
Săpânța is a village at the far north of Romania, hard against the Ukrainian border along the Tisza river, and it is known for a graveyard that makes people laugh and then think. The Merry Cemetery, Cimitirul Vesel, is packed with wooden crosses painted in a deep blue, each carved with a small scene from the life of the person buried below and a short verse in rhyming Romanian, sometimes tender and sometimes teasing. A shepherd with his flock, a weaver at her loom, a driver beside his lorry, and occasionally a verse about the dead man's unfortunate fondness for drink.

The idea came from a local woodcarver, Stan Ioan Pătraș, who started carving these crosses in the 1930s and carried on for decades, training apprentices who still keep the tradition going. There are hundreds of crosses now, and the cemetery has become one of the most visited places in Maramureș. The philosophy behind it is gentle: death is part of a life that was worth living, and the honest summary is better than a solemn one.

Maramureș is one of the best-preserved rural regions in Europe, where the wooden churches, tall and shingled with needle-sharp spires, are listed by UNESCO, and carved gateways stand outside farmhouses. The ride up here is easy and slow, along valley roads through haystack country, with scythes still in use and horse carts sharing the tarmac. The surface is mixed, so keep your speed modest, watch for potholes and for animals, and remember that many roads here have no hard shoulder.

The village has plenty of small guesthouses, and the restaurants near the cemetery serve hearty local food: stuffed cabbage, polenta with sheep cheese and sour cream, and the plum brandy called horinca or țuică, which is stronger than it looks. For fuel, ride to Sighetu Marmației, the main town of the area, about fifteen kilometres to the west, and fill up there before you set out for the mountains. A final point: because the Ukrainian border is close, keep your passport with you and do not wander towards the river banks and border posts, which are monitored.
t.zdiar@49.3,20.3:
Ždiar is a long, thin village stretched along a single road at the foot of the Belianske Tatras, and it has a character that sets it apart even in the Tatras. The people are górali, mountain folk like their neighbours across the Polish border, and the old farmhouses are low, dark timber with white-painted trim and carved decorations under the eaves. The fields behind the houses are laid out in narrow strips running up the slope, an arrangement that has survived for centuries and gives the hillside a combed look.

Riding here means arriving along the Freedom Road, the old name for the high road that links the villages along the southern foot of the High Tatras. Between the resort settlements, the road runs through sleepy villages and open meadows with the toothy limestone ridge of the Belianske Tatras to the north. It is a smooth, undemanding road with modest bends and good views, and the best light comes in the evening, when the ridge goes pink and the traffic thins out. Summer weekends bring crowds and tour buses, so choose your timing carefully.

The Belianske Tatras differ from the granite High Tatras next door, because they are made of limestone, with white crags, caves and meadows of alpine flowers. Much of the range is a strict nature reserve, closed to casual walkers, which helps to keep chamois and marmots at ease. Ždiar sits at a high altitude by Slovak standards, so the air is crisp and the winters are long and snowy.

Ždiar has a long tradition of hospitality, and many houses offer rooms and a hot meal. Typical dishes are halušky with sheep cheese called bryndza, plus pierogi, grilled cheese and thick soups, washed down with a local beer. Fuel is not always at hand, so ride to Spišská Belá, about seventeen kilometres away, or Kežmarok, for a reliable station and supermarket. Across the border at Łysa Polana and the Polish side there is a lot more, but it is a long ride, so it is best to plan ahead before the evening.
t.swellendam@-34.0,20.4:
Swellendam is the third-oldest town in South Africa, and it wears its age with an easy dignity. The Dutch East India Company established a magistracy here in 1743, and the settlement grew up under the Langeberg mountains, which stand along the north side of the town like a blue wall. In 1795, discontented local farmers declared a short-lived republic, with their own flag and officials, which lasted only a few months before the British arrived. The old Drostdy, the magistrate's residence and offices, is now a museum, its thatched roof and white gables intact.

Walking the main street, you pass lines of old oak trees and whitewashed houses with Cape Dutch gables, many of them guesthouses, galleries and cafés. The Dutch Reformed church, with its grand tower, dominates the centre, and nearby is the Bontebok National Park, a small reserve created to save a rare antelope from extinction. In spring, the fields glow yellow with canola, and the air smells of cut grass and woodsmoke.

For a rider, Swellendam is the start of the Tradouw Pass run, one of the loveliest short rides in the Western Cape. It sits on the N2, the long highway that links Cape Town with the Garden Route, so traffic in the town can be dense, with trucks and holiday cars, and turning off toward the mountains is a relief. Heading north from the town on the R324, the road runs through farmland and then climbs into the folds of the Langeberg. The weather can change fast, with cold fronts and rain in winter and strong winds in summer.

The town has a population of about fourteen thousand, so it has fuel stations, restaurants, banks and workshops, and many places to stay, from farm cottages to old town houses. Try the farm stalls and cafés for a slice of koeksister, a sweet twisted pastry, or a hearty plate of lamb, and take your time in the late afternoon, when the mountains turn orange. Montagu, forty kilometres north-west, and Barrydale, in the other direction, are smaller towns reached by quieter roads.
t.tradouw pass@-34.0,20.7:
The Tradouw Pass is a short, pretty road, and it has a good claim to being the best-surfaced mountain road in the Cape. It slices through the Langeberg mountains for a few kilometres between Swellendam and the Little Karoo, following the Tradouw river as it cuts a narrow gorge through red and orange rock. The name is said to come from Khoi words meaning pass of the women, though the exact meaning is debated, and the road was engineered in the 1870s by Thomas Bain, son of the more famous Andrew Bain, who built so many of the great Cape passes.

The ride starts in green farmland on the southern side, with orchards, wheat fields and fynbos, then enters the gorge, where the road bends from side to side with rock walls on either side and the river glittering beneath. Corners are smooth and well banked, the surface is excellent, and the pass is short enough to ride twice, once in each direction, which a lot of riders do. A few viewpoints let you stop and look at the layers of rock, which are tilted at dramatic angles, a reminder of the forces that folded these mountains.

Beyond the northern end, the landscape changes abruptly, from lush green to the dry scrub and red earth of the Klein Karoo, where the villages seem to sit in a different country. Nights can be cold, and in winter, snow sometimes lies on the highest peaks. Spring is best for flowers and clear light, and in summer the heat is dry and the air is full of the smell of fynbos. Rock hyrax and baboons appear on the roadside, and birds of prey ride the thermals above.

There are small settlements around the pass, and Swellendam, about twenty-six kilometres to the south-west, is the nearest large town and the best place for fuel and supplies, with Barrydale just beyond the pass offering a few cafés and craft shops. A stop at a roadside stall for a drink and a snack makes a good break, and the quiet at the northern end is a pleasure. If you can, stay overnight in the Barrydale area and ride back in the early morning, when the pass is empty.
t.swartberg pass@-33.3,22.1:
Swartberg Pass is gravel, and that is exactly why people love it. It crosses the Swartberg range between Oudtshoorn and Prince Albert, rising to about 1,585 metres at the summit, and it was built between 1881 and 1888 by Thomas Bain with convict labour, who cut and packed the stone walls and zigzags by hand. Today it is a national heritage site, one of the finest examples of pass-building in the country, with dry-stone retaining walls that look more like medieval masonry than road engineering.

The surface is a mix of packed gravel and loose stones, and a careful rider on a reasonably capable bike can manage it in dry weather, though conditions change with grading, rain and washouts, so it is wise to ask locally. Corners are tight, hairpins are steep and sometimes very exposed, with long drops from the outer edge, and in places the width is just enough for two vehicles. Take it slowly, stay alert for oncoming traffic, and treat the descents with respect. Do not attempt it after heavy rain or when snow has fallen, as it can close for days.

The views are the reward. From the top, the land falls away to the Little Karoo on one side and the Great Karoo on the other, with the contrast between green valleys, orchards and dry, rocky plains. Rock formations are bent and folded into dramatic shapes, and the light at sunrise and sunset is magnificent. A side road from near the summit leads into Gamkaskloof, a hidden valley known as The Hell, once home to a remote farming community, though that track is rougher and much longer.

Prince Albert, about fourteen kilometres from the northern foot, is a charming village of whitewashed houses, with fuel, a few restaurants and some excellent olive and fruit farms. Oudtshoorn, a larger town on the other side, is known for its ostrich farms and has all services. There are none on the pass, so fill up beforehand, carry water, and wear sunscreen. A flask of coffee at the top, with the whole range stretched out below, is one of the best breaks in the Cape.
t.de rust@-33.5,22.5:
De Rust means the rest, and the village earns the name by being a pleasant place to stop before or after a day in the Swartberg. It lies in the Little Karoo between Oudtshoorn and the mouth of the Meiringspoort gorge, a small settlement of about three and a half thousand people, with a single main street of low whitewashed houses, shady trees and gardens, and the long wall of the Swartberg mountains standing dark to the north. The land around is dry, with farms along the river and fields of lucerne laid out like green patches on the red earth.

Most visitors pass through on the N12, the main route from the Garden Route toward Johannesburg, and the village has the feel of a place that has learned to be gracious to strangers. Guesthouses with thick walls and cool courtyards line the streets, and a few small restaurants serve Karoo lamb, ostrich and homemade pies. The area is known for ostrich farming, a business that boomed in the early twentieth century when feathers were fashionable in Europe, and you see the big birds in paddocks along the road. Cango Caves, a spectacular limestone cave system, lie not far away on the other side of Oudtshoorn.

For riders the attraction is what lies on either side. To the south, the road passes through open Karoo country with long straights and wide views, and to the north it enters the gorge, with the road rising along the river. Summer afternoons are hot, often well into the thirties, so riding in the morning is best, and winter nights can drop below freezing, with frost on the fields. Wind is common on the plain, and thunderstorms in summer can bring flash floods to the dry riverbeds.

Fuel is available in the village, but supplies are modest, and the larger town of Oudtshoorn, thirty-three kilometres away, has everything you need in the way of workshops and shops. De Rust is an excellent place to spend the night before tackling the gorge, with quiet evenings and a sky full of stars, since there is almost no light pollution. Walk down the main street at dusk and listen to the quiet.
t.meiringspoort@-33.4,22.6:
Few roads in South Africa cross the same river as many times as this one. Meiringspoort is a gorge cut by the Groot River through the Swartberg range, and the N12 follows it for about twenty-five kilometres, crossing the stream some twenty-five times on low bridges and causeways, with cliffs that rise on both sides in tilted, twisted layers of red and grey rock. The road was built in the 1880s by Thomas Bain, and the gorge takes its name from a farmer called Petrus Meiring, who lived in the area in the early nineteenth century.

The riding is a calm and enjoyable one. The road is paved and well maintained, with gentle bends and a constant change of light as the cliffs close in and open out. There are picnic spots along the way, shaded by trees, and near the middle a waterfall of around sixty metres drops from a side valley, with a viewing point and toilets. The rock strata are the great show: huge slabs have been folded and tilted until they stand on end, a reminder of the mountain-building that shaped this part of Africa.

Take care in wet weather. In 1996 a great flood tore through the gorge and washed away much of the road and its bridges, closing it for months, and flash floods remain a danger after heavy rain in the mountains. Check conditions before riding in the rainy months, and do not stop in the riverbed. Baboons are sometimes seen on the road, so keep your distance. Lorries use the route all year, as it is part of a major freight corridor, and slow vehicles may hold you up, so be patient on the bends.

The village of De Rust, a bit under ten kilometres from the southern end, has fuel and refreshments, and Oudtshoorn, about forty kilometres away, is the large town with everything else. There are no services in the gorge itself except for the picnic areas, so bring what you need. Early morning is the best time, with fewer lorries and soft light on the cliffs, and the ride through takes less than an hour, though most riders spend longer, stopping to look and listen.
t.prince alfred pass@-34.0,23.2:
Thomas Bain built a great many passes, and Prince Alfred, finished in 1867 and named for Queen Victoria's son, who visited the Cape in 1860, is one of the longest. It runs from Knysna up through the Outeniqua mountains to Uniondale, over a distance of nearly eighty kilometres, and most of it is gravel. The route was built to link the timber country of the Garden Route with the farms of the Karoo, and for decades ox wagons carried wood, wool and supplies along it.

The climb leaves the coast behind and enters one of the greatest indigenous forests in South Africa, where yellowwood and stinkwood trees, tree ferns and creepers hang over the road, and the air smells of damp earth and leaves. The surface can be rough in places, with loose gravel, corrugations and washaways after rain, and the road narrows to little more than a lane on the steepest sections, so go slowly and expect to take most of the day. Fog and drizzle are common near the top, and the temperature drops noticeably as you leave the coast.

Beyond the forest the scenery opens up. The road passes through fynbos, rocky ridges and, eventually, the dry farmland of the Little Karoo, with long views over folded mountains. The old stone bridges and culverts are a delight, and the road has a sense of quiet history. Occasionally you will see the Outeniqua Choo Tjoe, a heritage train, running on a line in the distance, and birds such as Knysna turacos flash green and red in the trees.

There are no services on the pass, so fill up in Knysna, which is a sizeable town of nearly seventy thousand people with every facility, and Plettenberg Bay is an alternative on the coast. At the northern end, Uniondale is a small village with fuel and a few cafés. Check the condition of the road before you set out, particularly after rain, and tell someone where you are going, as mobile signal is weak in the forest. A day on this road, with a picnic by a stream, is a good way to understand the country behind the coast.
t.transalpina point 1@45.4,23.7:
Up here the Parâng Mountains show their true shape, a broad, grassy massif that rolls away to the horizon more like a Scottish moor than an Alpine peak. The Transalpina, Romania's DN67C, climbs onto this high plateau above the treeline, where spruce forest gives way to open pasture, juniper and heather, and the road becomes a thin ribbon across a vast, empty landscape. Its high point, the Urdele Pass, reaches 2,145 metres, which makes it the highest paved road in the country, and the surrounding country has the lonely, windswept feel of the roof of the Carpathians.

The history of the road is longer than you might guess. Romans and medieval shepherds used a track over these mountains, and in the 1930s King Carol II had it improved as a showpiece, giving it the grand name of the King's Road. During the Second World War, German troops widened it for military use, and for decades afterward it was little more than a gravel track used by shepherds and foresters. A major rebuilding programme over the last fifteen years has paved most of it, and riders from across Europe have since found it.

The riding is spectacular but demands respect. The road is a succession of long, open curves and tight hairpins, climbing and dropping across the grass, and the surface, though paved, can have frost heaves, potholes and loose gravel, particularly after winter. Sheep, cows and horses graze freely, and herding dogs, large and sometimes aggressive, may run alongside. Slow down for animals and for blind crests.

The nearest reliable stations are in the towns at the foot of the mountains, such as Novaci to the south, about nineteen kilometres away as the crow flies, and Petroșani to the north, and it is wise to start with a full tank and carry some spare food and water. Mobile coverage is poor in the high valleys, so tell someone your route.

The road is closed in winter because of snow, usually from late autumn until late spring, and the exact dates vary, so check before you set out. Even in July, the weather can swing from blazing sun to fog and cold rain in an hour, and storms build quickly over the ridge. Pack waterproofs and a warm layer, and aim to cross the high plateau in the morning, when the air is clear and the light long and low across the grass.
t.transalpina point 2@45.5,23.7:
Here the road leaves the bare plateau and drops into the valley of the Lotru, a long, wooded corridor threaded by one of the main rivers of the Southern Carpathians. The river has been tamed for hydroelectric power, with large dams and reservoirs, notably Lake Vidra, and from the road you catch glimpses of still, deep blue water between steep slopes of spruce. After the exposure of the high pass, the forest comes as a relief, with the smell of resin and damp earth.

The area is thinly populated. Small villages like Voineasa and Obârșia Lotrului sit among clearings of hay meadows, with timber houses and haystacks, and the pace of life seems slower than in the lowlands. In summer, shepherds bring flocks up to the high pastures, and you may pass them on the road, with their dogs and a small caravan. Sheep's cheese cured in a wrapping of spruce bark is a speciality of Romanian mountain communities, and it is worth asking after in a roadside shop.

For the rider, the road in the valley is a pleasure, with a more relaxed rhythm than the high section. The corners are long and flowing, the gradient is gentle, and the forest shelters you from the wind. But it can be damp and shaded, with moss and fallen needles on the surface, and sections remain rough, so keep your speed within the limits of what you can see. Watch for logging trucks and for bears, which live in these forests and sometimes cross the road at dusk.

Services are limited. Voineasa has a few small shops and pensions, but hours are short and supplies may run out, so plan to fill up in Petroșani or in the town of Brezoi down the valley if you can. Cash is useful, since small places may not take cards.

The best time to ride is from June to September, when the road is clear of snow and the weather is mostly fair. In late September, the beech and maple turn gold and orange, and the valley glows. Keep a rain jacket handy, because afternoon storms are common, and the forest road can be slippery after rain. If you find a pull-off beside the lake, stop for a while, and listen to the wind in the trees.
t.garden route point 6@-34.0,23.9:
East of Plettenberg Bay the coast turns serious. The Tsitsikamma, whose name comes from a Khoisan word often translated as place of much water, is a narrow band of forest and cliffs where the mountains run almost straight into the Indian Ocean. The N2 follows the high ground behind the shore, crossing deep river gorges on tall bridges, and these coordinates sit in that country near the Storms River Mouth, one of the most photographed places on the Garden Route.

The riding is the real draw. Beyond Plett the highway climbs and drops through a series of passes and bridges, with forest on both sides and a shifting light that makes the green seem almost black in the shadows. The Bloukrans and Storms River crossings are high, and a crosswind from the sea can get hold of a bike on the bridge decks, so keep a relaxed grip and a margin for gusts. There is a toll plaza on this section of the N2, so carry cash or a card, and motorcycles pay a reduced rate.

The coast itself is protected as part of the Tsitsikamma section of the Garden Route National Park. A short road leads down from the highway to the Storms River Mouth rest camp, where a suspension bridge swings across the rocky mouth of the river and the sea pounds in from below. The walk to it is a gentle path through coastal forest, with yellowwood trees and ferns on the path, and the noise of the surf grows as you approach. Park entry is paid, and the descent road is steep with tight corners, so ride it slowly and watch for baboons and loose gravel.

Geologically this is a remarkable coast, a rim of old sandstone cut by rivers, with a marine reserve offshore that has been protected for decades. Otters live along the rocks and the Knysna loerie, a green bird with a crimson flash, calls from the canopy. It rains often, and fog is common, so a light waterproof is worth carrying even on a fine morning.

Practical matters need some thought. There are no large towns on this stretch, and the small villages along the N2 have limited services, so the sensible plan is to arrive with a full tank from Plettenberg Bay. A coffee and a simple meal are available at the rest camp and in the small village inland, but you should not count on much more. The reward is the quiet, the smell of wet earth and salt, and the odd feeling of riding along the edge of a continent.

t.levoca@49.0,20.6:
Spread across a ridge in eastern Slovakia, with the jagged peaks of the High Tatras rising on the northern horizon, the Spiš region holds one of Europe's great clusters of medieval monuments. The town of Levoča, the old regional capital, was a wealthy royal free town, and its walls, burgher houses and Renaissance town hall still surround a long central square. Inside the church of St James stands Master Paul of Levoča's carved Gothic altarpiece, finished in the early sixteenth century and the tallest of its kind in the world, an astonishing tower of limewood saints and filigree.

Close by, above Spišské Podhradie, Spiš Castle sprawls across a travertine hill: one of the largest castle complexes in Central Europe, its ruined walls covering a whole summit and visible for miles. Opposite it, on another hill, Spišská Kapitula is a small walled church town with a cathedral and canons' houses, little changed in centuries. Levoča, the castle, the Kapitula and the Gothic church at Žehra, with its remarkable medieval frescoes, are listed together by UNESCO, and riding between them gives you a day of shifting perspectives on the same few hills.

The riding is easy-going and scenic, across rolling farmland, rapeseed fields and woods, with the castle appearing and disappearing on its hill as you approach. The main road between Prešov and Poprad passes through the area and can be busy with trucks; the minor roads to Žehra and towards the Slovenský raj national park are quieter and more fun, with gentle curves and occasional rough patches. Weather can turn quickly, especially with the Tatras so close, and on clear autumn evenings the castle glows orange in the last light.

Spišské Podhradie and Levoča both have fuel and places to eat; Krompachy is another option. Try bryndzové halušky, potato dumplings with sheep's cheese and bacon, and a cold Slovak beer once the riding is done. The castle is a steep walk up from the car park, worth every step for the view over the Spiš basin. In summer the castle hosts historical events, and if you are around in early July, Levoča's pilgrimage to the hill above town draws huge crowds.
